# THE AMPHITHEATER OF ANATOMY
## DESIGNED WITH A TRIPLE IMAGE, IN VARIED MANNER AND CONDITION
->*By the Author*<-
->**Robert Fludd, also known as de Fluctibus, Esquire and Doctor of Medicine of Oxford**<-

<note>Robert Fludd (1574–1637) was a prominent English Paracelsian physician and mystic who sought to reconcile scientific observation with spiritual truths.</note>

<image-desc>
An elaborate engraved diagram centered on a large circle, topped by the head of a man <note>representing the "World Soul" or the divine intellect overseeing the human form</note>. The large circle contains three primary medallions and three smaller connecting circles. 

The large outer ring contains the text: "MAN OR THE MICROCOSM, THE WONDERFUL RECEPTACLE OF THESE SUBJECTS." <note>original: "HOMO SEV MICROCOSMVS ADMIRABILE HORVM SVBIECTORVM RECEPTACVLVM." The "Microcosm" is the idea that the human body is a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note>

1. Top Medallion (Mystical Anatomy): Titled "IMAGE OF THE MYSTICAL ANATOMY OF MAN." <note>original: "ANATOMIÆ HOMINIS MYSTICÆ IMAGO."</note> It depicts a sun-burst with the monogram "IHS" <note>The Christogram, representing the divine light within humanity</note> at the center. It is oriented with the four cardinal directions and their presiding archangels: 
   - North: Gabriel presiding. <note>original: "Boreas s. Gabriel præfes."</note>
   - East: Michael presiding. <note>original: "Oriens s. Michael præfes."</note>
   - South: Uriel presiding. <note>original: "Merid: s. Uriel. præfes."</note>
   - West: Raphael presiding. <note>original: "Occidens s. Raphael præfes."</note>
   Inside the rays are terms such as "Spirit," "General," "Heaven," and "Splendor."

2. Bottom Left Medallion (Nutrition/Wheat): Titled "THE MIRROR OF WHEAT OR BREAD." <note>original: "TRITICI SEV PANIS SPECVLVM."</note> It shows the process of nutrition and the essence of wheat, featuring a loaf of bread (A), an ear of wheat (B), and a large chemical distillation furnace or vessel (c, e, f, g) labeled "The Nourishment of Man."

3. Bottom Right Medallion (Vulgar/Physical Anatomy): Titled "A LIVING LIKENESS OF VULGAR ANATOMY." <note>original: "VIVVM ANATOMIÆ VLGARIS SIMVLACRVM." "Vulgar" here means common or physical, referring to standard medical dissection.</note> It shows a realistic scene of a human dissection (anatomical theater) with several men gathered around a cadaver on a table, surrounded by surgical tools.

Connecting circles:
- Left: "The triple members of the internal man: Spirit or Air (A); Soul (B); Jesus, the light or center of Men."
- Right: "Three things pertain to vulgar Anatomy: The subject to be divided (A); The divider (B); The dividing instruments (C)."
- Bottom: "Three things are necessary for Vulgar Anatomy: The subject (A, B); The dissected members or the 3 elements (c, d, e, f, g); The instruments (h, i, k)."

The central space between the three medallions is labeled "THE BRIGHT NOURISHMENT OF MAN." <note>original: "LVCVLENTVM HOMINIS Nutrimentum."</note>
</image-desc>

->Frankfurt, at the expense of **Johann Theodor de Bry**, 1623.<-

<summary>The title page of Robert Fludd's 1623 work, illustrating his "triple" approach to anatomy: the mystical/spiritual, the nutritional/chemical, and the physical/dissection-based. It presents the human body as a "Microcosm" that mirrors the divine and elemental structures of the universe.</summary>

<keywords>Robert Fludd, Microcosm, Mystical Anatomy, Dissection, Johann Theodor de Bry, Archangels, Alchemy, Nutrition, 17th-century medicine</keywords>

# TO THE HONOR, PIETY, AND MEMORY
## OF THE BEST, MOST UPRIGHT MAN, WHO DESERVED THE HIGHEST PRAISE FROM THE PUBLIC LITERARY GOOD, AND THE GREATEST ARTIST
of our times, JOHANN THEODOR de Bry, citizen of Frankfurt, who on the 8th day of the month of August, in the year 1623, was translated to the dwellings of the blessed.

<image-desc>An engraved portrait of Johann Theodor de Bry within a rectangular frame. De Bry is depicted from the chest up, wearing a doublet and a large pleated ruff. He holds an engraving tool in his right hand. His left hand points to a small print of a child blowing bubbles (the 'Homo Bulla' motif <note>A common Renaissance allegory meaning "Man is a bubble," signifying the fragility and brevity of human life.</note>) which bears the text "WHO ESCAPES?" and a biblical quote from John 8. In the background are various inscriptions. On the table before him are stacked books with the titles "HISTORY", "EAST INDIES", and "WEST INDIES".</image-desc>

->To the man who engraved his own likeness in copper<-

Many sculptors are often skilled enough at fashioning
the likeness of the body: but they are unable to capture the soul.
<column-break/>
Yet, Johann Theodor, this small tablet reflects your own
likeness of both body and soul, through your own art.
<column-break/>

->Placed out of friendship by J. C. D.<-

---

Let others accuse the cruel fates in verse—
the fates that know not how to spare illustrious men;
Let them draw out mournful songs in light Elegies,
and let so many monuments groan, orphaned of their parent.
Others will mourn the loss and the public damages;
they will weep for the genius and the craftsman’s hand.
O, your loss, Theodor de Bry, longed-for father-in-law,
whom a sad disease and a dark day have snatched away.
A cause closer to home squeezes wet tears from me
and weighs down my breast with a mass of sadness,
For your piety, love, indulgence, and virtue
desert me, and press upon me with a more immediate grief.

<column-break/>

Alas, uprightness! Alas, ancient faith! Alas, the white
fiber of a mind <note>A poetic way of describing a pure or sincere character.</note> lies here, never to be lamented enough.
I had scarcely been chosen as your son-in-law by a favorable deity,
O holy old man, and your daughter had not yet been made a mother:
You fall, and you break the fellowship of the pleasant table,
O father-in-law, and father more to be revered by me!
So death, the enemy, once snatched away boys who had
scarcely reached the light of the Sun at the beginning of life.
Therefore, take these tears, and these small verses,
witnesses of a bitter lot, mottos placed by a trembling hand:
And farewell; and may Christ (nor will the delay be long)
place you, snatched from the grave, in the citadel of the heavenly Pole.

---

->Johannes Ammonius of Amberg placed this with tears<-
->for his most deserving father-in-law.<-

It includes a poignant funeral poem written by his son-in-law, Johannes Ammonius, lamenting the personal and professional loss caused by De Bry's death in 1623.</summary>

# THE FIRST SECTION
## THE THIRD PORTION

->CONCERNING<-

# THE TRIPLE
# ANATOMY.

->Divided into three parts.<-

<note>The following diagram outlines the philosophical structure of the book, comparing the "anatomy" of food to the "anatomy" of the human being.</note>

Of which:

The First Part: Treats **Bread**, the principal nutrient, whose elements and hidden properties are discussed through dissection by fire <note>original: "per ignis resolutionem," referring to alchemical distillation</note>.

The Two Following Parts: Concern **Man**, who is most excellent in the dignity of nutrition. This is further divided into a twofold anatomy:
*   The **Common or visible** anatomy <note>The physical study of the body through dissection</note>.
*   The **Mystical or invisible** anatomy <note>The spiritual or "vitalist" study of the soul and life force</note>.

->BY THE AUTHOR<-

## ROBERT FLUDD, ALSO KNOWN AS DE FLUCTIBUS,

# THE SUBJECT OF THIS THIRD PORTION

<margin>This third portion is divided into two types of Anatomy, the first of which deals with:</margin>

{ That most ancient and most highly esteemed nourishment or nutriment, namely **BREAD**, whose internal nature is revealed through "fiery section" <note>original: "sectione ignea"; likely referring to chemical or alchemical analysis by fire/heat</note>. That is to say, all the elements hidden secretly within it are revealed, separated from one another, and purified by rectification. At the same time, their hidden virtues and properties are uncovered by the watchful observation of the craftsman, recognized by their effects, and demonstrated clearly enough to the eyes. The first part of this section deals with this.

{ That nourished or sustained being which is easily the prince of the animal kingdom, namely **MAN**. And this is subdivided into two species of Anatomy. Specifically:
*   { The Common <note>original: "Vulgarem"</note>, by means of which his exterior is dissected in the common manner; the parts and organs are distinguished from one another, each of them is described by itself, and is correctly applied to the use destined for it by Nature. The second part of this section deals with this.
*   { The Mystical, through which both his exterior and interior, divided into distinct portions, are treated in a mystical manner. They are laid open equally by the "sharpness of words" and are described as if by a living dissection. The third part of this section is concerned with this species.

It depicts several figures in what appears to be an interior or landscape setting, possibly an anatomical or alchemical scene, though the details are severely obscured by the ghosting of a large circular diagram and text from the opposite side of the paper.</image-desc>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page serves as the formal dedication of the work. The author addresses a high-ranking clergyman known for his interest in alchemy and natural philosophy, establishing a tone of mutual intellectual respect.</meta>

<image-desc>A large rectangular woodcut headpiece featuring symmetrical elaborate scrollwork, floral motifs, and two seated figures or putti on either side of a central circular wreath.</image-desc>

## TO THE VENERABLE AND REVEREND MAN, AND
->one most diligent in the accurate investigation of the mysteries of Nature;<-

# JOHN THORNBURGH,
## BISHOP OF WORCESTER, MY REMARKABLE
### FRIEND, IN HIM WHO IS THE TRUE
### LIGHT OF THE WORLD, AND THE TREASURE OF TREASURES,

->GREETINGS:<-

<image-desc>A square decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing an illustration of a seated figure in a pastoral landscape with a building in the distance.</image-desc>

Concerning to whom I should dedicate these internal revelations of things or the hidden mysteries of Nature, I was made uncertain by the vain multitude of common men—those occupied only with coarse, corporeal, and external matters. This ignorant and profane crowd of mortals made me hesitant, since among a thousand men, scarcely one can be found who is a worshiper of naked Nature or who rightly knows himself. Therefore, the worldly hold in hatred and pursue with vain derision anyone who is least concerned with deceptive and outwardly visible things. To such people, wandering in darkness and constantly traveling around the "bark" <note>original: "corticem" - a common alchemical metaphor referring to the outer shell or superficial appearance of matter as opposed to its inner essence</note> (as they say) or the plainly cloudy circumference, the entrance to the most fixed center of virtue—the palace flashing with divine light—is denied as if they were profane. This man, I say—truly a son of light and charity—they reject with contemptuous custom. From this sort of worldly grain <note>original: "farinâ" - literally 'flour' or 'batch,' meaning 'of that ilk'</note> my Muse, burdened with the reward of truth, turns away; having been instructed by experience, she has become entirely estranged from them. Furthermore, we are taught by the admonition of Holy Scripture that pearls are by no means to be cast before swine, nor the bread of the children of men to be given to dogs.

To whom, therefore, shall I better direct this ship of mine—laden with no small riches of chemistry (even if common <note>original: "chemiæ licet vulgaris" - likely referring to laboratory chemistry as the starting point for higher spiritual alchemy</note>), and even now plowing the turbulent seas of worldly opinions—than to a man learned, grave, and studious in tracking and inquiring into the mysteries of Nature? And finally, to one looking into the centers of hidden things with the most sharp telescope of genius? For the sons of light exult and rejoice among themselves, since experience has shown that like things, by a certain natural instinct, enjoy and take delight in like things.

Therefore, toward your shores (Reverend Sir, most to be honored for your profound learning in chemical matters), the full sails of my ship stretch out. With a favorable breath of love and benevolence, she directs her course toward you; the skiff of this my History strives with all its might to put into your firm and auspicious shores of judgment. This it does under this secure confidence: because the rays of the Triple-One <note>original: "Trivnius" - likely a reference to the Trinity or the "Hermetic Trinity" of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note> have shone upon your mind, since the *Nothing*, the *Something*, and the *All* of the ancient sages are by no means hidden from you. For you have nobly acknowledged the Chaos and the Darkness in your writings—

<sig>A 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: ...acknowledged (gnouistis)</meta>

<summary>This page is a formal Latin dedication to John Thornburgh, Bishop of Worcester, praising his expertise in "chemical matters" and natural philosophy while distancing the work from the "profane" masses. The author uses maritime metaphors to describe the delivery of his alchemical knowledge to a worthy peer.</summary>

<keywords>John Thornburgh, Bishop of Worcester, alchemy, natural philosophy, mysteries of nature, sons of light, chemical art, Chaos, the Nothing, the All</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory address (Prooemium) from the previous section, maintaining the author's defensive and celebratory tone regarding natural philosophy.</meta>

You have known this: and with a clear thread of discourse, you have preached the light—the life of every creature—emerging from these things, and you have done so quite brilliantly. Indeed, you have explained with golden words the terrestrial sun reigning with wondrous splendor in the center of the darkness. Therefore, let the foolish worldlings—who mock mysteries of Nature of this sort (inasmuch as such things are utterly unknown to them)—tell us, by the immortal God: what is more unjust than that they should hate what they do not know? And even if the matter deserved hatred, what, in the end, is more futile? Or what greater madness and senselessness is there than to condemn that science in which they have smelled out absolutely nothing? These are men, of course, who have learned neither of blessed Nature, nor the majesty of Nature, nor her properties or her hidden operations within worldly things, whether in the elements <note>The four classical elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note> or in things composed of elements. However, even as these critics <note>original: "momi" – referring to Momus, the Greek god of mockery and blame.</note>, filled with envy or swelling with ignorance, continue their croaking and babbling, virtue shall nonetheless enjoy that perpetual trophy of truth which she herself has fixed for eternity; and she will, at long last, adorn the brows of her sincere worshippers and intimates with a crown of glory.

->The most devoted admirer of your Dignity,<-

->ROBERT FLUDD<- <note>Robert Fludd (1574–1637) was a prominent English physician and mystical philosopher known for his works on the macrocosm and microcosm.</note>

<summary>In this concluding portion of the preface, Robert Fludd defends the study of Nature's hidden mysteries against ignorant critics and asserts that the pursuit of truth will ultimately be rewarded with eternal glory.</summary>
<keywords>Robert Fludd, natural philosophy, alchemy, elements, defense of science, light of nature, mysticism</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page begins the preface (Prooemium) of the work, establishing the theological and philosophical foundation of the author's study of nature. It connects the previous introductory matter to the specific discussion of the divine presence in all things.</meta>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut headpiece consisting of a horizontal rectangular border filled with intricate scrolling foliage, floral patterns, and small figures of animals or birds.</image-desc>

# P R E F A C E

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring scrolling acanthus leaves and floral motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

So immense was the benevolence of <term>Natura naturans</term> <note>literally "Nature naturing"; a philosophical term for God as the creative force acting within the world</note> toward its creatures, that it wished to leave or permit none of them to be destitute of a spark or small portion of its goodness; inasmuch as it is accustomed to be present everywhere—both presently and consequently essentially—and to inhabit all created things, both simple and composite, being immediately within them by means of its spirit (whose role it is to attribute power, and consequently life, to any thing). For as the most holy scripture testifies: (a) *God is present throughout the whole world, namely in hell, in the furthest reaches of the sea, in the night, and in the darkness;* (b) *in the heavens above, and on the earth below.* 
<margin>
a Psalm 139:7
b Deuteronomy 4:39
</margin>
For if we truly investigate the matter, it is permitted to draw from and explore the fountain of all truth: that this divine nature has been clothed in all the garments of the world, both subtle and coarse, from the world's beginning. The thinnest of all these, and the closest to its essence, was the light, which it is said to have put on in the <term>Empyrean</term> <note>The highest heaven, believed in ancient cosmology to be composed of pure fire or light</note> or angelic heaven; for the Royal Psalmist says: (c) *God is clothed with light as with a garment* and (d) elsewhere, *God reigns clothed in majesty and loftiness.* 
<margin>
c Psalm 104
d Psalm 93:1
</margin>
His middle garment is the solar body, in which he is said to inhabit the ethereal or stellar heaven; hence David said: (e) *In the sun God has placed his tabernacle.* 
<margin>
e Psalm 18:2 <note>original: "In sole posuit Deus tabernaculum suum"</note>
</margin>
After this, the divine and life-giving nature of the Creator, penetrating further downward, made the thick cloud his tabernacle in the elementary heaven, whence we find it written: (f) *that God made the clouds his chariot;* and elsewhere: (g) *Thick clouds are the hiding place of God, so that he may watch us, and he walks upon the circuit of the heavens.* 
<margin>
f Psalm 104:3
g Job 22:12
</margin>
Furthermore, descending even to the center of the entire machine, this uncreated light, or the most holy spirit of Jehovah, (h) is declared there to fill the entire world. 
<margin>
h Wisdom 1:7
</margin>
And we also find written elsewhere, that *the Earth shall be opened and bring forth a Savior.* From these things it seems clearly enough established that God is present everywhere in the simple elements of the world, both in the higher heavens above and in the lower and sublunary regions.

It remains now that we seek out with diligent intuition and sincere inquiry whether this holy spirit is present in every composite creature in this world or not. To begin, therefore, with the prince of the animal kingdom, namely Man: we find infinite things committed to eternal monuments concerning his exalted dignity and praises, among which these are expressly found written in the sacred letters: (i) *Your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God.* 
<margin>
i 1 Corinthians 6:19
k Deuteronomy 32
l 1 Corinthians 3:17
</margin>
And elsewhere: (k) *His people are the portion of God.* And elsewhere: (l) *The temple of God is holy, which you are.* Hence it is that just as the Earth, so also the Heaven concurs in the admirable composition of man; for his heaven is the internal man or spirit, while his earth is the external man or body. And just as the spirit of the Lord is said to be everywhere in the heavens and the earths of the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The "Great World" or the universe as a whole</note>—inasmuch as the heaven is his seat and the earth his footstool, for he fills the orb of the lands as the wise man testifies—so also he is present everywhere in the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "Little World," referring to Man as a reflection of the universe</note>, although he is most conspicuous in its heaven. 

Hence, those most skilled in both philosophy and theology have, not ill-advisedly or uselessly, consumed nights and days in such tedious inquiry and speculation upon the internal part of man and his central act; following which, they all finally fell upon this position with unanimous consent: That the most intense labor and most worthy industry of a wise man is *To know himself* <note>original: "Noscere seipsum"</note>; that is, to look into and behold his own internal self with the eyes of wisdom or intellect. Without this speculation, man is observed not to differ much from a beast or irrational animal. By the virtue of this admirable vision, man is entirely sublimated on high and flies out with full wings to God—that is, he penetrates to the innermost center of himself, where he beholds God, and dwells in him and around him. By this vision, I say, man expands himself to both the lower and higher things, and is wonderfully illuminated to know and contemplate God above him, himself within him, the Angels beside him, and whatever is contained within the circuit of heaven below him.

But truly, so that we may now arrive at the vegetable kingdom or composite, and treat of the easy prince among vegetables: which is <term>wheat</term> <note>original: "triticum"</note>, from which our common bread is usually made,

# PREFACE.

...it may be, Bread, I say, that most ancient of human nourishments, of which mention was made immediately upon Adam’s departure from Paradise. In this vegetable, therefore, that spirit which gives life to all things and fills the world abounds in great plenty. Whence it happens that it is so necessary to human life that no bodily food is found in the world that is more common among men, or more ready and useful for repelling their hunger, than is that bread fashioned from the grain of wheat. Without a doubt, its nutritive power proceeds immediately from the very act of the divine spirit, which from the sun—its tabernacle—rejoices to rain and flow abundantly with rays of life into this composition daily. For all the power and goodness of life is sent by God into his creatures, according to that saying of the royal Psalmist: *By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the spirit from his mouth.* <note>Psalm 33:6</note> But truly, no faculty is granted to creatures by the Creator more desirable or more clear than that of life; and consequently it follows that the act, and therefore the essence, of the uncreated spirit is in the nourishment of the creature, without which it is least able to reach its good effect. Hence, therefore, it was said by Saint John: *By the word all things were made, and without it nothing was made; in it was life, and that life is the light of men.* <note>John 1:3-4</note> By which he seems to conclude that the essential footprints of the divine word are in every creature, but more eminently in man in the animal kingdom, and then in wheat in the vegetable kingdom. For the gifts of the spirit shine forth more in one place than in another; but I shall gird myself a little more closely to the grain of wheat, so that I may then approach more nearly to the description and dignity of bread. Odo, that most learned Abbot, <note>Likely Odo of Cluny or Odo of Morimond, medieval theologians.</note> in his *Harmony of the Trinity*, relates that Wheat is taken analogically for the second person in the Trinity in many places of Holy Scripture, and he brings forth this first passage from the Prophet Joel: *The floors shall be filled with wheat, and the winepresses shall overflow with wine and oil.* <note>Joel 2:24</note> Moreover, he treats this passage allegorically thus: The Spirit fills the winepresses with wine, the Son fills the floors with wheat, and the Father fills the winepresses with oil. And indeed, by examining the matter a little more accurately, we shall discover that these three vegetable creatures may not unsuitably be referred in their condition to the three persons in the Holy Trinity by metonymy <term>metonymy: a figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it</term>, if it be lawful to compare created things with the uncreated. For oil is referred to mercy, as it is accustomed to soothe pains; Wheat fills with abundance; and wine is accustomed to refresh and recreate. In this sense also we shall find many other places in the sacred writings; for in Deuteronomy 18:12: *All the choice oil, and the wine and the Wheat, as firstfruits, they shall offer to the Lord.* And elsewhere: *You may not eat in your towns the tithe of your wheat and oil and wine;* Deuteronomy 12:17 and 18:4 and 2 Chronicles 18:5. And elsewhere: *He will give rain to your land in due season, the early and the latter rain, that you may gather in your wheat and oil. Deuteronomy 11:14.* From these and many other places, therefore, it appears in how much honor and excellence wheat was esteemed among the Prophets. Moreover, that the internal balsam of wheat is held as the greatest blessing of earthly things, the royal prophet testifies in these words: *Jehovah fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock;* <note>Psalm 81:16</note> And elsewhere he says: *He satisfies you with the fat of wheat;* <note>Psalm 147:14</note> By which he seems to hint that the greatest blessing resides in wheat. So also we read in Leviticus 23:6. But concerning the further dignity and excellence of this grain, we shall speak more richly below in its proper place.

As for what pertains to the dignity of bread, mention of it fills the Holy Bible everywhere, in which as two kinds of bread are reckoned, so indeed it is necessary that the internal and heavenly bread be found in the external and elementary no differently than the internal man is found in the external, or the soul in the body. Moreover, the benefit of the external is stirred up to nutrition by the internal, and the external is accustomed to be nourished by the internal; for it is heaven that refreshes the failing spirits, and not the earth. Whence, wherever mention is made of bread in the sacred texts, there indeed the internal bread is signified through the external, which is difficult for the coarse common folk to understand, as they are chiefly occupied with the external sense. And hence it is that bread was to be preferred to riches and wealth, as is held in Numbers 15:19, where we find: *Of the riches of that land you shall participate, but of the bread of that land you shall eat.* Concerning the virtue of bread, the Prophet writes thus: Psalm 103:15: *Bread strengthens and supports the heart of man, as that wine gladdens it:* Furthermore, we read elsewhere that *bread is brought forth from the earth by the favor of God.* Psalm 104. Indeed, we have in Saint Matthew with how much divinity this nourishment was to be honored, where we read 26:26: *He blessed the bread and broke it and gave it to the disciples and said, Take and eat, this is my body.* And in Luke 24:30 this is found: *And it happened while he sat at meat with them, he took bread and blessed it, and broke it, and handed it to them, and their eyes were opened and they knew him.* From which it is declared clearly enough how great a [connection] there is between bread, or this earthly creature...

-># P R E F A C E<-

<note>original: "PROOEMIVM"</note>

...relation to our heavenly author and creator. It is for this reason that King David in *Psalm 53:5* <note>Modern Psalm 53:4 or 14:4</note> goes on to recount how barbarous and profane it is for men *to eat bread without the most humble giving of thanks and invocation to God.* Furthermore, when God purposed to punish the impious and rebellious, *He threatened to take bread away from them in many places. Whence in Psalm 105:16: He broke the staff of bread, and brought a famine upon the land.* We could bring forth infinite other examples of the dignity of bread from Holy Scripture, by which we might more clearly declare that a spirit of goodness has been abundantly present and inherent in it from the beginning, seeing as it has been endowed with such virtue and goodness since the world’s origin.

This, therefore, is the reason why a desire for knowing hidden things has eagerly led me to the <term>anatomy</term> <note>In this context, "anatomy" refers to the alchemical "cutting open" or chemical analysis of a substance to find its components.</note> of this most noble vegetable creature: so that I might elicit or reveal its internal and latent mysteries according to the possibility of common <term>chemistry</term> <note>original: "chimia"</note>. I have undertaken to attempt this in the prince of the vegetable kingdom rather than in that of the animal (namely, man) or the mineral (namely, gold). This is because to perform an internal anatomy of man by the way of common <term>Alchemy</term> would be useless and impossible; for his nature is so fiery and subtle that to reveal the parts hidden within him—which are more spiritual—and to subject them to the senses by the art of common fire would be either most difficult or plainly impossible. Indeed, the subtlety of his fiery spirit is such that it sustains the violence of fire less than that of quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, which quickly vanishes into smoke at the touch of violent heat. Nor, certainly, would I wish to lose my "effort and oil" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to waste time and resources</note> in the destruction of gold (so that I might speculate upon its internal elements). For although the mineral disposition tastes of the earth, just as the animal tastes of fire—and consequently their divided parts can be brought before the senses—and although the Holy Spirit of discipline has placed his tabernacle in this "earthly Sun" <note>gold</note> no differently than in the celestial sun (insofar as this spirit fills the orb of the earth, and according to that saying of Augustine: *as much light as a thing has in itself, so much of God it seems to claim for itself*); nevertheless, because according to the opinion of the wisest philosophers, *it will be easier to build gold than to destroy it*, and consequently to segregate its elements from one another would be one of the Labors of Hercules. Therefore, I have chosen for this work of ours this intermediate subject—that is, one consisting between the mineral and animal disposition—inasmuch as it participates greatly in water. Since its species is vegetable, it can most easily be destroyed and corrupted by the force of common fire, and its internal elements distinguished from one another. Thus we have in a way manifested its secrets, because in its watery vehicle the elements appear better after its corruption than they do in the animal (in its airy vehicle, on account of its intense heat and overly volatile moisture) or in the mineral (on account of its extreme dryness arising from its earthly fixation or coagulation).

And although I may seem to treat of common bread in this place, I wish you to candidly recognize that under its veil or shadow I have dealt abundantly with the **mystical bread** in its own proper region or subject; that is, I have demonstrated it clearly enough in the type of common bread. Nor indeed should <term>Momus</term> <note>The Greek god of mockery and criticism; a personification of the unfair critic.</note>, filled with malevolence and envy, deride me for this, nor should the ignorant proclaim that I have brought frivolous things to light because he either least understands the interior sense of this history or does not wish to understand it. Nor let anyone rashly accuse me because I describe this anatomy of bread of ours parabolically or analogically—that is, in a double sense—since in this thread of discourse I imitate the Holy Scriptures, the interior of which is the spirit, while the exterior is the letter. The spirit explains the mystery of the thing and relates to it as the soul to the body; the letter describes the historical or moral sense of the thing at first glance and relates to it as the body to the soul. What the Evangelists wrote, both external and internal, was entirely true and useful for establishing the life of both soul and body; for the internal essentially led to the life of the soul, and is a divine mystery that divinely governs the internal man, while the external looks to the institution of the body, both physical and moral, and conforms the body to the disposition of the soul. Therefore, both the external and internal of the holy letters are infallible and most necessary for the governance of human life, and there is no lie in them. But truly, their internal sense is revealed only to a few, while the external is open to almost everyone; hence, as the disciples spoke commonly in parables, *the Savior of the world commanded that they should have ears and not hear, eyes and not see.*

But as for what pertains to this little work of mine, although I know well it is not right to compare small things with great, and a hillock so humble with a mountain or mass so lofty as is...

# -> P R E F A C E <-

...to equate this with Holy Scripture, yet I have dared to say this: that its internal as well as its external nature is not at all distant from the truth. If its interior spirit and even its external face were weighed in the scales of Justice—that is, the balances of equity—you will perceive that no small amount of truth and utility in physics (or the study of nature) and even in the arrangement of Ethics (that is, in the harmonious arrangement and ordering of all creatures) is to be drawn out and found through these external visions. Furthermore, you will find a contemplation directed toward divine and super-celestial things through its internal and hidden mysteries. 

But the action of these mysteries consists in the Divine Word, the light of the world, and the life of all creatures. From that **cornerstone** <note>original: "lapide angulari"; a reference to Christ as the foundation of all knowledge</note>, the sole fountain of mysteries, the virtue and power of performing miracles is accustomed to flow. Because bread is appropriated to Him in the Holy Scriptures (whence the Word said: *This is my body* <note>original: "Hoc est corpus meum"</note>, and elsewhere, *Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word proceeding from the mouth of God*), we have therefore said that there is a great mystery in bread. Or rather, through bread, we attest to the greatest mystery—namely, the Word—in a **hieroglyphic** <note>The author uses "hieroglyphic" here to mean a sacred symbol or a physical sign that contains a hidden, spiritual reality</note> manner. 

Nor indeed do I hope that I can be justly condemned by anyone for this, since in this effort of mine I am an imitator of the Savior. While I write these things under the secure shadow of His wings, so that I may more safely escape the viperous tongues of the malevolent, I shall hide myself, preceded by the central prayers of my heart. 

Finally, the principal reason that induced me to publish this treatise to the world is this: because in this are contained the foundations of my **macrocosmic** <note>The study of the universe or "great world"</note> as well as **microcosmic** <note>The study of man as a "little world" reflecting the universe</note> philosophy, supported and confirmed by the pillar of truth. All these things my promise in preceding volumes compels and urges me to offer here to your eyes and judgment and to publish openly. To this end, without further hesitation or doubt regarding my previously published philosophy, my labors and late-night studies may at last be received by you with a more grateful and certain embrace; inasmuch as they are supported by infallible demonstrations and reasons derived from the very storehouse or sanctuary of Nature herself. Farewell.

## BOOK ONE

->Concerning<-

# BREAD AND WHEAT IN GENERAL, AS WELL AS THEIR EXCELLENCE.

### CHAPTER I.

#### *Concerning the three composite kingdoms of Nature, in which she herself, like a sole queen and most radiant Empress, holds dominion.*

Just as universal nature—the absolute mother of the world’s structure and its creatures—is observed by the more skilled <note>The "skilled" or "experts" likely refers to alchemists and natural philosophers.</note> to be pure, simple, transparent, and invisible in and of herself, so too does she strive to hide and conceal her secrets from the eyes of the unworthy. She does this within this lowest region of the world across three special and notable kingdoms, which are composed of her simple elements as if under the covers of obscurity or shadows. Each of these kingdoms is distinguished from the others by the admirable property of their Empress, who holds her royal court in their center or heart; from there, with just equality and due proportion, she divinely rules and governs every member of their circumference. We observe this universal governess of things inhabiting the splendid palace of the worldly sun (as if she had directed her fiery and flashing chariot through the vast ocean of the world), possessing its internal and central point. In this way, by her daily motion, she leads the horses of Phoebus <note>Phoebus is a classical name for the Sun god, Apollo.</note> around the sphere of equality, so that she may send her radiant peripheral virtue everywhere—downwards to the very lowest earth and upwards to the highest heaven. Thus, she adorns all things, both superior and inferior, with equal symmetry and harmony, and brings them to life through the influence of her rays. And just as this same queen governs the active and throbbing tabernacle of the microcosm <note>term: Microcosm (the "little world"). In Renaissance philosophy, the human body was seen as a miniature map of the entire universe (the macrocosm).</note>—namely, the heart—and liberally distributes the vital spirits in a circular motion everywhere, from the virtuous center to the circumference via the flowing vessels and arterial channels; in a similar way, I say, this most powerful queen, ruling in her central palace in a hidden manner, is perceived to daily nourish and gradually increase the composition of these three kingdoms of hers by ejecting and sowing the essence of her rays from the midpoint of each toward the margins or periphery of the subject. This, then, is that royal virgin and handmaid of the eternal Creator; this is the invisible fire of Zoroaster and Heraclitus <note>Ancient philosophers associated with the primary element of fire and the hidden energy of nature.</note>: this essential bond of the elements, and that virtue of true mixing, which is accustomed to procreate so complete a union among the clashing natures of the four aforementioned kingdoms found in the sublunary world. This is that princess of creatures, who desires to imprint upon every species of composite thing a fitting character and a decent form, by which property one thing is distinguished from another by an essential difference. Indeed, I say, this is that very Empress who has placed her palace in the heart of these three kingdoms of hers; in them she reigns triumphantly and holds the scepter. In one of them, she is seen to express her majesty more abundantly than in another, and yet nature is not manifold but one alone—not indivisible, and simple only in number—bearing the image of the general Creator in her governance, predominating over all and above all. Since she is the life of all things, she is said to be with the universal soul in every thing, and consequently in every particle of the microcosmic fabric. Therefore, it must be seriously considered that she has chosen the human frame for her principal mansion in the animal kingdom, as it is the most excellent of all sensible creatures; while in her vegetable empire, she seems to claim Wheat—the most worthy of all plants—for her richest tabernacle, as it is in this that she holds her open court more copiously and sumptuously, [distributing] her vegetable gifts...

# Section I. Portion III. Part I. Book I.

...and she rejoices to impart her multiplying power more abundantly and fluently. In her mineral nature, however, she delights in the golden mass, in which her splendid glory—shining as if with fiery rays—is openly revealed to mortals. O, how eminent that artist would appear above his peers who, having completed the act of Alchemy and by the virtue of celestial fire, understands how to distinguish the parts of this animal queen’s palace, both spiritual and corporeal, with just scales! For by the exact revelation of these hidden regions and the manifestation of the secret palace, he shall arrive at a perfect knowledge of himself and the vision of the internal man. He shall visit the highest point in the microcosm <note>The "little world," referring to man as a reflection of the universe.</note> of heaven—that is, the most secret sanctuary of man, hidden in his lowest spirit—in which the Divine Presence, surrounded on all sides by intellectual rays, has its residence. By this sacred presence, man not only excels the other creatures of the world but also holds eternal dominion over them.

Similarly, what great happiness and what joy shall be poured into that faithful operator who is so favored by fortune that he can, with a skilled right hand, properly uncover that most nourishing nurse among the vegetables and anatomize <note>To "anatomize" here means to chemically or alchemically separate a substance into its core components.</note> her by the way of nature. In her center, the endowments and influences of this multiplying queen abound as if in her own vegetable temple. For here, as if in a universal Mirror <note>original: "Catoptro"</note>, he shall behold the secret mysteries of nature.

And finally, with what riches and true happiness shall he be endowed whose fortunate birth and bright guiding star direct and lead him to reveal the various acts and ineffable effects of those well-polished and illuminated elements. These are the materials of that golden mineral castle in which the royal nature has her residence. For by his art or science of this kind, he is able to redeem that flashing and spiritual gold, bound and captured in a dark prison, and restore it to its original liberty. He is powerful enough to uncover the divine glory of nature—the first and noblest creature—and to strip off and lay aside her garments of obscurity, so that, with her elementary coverings removed, it is granted to see her in her simple and naked disposition. She will look back benevolently with a celestial gaze and a pleasant intuition upon her faithful minister and great-hearted soldier, who so faithfully freed her from her dark prison.

And truly, although I confess myself to be lacking in such exquisite art—or at least I do not publicly confess myself as knowing—namely, that I understand those hidden mysteries of nature or the governance of that celestial fire by whose help such glorious effects in nature are perceived; and consequently, entry into so narrow a path leading to the vision of happiness is perhaps denied to me; although (I say) the bitter and severe punishment of Prometheus <note>The Titan punished for stealing fire from the gods.</note> has perhaps struck terror into my thoughts and rendered me timid and not bold enough to snatch this most noble fire from the heavens; and perhaps my ignorance or the unworthiness of my merit does not allow me to obtain such great grace from the powers above; or some piety, or despair, or at least the fear of Jove’s wrath commands and warns me not to attempt to snatch it violently and in vain from the adamantine firmament by force, lest, like the ambitious and bold Typhon <note>A monstrous giant who challenged Zeus/Jove and was struck down by lightning.</note>, I be plunged by the impulse and strike of a lightning bolt into the bowels of the dark earth, and for this my insult and rebellion, I perpetually vomit out the fiery sighs of torture: (for we are taught by the Holy Scriptures, *it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that showeth mercy* <note>Romans 9:16</note>).

Although (I say) these obstacles seem to meet me, by which I either do not possess such great faculty, or if I did, I would refuse to reveal it openly to the world; nevertheless, while it is permitted for the common and false Alchemist—that fantastical ape and superfluous imitator of nature—to aspire, I may in this place immerse myself and penetrate as deeply into the hidden parts and the obscure composition of that richest and incomparable vegetable (hidden from the common eye) as that super-celestial spark infused in me by the Creator shall direct me by the common way. For if the mystical way were known to me, it would not be lawful or right to publish and reveal it to the world. It shall suffice you, therefore, that I begin to reveal to you in plain words those things which I have learned by my own experience and investigation into the nature of this vegetable thing.

In this attempt to reveal nature and anatomize this vegetable, we use an earthly agent—elementary fire or heat—in place of the celestial one. By its edge, I have attempted to divide the elementary parts of this compound from one another. And although the property of that ethereal and exalted heat (to whose proportion of action we have adapted the edge of this inferior fire in our anatomy) is to subtilize and spiritualize all those things which the biting cold has incorporated in its merciless and icy arms and gathered into a dark labyrinth to incorporate bright and active forms; nevertheless, since these inferior fires or earthly agents, both visible and invisible, are derived from that pure and essential light (for they are like the offspring or various infants of one father, according to the variety of the spirit or medium in which they are present in a hidden way), I judged it a suitable thing to choose one of those inferior agents for this our purpose. By means of this agent, with the degrees of nature well observed in it, I shall begin to bring to light the internal spirit of this most excellent vegetable—namely, of wheat and bread, in which nature so greatly abounds—and to uncover the naked nature of Nature, though not exactly in the manner of natural and supreme Alchemy.

Therefore, this shall be the subject <note>original: "patiens"</note> of our anatomization, concerning whose dignity and internal mysteries I have proposed to discourse in this my present treatise. I have chosen to distinguish it by the title of the **Lesser Philosophical Key**, because just as that **Greater Key of Philosophy** explains the exact and infallible reason for creating and disposing the world and the elements, and is said (to speak with Solomon) to express the mysteries of all things both hidden and manifested (as one whose governance is guided by the virtue of Wisdom itself, proceeding from the mouth of the Most High, and consequently can never deceive or fail); for this is the highest mystery of all, from which, as the wise man testifies in *Wisdom 7:17*: *For he hath given me certain knowledge of the constitution of the world, and the forces of the elements: the beginning, ending, and midst of the times: the alterations of the turnings of the sun, and the change of seasons: the circuits of years, and the positions of stars: the natures of living creatures, and the furies of wild beasts: the violence of winds, or spirits...*

# On the Exact Anatomy of Bread or Wheat.

<note>original: "De Exacta Panis seu Tritici Anatomia"</note>

...of the powers and thoughts of men, and the differences of plants, and the faculties of roots, and also to know whatever is hidden and manifest:) So also is this our **Lesser Key**, whose subject is not wisdom itself, but the *effect* of wisdom. We are admonished to demonstrate and contemplate God not otherwise than from the "posterior" <note>Latin: *à posteriore*—reasoning from effects back to causes</note>—that is, through His creatures—inasmuch as He is known through His wonderful works; rather than from the "prior" moving wisdom in the aforementioned most hidden mystery of all. It shall suffice us, therefore, in this our treatise, not to forge a new world and make all things new—that is, to strive from the prior to the posterior (since this is the subject of the aforementioned **Greater Philosophical Key**, of which the most enlightened **Brothers of the Rosy Cross** <note>The Rosicrucians, a secret society of mystics and alchemists</note> have sung so much, whose song is not to be rashly despised or held as frivolous by the wise)—but conversely to proceed from the posterior to the prior. This means not in constructing, but in destroying the compound and reducing it into its primary and simple elements. By this, we may gaze upon the simple parts of the composition; notice the natures, positions, and dispositions of the elements according to the possibility of "spurious alchemy" <note>The author uses "spurious" or "adulterated" alchemy to refer to laboratory chemistry as opposed to divine "true" alchemy</note>; gather the reason for the compound's growth and quickening; contemplate the union and harmony for life of the clear spirit and the flashing light; conceive, albeit from afar, the intentions of corruption and generation; see with open eyes the reason for the body's darkness and opacity; and finally elicit and make manifest many other things hidden in the sanctuary of nature. 

This, I say, is the "Lesser Key" of philosophy, because although the five elements—and even its own absurd and dark chaos—are drawn out by this artifice so that each seems distinguished from the other, nevertheless the pure element in its simple nature cannot be demonstrated by the industry of this spurious art. Nor can nature in her golden and flashing purity, as she truly is, be unshelled and brought into the light, but only separated from one another in her defiled nature, insofar as each part, though still impure, participates more in this or that element. For despite the art of spurious chemistry—however it works through distillations, cohobations <note>The process of redistilling a liquid over its own solid residue</note>, digestions, circulations, putrefactions, filtrations, calcinations, separations, or conjunctions, as well as fixations or dissolutions—nature will still have her labyrinthine hiding places in which she conceals her "Phoebian face" <note>The sun-like or golden essence</note> from the artist who is a stranger to her. For she does not recognize, nor will she greet with a naked and uncovered face, anyone except her own proper minister: one walking in the simple path of nature, simple in his works, and always having his eye fixed on the act of nature’s operation. To such a true Alchemist, favorable Nature will be present, her garments of darkness cast off; to him (I say) the first wisdom of all creatures will be present, and will greet him with a lucky and favorable omen. But let us pass on to our purpose.

## CHAPTER II.

### *Concerning wheat or bread, and the name appropriated to it among both the Greeks and Latins. Its excellence, its rationale, and likewise its manner of growth and the formula for its multiplication are clearly explained in this chapter.*

Wheat, therefore—that most excellent vegetable temple and dwelling place of Queen Nature—is the subject upon which we have placed the foundation of this our ocular demonstration. Among the Greeks, it is called <term>pyros</term> <note>original Greek: πυρὸς</note> from its "fiery" disposition (as I think), inasmuch as it is filled with the bright and lively ray of nature. By the Latins, it is called *triticum* from *triturando* <note>threshing or grinding</note>, as some would have it, because it must be crushed and reduced to a barely palpable powder before it can be brought into use. In this vegetable creature, even the coarse country folk have found no small difference through their experience, as they are accustomed to divide it into chaff, bran, flour, and fine flour <note>original: "similaginem"</note>; although in truth, flour is nothing other than a composition of bran and fine flour, just as fine flour is observed to appear upon the separation of the bran. This seems to be the sole king and prince of vegetable grains, because in it, nourishing Nature—the mother and nurse of the whole world—has her chief residence. Whence it is not unsuitably called by some (as was said previously) the most perfect temple or palace of the vegetable kingdom. And for this reason, this grain is imbued with infinite power both in multiplication and nutrition, by means of which it is observed to be more fruitful as well as more nourishing than any other grain of the entire vegetable kingdom. Furthermore, it approaches so closely in its essential parts to the well-tempered nature of man, that learned physicians notice it conforms itself to the vital and natural faculty of man by reason of its similarity in disposition; for it nourishes the parts or members of man more than any other vegetable, the effective reason for which I shall not fail to explain to you in its proper place and time. But now, although it may seem an impossible thing to the ignorant to give a certain reason for the growth and multiplication in this beneficent creature, it will nevertheless be very easy for one with true speculation to unshell this doubt—one who first understands how to anatomize this body well, and then afterwards honestly weighs the qualities of the four elements, as well as the contiguity of each to the other; but especially one who rightly contemplates that precious balsam of nature, derived from the bright essence of the celestial sun, and hiding in the hidden marrow of the cavity, by means of which this vegetable body lives and abounds in multiplication. For this is that crystalline mirror, and the clear spirit of the **quintessence**, in which the presence of bright nature [does] not...

# Section I. Portion III. Part I. Book I.

It never appears visibly, yet it yearns to reveal itself even to the common eye through a certain external effect. If, therefore, in the first place, we observe through the intellectual contemplation of philosophy how the element of earth is linked by an essential and inseparable bond with that of water, and by what path again the element of water is joined to that of air, and that aerial one to the fiery, and finally how the fire is bound to the fifth element or the luminous **fifth essence** <note>original: "quinta essentia"; the "quintessence" or purest celestial substance beyond the four terrestrial elements</note> (which indeed participates in the golden disposition of the sun, for the fifth essence is the purest spring of life, in which the light and fiery ray of eternal wisdom, or of the sacred desire of the world, rejoices to bathe itself as if in the most chaste bosom of **Psyche** <note>The personification of the Soul</note>); then it will be a most easy thing for us (as I think) to know and gather why the ear of wheat rises directly and perpendicularly from the earth and is lofted upward, stayed on high as if by the trunk of a tall pine.

For when **putrefaction** <note>The process of decay which alchemists believed was necessary for rebirth and growth</note> is finished (without which, according to the testimony of the Sacred Scriptures, nothing dead can rise again or be exalted), that eternal and never-dying spark of the fifth essence—derived immediately from the celestial progeny of most holy **Apollo** <note>The Sun god</note> (who set his tabernacle in the sun)—now finding its freedom through putrefaction from the bonds of the four elements in which it was enclosed in its dark prison, attempts to take flight toward its ethereal fatherland from which it originally descended. Thus, step by step, it first exalts its crest or head above the dark or heavy earth.

Next, the element of fire (which is connected to the spirit of the fifth essence by an admirable inclination and inviolable knot) rises up from the earth after that fifth essence in subtle smokes and exhalations, not otherwise than we see in Arithmetic the number 5 following consequently after 4. Thus, by a certain natural glue, the element of fire adheres to that of the ether, either because it would be impatient to leave and lose its sweet and formal companion, by whose presence this element, along with its three lower companions, is adorned with such beauty; or in that respect that every thing aspires by natural instinct to its native freedom and longs to return to its own mansion or fatherland.

By a similar reasoning, air follows in the form or image of an invisible or subtle vapor, and ascends from the earth immediately after the fire, inasmuch as it is united to the element of fire by a plainly similar bond of nature as that by which fire is joined to the fifth essence. Finally, the element of water follows the air in its own series and order, whence it is perceived to leap upward from the matrix of the earth immediately after the air; for it claims for itself the same privilege of combination with air that air had with fire.

And although, in the last place, the earth embraces the volatile and fugitive element of water by the same reasoning, nevertheless, by reason of its heaviness, and also because of its desire for resting in the sphere assigned to it from creation, it halts the water in its motion and hinders it from being carried further upward. And again, the water hinders the air, to which it is joined by natural friendship; and again, the hindered air stands by the fire as a bridle, restraining it in its motion; and here, finally, it wretchedly retains the enclosed ray of the sun and prohibits it, appearing to withstand its motion in every way so that it may not tend further upward.

From this it happens that this celestial ray is forced to remain fixed in the summit or top of the plant against its own appetite; which plant is bound by its roots to the dark earth, so that this solar spark is again imprisoned—partly by the air besieging it on all sides and enveloping it like a net through degrees of thickening, and partly by the other elements, and especially by the earth—and is captured no differently than it was before.

And yet, nonetheless, this peculiar spark of vital fire so enclosed does not cease at every moment, by a certain magnetic faculty, to attract to itself and to call down from on high (as if to its aid and assistance) formal sparks and solar fire similar to itself, to dissipate and break those newly knotted and bound chains. For the air is always filled with the multiplying rays of nature, which wander invisibly to and fro in the aerial waves; and these are ready to bring aid to their captive companions, just as we see cohorts of armed soldiers, divided from the battle line of the army, are ready on every occasion to offer help to their comrades remaining in the line when necessity demands.

But to these sparks of light possessing freedom and wandering everywhere in the aerial ocean, the same thing happens as to hungry and bold flies, which, preferring rashness to danger, are observed to immerse and plunge themselves so deeply into that slime of muddy honey or sugary syrup that at last they adhere so firmly to that lethal and deadly glue that they cannot return to their dwellings. This same thing, I say, happens to these bright children of **Phoebus** <note>Another name for the Sun</note> or celestial freedmen, who, wandering invisibly in the air, attempt to liberate their imprisoned brothers, and being ignorant of material snares or treachery, are suddenly captured and cling to the nets of the gross elements. Thus they are deprived of liberty and are shut up in various prisons or dark bodies with their companions captured before.

Do we not also see that the visible winged creatures of the air are betrayed and deceived in plainly the same way by the viscous machinations of the cunning bird-catcher? What doubt can there be, then, that those invisible fires are sometimes captured and imprisoned in plainly the same way by means of the deceitful engines of the earth? This, I say, is the sole reason that every thing is multiplied unto infinity through this enclosed spark alone; this is the manner by which any vegetable, though in itself corruptible, is nonetheless perpetuated through multiplication.

And indeed, I cannot produce any member in the whole vegetable kingdom more exquisite and excellent in multiplication than is this grain of Wheat; for the lowliest of peasants, taught by experience, can prove to us that from the putrefied body of one single grain, sometimes three stalks of wheat arise with their complete ears or their heads abounding with hair, and reach perfection and maturity. The reason for this thing, as I think, is the abundance of **radical moisture** <note>The essential fluid of life in medieval physiology</note> and **innate heat** which this plant possesses, since it is always a faithful and greedy receptacle of the vital rays which the sun liberally darts down from his golden palace into these lower regions. But lest you think this a fiction derived from my own imagination, I shall [demonstrate] the truth of this matter by a certain ocular demonstration...

# On the Exact Anatomy of Bread or Wheat.

...I shall attempt to indicate below. From the effect of this chapter, it will be permitted for us to observe that the motion or progress in generation or resurrection in a plant is in every way contrary to that of extreme deprivation or destruction; for in the former, the elements rise up in their dignity and order according to the disposition of nature, which is in this manner: namely, ether, fire, air, water, and finally earth, which is the basis and foundation of all. But in destruction, things are perceived to be held in the opposite direction, for first the water ascends, then the air, afterwards the fire, and finally the ether, etc.

### CHAPTER III.

### On the Elements of Wheat or Bread, and on their Manifest Qualities.

From wheat, therefore, is fashioned that earthly bread of the highest grade, which our Savior Christ—by reason of the nobility and excellence of that vegetable—chose for the representation of his own body. Some have made this bread the real body of our Savior, with consecration preceding; others have received it as a certain memorial sign of his passion, with a blessing preceding; concerning which we shall speak more broadly and clearly below. For through the whole thread of this chapter, it has come to mind to insist upon the detection and revelation of the natural elements of wheat or bread and its qualities. For although wheat is but a single simple thing in the vegetable kingdom, it is nonetheless composed of members and parts more pure and homogeneous than its whole, which we call its elements. By the union or conjunction of these (by means of the knot or bond of the <term>quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth essence" or ether, thought to be the celestial spirit binding the four earthly elements together.</note>), the entire body or grain of wheat is contracted into this vegetable species, in which, by means of corruption, it is multiplied.

Experience, therefore, relying on other infallible proofs, has taught us that water abounds more in the mass of this vegetable than any other element; which indeed, as it is superfluous and of very little nourishment, must be exhaled and evaporated from the bread by the advice and admonition of the most skilled physicians. And for this reason, Hippocrates left us an entire treatise on the preparation and roasting of bread. Hence it is that this vegetable, once the threshing is done so that it may more easily be reduced into bread, is exposed to artificial heat, so that the said superfluous moisture may expire and evaporate, whereby its substance might be moderately dried. For it is concluded by those most skilled in medicine (who are instructed by common observation and practice) that this kind of superfluous and useless moisture is the occasion of many diseases in the human body, inasmuch as it generates thick and viscous humors, and consequently is the origin of those phlegmatic <term>crudities</term> <note>Undigested or "raw" humors in the stomach believed to cause illness.</note> which very often afflict the stomach and produce flatulent vapors with indigestion; whence it happens that this humor nourishes little or not at all. Furthermore, it even produces pains in the sides and ribs, and causes the substance of its <term>chyle</term> <note>The milky fluid of digested food.</note> or juice to be suddenly converted into putrefaction; and from this, worms of various kinds arise.

But on the other hand, physicians acknowledge and confess that if it is well-baked, it nourishes wonderfully and generates good blood; it is seen to procreate little or no windiness in the stomach, and renders the whole mass more <term>styptic</term> <note>Astringent or contracting; here meaning it firms the digestion.</note> in its disposition. From this, therefore, it appears that the element of water, so abundant in this grain, is of either little or plainly no utility, but rather superfluous and more harmful to nourishment than useful, as was said before. And certainly the manifest reason for this superfluity of water in wheat or bread ought not to be hidden from the skilled physician, to whom it is not unknown that the effective heat lurking in this kind of vegetable grain—and breathing into the summit of that cedar-like plant—by a certain natural inclination greedily desires watery moisture. For this reason, it draws to itself subtle water from the earth by means of the trunk or the pipe of the stalk, at every moment to refresh and sprinkle with moisture its warm dwelling; not otherwise than the hidden sparks of celestial heat, which are suspended in the middle region of the air, by their magnetic attraction draw up lakes and rivers from the lower parts to the upper sphere which they inhabit, to mitigate and temper the fires of the flashing lightnings. Whence it also appears that wheat, in its manifest quality, is moist by reason of its moisture, in which it abounds in plenty, and hot in respect to the exuberance of its natural heat, which acts essentially within it. And the herbalists seem to agree with this assertion of ours, who seem to estimate this simple as hot and moist in a temperate degree.

Besides this aqueous element, we shall perceive that subtle and clear air lurks in this subject of ours, which contains many hidden faculties in itself, as we shall explain clearly enough in its proper place below.

Furthermore, even the fetid element of fire (the perfect agent for all corruption) is elicited from it, which without doubt is the cause of many preternatural effects in the human body, so that by means of it, one is subjected to many infirmities. Finally, that glorious and ethereal spirit, dispersed and sown through the universe by the rays of Phoebus's <note>The sun's</note> light, betrays itself to the eyes by leaving its dark prison, deprived of all grace, light, life, and solace; since, once that fiery spirit is lost, it is like a void, damned earth, and that <term>caput mortuum</term> <note>Latin: "dead head." The useless residue left after a chemical distillation or sublimation.</note> of the chemists.

We shall observe, therefore, and with due inquiry preceding, we shall find that all these elements are present in bread or wheat: namely, earth, which is the final dregs of separation; then water, which appears first; then afterwards air, which claims for itself the second series after water; fire follows this, which is immediately succeeded by the quintessence, or fifth element, ascending from the region of night into the horizon of day, from whence it previously proceeded. Nor would I wish you to understand in this place that I have meant the simple elements in nature, for so it pleased the most august majesty and most renowned in learning, the Monarch of Britain, to me not unjustly...

# Section I. Portion III. Part I. Book I.

One might justly object that there is no such thing as a pure element in the nature of things; but as I have responded to such a person, so I would also have you know: these parts of a compound are called "elements" because they participate more greatly in one specific element or another. For we acknowledge that nothing absolutely pure or clean is to be found in the progression of nature, for even the simplest element among us is observed to participate in a foreign nature. Indeed, these elements are said to have put on a polluted and corrupt nature immediately after the Fall of Adam <note>The theological idea that nature itself became "degraded" or less pure after the biblical Fall of Man.</note> and to have wandered from their original simplicity. And yet, the wise and those well-versed in true Alchemy have not doubted that they might reach the sanctuary of the pure element.

### CHAPTER IV.

->How the elements of bread concur for human nutrition, and concerning the peculiar office and function of each of them.<-

Now, although it may seem a very difficult thing for an ignorant person to demonstrate—namely, what portion in this vegetable <note>original: "vegetabili"; referring here to the wheat/bread</note> procreates the blood in the animal, by means of which its natural faculty is refreshed and satiated; and then to distinguish that element in it which primarily regards the heart and the vital spirits; and furthermore, what that vegetable substance is which passes through the ureters (or small urine channels and conduits) into the bladder; finally, from whence proceeds that which fills and nourishes the gall bladder, and what nature claims the spleen and the viscera for its receptacle—nevertheless, to him who diligently attends to the order of this anatomy of ours, all these doubts will become clear and manifest.

For he will perceive that the **airy part** is that which is converted into blood by the blood-making virtue and nature of the liver; for gross blood comes closest to that pure spiritual humidity which fills the arterial vessels. In its property, this stands in relation to the blood of the liver as **spirit of wine** <note>An early term for concentrated alcohol or ethanol.</note> stands to common **water of life** <note>original: "aqua vitae"; here referring to a less refined distillate.</note>. For the vital spirits contained in the arteries behave like the cream or the purest and most subtle portion of the blood, which is nothing other than the thinnest substance of air, mixed with the subtle nature of the **ether** or **quintessence** <note>The "fifth element," thought to be the celestial essence of life.</note> by whose benefit we live. This portion of arterial blood is preserved partly through the bright spirits of the blood, but principally through the air attracted every moment by inhalation. In that air, the invisible and celestial spirits of life lie hidden and concealed; as soon as the heart receives them through inhalation, it retains them firmly, ejecting through exhalation the smoky and vaporous air that had carried them, as being useless for its purpose.

The **element of fire** preserves and occupies the gall bladder; while **aqueous humidity** distills from the principal blood vessels to the bladder through a double channel. The **thicker earth** is received by the viscera or intestines, as it is too thick to pass through the tiny mesenteric veins <note>The small veins that carry nutrients from the intestines to the liver.</note>; for it is the office of these veins to convey the **chyle** <note>The milky fluid of digested food.</note> to the liver. But if by chance a little of its thinner viscosity enters through these narrow branches along with the thicker waters, the dark spleen is immediately ready to attract that slimy matter to itself, sucking it greedily into its spongy substance. 

For Nature ordained these internal tracts and conduits in man and other animals for this sole end: without them, such terrestrial and dreg-like matter would contaminate, pollute, and infect the entire mass of the red substance prepared for the nourishment and preservation of the fleshy part. Therefore, it is manifest that when retention has been made by the virtue of the transverse fibers in the stomach until the bread and food are cooked into perfect chyle, then that chylous pulp—consisting of the aforementioned elements (namely, viscous **earth**; fluid and slippery **water** serving as a vehicle for all the rest; subtle **air**, which is like a volatile salt or an invisible **Ammoniacal** or **Nitrous** humor <note>Chemical metaphors for the "life-force" found in the air.</note>, whose thicker and more tenacious substance is sent to the bladder after the airy element has been reduced into blood; and finally the spiritual **quintessence** which holds itself between air and fire and mixes itself with every element, being by its amiable nature a friend to all and an enemy to none)—this chylous pulp or substance, I say, thus prepared, is attracted to the liver. There, as if in a furnace, every humor is examined by the fire of nature, as it were, and divided from one another, and according to its dignity and quality, is disposed and infused into the competent or convenient vessels ordained by Nature to receive it.

And so it is very easy for a diligent anatomist to discern and perceive the disposition, office, and property of each of these elements in wheat, ordained by Nature for the nutrition and preservation of the human body. From this, I would also have the ignorant be admonished to observe how a true transmutation is made by means of this **natural Alchemy** in the **microcosm** <note>The "little world," i.e., the human body as a reflection of the universe.</note>: namely, the conversion of one species into another—that is, of the vegetable into the animal—since every essential and elemental part of the wheat is transformed by a certain natural agent into the vital and natural parts of both man and any other animal.
