# On the Exact Anatomy of Bread or Wheat.

## CHAPTER V.

### On the miraculous properties of wheat in Medicine, and how it contributes to the curing of diverse kinds of diseases.

Just as we have explained—by the consensus and authority of the most learned philosophers, as well as by the reasons alleged therein—that an excess of water in this vegetable has given rise to many diseases and infirmities in the human body, so too must the perfect method for bringing about human health be found within it. For from the monuments of the most ancient and knowledgeable physicians, it is right to gather how much excellence and eminence this vegetable possesses and conducts itself in certain diseases invading the human body. For what, I ask, is more effective for repelling diseases, resisting the enemies of health, and restoring human life, than the fullness of that very thing by which life is chiefly preserved? Or what is the reason why vicious humors are so irregular and violent in the human body that they produce diseases and thus hasten premature death (unless it be countered), except for a defect in the universal bond or "knot of Nature," by whose presence and preternatural help the four elements are peacefully bound together in the external mass? 

For just as we see a fierce horse in a stable, once its bonds are broken, never ceasing to kick and attack the others until it remains the sole victor of the place, so also a specific element, feeling the lack of its bridle or ligament (which participates in the nature of the <term>quintessence</term><note>The "fifth essence" or ether, believed by alchemists to be the purest, most potent part of a substance.</note>), wanders outside its circle and prison. It leaves the order destined for it by nature and does not cease to inflict violence upon the elements contrary to it in the same composition, until the entire economy of the human palace is destroyed and the spirit of life is claimed by liberty <note>i.e., the soul is released from the body in death</note>. And all these things proceed from the defect and poverty of this celestial and sympathetic ligament, by the virtue of whose harmony and concord the essential form ought to be preserved and retained in its state throughout the entire fabric of the body. Therefore, human industry or science knows no better work to undertake than to recover that by which the weak and feeble ligaments in this body may be repaired and strengthened. 

And indeed, it is a most evident sign of death when the universal ligaments of nature are perceived to be violated. But where this knot of the quintessence is loosened only in some part, it signifies the mortification or at least the temporal depravation of the life of that specific part. But if by chance weakness or debility occupies only one or more portions of the body, the evil grows into a disease or infirmity that is more dangerous the more their symphonic bonds are thinned and violated. This being the case, it appears (in my opinion) most evidently that through the nutrition and recreation of these weak and debilitated bonds of nature by something similar to themselves, the vigors of the human body can easily be repaired and restored—provided that excellent human industry can skillfully acquire and prepare this <term>balsam of nature</term> aptly, as befits a good philosopher and skilled physician. 

And certainly, I am forced to confess in truth that I was once affected by a great trouble due to pain and weakness arising in the outer part of my hand, at that very time when I was engaged in this same experiment of which I now treat. Whereupon I took a little of this raw <term>balsam of the quintessence of wheat</term> and anointed the hump or back of my hand with it; and from that very hour, though three years have now elapsed, until this present time, I have never felt the pain by which I used to be affected before that time. And yet I confess (not without a blush) that either my negligence or other occupations were the cause that neither before nor since that time have I ever made any other examination or trial of that virtue or property. For I have longed to be instructed by those experienced philosophers (who are better exercised and versed in the secret virtues and nature of this fifth element) and to be fully and faithfully led by the way of exaltation to the highest effect of its purity. But what this balsam of the quintessence may be, I have proposed (God willing) to express and relate more fully in the second book, where I shall demonstrate that it is the true spirit of the starry heaven, filled with bright solar rays.

Ancient and Modern Physicians, who were ignorant of the method of extracting this quintessence and perceived the splendor of its beauty not at all, have nonetheless perceived through experience and practice its hidden and singular effects, both in the preservation of debilitated and consumed natures and in the extinction of raw humors, resistance against poisons, and the cure of many diseases of the human body. And to this purpose, **Almanzor** <note>Likely Al-Razi (Rhazes), the Persian physician</note> professes that wheat well-cooked or boiled in milk better nourishes and strengthens human nature, and hence it is that he seems to commend it in consumptions and <term>Hectics</term><note>A wasting fever associated with tuberculosis</note>. **Trallianus** <note>Alexander of Tralles, a 6th-century physician</note> published in a public writing that warm bread dipped in wine is beneficial for those oppressed by <term>syncope</term><note>Fainting</note>, or swooning, or vertigo. And all the princes of physicians generally assert that it procreates good blood, multiplies sperm or seed, and nourishes abundantly. **Isaac** <note>Isaac Judaeus, a 10th-century physician</note> affirms that it wonderfully confirms and strengthens the limbs. **Avicenna** teaches us that this grain contains within itself the cure for the bite of a mad dog, whence he also makes this a special antidote against poison; with whom **Dioscorides** agrees, testifying that it cures the strikes of serpents when used with Rue. And for this reason also, in respect of its nutritive faculty, **Actuarius** commends it for the composition of <term>ale</term><note>original: "cereuifiae"</note> and prefers it by far to barley or oats. Section I. Portion III. Part I. Book I.

...cially from its ethereal disposition, which is joined by the tightest bond of friendship to the life of all animals; because of this, it is an enemy to poisonous and infected humors, which attempt to violate or weaken those precious ligaments of the human composition <note>original: "hominasiae," likely a Greek-derived term for the human constitution</note> previously mentioned. For it must be known that the ligaments of the composition of every single creature are of one kind, and therefore like is nourished by its like, and like rejoices and delights in its like. Indeed, this balsam can be extracted from any thing of whatever condition, since without it nothing can endure for even a moment of time.

### CHAPTER VI.

->*On the mystical significance of wheat in the Holy Scriptures.*<-

Abbot Odo <note>Likely Odo of Cluny or Odo of Tournai, medieval theologians</note>, the most learned man of his age, observed in his *Harmony* attributed to the Most Holy Trinity that wheat, above all other plants in the sacred scriptures, is many times taken to represent the second person of the Trinity. In confirmation of this, he brings forth this example from the Prophet Joel: *The floors shall be filled with wheat, and the presses shall overflow with wine and oil.* In this, he attributes the individual members to the individual persons of the Trinity in this manner: the Spirit fills the presses with wine, the Son fills the floors with wheat, and the Father fills the presses with oil. Furthermore, we shall find the natures of these three to be aptly applied to the persons of the Trinity in respect to their properties: such as oil to mercy, for it mitigates pains; wheat fills with abundance; wine refreshes, etc. Wherefore, in this sense, we find many other passages of Holy Scripture in which mention is made of this triple harmony in clearly the same words, such as: *All the best <note>literally "marrow"</note> of the oil, and of the wine, and of the wheat, whatever first-fruits they offer to the Lord, I have given to thee. Deuteronomy 18:12.* So also elsewhere: *Thou mayest not eat within thy gates the tithe of thy wheat, and of thy wine, and of thy oil. Deuteronomy 12:17 & 18:4 & 2 Chronicles 8:5.* Similarly: *He will give rain to your land in due season, the early and the latter rain, that thou mayest gather in thy wheat, and thy wine, and thy oil. Deuteronomy 11:14.* And many other such passages are drawn from Holy Scripture, which abundantly prove with what honor and excellence wheat was held by the holy prophets. Furthermore, the utility of this simple <term>simple: a medicinal herb or plant used as a remedy</term> is explained in express words by the Prophet David in Psalm 81:16 and Psalm 147:14. Thus, the abundance of this balsam or "fifth essence" <term>quintessence: the purest, most concentrated medicinal extract</term> of wheat seems to be among the highest earthly blessings that a man can attain in this world; for he says: *Jehovah fed them with the fat of wheat, and with honey out of the rock he satisfied them;* and in the other place: *He satisfieth thee with the fat of wheat,* etc. We also read in Leviticus chapter 23:10 <note>corrected from 23:6 in source</note>: *When you shall have entered into the land which I will give you, and shall reap your corn, you shall bring sheaves of ears (the first-fruits of your harvest) to the priest, who shall lift up the bundle before the Lord, that it may be acceptable for you on the day after the Sabbath, and he shall sanctify it.* From this it clearly appears how precious wheat was in the eyes of both God and men. Furthermore, if we read how seriously and effectively the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 15 <note>corrected from 2 Cor 15 in source</note> teaches us the effects of our resurrection through a grain of wheat—which, after its corruption in the earth, is restored to life and rises much more gloriously—we can boldly assert that there is a great internal mystery which is hidden and lies concealed in this most noble grain. And we shall consider even more attentively the great and stupendous secrets and allegorical relations which this plant, under the shadow of bread, has to the person of our Savior Jesus Christ, as the sacred volume widely testifies, and as we shall further explain in the following chapter.

### CHAPTER VII.

->*On the two kinds of bread, of which one is earthly and common, the other celestial and*<-
->*proceeding immediately from God; and on the wonderful virtue found in physical bread,*<-
->*as well as the natural bond and joining*<-
->*which it has with that*<-
->*spiritual bread.*<-

And because, for the reasons we brought forward above—namely the abundance of that superfluous watery substance—it is not expedient to put this vegetable grain to the use of nutrition without skillful preparation and necessary correction preceding it, it was seen to be required (by counsel, use, and approved experience, and that from the very beginning of things) that after threshing it should be reduced into a mass. This mass Adam himself (instructed by the mouth of the most high Jehovah) saw fit to call *Lechem* <note>original Hebrew: לחם</note>, that is, bread; whence Genesis 3: *In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread* <note>original Hebrew: בזיעת אפיך תאכל לחם</note>. Truly, to recount here all the labors discovered in the cooking and baking of it, of which mention is made among the most learned physicians, namely Hippocrates and his disciples, would be too tedious and neither useful nor fitting for my discourse. Therefore, I will omit all that, so that I may proceed immediately to the general division of bread, of which mention is so often made in sacred writings. In these we shall find that just as the entire machine of the world is divided and distributed into two principal natures, namely heaven and earth,

# On the Exact Anatomy of Bread or Wheat.

In this way, we shall find bread to be divided into its two-fold species: namely, the spiritual and the earthly. Earthly bread was produced in the first creation and has been continued through multiplication in this vegetable grain until this very day; but that celestial bread proceeds from God, in whose power it always remains to dispose of it as it pleases Him, as we shall declare in the following chapter. And indeed, it appears by many manifest arguments that God has infused no small power of His own splendor into the nature of this lower bread. For this reason, it is so highly esteemed and held in such great value among all nations of the world that even gold itself is not held in such high price by man. For although gold, gems, and precious stones are sold at a higher price by weight and quantity, bread is observed to far excel them in both value and utility. First, because it abundantly nourishes and refreshes the tabernacle of the human soul <note>The author uses "tabernacle" to refer to the physical body as a temporary dwelling for the soul.</note>, whereas the function of gold and precious gems is only to adorn it and make it splendid on the outside. Furthermore, bread is capable of multiplying itself unto infinity, which gold or gems cannot provide—unless they be the "Gold of God" and the "mystic gems" of the Magi <note>A reference to alchemical or Hermetic concepts where "philosophical gold" possesses life-giving properties.</note>. And therefore, it is much more precious in the eyes of God and men than even the gold or the most precious and rarest stones of princes. For this reason, it was not said in Numbers 15:19, "You shall participate in the riches of that land," but *you shall eat of the bread of that land*, proving by that very fact that bread is the highest good and the price required for the life and sustenance of man. This the Psalmist also manifests to us in Psalm 104:15 <note>Original text cites Psalm 103:15 following the Vulgate numbering.</note> in these words: *Bread strengthens and supports the heart of man, just as wine gladdens it.*

Furthermore, we find so close an affinity between earthly or material bread and the spiritual bread descended from heaven, that if we look rightly and deeply into this lower bread, it would be a matter of no great difficulty to behold and contemplate the images and shadows of the mysteries contained in that more sublime bread. And for the sake of this matter, we can observe in Holy Scripture itself how effective a comparison has been established between these two, as if one were joined with the other by a certain secret and essential connection. Whence the royal Psalmist, in Psalm 104, ingenuously confesses that *Bread is brought forth from the earth by the favor of God*. So also in Saint Matthew 26:26 we find: *He blessed the bread and broke it, and gave it to his disciples, and said, take and eat, this is my body.* From this it appears how great an excellence is in the bread of that earth, since Christ Himself compares His own body with it—a discourse certainly of such consequence that it has effectively set the entire Christian world on fire regarding this doubt: namely, whether the consecrated and sanctified bread is the real body of Christ or not? So also we find in Luke 24:30: *And it happened, while he sat at table with them, he took bread, and blessed it and broke it, and handed it to them, and their eyes were opened, and they recognized him.*

Our Savior Christ manifested this miracle in bread after His resurrection, from which we may clearly recognize that there is an admirable correspondence situated between this earthly creature and the celestial Creator. We read also how many miracles Christ performed concerning this subject on the mountain, where *with seven loaves he satisfied four thousand men, with a great abundance of leftovers and fragments remaining*, Matthew 15. And in another place, *five thousand hungry men, exhausted by lack of food, were sustained by only five loaves, leaving aside the baskets filled with the remaining fragments*, Matthew 16. Furthermore, the world cannot deny the blessings which God imparts to the grain of wheat every year, which supplies the people abundantly in its season, as it is their life and the sustenance by which they live. For which reason King David in Psalm 53:5 shows how detestable and barbarous it is to feed on bread without a humble invocation of the name of the Most High and due thanksgiving for such great beneficence, deeming such a man impious who devours bread without grace preceding it. And it was held as a vice and transgression by the Pharisees and Scribes to eat bread with unwashed hands, for they exhibited such reverence to this principal nourishment, Matthew 15:2. Does not Jehovah, when He is about to punish the wicked, threaten them with a lack of bread? *He broke the staff of bread, and brought famine into the land*, says the Psalmist, 105:16. How many commands and statutes were divinely ordained for the people of Israel concerning this kind of nourishment—namely, leavened and unleavened bread—let him who reads Exodus and Leviticus judge and determine. For in one place it is said of it: *You shall not eat leavened bread on that day when you went out of Egypt.* Exodus 13:3, 7. By these things, therefore, we can perceive how precious this earthly bread is in the eyes of the Creator, and how it is connected to His secret mystic will. Nor can we deny that it draws its life, multiplication, and consequently its preservative virtue from the secret workshops and treasuries of Jehovah Himself, since the dew and rains, which are the causes of the true fertility of this royal grain, are established in the hand of our God Jehovah. He preserves them in His secret treasures, as if in a storehouse, to either impart them to the earth or deny them according to His pleasure—namely, so that by such retention and denial, wheat is denied to the wicked living on earth, but conversely, by their emission and pouring out at the opportune time, God bestows it and supplies it abundantly to the pious and to men pleasing to God, as the sacred histories teach us in many places. Furthermore, we find not only that the offering of wheat was pleasing to God (as we hinted above), but we also read that bread was consecrated to Him in place of a principal offering: for thus we gather from Leviticus 23:17, *Two loaves are to be offered to Jehovah*. And Job 28:5 seems to assert *that a certain bread comes out of the earth, and that which is under it is turned into something like fire.* What this bread and the earth from which it emerges signify in mystic theology, I leave to be explained by those far deeper and more learned than myself. To me, indeed, it is very easy to bring forth for you testimonies of even greater importance attesting to the mysteries of this most noble vegetable, both to explain its sanctity—which is verified by that offense and sacrilege committed by the Prophet David in the taking and eating of the consecrated loaves—as well as many other examples of a higher nature: but I must fear, lest to you...

Section I. Portion III. Part I. Book I.

### CHAPTER VIII.

#### Concerning the heavenly or spiritual bread, with its infinite mysteries and effects.

Just as earthly grain is reckoned to exist among us, so also is heavenly grain granted; and it follows consequently that, in a similar respect, earthly bread holds a relation to that heavenly bread. What this heavenly grain or spiritual bread truly is, the prophet David describes most excellently for us: <margin>Psalm 78:24</margin> *He rained down manna upon them to eat, and gave them the grain of heaven, so that every man ate the bread of the mighty* <note>original: "panem robustissimum," often translated as "angels' bread" or "bread of the strong."</note>. And this same thing is confirmed by Moses in these words: <margin>Exodus 16:5, 9, 14</margin> *Manna, the bread from heaven,* etc. What this manna was, whence it came, and by what discrepancy it differs from wheat or earthly bread, the same supreme Prophet <note>Referring here to Moses</note> sufficiently teaches us in these very words: *He afflicted you, and made you hunger, but fed you with Manna, which you did not know, nor did your fathers know, that he might make known to you that man lives not by bread alone, but by everything that proceeds from the mouth of Jehovah.* <margin>Deuteronomy 8:3</margin> Now indeed we can confess how excellent a thing this heavenly bread is, since it proceeds from the very Spirit of God, and is as if it were his very word, which nourishes both corporally and spiritually. And hence it is that the wise man says: <margin>Wisdom 16:26</margin> *The natures of fruits do not nourish man, but the word of God preserves them.* From this it evidently appears that this bread proceeds from the very word of God, which is also confirmed in the following passage: <margin>Exodus 16:5, 14, 16, 17</margin> *Bread is rained from heaven called Manna; This is that bread which Jehovah gives you to eat. This is the word which Jehovah commanded: gather from it.* This same was the sweet bread of angels of which Solomon speaks, <margin>Wisdom 16:20</margin> saying: *You nourished your people with the food of angels, and you provided for them prepared bread from heaven without labor, having in itself every delight, and the sweetness of every taste.* From this it appears first, that this heavenly bread was ordained by God to be the food of angels, and also that it was a most delicate nourishment, most pleasing to the taste and palate. To be brief, this bread hidden under the type <note>A "type" is a biblical person or event that foreshadows a future reality.</note> of the heaven-sent Manna contains within itself a greater mystery (as I believe) than can be explained in words by the majority of men. And although I freely confess that I have not yet fully progressed in the knowledge of such arduous and mystical food, nevertheless I dare to affirm that the sole vow and desire of my soul is to know as much of it as anyone possibly can; for my own internal spirit, as well as that sharpest sting of the mind implanted in man by God and his own nature, urges and impels me toward such blessed contemplations—a mind which continually strives to elevate itself to the highest contemplation of that happiness and bliss where unity dwells. My mind has taught me, teaches me, and will teach me (God favoring) the way to the palace of bliss, to the center of creatures, to the light of the world. What? Does not the Wisdom of Solomon teach us the same, namely that it is the delight of wisdom to dwell and live among the sons of men? <margin>Proverbs 8</margin> Was she not sent upon the earth from the bright heaven itself, so that she might remain and cooperate with man for this end: that he might learn and know what is acceptable to God? <margin>Wisdom 10</margin> And for this cause God himself said: <margin>Job 38:36</margin> *Who has put wisdom in the inward parts? or who has given understanding to the heart?* From this, therefore, it clearly appears that God infused wisdom into man from above, and that wisdom is a bright emanation proceeding immediately from the Majesty of the eternal God. <margin>Wisdom 8</margin> Wherefore, let no one think it a matter of presumption or ambition to strive, as much as possible, to climb to the true knowledge of divine mysteries, since by divine grace we have tasted from the bright fountains of eternal wisdom, which by their benefit lead and accompany us even to the very throne of Jehovah himself, so that with a joyful and eager soul we may contemplate and behold glory through the spirit. But what shall I say? This thick and dark body (a blind spring of darkness) veils and covers our captive spirits so that we can only with difficulty discern those things which are set before our bodily eyes, and much less the things enclosed in the spiritual heaven. Did not the wise man testify that he felt the same in express words when he said: <margin>Wisdom 9:15</margin> *The body infected with corruption weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses the mind full of many cares? And we hardly guess the things that are on earth, and with labor we find the things that are at hand; but who shall search out the things that are in the heavens? and who has known the counsel of God? unless God has given wisdom, and sent his holy spirit from the highest places.* Thus the paths of those who live on earth were corrected, and men were taught the things that please God. It is therefore the flesh which draws the spirit away from the high contemplations of heavenly things, and not the will of God, who liberally rains down his wisdom upon us to lead and direct us to himself. But to return to our subject, which is the spiritual manna or heavenly bread, it is very easily gathered how sublime and mystical that nourishment is from various citations of the Holy Bible. And to begin from the speech of our Savior himself: <margin>John 6:32</margin> *It was not Moses,* he said, *who gave the true bread from heaven, for the true bread is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.* They said therefore to him, "Lord, always give us this bread," but Jesus said, "I am the bread of life; he who comes to me shall not...

# On the Exact Anatomy of Bread or Wheat.

...will hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst; from which we see here that Jesus himself (who is the Word, which is God himself) is the true Manna or the true bread which was sent from heaven. I know not what to say of that miraculous bread which the Angel offered to Elijah during the second visitation, of which it is written <margin>*3 Kings 19:6* <note>In modern Bibles, 1 Kings 19:6.</note></margin> *that the hearth-baked bread and the vessel of water comforted Elijah, by means of which food—that is, in the strength of which—he walked forty days and nights.* That nourishment was, beyond all doubt, of the same nature as that heavenly manna by which Moses was nourished when he remained for forty days and as many nights on Mount Sinai: just as our Savior Christ, when tempted by the tempter, was seen to imply in some way by these very words (who was also sustained in the same manner in the desert for forty days and nights) <margin>*Matt. 4*</margin> *Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word proceeding from the mouth of God.* <margin>*Ecclesiasticus 15:3*</margin> *She fed him with the bread of understanding, and gave him the wine of wisdom to drink;* was not Ezra also sustained in a miraculous way by this nectar-like cup for forty days and nights, bringing forth throughout that entire space the <insert>laws</insert> and precepts of wisdom? <margin>*2 Esdras 14:39* <note>Original: "Efdr. 4. 14. 39." refers to the apocryphal 2 Esdras.</note></margin> *Behold, a cup full of a liquid thing like water, but of a fiery color, by which my heart was burdened with understanding, and wisdom swelled in my breast.* So also we shall find in *Ezekiel 3* that very same nourishment—namely the Word of the Lord—was presented to Ezekiel, though in another form, by which he was filled with wisdom and pronounced the will of the Lord, who said to him: *Rise, son of man, eat of this which you find, eat these writings <note>original: "literas" (letters/writings)</note>, and go and speak to the house of Israel; then I opened my mouth, and he gave me these writings to eat, and he said to me: Son of man, cause your belly to eat, and fill your intestines with these writings which I give to you; then I ate them, and they were in my mouth sweet as honey.* Saint John also in the *Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> made mention of a similar nourishment which he confessed was sweet to the palate, but bitter in the intestines. What then was this precious nourishment? Did it not bear the true type of Christ, or Christ the type of it? Was this not that spiritual rock which followed the Israelites in the desert, by whose protection they were fed? And was not Christ himself that spiritual rock? Let us hear the doctrine of Saint Paul on this matter <margin>*1 Corinthians 10:1* <note>Original cites 2 Cor, but text is 1 Cor 10.</note></margin> *Brothers, I would not have you ignorant that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized by Moses in this cloud and in this sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from that spiritual rock which followed them, and the rock was Christ, etc.* Therefore it is evident that Christ (who was before every beginning) was that spiritual rock, and this rock was the spiritual food and drink which feeds both body and soul, by which both the internal and external man is regenerated and called back into life. What then? What is this heavenly and hidden Manna which shall be given to him who overcomes? *John 2:17* <note>Actually Revelation 2:17.</note> Here, I say, this same bread is without any doubt the fruit of that tree of life planted in the midst of the paradise of God, promised to him who shall overcome, *John 2:7* <note>Revelation 2:7.</note> which brings with it that white stone in which a new name is inscribed, known to no one, saving him who receives it. Does not our Savior acknowledge this same thing when he says, *I am the true bread of life, the true rock, and the cornerstone, which St. Paul calls the spiritual rock with which he fed the Israelites (as was just said).* Indeed, this is that unique rock, that true hollowed stone, I say, fallen from heaven, which Jacob recognized to be the gate of heaven and the house of God, *Genesis 28.* Since, therefore, Christ is perfect wisdom in whom, according to the wise man <margin>*Wisdom 7:22*</margin> *the spirit of understanding resides, which (I say) is holy and only-begotten, manifold, subtle, mobile, clear, undefiled, open, free from deceit and harm, loving the good, sharp, which cannot be hindered, doing good, lovable, constant, faithful, without care, having all power, circumspect in all things, permeating all intellectual, pure, and subtle spirits; since it is more agile than all things, and for this reason penetrates all things because of its purity (for it is the true spiritual power of God, and a true influence flowing from the glory of the Almighty, and therefore can be contaminated by nothing, as it is the brightness of eternal light, the unspotted mirror of divine majesty, and the image of his goodness; which, though it is one, can yet do all things, and looking constantly into itself it renews all things, and having considered the distinction of ages, it enters into all holy souls and makes them friends of God and of the prophets;* This is, I say, that true gem of the world, the spiritual rock, the true manna flowing down from heaven, which sustains the entire world both spiritually and corporally, which is one with Christ. This is the light and life of men according to St. John, chapter 1. And this, finally, is that universal spirit which gives continuous being and essence to earthly wheat, without which no one can live, since life is virtue, and all virtue proceeds from the Spirit of Jehovah; for thus we are taught by the psalmist David <margin>*Psalm 33:6*</margin> *By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit from his mouth, all their power.* Nor has this holy spirit deserted the world, as some profanely devise, who banish it into the heaven of the greater world <note>The macrocosm.</note>, since the effects of the world, the multiplication of things, and the constant renewal of creatures after corruption seem to testify that it is even now as powerful in its operation as it ever was. But what need is there for words, when Solomon himself is a witness of this thing? saying, <margin>*Wisdom 1*</margin> *The spirit of the Lord fills the orb of the earth, and that which contains all things; the heavens and earth are full of the glory of God,* and <margin>*Isaiah ch. 6*</margin> teaches us that God fills heaven and earth; so also we read in <margin>*Jeremiah ch. 23*</margin> *that heaven is the throne of God, but the earth is his footstool;* all of which persuade us that God is even now as much in all things as he is above all things—namely in you, in me, and in any thing whatever, at any time and place, as much in this instant of time as in the beginning, according to that saying of the wise man: *God is the center of every thing, whose circumference is nowhere,* as if he were saying, the Spirit of God is uniquely within and without all things, and consequently incomprehensible. Whence it is clear, according to Solomon's saying, that the same true wisdom takes pleasure in dwelling among men as much in this present time as from the beginning of the world; for the power of the divine arm cannot be diminished in the least. # Section I. Portion III. Part I. Book I.

She even attempts to entice people to herself, if by chance they might be seriously induced to seek her: For we find in Proverbs 1:20 <note>The author provides a paraphrased Latin translation of the Vulgate</note> *Wisdom cries out and raises her voice in the streets, calling out in high places, in the crowd of men, at the entrance of the gates, and uttering her words in the city, saying: How long, O simple ones, will you embrace folly? How long will mockers and scoundrels delight in their scoundrelry? How long will fools hate prudence? Receive my reproofs; behold, I will open my mind to you and make you understand my words, for I called, but you turned away; I stretched out my hands, but no one took it to heart.* From this it is clear that it is not by God's fault that such power and familiarity between us and Him—and the sacred wisdom flowing from Him—does not intervene, but it must be imputed to our innate darkness. It is not the severity of Jehovah, nor of that kind and gentle spirit of all power, but the envious perversity of the Devil that keeps and restricts us from performing miracles and seeing miraculous visions, which it happened that our fathers, namely the Patriarchs and holy Prophets, saw, according to that passage in Wisdom 1: <note>Wisdom of Solomon 1:13-16</note> *God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of men; for he created all things that they might exist, and that the generations in the world might be preserved, and the poison of destruction is not in them, and the kingdom of hell is not upon the earth; but man brings destruction upon himself by the works of his own hands,* and likewise in Wisdom 2: *God created man incorruptible, and formed him in the image of his own likeness, but by the envy of the Devil death entered into the world etc.* What then shall we say of wisdom, except that she was sent by Jehovah to counter the tricks and machinations of the Devil and death; by instructing man in what is right before God, and preserving us like a true tree of life and spiritual bread from the stings of hunger and death, both spiritual and corporeal. Wherefore it was said by the wise King <note>Solomon</note> that wisdom holds prosperity and longevity in her right hand, and honor and riches in her left, for which reason she is preferred above gold and precious stones: for Job 28 denies that *man knows the price of wisdom; gold shall not be given for it, nor shall its price be weighed in silver, no one can value it with gold, or the shining gem or the Adamant <term>Adamant: an archaic term for diamond or an incredibly hard, unbreakable stone</term>,* and for this reason Solomon judges the man most blessed who attains her in Proverbs 3. And let no one of our age flatter himself, saying that he possesses wisdom: for this imagination of theirs is a type or index of double ignorance; for in the first place, these men are not wise except in their own judgment, and then afterwards they are entirely ignorant of that discrepancy which exists between human wisdom and divine wisdom. If they knew this, they would candidly confess human wisdom to be mere folly and a "fantastic" science <note>meaning a science based on fantasy or appearances rather than reality</note>, propagated by the vain inventions of men, while on the contrary divine wisdom was with God himself then when he fitted the heavens, and fixed the highest clouds above, when he established the earth and the fountains below, and as if she served him in the place of a helping right hand in that all-encompassing composition, who also continually plays before God, as we find in Proverbs 8:22. *This wisdom built her house with seven columns skillfully polished, to which she invites all to drink of her wine and eat of her food, saying in Proverbs 9:5: Come, eat of my food, and drink of the wine which I have mixed.* This is she who says to her friends in the Song of Songs 4:17: <note>Likely referencing Song of Solomon 5:1 in modern numbering</note> *Enter into my garden, pluck my myrrh with my spices, I will give my wine with milk: eat, friends; drink, and be inebriated, my beloved.* This is she in Wisdom 5:24 <note>Likely referencing Wisdom of Solomon 6 or 7</note> *who never wilts or withers, who is easily perceived or found by those who praise her, and is quickly found by those who seriously investigate her; she goes to meet those who desire her, and offers herself freely to those who long for her; she moves among those who require her, and manifests herself to them in the royal way.* This is that true wisdom which can teach man all things; for she herself is certain knowledge etc. Wisdom 7:17: Inquiry provides the science of all things, shows the knowledge of the creation of the world, and reveals the powers of the elements, the beginning, end, and middle of times and their successions, and the changes of the parts of years, the course of the year, and the situation of the stars, the natures of living things, and the impulses of beasts, the powers of the winds, and the imaginations of men, the diversities of plants and the virtues of roots. Finally, she discloses all things both abstruse and known: What then is human wisdom in respect to this but mere fatuity and spontaneous ignorance, which produces nothing but delusory imaginations? O blessed man then (let me repeat the very words of the wise man in Proverbs 3) and thrice blessed is he who possesses and rightly governs this splendid celestial manna! How well he can be numbered here among the elect sons of God, who is adorned with the presence and power of Christ! For he acquires whatever treasures there are of health, wealth, and prosperity both spiritual and corporeal, of which mention was made above. Nor indeed do I doubt that such men are found in the world, for sacred scripture teaches us that wisdom delights most of all among the sons of men, and she also blesses with all these gifts of hers those who perhaps incline themselves toward her, and hold her in honor and esteem, and in the place of a most splendid queen. So that I may conclude this chapter, and at the same time this part of my discourse, I say that this celestial bread, this celestial manna, this spiritual rock, this divine wisdom, this "all in all" of life—this, I say, is Christ Jesus, according to that kind of bread which differs from common bread as heaven differs from earth, or light from darkness; which is a companion so excellent that whoever has attained it can by the best right say with the Philosopher <note>Attributed to Bias of Priene or Stilpo</note> *I carry all my things with me,* or with Morienus, that pious hermit, <note>Morienus: A legendary figure in alchemy</note> *He who has all things with him stands in no need of foreign help.* But because perhaps I may seem to you a stranger in this arduous science, and to have wandered very far from the investigation of this real divine wisdom, I will nevertheless show myself a supporter of its investigation, and I will give my greatest effort (God assisting and being propitious) toward me journeying toward this palace of happiness. Finally, as much as pertains to the internal secret which I have contemplated with this external and earthly bread, it confirms me constantly that there is such a certain eternal and life-giving essence among men, which is the true celestial bread, the spiritual rock, the celestial manna, and the most divine wisdom, through which every single thing participates more or less in the nature of its creator; but principally her delight is to be preserved with man, the most excellent image or icon in the composition of the divine creator, as one to whom this very wisdom, the immediate offspring of the Deity, is most nearly present and within.

Section I. Portion III. Part I. Book II.

<image-desc>A decorative horizontal woodcut border featuring repeating symmetrical scrollwork and floral elements.</image-desc>

### CHAPTER I.

->*The first intention of the Author agrees with the labor of the Archeus, who is the chemical operator of Nature;* <note>Archeus: A term used by Paracelsus and his followers to describe the "internal chemist" or vital force that directs life and growth.</note> *but his second agent is contrary to that Nature.*<-
->*Finally, the four regimes of nature are described here in good faith.*<-

In this invention of mine, by vigilantly and somewhat accurately observing the action of Nature (inasmuch as she often emits hot vapors from the center of her hidden furnaces, or the cavities of mother earth; not unlike that fire which the sophisticated Alchemist calls the *Mary’s bath* <note>original: "balneum Mariæ" — a water bath used for gentle heating.</note>, but the subtle and true one, to mock the ignorant, calls *Horse dung*, or the heat of a horse's belly or manure, (for by this kind of action Nature is accustomed to subdue and rot the seeds committed to the earth): I chose (I say) that very time of year in which the skilled head of a household, sensing that nourishing nature is working with such a fire, is accustomed to hide his grains of wheat in the womb of the earth, so that they might better rot, and through that rotting <note>original: "putrifactionem" — in alchemy, putrefaction was considered the essential first step for transformation and rebirth.</note> might sprout again with greater glory and multiplication; I chose (I say) that same time, a similar kind of furnace, and an equal degree of fire, to break through corruption these four bonds of the elements in the grain of wheat, by which this vegetable form was sustained. I did this so that in this way I might strip it of all its form, for in this manner its whole body was reduced into a viscous substance, which was indeed an evident sign of the elements being claimed back into their freedom.

Thus I also perceived that a grain, perhaps cast out and inserted superficially into old manure, began after the time appointed by nature to thrust out from its rotted center some slight sign of its resurrection. Furthermore, just as the intention of the Anatomist is not to compose and join together again the body which he has destroyed by the fiery incision (nor could he even do so if he wished, since he is not God), so also in this work of mine, I must necessarily transgress the rule of our teacher Aristotle, since in this work the "corruption of one is not the generation of another" <note>A reversal of the Aristotelian maxim "corruptio unius est generatio alterius." The author is destroying the form without intending to create a new life form.</note>; for I conclude this experiment with an external deprivation. Inasmuch as when I have the body dissolved into its principles, I here indeed finish my work and proceed no further toward generation.

Therefore, I had this prepared grain of mine disposed in such a way that, according to the changes of the seasons and the custom of Nature, I might resolve its bonds—namely, by reducing the body into rot; and afterward, just as we observe the central Archeus, the laborer and craftsman of Nature, to work through four principal and distinct degrees of fire: namely, by the **winter fire** by which he rots; then the **spring fire** by which it grows and sends forth its green sprout or stalk; then afterward the **summer heat** by which the crest or helm is adorned with a clearly golden color, and in this way hastens to maturity; and finally he changes this fire into the **autumnal operation**, by which the goal of maturity, at which Nature aims through the entire year, most exactly occurs.

So also I, in this anatomization of mine, restrict myself to four kinds of actions, although not in the same way and method by which the Archeus works; for we have (as I said) different ends proposed, and therefore it is necessary that we also vary in order and reason. Since he is the true operator of Nature, I am nothing but an ape or an imitator of the same in some things; he compels the creature to rot so that he may afterward renew the same abundantly in its kind; I, driving it backward through that corruption, lead it away from its specific essence which it had before, so that it may return to the nature and being of its principles—namely the elements and its **prime matter** <note>original: "primæ suæ materiæ" — the fundamental substance from which all things are made.</note>—from which it was derived from the beginning.

But truly, nature works gradually and calmly after rotting, lest the elements break out in the tender age of the plants and desert the bonds of the composition. For the same reason, we see that a milder regime and governance is required in childhood than in adulthood, because that age is of a softer constitution and more fit to receive any impression. But I, on the contrary, work here with greater effort and violence, because my intention was to separate those volatile and agile elements from the slow and fixed mass, and that immediately after the rotting was done, so that I might more easily destroy the species. Wherefore, just as Nature, with corruption or rotting going before, works calmly to produce a second generation, so I, on the contrary, labor to lead the composition to the peak of the destruction of the final species by the violence and sharpness of fire.

# On the Exact Anatomy of Bread or Wheat.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting an alchemical or chemical apparatus. In the center is a tall, cylindrical brick furnace with a small arched opening at the base showing a fire. ### CHAPTER II.

->The author’s subterranean agent: a fitting comparison of the appearances of this, his first vision, with those of the universal creation; an evident demonstration that all things are water; the reason why the matter of the world is thicker in one place than another; a description of his first vision with the relationship between it and the effects of the creation of the greater world.<-

By the very same subterranean agent <note>The "agent" refers to the heat of the furnace, which the author likens to the natural heat found beneath the earth's crust.</note>, which is entirely similar to that of a scorching summer—though of a coarser and baser disposition—I separated the specific elements proper to this creature <note>The "creature" here is the grain of wheat being analyzed.</note>. This was done by means of putrefaction <note>term: putrefaction (the process of breaking down a substance through gentle heat and moisture to release its constituent parts)</note> following the imitation of Nature, so that by this method the integral parts of the compound might be better separated from one another. And just as we read in the divine and supreme philosopher Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with alchemy and wisdom.</note> regarding the beginning—namely, at that very moment when God revealed himself—that all things suddenly emerged from darkness, and Matter <note>original: "Hylam" (from the Greek hyle, meaning primordial matter)</note> was disturbed, and immediately a certain obscure and terrible shadow fell downward, changing by a slanting revolution into a moist nature, having been previously agitated and stirred in the ineffable likeness or form of a great smoke or thick cloud; in the same way, by means of the sharpness of this subterranean agent of mine—I mean the violence of common fire—the dark and obscure mass of this shapeless grain manifested itself and showed itself to our senses through an artificial putrefaction and by the mediation of vapor. For the appearance of a spiritual vapor is the intermediary mode in generation and corruption, just as in the creation a moist nature intervened between nothing and something. And from this, Saint Peter seems to conclude when he affirms <margin>2 Peter 3</margin> that the heavens and the earth, with all things contained in them, consist of waters and through waters by the power of the word of God; and he infers from the same that water is as thin and subtle a spirit as that dense moisture from which both the heavens and the earth were primordially procreated. But the most acute Hermes, whom we mentioned above, expressly writes this: *That which is below is like that which is above, and vice versa:* as if he wished to imply that that which is thick is one and the same with that which is subtle, and vice versa, that which is subtle is nothing other than that which is thick. If we examine this properly and accurately, we shall find that earth is reduced into water, and water by the power of heat into air by thinning; and by that very act, air is transmuted into fire, all of which occurs through subtilization <note>The process of making a substance more refined or "thinner."</note>. From this we can infallibly conclude and argue that Earth is thick water, and water is thick air, and in turn Air is nothing other than dense and thick fire. Therefore, the truth of this matter is declared by ocular experience in reverse: that fire by condensing becomes air, and air by the same labor becomes water, and finally water is thickened and coagulated into earth. Since this is manifest to human sense, it will also be clear that all things are nothing but one, because all compounds are made of the four elements, which in reality are nothing other than that very "one" which Saint Peter says is water; and Moses asserts that the Spirit of the Lord was carried not over heaven and earth, but over the waters, by whose separation and distinction into parts the heavens and earth were afterwards created. We conclude, therefore, that the substance of the highest heavens is nothing other than a most subtle exhalation consisting of the thinnest water; that of the middle heavens is an exhalation of intermediate composition, which is a thin vapor, namely water of a middling substance. The lowest heaven, however, is like a certain thick vapor, which the higher it goes, the thinner it appears; and the dreg-like substance of this entire watery mass is the earth. Whence we may observe that all things which the universal frame of this world embraces are nothing but thick water...

# Section I. Portion III. Part I. Book II.

...or subtle, and that all water is nothing other than spirit, whether dense or thin; and therefore all things, in respect to their matter, are nothing but one thing—namely water. This was that sole and unique substance in creation, upon which that unique *Elohim* <note>Hebrew: God</note>, that God alone, was carried over the waters to work toward the perfection of the world and all things contained within it. Furthermore, lest anyone here should quibble and object: "What then is the reason for the thickening and thinning through so many degrees in the whole element of water, such that it is divided and separated into diverse heavens, spheres, and elements?" I respond that, just as we gather from ice, snow, and similar effects of winter, cold is the most powerful agent in the mutual constriction and condensation of diverse, discordant substances. So, on the contrary, heat is found to be the attacker of the frozen actions of cold, by means of which those substances are weakened, melted, and finally dissolved entirely into the liquid nature of flowing water. 

Hence it happens that where cold (which is the origin of dark *Chaos*, and therefore an enemy and contrary to heat, which is the offspring of light and *Demogorgon* <note>A primordial deity often associated with the underworld or the deep origin of nature</note>) claims dominion for itself, there thickness and density reign in the general mass of water. But where heat—the most noble officer of the universal Emperor, namely Light—is present and powerful, there conversely an effect opposite to cold is produced. Where they run together and rule with equal dominion, there also is the sphere of equality, or the orb or circle of the *Soul of the World* <note>Latin: Anima Mundi</note>, about which the *Platonists* treated in such a perplexed and intricate manner. By means of this (as we hinted in the physical history of our Microcosm), the most splendid *Sun* of the greater world is moved, or in which (as we explained in that history of our microcosm) that life-giving heart in the microcosm thrives and leaps. 

Wherefore it appears manifest to the wise man that where light most abounds and dominates, there the watery spirit is rendered most subtle and thin by the operative virtue of heat, proceeding and flashing forth from the act and motion of the lucid rays. For the succeeding heat, by its presence, so repels and drives away its adversary, cold, that it denies it the matter, time, and place to bring the natural effects of condensation into act. On the contrary, where light, and consequently heat, is weak, there its contrary is necessarily rendered stronger. And although the degrees of heat and cold in this semi-diameter—the measure of which is taken from the lucid circumference of the world to the dark center—are infinite in number, nevertheless, we (dissenting very little from other philosophers in this matter) have distinguished them into only six natures evidently differing from one another, which, like *Jacob’s Ladder*, tend upward from the center of the greater world to its very circumference. And the order of the ascending degrees or intervals of this ladder is as follows: *Earth*, *Water*, *Air*, *Fire*, *Ether*, and the *Empyrean Spirit*. Furthermore, just above this highest sixth degree, a seventh or supreme one stands out, where the general *Sabbath* <note>original: Saboth; the day of rest</note> of all rest resides, as it is where the presence of God is permanent. 

From these things it is right to gather that the further we recede from this source of light, the thicker and denser the substance of water becomes. For just as light, by the service of its heat, works through thinning and purification by penetrating downward from the highest heaven or the circumference of the waters toward the center; so also darkness, by its instrumental cold, tending upward from its center in the opposite way (that is, through opposition), strives and attempts by its natural inclination to meet and receive the actions of the descending messengers of light. This is the reason for the comparison established by me in both my microcosmic and macrocosmic history: namely, of heat and formal motion in the region of light, and of dark matter, to two pyramidal figures of equal dimensions. The material cone of one, ascending, touches the base of the formal pyramid which is above; and on the contrary, the formal cone of the pyramid descends downward and reaches all the way to the center in the base of the material pyramid, which is in the earth—about which I have indeed proposed to discourse more widely below. We have set forth the figure and position of the said pyramids in this place so that our intention may be more clearly explained to you.

Therefore, after the vigorous act of my earthly fire or heat had penetrated the dark vegetable mass (prepared in such a way) by a certain secret reverberation, and because in this cast-off, putrefied, and almost deformed substance it had imitated by its remarkable agility the virtue of that first and most excellent light leaping out of the dark *Hyle* <note>Greek: Matter</note>: it immediately sublimated a mist or dense cloud from the putrid mass to a height of nearly ten cubits, not unlike that huge smoke or most foul shadow in the universal creation of all things from nothing (which *Moses* and *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with alchemy and wisdom</note> mention in the places cited above). In this action of the art, it made oblique motions in its ascent, and it was worthy to consider the revolutions made: namely, in what manner the mass was disturbed by the contact of that earthly fire. In the very same way, it is written that the water of the abyss in the first generation or creation was disturbed and terrified because of the lucid presence of that illuminating fire which lives for all eternity (*Psalm 77:17*). And the same prophet relates (*Psalm 18:12*) that the clouds and dark waters fled from the splendor of His presence. So also this dark and putrefied cloud leaped from its abyss away from the sight and contact of this lower light or fire, and flew into the heights, and again tended downward; and withdrawing itself for a long time in hesitation at the upper part of its vessel, it flew about like a thick mist, until by the virtue of condensing cold it is coagulated (just as in the middle region of the air we see vapors frozen into dense clouds by the force of cold) into denser water, which because of its weight and by natural impulse was forced to fall back toward the earth, from which it had ascended by violent motion. By this progress, therefore, through coagulation, it is seen...

# On the Exact Anatomy of Bread or Wheat.

Although the thicker and thinner waters of the sublunary region <note>The "sublunary region" refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, which according to ancient science were subject to change, unlike the perfect heavens.</note> were produced in the universal structure of the macrocosm—namely, from an infinite moist vapor or smoking and misty cloud reduced into a watery substance—this substance, by the force of the cold quality hidden in the dark matter of every thing, was more tightly constrained and condensed in this sphere of the greater world than in that [the vaporous state]. Therefore, it is heavier and more exposed to sight in one place than in another: by which distinction *the waters are said by Moses to be separated from the waters, and the dry land from both.* And so, I have set forth to you, revealed through this common dissection or anatomy of ours, the full substance of this first mystical vision of mine, which first presented itself to my eyes.

This vapor rises and splits into two distinct paths, each leading to a large, stylized circular cloud or globe. ### CHAPTER III.
#### On the second appearance, exhibited by the Water itself.

<margin><unclear>Genesis 1.</unclear></margin>
Just as we observe a thick mist gather on the peaks and ridges of the Alpine mountains—while the solar rays nevertheless shine all around in their most excellent glory—which, suddenly converted into a dense cloud by thickening, finally vanishes and drips drop by drop, dissolved into rain that fills the surrounding wells and pools: so also it happened in this work of ours. For in the second appearance, the dark mist or misty vapor, gradually vanishing from the sight of the eyes, was converted into downward-dripping drops, representing that golden rain which the Poets fable to have rained into Danaë's tower <note>In Greek mythology, Zeus visited Danaë as a shower of gold; here, the author uses it to describe the appearance of golden-colored chemical distillates.</note>. Thus, I observed a sea, as if it were a small abyss of water, succeed that dark mist; it was everywhere splendid, animated and decorated by the tincture of spiritual light. And from that moment, I immediately recalled to mind how it is related by Moses that *the Spirit of God <note>original: "Spiritus Elohim"</note>, in the first creation of the world, was carried over the waters*, liberally imparting to them from his fiery act or virtue. 
<margin>Augustine on Genesis.</margin>
Regarding this passage, Saint Augustine remarks in his commentaries on Genesis: *The Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters, giving to them a fiery vigor;* 
<margin>Hermes Trismegistus in the Pimander.</margin>
And Hermes Trismegistus says: *Moreover, the Holy splendor flourished, which led the elements beneath the sandy and moist nature.* In exactly the same way, I discovered that the universal water of this experiment of mine contained within itself the image or traces of that same light which was infused into it by the vivifying spirit in the threefold creation—inasmuch as it received its essence from it. Thus, with due contemplation leading the way, I clearly speculated that this lesser world of water <note>The liquid in the flask.</note> encompassed within itself all those things which the Water of the universal greater world contained at that very time when the Spirit of the Lord was carried over them: namely, the universal spirit of light or splendor, which was the soul of the world, or a certain universal spiritual and volatile Air containing within itself the chaos of the five particular elements—namely, Ether, Fire, Air, Water, and Earth—concerning which [I will speak] later.

we shall speak of this later in its proper place. I say, therefore, that in this mass of the watery element I observed a thing worthy of note: namely, that after I had separated its airy tincture and spirit from it by the common way of Alchemy <note>original: "Alchimiæ"</note>, it nevertheless strove daily to attract to itself more and more of a new tincture. This occurred by the power of that remaining vegetable and multiplying spirit which could not be separated. Furthermore, the abundance of the watery element springing forth from so small a subject showed me the reason why bread or wheat in its own nature—if the proper preparation and correction has not first been made through both fermentation

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of an alchemical glass vessel, specifically a cucurbit or flask with a rounded body and a long, narrow tapering neck, placed on the left side of the page with the following text wrapping around it to the right.</image-desc>

and cooking, by which this superfluous moisture is consumed and worn away—is so adverse and harmful to the human body, producing many infirmities in it through putrefaction. On the contrary, I am certain that this is that very excrement or moist superfluity in bread, swallowed along with the nourishment, which nature purges from the blood mass through the kidneys into the bladder. This salty spirit, which can only be separated with difficulty due to its volatile disposition, is the reason why human urine is salty and infected with such sharpness. This, then, is that very salt which is extracted by Alchemists from the multitude of urine, which they call salt ammoniac <note>original: "salem ammoniacum"; likely ammonium chloride, prized by alchemists for its volatility</note>. And so, I shall lightly pass over this second appearance of this subject concerning the universal water, so that on swifter wings of dispatch we may approach the anatomy of its more central parts—namely, their formal qualities, figures, and occult virtues, by means of which it was preserved from corruption.

### CHAPTER IV.

->*The third vision was the spirit which was covered by and mixed among the waters. The method of separating the airy part from the foul watery part: How this airy liquor differs from common water. Its use and properties in both the vegetable and animal nature. Furthermore, many experimental conclusions are revealed in this place, by which the faculties of this spirit are disclosed.*<-

But since I discovered a twofold nature in this watery abyss, one of which seemed to act, while the other sustained it as a passive subject in just proportion, a vehement desire immediately seized me to investigate that disposition. Thus, I attempted by a subtle operation to distinguish it from its thick matter which receives its actions, so that I might subject its naked and open nature (if it were possible) to my eyes. To accomplish this, I changed my agent—that is, the heat serving the aforesaid operation—from the boiling heat of a scorched summer to the temperate disposition of a misty spring. I was forced to divide this degree of heat, or "governance of fire" <note>term: "regimen ignis" - the controlled application of heat in alchemical work</note>, into three natures. The first was hot in the first degree and less moist, and because of this, the coldest of the three; I adapted and appropriated this to the first entry of springtime, which refers to the month of March, namely after the Sun has entered Aries <note>The first sign of the Zodiac, marking the spring equinox</note>. The second degree of this spring fire was hotter and most moist, proportioned to the entry of the Sun into Taurus, producing those April showers by whose power plants yearn to put forth their shoots and leaves, and the crops are accustomed to germinate. The last was the hottest and more moist, which can be conveniently referred to the entry of the Sun into Gemini; by their most delightful temperament, the most beautiful and regular state or circuit of the year is established—namely, that lovely time of May, when the meadows, distinguished by sweet-smelling and variegated flowers, laugh on every side. Thus I adapted the degrees of my fire to perform this act of separation, so that by the first heat I might separate the thinner water from the thicker mass, in which the hidden spirit (though previously indicated only by its effects) now appeared in its visible substance. By the second, I segregated the pure vegetative spirit from the thicker residues of the water. And finally, by the third of my spring degrees, I exhibited the spirit in various forms and at last in its own proper disposition.

# On the Exact Anatomy of Bread or Wheat.

<image-desc>An alchemical or chemical distillation apparatus. At the base is a large, rounded glass vessel (cucurbit) filled with a wavy-textured liquid. When, therefore, in my first action I had separated the thinner water from the spirit (which was still held back by the viscous ligaments of the fundamental or drossy mass), I perceived that the entire residue had taken on the form of a honey-like and thick liquor, marked by rays on all sides, and distinguished and suffused with a bright tincture like gold. After I had considered this sufficiently, I extracted the purer spirit from the drossy substance by the power of my second heat or agent; however, it appeared everywhere defiled with spots of earthy parts, which strove to ascend with it into the head of the <term>alembic</term> <note>The top part of a still used for distilling liquids</note>. For this reason, I adapted this still-impure spirit to the lowest degree of my heat, by the power of which (a thing wonderful to relate to the ignorant) a spirit—entirely pure, white, and crystalline, composed (as far as I could discern) of pure volatile salt—ascended into the head of a certain crystalline vessel and fell back into its receiver. 

And this liquor (although by its clarity and liquidity it seems to be the purest water, yet by its body, fluidity, and the quality of its substance, it seems to be of a nature far more excellent than common water) was to the sight liquidly flowing, penetrating, and agile in action. By well-known experience, it clearly appears to be that other <term>Psyche</term> <note>Soul or animating principle</note> of that celestial Desire, and the active principle of all things, seeking that beautiful heat and the golden tincture of the Sun as ardently as a woman seeks union with a man. And I know for certain that this is that hidden "patient" <note>The passive substance that receives an active influence</note> in the world which receives the secret influences of celestial action, and not that common water, which is rather the helper and cause of putrefaction, or the patient of the choleric fire of the elements, by which all lower things are reduced to corruption. 

This is that hidden vegetable balsam in every living creature, whether plant or animal, which causes growth in plants by extracting its like from the air or the water that falls from heaven to moisten the plant. Yet, it is not the entire substance of that rainwater that leads to growth, but a certain insensible part of it, which is drawn out from that rainwater by a true and natural <term>Alchemy</term>, leaving what remains in the grain as superfluous, of which I spoke a little before. In this way, I say, the plant multiplies itself in its material substance, which, continually drawing and deriving its form from the golden palace of heaven, abundantly distributes the power of multiplication to all things. When this matter has attracted a form worthy of itself, a <term>Hermaphrodite</term> <note>A being possessing both male and female qualities; in alchemy, a perfectly balanced substance</note> is created—that is, most fertile in both sexes, namely male and female ruling under one vegetable form. Nevertheless, it will produce offspring of its own kind no less than a man will procreate offspring, provided it is enclosed in the matrix of the earth (the general mother of all vegetables), just as a man must first immerse his seed in a woman's womb. This is that hidden water which follows the animal with such love, which generates blood and increases seed in the living creature, and consequently is the sole support or pillar of the natural faculty in both man and beast. But because all these things may seem impossible to the incredulous and the ignorant, I shall proceed to faithfully cite in this place those experiments which came to my sight in this work, even unexpectedly, so that you may give credit with more certain demonstration to those things reported by us.

### The first experiment by which it is proved that this spirit participates in the nature of the universal air.

After I had manifested the crude spirit to my eyes (prepared, as I said before, by the "vernal fire" of the second degree), I set about purifying it by the moderation of the first heat. By means of this work, I observed the spirit ascending in the head of the Alembic coagulating into small pieces of a whitish substance, some of which were like snow, while others were turned again into tiny particles like hail; the residue, however, which felt the external cold the least, distilled downward into the Receiver in liquid form. From this, one can see that snow or hail is nothing other than air in the middle region of the air, coagulated by the power or force of freezing cold. Therefore, this operation by artificial heat, just like the air of the world by natural heat, demonstrates that this spirit draws its origin from the universal spirit of the air. Conversely, I gathered from this frozen snow or hail that although the external and manifest appearance of the aerial spirit is translucent and white, its internal and hidden nature is fiery and shining like gold; for this white substance, even when touched or treated with a tiny amount of heat, immediately [turns] into

...a golden liquid, pleasant to the sight, and not at all unlike "potable gold" <note>original: *auro potabili*; a legendary alchemical medicine consisting of gold dissolved in a liquid state</note>, it melts quite readily. This, therefore, reveals to us the mind of the philosophers through a somewhat raw example, when they say: *Its manifest part is white and watery, but its hidden part is red and fiery; and again when they say: Make the hidden manifest, and the manifest hidden.*

->[Image: A glass distillation apparatus (alembic) resting on a stand, with liquid dripping from its long neck into a collection jar.]<-

The reason why common snow or hail of the "greater world" <note>The Macrocosm or the universe at large</note> does not obtain this tincture or hidden essence in a manifest state after its dissolution is the crude abundance of water within them. The presence of this water infects and contaminates the nature of the congealed spirit; therefore, because the water predominates after dissolution, it appears to be nothing other than clear water. Nevertheless, just as seeds or grains draw out this invisible and spiritual essence or "tincture" from raindrops after a natural putrefaction <note>The process of breaking down or "rotting" in alchemy, necessary for new life to emerge</note> in the earth, so too does this essence lie hidden in the secret workshops of the raindrops to aid in both its growth and multiplication. This spiritual moisture, therefore, is nothing other than air, and for this reason, it is nourished by its own kind.

### *The second experiment, by which it is proved that the golden spirit is enclosed secretly within the watery element.*

To prove that air is contained in every particle of water, no argument can be produced more pregnant and evident than this visual demonstration, by which we clearly perceive how this airy spirit is within every part of the universal water, just as the soul is said to move in every member of the body. For this spirit in the water is truly the "radical moisture" <note>The fundamental life-sustaining fluid of a being</note> of the world, or that occult and latent spirit which receives that life-giving light from the Spirit of God <note>original: *spiritus Elohim*</note> which moved over the universal waters (from which both heaven and earth were made). By means of this spirit, all things live, move, and receive their life-giving essence, as will be declared more clearly below. I have found it to be a matter of immense difficulty to separate water from its spirit, as the water is not at all prone to lose or leave behind its vegetable soul; indeed, it is quite difficult. However, we have learned from another experiment what this spirit is that is diffused everywhere through the waters, besides the demonstration in this our subject, which also confirms our assertion: for while I was practicing swimming (during my stay in the city of Nîmes <note>original: *Nemosiensi*</note>), I dove to the bottom of the river and struck two flints together with a strong collision. From this, a terrible crash was produced because of the air enclosed in the water. But since the medium or means of the sense of hearing is air alone, according to the doctrine of the philosophers, it follows from what is granted that air is contained abundantly in water, and it is proved by that experiment.

### *The third experiment teaches that this airy spirit abundantly incites growth.*

Now we shall bring forward the reason by which it will be proved that this spirit is the sole and unique cause of growth <note>original: *vegetationis*</note> in every seed or plant. Generally, we observe in the first place that celestial rains (which embrace much of this airy spirit within themselves), when poured out in due time upon the dry earth, are the chief cause of the germination of seeds and plants. But I shall proceed to an experiment which, although it may perhaps seem impossible to the incredulous, I shall not fear to bring forward at least on my own faith, because I know it to be so and because I have beheld it with these very eyes. One day my operator, a Frenchman by nationality, called me suddenly into the laboratory or workshop <note>original: *ergasterium*</note>. There he showed me a thin and simple iron plate which well-covered a clay pot, into which he had, by chance or fortune, placed part of those dregs from which this spirit had been extracted a second time. The time during which it stood covered by that iron plate was, if I am not mistaken, about five weeks—the very time when wheat committed to the earth and putrefied within it is accustomed to emerge again and sprout. At this time, I say, the vegetable power of the covered matter was observed to be so great (a thing I would not have easily believed myself before) that for lack of a vegetable or animal substance, which would be natural to it elsewhere, it even worked upon the mineral body itself, or the iron plate. For this spirit, ascending more penetratingly upward from the pot in which it was enclosed, perforated its iron lid; and by the effect implanted in it by nature, it worked so powerfully that it caused ten thousand little spikes or stalks, like saffron or like grain emerging from the earth, to rise up, grow, and sprout from the iron. All of these had grown to the length of a small needle...

->[Image: A flat rectangular plate with hundreds of tiny, thin spikes growing vertically from its surface, resembling metallic grass.]<-

...and this sight truly seized us both with no small wonder. It most clearly persuaded us that this is the unique and very same vegetative part of the plant. I conclude, therefore, with this maxim of the philosophers: *That which makes a thing such, is itself more such.* This, moreover, is without doubt the substance from which animal blood is generated, as I have proposed to demonstrate more clearly in the following experiment. The present conclusion demonstrates to the eye, as it were, the manner through which plants and herbs grow and germinate from the earth, since this spirit is the vehicle of that vital spark which, after the corruption of the grain in the earth, strives with all diligence to ascend and return to that ethereal palace from whence it takes its origin.
