# On the Exact Anatomy of Bread or Wheat.

### The fourth experiment reveals to us the true method of growth and multiplication for both plants and animals.

Therefore, having taken this volatile spirit—which was white, and as transparent and clear as crystal—and having finally exposed it to the rays of the sun, I perceived such a great mutual sympathy between them that this material spirit, by a certain magnetic power of attraction, drew out for itself a certain formal tincture <note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is a spiritual principle or soul-essence capable of transforming and coloring matter.</note> from that shining orb. I observed that within the space of a few hours, the spirit was transmuted from its crystalline whiteness into a ruby red; indeed, I noticed that the longer it was exposed to the solar gaze, the more excellent its tincture became. From this experiment, I gathered the perfect reason for multiplication in both the vegetable and animal kingdoms. For just as a woman (to whom we may not inaptly compare this spirit) cannot conceive or multiply without the help or coupling of a man (to whom this formal light has a relation), so neither can this spirit have any increase or multiplication unless the act of light is joined with it. For a passive nature cannot suffer <note>In the sense of "undergo change" or "be acted upon."</note> within itself, and therefore it awaits the impressions of some natural agent, previously well-prepared and refined by Nature for this purpose. The subsequent natural action and passion <note>The interaction between the active (male/light) and passive (female/matter) principles.</note> of these two are the cause of increase and multiplication in the same species which they inhabit, and this occurs in each of the three kingdoms of Nature, without which there would be neither generation nor multiplication in them.

Thus, this spirit, once putrefaction has occurred in the earth and it is restored to its freedom, deserts that dark tabernacle in which it dwells and wanders more freely toward that celestial fire, by whose power it is multiplied, quickened, and effectively moved. For this is that unique active fire which moves toward generation through multiplication; and this is that passive spirit or medium through which the life-giving light moves in a composition. By means of this spirit—as if by the most precious juice and substance of all sublunary things—the species is best nourished. And because a tiny portion of the formal light of that spirit is sufficient to inform <note>To give "form" or life-blueprint to the grain.</note> the multiplication of a grain, it follows that this spirit sucks in matter for itself and its kind, and that the matter, by a certain natural appetite, attracts the portion of light required for its formation. And this is the cause of multiplication, following its liberation through putrefaction in the earth, as we are taught by experience every year.

Furthermore, even in animals, as they are introduced into the body—both through nourishment and through inspiration (namely, the attraction of this kind of spirit by the lungs)—they grow and multiply in each of their members and expand in dimension, just as their spermatic substance is increased and rendered fit and capable for generation. It must be noted, however, that for the multiplication of an animal, a larger portion of this ethereal or celestial spirit and fiery form is required than for that of a vegetable creature. How this spirit attracts its like to itself, we are taught by the example of Salt of Tartar <note>Potassium carbonate, known for its ability to absorb moisture from the air (deliquescence).</note>, which allures the hidden volatile spirit in the air to itself by a certain magnetic vigor, until, on account of the attracted aerial substance, it becomes so raw and liquid that it is accustomed to flow in the form of a liquor like common water.

->[Image: The sun shines its rays upon a seed or egg held within a tripod, symbolizing the celestial light "informing" the material spirit.]<-

### The fifth experiment proves that this spirit is in the universal air, because it participates in water, fire, and the quintessence.

I discovered that this spirit is also diffused through the entire space of the world and fills every part of the world, insofar as I perceived it to agree and mix with the element of water by a natural instinct, no differently than form is accustomed to embrace matter. So also it had no less familiarity with fire, since it easily embraced it on the other side; indeed, I found this formal essence of the air to be nothing other than a sort of coarser and more material portion of the quintessence <note>The "fifth essence" or ether, the purest element above the four earthly ones.</note>, supplying the place of a bond for the discordant elements in the sublunary region. For by diligent speculation, I observed that this spirit was received into a close and inviolable familiarity by the quintessence, and relates to it in the same way that water relates to air, as we shall explain in its proper place.

# Section I. Portion III. Part I. Book II.

### *The sixth experiment, proving that all things are fashioned and composed of atoms, as certain Philosophers have judged.*

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration showing a scientific or alchemical experiment. It depicts a vessel or lamp with a lit wick at the base, providing heat to a glass bulb (cucurbit) above it. In the first experiment, it was observed that this universal spirit, through the process of thinning <note>original: "subtiliando"</note>—and indeed by the slightest contact with applied heat—was converted and resolved into a myriad of sensible atoms flying everywhere through the glass. This event immediately brought to my mind and memory the dogma and opinion of the ancient Epicurean philosophers, who did not hesitate to affirm that all things are formed and made from Atoms; indeed, I even discovered that the body of the *quintessence* <note>The "fifth essence," a celestial or pure substance distinct from the four earthly elements.</note> itself is of exactly the same nature and condition.

### *The seventh experiment, by which it is proved that this spirit works by way of purification.*

Furthermore, necessity requires that I add to these aforementioned experiments a seventh and final one, by no means to be despised, which proves that the nature of this spirit is such that it purifies by a certain natural instinct. For when I had immersed one of the natural grains of wheat (as if it were a certain *Philosophical egg* <note>A sealed glass vessel used in alchemy, shaped like an egg, symbolizing the containment of life or transformation.</note>) into this purified spirit, bathing it as if in its own blood, I perceived that within the space of a few days its dark nature was so purged—by the mediation of the nature of that purified and clarifying spirit—that from an opaque body it became transparent and pellucid, as if it had been fashioned out of glass. I could relate and express many more observations of no small importance drawn from this spirit in this place, but lest I perhaps detain you in discussing a useless matter (as some, I know, wish to object), I shall proceed directly in this my *Anatomy*. I say, therefore, that the spirit mixed with water covered a certain opaque and undigested chaos on all sides, just as the ocean of the clear and translucent heavens or the universal spirit (which is nothing other than pure and subtle water) surrounded the earth, which was an opaque, thick, and deformed mass, or like the *dead head* <note>original: "caput mortuum"; a term for the useless residue left after distillation.</note> of the universal waters of the greater world. Wherefore, we have proposed to address this very subject in the following chapter.

# CHAPTER V.
### *What the author understands by "Chaos," from which he extracted the five elements.*

It is not that universal or infinite *Hyle* <note>Greek: "matter"; the primordial, formless substance of the universe.</note> of Plato or Aristotle that I strive to demonstrate in this place and expose to your sight (O perspicacious and censorious eyes of this age), seeing as it can neither be discerned by human senses nor comprehended by Geometric calculations or figures. For even the wisest philosophers of all ages, even with the highest sharpness of their mind or genius, could never attain or reach a perfect and complete knowledge of it. Whence those who approached closer to the mark of truth described it only in a symbolic sense and through the path of comparison: sometimes comparing it to a forest <note>original: "sylua"; a play on the Greek "hyle" which also means wood or forest.</note> whose wood is fit for shaping or building any image; sometimes they adapted it to wax, which is ready to receive any impression of a seal. Others, however, liken it to a monstrous image appearing in a dream, which a man waking from sleep finds to be either vain or nothing. But St. Augustine said that it behaves in the manner of silence, which in respect to speech is no less a "thing" than a shadow. This, I say, is not the principal mark at which my curiosity aims, knowing that it is a thing utterly impossible to grasp, since it is deformed—indeed, truly destitute of all form or essence—and nothing other than empty darkness.

Nor, indeed, is this that rude and undigested chaos dedicated to the memory of eternity by the ancient philosophers, and so celebrated in the monuments of poets, poems, and mystical meteors, which is so universal. For it is not credible that a mountain or a mass so huge could be transmuted or converted into a hillock as tiny as that about which I have decided to speak. Rather, the wings of my labor and effort show themselves more humble and lowered, lest by plucking things too high and exalted like Icarus, the feathers of my ambition be scorched by the heat of the reproach and censure of the sharpest men, or the wax to which they are fixed melt, and so at last I fall headlong into the turbulent lake of public ignominy—namely, by professing that I will reveal that of which I am perhaps ignorant, or if well-versed in it, am by no means prepared or disposed to reveal to the world.

My "Chaos," therefore, is only an external and visible figure, and light as a shadow, or the smallest atom of that universal one, which in truth appears to be (as I call it) a positive corruption or privation of the body, just as that great chaos of the world manifested itself immediately after the first creation. I would not have you, therefore, expect wonders and miracles from me, for I do not profess such things. But this alone I promise you: that in this my experimental conclusion I will imitate nature as far as I am able, and I will seek out a "small chaos" in this creature in as subtle a manner as I can, which will be an image of that greater world—just as the *microcosm* (or man) is the effigy and exemplar of the greater, called the *macrocosm*. I shall therefore relate to you here in a few words how I manifested this particular chaos to my eyes, so that afterwards, by the "anatomizing" of the same, you may understand how the individual elements in the greater world were produced from the dark and obscure chaos: for in this kind of mirror or looking-glass <note>original: "catoptro"</note> [you may see] the true nature, quality, form, and consistency of each element in its own sphere,

# CHAPTER VI.

## *Concerning the true universal Chaos of the greater world, its difference from Hyle <note>Hyle: A Greek term for "prime matter" or raw substance without form.</note>, as well as the extraction of the five elements of the world from it, and the power of the fire or heat of the universal light in the great furnace of Nature: Finally, concerning the allusion and comparison of that to the author's small chaos, and the image of the double water.*

I have explained myself directly enough (as I believe) and sufficiently in my history of the macrocosm <note>The "Macrocosm" refers to the universe as a whole, as opposed to the "Microcosm" or man.</note>, namely that the true chaos was a triple dark mass—that is, that deformed and potential existence which deprived the third and highest heaven or the Empyrean region of its bright form, and that which, before the existence of the second, middle, and starry region of the world, hid it from every sight, form, or habit. Both of these deformed darknesses, on the second day, by a conglomerated and involved motion through the power of the light appearing in both these heavens, were reverberated by a repercussion into the lower or elemental region of the world. This region was even then rude, dark, and undigested, and outwardly appeared to the sight to be mere nothingness, because the powers of the four contrary and fighting elements lay hidden under the dark and obscure cloak of privative darkness. In exactly this same state the sublunary region remained on the second day of creation: namely, without light, without form, without manifest act, or any existence.

And yet it differed greatly from *Hyle* <note>original: "hyla"</note>, in which no internal light, action, passion, or element was found, insofar as it remained absolutely annihilated in its nature before God shone out of the darkness or revealed himself in the structure of the world; so that the supposed capacity or circuit of the world was called *Hyle* or the Abyss, before the Spirit of the Lord, by its splendor, caused the waters to appear in the vast cavity of the world.

But as I said in my Macrocosmic history, the deformed waters, or denser spirits lurking in the deformity of darkness, being greedy and longing for formal light in that repercussion made by the darted rays of light, embraced some of those rays which had immersed themselves more deeply into their substance. They held them fast, entangled in their natural viscosity and slime; and for this reason the nature of potential *Hyle* was converted into *Chaos*, which embraces an active force within itself. Indeed, it contains all elements in itself and is only potential from the outside, being entirely opaque and formless. Therefore (I say) this chaos has fire in itself, since the spirits lurking in darkness are informed by the light of the retained rays; and it also contains air and water, because the spirit retained and enclosed is thick or thin according as it participates either copiously or sparingly in the gifts or portions of the rays or sparks of light. Finally, Earth is the manifest part of this chaos, as it is the more opaque and thicker member of the universal chaos.

From this, therefore, it appears that the universal chaos was that triple mass of darkness: namely, the obscure deformity preceding the first day, and also that immediately preceding the second day, both of which were mixed together by the mediating lucid act of these days, and were thrust down further toward the center of the machine for the works of the third day to be brought forth. Thus the chaos of the greater world was completed, and this immediately before the third day, from whose belly leaped forth the substance of the entire lowest region of the world, which is divided among the four elements in order of their dignity and eminence.

From this (I say) rude and undigested chaos, the elements—discordant among themselves—were extracted, and this by the power of the universal light, which surrounded it on all sides on the third day in the reverberatory furnace of the greater world. Then the darkness sank down slowly and gradually toward the center, and the thin elements extracted from the mass filled the entire concavity, lest any vacuum or emptiness be left in it. And so every portion of the spirit now enclosed, according to the greater or lesser wealth of light reigning in it, was either exalted above its companions or depressed, and was confirmed in the seat and sphere suitable to it by the bonds of the *quintessence* <note>The "fifth element" or purest essence that binds the other four.</note>. In this way (I say) the elements were formed from the universal chaos, and according to this same reasoning they still behave: Earth is seen to occupy the lowest place, like a drossy base in the fabric or the almost dead head of all the rest; and yet, notwithstanding this, it exists as the receptacle and mother of Minerals, Vegetables, and Animals.

In a plainly similar way, we find in this small subject of ours <note>Referring to the author's laboratory sample of wheat/bread.</note> that the universal water with its spirit, illuminated by the tincture of light, represents the works of the first and second day; for just as in the creation of the first day the first heaven imparted life and essence to the second heaven,

In the same way, a certain spiritual tincture (most rightly compared to the fiery heaven or the **Empyrean** <note>The highest heaven in ancient cosmology, believed to be composed of pure fire or light.</note>) bestowed life and action upon the denser water. Just as these two heavens covered the Chaos with immense depth before the creation of the third day—filling the concavity of the lower heavens—so too the water, mixed with the spirit of the tincture, moved like a deep abyss above my dark chaos, covering and submerging it on all sides, no differently than the heaven covers the earth. Having thus separated the twofold dark mass, I found it to be as dark as the blackest pitch and as tenacious as birdlime, namely on account of the deformed spirits and viscous slipperiness contained within it. I therefore took that double water and applied a very slow fire, observing with the greatest care I could manage all the artificial degrees of fire; yet, I call God as my witness, it was only after a long period of time that I was able to distinguish and separate them from one another. For this reason, I erred many times regarding this work and applied my labor in vain. Therefore, I diligently set myself to imitate that circular light of Nature, and I administered strength to my fire as reason persuaded me was necessary. First, I extracted a portion of the thicker water, which I compare with the aqueous element of the sublunary sphere; afterwards, I drew out a portion of the airy spirit. I omit a specific mention of this here, because I have said enough words about it in the preceding pages, so that I may discuss more fully the element of fire, or the fourth element, and then afterwards the **Ether**, which is the **quintessence** <note>The "fifth essence" or purest element, distinct from earth, air, fire, and water.</note>, or the fifth element, which is still drawn away by a thick garment. Finally, I shall bring an end to this book with a description and consideration of the earth, comparing it in this experiment of mine with that of the greater world <note>The Macrocosm.</note>. Because this will seem very difficult and (as I divine) obscure to those who are not well-versed in my volume on the Macrocosm, I refer them entirely to the first book of that work on this matter, where they will find all these things explained plainly and lucidly.

# CHAPTER VII.

### *In which the appearance of the airy moisture of the succeeding fiery Element is explained, as well as the inclination of its nature toward the corruption and putrefaction of all things.*

AFTER the spirit of the subtle Air succeeded the element of water, immediately fire in the form of a fiery liquor, or a thick and reddish oil, showed itself to the sight. This nature was thoroughly distant from water and of a different form than air, also breathing out a foul stench and a heavy odor. Once this was purified by circulation or **rectification** <note>The process of refining a substance through repeated distillation.</note>, it took on a saffron or red color not unlike the flame of a kitchen fire; however, even when cleansed, it refused to leave behind or lose its heavy odor. Therefore, with due contemplation leading the way, I noticed that this is the sole active element in the sublunary sphere, by whose force those hostile alterations of corruption are produced in the world, and by whose violence creatures are driven to rot. For this element dominates in producing putrefaction in the body, and under its dominion the body itself rots most greatly; in the act of putrefaction, a most foul stench arises, so that the sense of smell is severely offended by the vaporous exhalations of this element from the rotting body. Furthermore, just as we find the airy spirit (which I mentioned above) to be feminine, well-adapted, and passive for producing generation—whose agent or husband is the celestial fire, or that light of the quintessence, disposing the air as a passive subject for this kind of alteration in the course of nature—so the element of water is a passive subject serving chiefly for mortification or corruption. Being liable to corruption, its agent is the fetid elemental fire, urging and promoting the composite body toward a privative progress of alteration, which motion is contrary to the progress of nature. And although water seems to nourish, yet in truth it does not nourish by itself, but only that unique spirit lurking within it, which alone is retained by Nature for nutrition in the body; the useless superfluity of the water is emitted through urine. But where water in its own nature exults or overflows in a composite body beyond the laws of its natural temperament, there, because of its exuberance, dull and **dropsical** <note>Related to edema or the abnormal accumulation of fluid.</note> diseases are usually procreated. This happens especially when its agent, the element of fire, holds the smallest place in the alteration; for from such possession of unnatural water follow faintings or swoons, **Lethargy, Apoplexy, Catocha, Catalepsy** <note>Various historical terms for states of unconsciousness, rigidity, or seizures.</note>, stupors, and other things of that kind. But where the agent is of equal power with the patient <note>The "patient" here refers to the passive element being acted upon.</note>, then false fevers, both phlegmatic and choleric, as well as composite **Apostemes** <note>Abscesses or swellings.</note> and such infirmities predominate in parts of the body, such as **Pleurisy** and all kinds of **Phlegmons** <note>Inflammatory tumors or boils.</note>. But if fire has dominion over the water, then all infirmities derived from false or burnt phlegm are usually procreated. Yet if the agent be more simple and inhabits a thin vapor of an aqueous nature, then it excites those fevers called **Ephemeral** or **Diaries** <note>Fevers lasting only a day.</note>. Where fire is destitute of its aqueous fuel, so that it is forced to act upon the thicker airy spirit, there it procreates burning fevers arising from the corruption of the blood called **synochus**. And for that reason, it inflames the entire mass of the body's humors. Truly, where the corrupted humor of water abounds with a thicker airy spirit, there a contagious putrefaction arises, which is wont to procreate smallpox and plagues; but where the corrupting water is thin and mixed with a similar airy spirit, there pestilential fevers are produced with spots which are called **Petechiae** by the Italians. Finally, all diseases, whether procreated from rawness or burning, are generated from a greater or lesser proportion of these two elements, the authors of corruption; so much so that the airy spirit itself is frequently disturbed. And thus these two elements never work by themselves and by their own nature except toward destruction; whereas, conversely, the Solar virtue or celestial fire lurking in the airy spirit acts naturally toward health and life. The Earth, truly, is the receptacle of all these.

# On the Exact Anatomy of Bread or Wheat.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of two chemical distillation vessels connected by a tube. The vessel on the left is a bulbous retort with a long neck, resting on a flat-topped base. A curved tube connects its opening to the top of a second, pear-shaped vessel on the right.</image-desc>

### An experiment demonstrating how the element of fire produces Melancholy and dark or Demonic diseases.

I have discovered an unexpected operation in this element; for although I purified it through many distillations and rectifications until it reached a most lucid splendor, it nevertheless possessed such an affinity with darkness that, in a short space of time, it contracted its old and former obscurity and blackness, quickly losing its clarity and the beauty of its shine. This matter brought to my memory the saying of a wise man named Artephius <note>Artephius was a legendary medieval alchemist, often cited in 17th-century hermetic texts.</note>, who in his book titled *The Key of Wisdom*, says: *Perhaps there are certain infirmities to which the Devil joins himself when a humor emerges from the temperament and disturbs health itself; and this happens most especially in infirmities arising from choler <note>Choler, or yellow bile, was one of the four bodily humors, associated with a hot and dry temperament.</note>, the cause of which is this: because the nature of choler itself is hot and dry like fire. Now, the body of the Devil is composed of two things, namely fire and air. And we have said (he says) in the preceding parts, that every subtle thing may enter into every gross thing. It is manifest, therefore, since fire is more subtle than air, that the visible part of the Devil's body is air, but his hidden part is fire; and this is the cause of his concealment from human sight, since the medium through which we see all things is air, which is joined to our eye. Since, therefore, the interior of the Devil is of the nature of fire, it is manifest that he is opposed and contrary to the nature of the soul itself, which is a nature of equality <note>The soul was often described as a "perfect balance" or "harmony" of qualities.</note>. When, therefore, some choleric sickness invades the body (since Choler is the Devil’s hidden part), it appears clearly that he joins himself most easily with Choler, and thus his dominion over the other humors is increased; indeed, that humor can predominate so much that the soul departs from the body and is utterly separated from it.* Thus he spoke.

For this reason (I say), the Devil is suited by natural instinct to insinuate and join himself into this element of fire. From this we can diligently observe that just as God, the King of Light, works through celestial fire toward life and preservation, so plainly on the contrary does this Prince of Darkness—who has his dominion in the sublunary elements—act through this corruptible fire toward death and destruction. Hence it is that this spirit of deprivation, wandering and roaming everywhere by the impulse of the darkness he has contracted (by which he has been vexed and agitated ever since his fall—that is, being compelled to hide the lucid rays of his first-born creation behind a dark veil as punishment for his ambition and disobedience), now shows himself ready to demonstrate through effects the affinity or consanguinity that exists between him and the choleric humor; from which even the good air suffers.

From this it happens that a man, by the force of this element predominating in him, becomes a "Lunatic" <note>In this context, meaning one whose mind is disturbed by planetary or elemental shifts.</note> and distracted from his senses; dark impressions blunt the most clear edge of his intellect and cloud the rays of his mind, while terrible and deceptive chimeras lead his imagination astray and make a mockery of it. Indeed, the Devil is accustomed to converse with many in this way in manifold forms, disturbing them with monstrous visions. From this also it arises that the life of a man laboring under a burning fever, or a disease arising from "gnawing melancholy," is infested either with delirium, or sleeplessness, or despair, or Lycanthropy <note>The delusion of being a wolf.</note>, or insanity; and for the most part by melancholic vapors procreated from the flatulent smoke emanating from this sulfurous element. This fiery smoke likewise strikes in "Hypochondriac passions," such as trepidations, anger, rage, solitude, insomnia, and a hatred of all human society and commerce.

What more serious thing can I add, when we find that by means of the assault of this element and its suffering Water, not only men, but the entire lower region of the universal worldly frame is affected by distress and sickness? For in the air, it is the cause of comets, fiery dragons, burning columns, fire-vomiting flames, and similar meteors <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including lightning and comets.</note>—specifically where the "agent" (fire) has greater dominion, but the "patient" (water/moisture) is not so abundant. But where its patient, namely water, is equally powerful and strong, there crashes, thunders, and lightnings weigh down the lower region. Yet if the patient is endowed with the highest power and overcomes the fiery faculty, then floods overwhelm the earth, and the middle region of the air grows dark with the veil of thick and gloomy clouds, from which infinite calamities arise. However (as the proverb has it, *There is no wind that brings no one an advantage*), sometimes a gloomy air presages abundance and fertility of the earth; and sometimes, led by experience, we observe that the vapors of a cloudy body are consumed and dried up by febrile heat, just as we notice that lightnings (which are the febrile effects of the air) dispel and absorb the morbid exhalations of the air. And this is as much as I have seen fit to declare to you concerning the nature and disposition of the element of fire.

# Section I. Portion III. Part I. Book II.

## C H A P T E R VIII.

### *The final appearance or vision, outlining the nature of the fifth Element, called the quintessence.*

Now at last we have climbed above the elementary heavens of the sublunary world <note>The region below the moon, subject to change and decay</note>, and we make our entry into that region which is distinguished by the Alchemists by the name of the **fifth essence** <note>original: *quintæ essentiæ*; the "quintessence" or purest part of a substance</note>, by philosophers as the **ether** or simplest matter, and by Poets as the sky, Olympus, or the Elysian fields. Here, however, I would like you to understand in passing that just as in the structure or composition of any thing we proceed from one to five—which is a round number and the true center of the ten—namely proceeding 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; so also in the destruction and resolution of a thing back to one, we must proceed from 5 to 4, and so backward all the way to unity. This region is therefore called the **fifth essence** by the Hermetic philosophers because it is distant from the earth by five steps. This is, I say, the reason: that the appearance of water closely follows that of earth, which air follows, and then fire follows air; and after fire, that golden moisture ascended, called the **fifth essence** because of its relation to the true fifth essence of the mystical philosophers. This is the final sign of this violent dissolution; for in this element is that true life, by means of which the remaining four elements act in the human body—that is, by a central virtue or internal moving principle, through which the entire compound subsists.

And just as we see that a man who is forced by compulsion to share something of his own with others usually offers first and before all else that which he himself values least and is of lesser price, thinking he will thus be set free; but perceiving that his first offering is by no means enough for the one compelling him, he is then forced to hand over from his treasury something a little more dear and precious to himself, which nevertheless he does not value as much as what seems to him of greater price in his chest; and so he proceeds step by step by bringing forth things of lesser prices, until he finally reaches the distribution of that of greatest value: namely, the dearest blood of his life. So also the matter stands in this dark **Chaos** or black **Corpse of the earth** <note>original: *Cadauere*; the "caput mortuum" or dead dregs left after distillation</note>; since the watery element (which portion is less useful for its preservation) does not suffice for the appetite of the false Alchemist, the earth offers him air as a more precious thing after water, and so it proceeds in bringing forth the richest dignity of its treasure, until the very **balsam of life** is withdrawn from it by fiery violence, and the mass itself—once raw and undigested—now remains as nothing but a **dead head** <term>caput mortuum: the useless residue remaining after distillation or sublimation</term> in the ignoble condition of damned earth, deprived of almost all grace.

It remains, therefore, that we finally approach the most precious gem of the vegetable chaos, or the solar and life-giving balsam in the wheat, which we have divided from its mass by the highest extremity of the fiery art. Indeed, the earth was so greedy and prone to hide this gem in its lap or center, and to deceitfully withhold it from the Alchemist, that it was a matter of greatest difficulty and labor to separate this from it—so much so, indeed, that if I had attempted to treat this chaos with greater harshness and violence to obtain its balsamic treasure, I would have extinguished and suffocated this spirit rather than conveniently separating it in its native color and property. Whence it happened that I was frustrated in a great part of my labor; and so I attempted a more expedited way and method to dig out and entice this golden treasure from its spongy hiding places. To accomplish this, I found it necessary to find a new kind of heat, which exerted its force from one part of the vessel, by means of which I drew out this ethereal moisture and reduced it to the highest purity of splendor, with various rectifications <note>The process of refining a liquid by repeated distillation</note> preceding it.

Then indeed, with eyes opened, I perceived a wonderful disposition to be in this balsam; for it became liquid from even the slightest heat, and red like blood, filling the entire vessel with atoms; and conversely, from the cold of the air, it immediately stiffened into a transparent and clear substance like a precious stone, partly of a bright crystalline color, and partly of a golden Hyacinth tint—that is, like crystalline glass, with sparks shimmering everywhere and planted as if with little bright stars. But here I strongly warn the reader to observe that I have not in this place brought to light the true and simple **fifth essence** or heaven of the true Philosophers in its purified and naked disposition, but only that which, because of its purity, seems to the common person to be distinguished from the 4 other visible elements, which we have therefore named the **fifth essence** insofar as it participates more in the nature of the fifth essence or ether than any of the other 4 elements cited above.

From this point, the resolution of these questions or objections occurred to me as I watched more attentively: namely, how the **soul** <note>original: *anima*</note> differs from the **spirit** <note>original: *spiritu*</note>, and how, notwithstanding this, both are sometimes—indeed usually—taken interchangeably for one and the same thing? And how the spirit is called the "vehicle of the soul" by the Platonists, as also what the "sphere of equality" is in which the **soul of the world** <note>original: *anima mundi*</note> reigns, of which they made such religious mention in their writings? Furthermore, what did the Platonists understand by the soul in the spirit, and by the spirit in the body? And consequently, what does **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: *Merc. Trism.*; the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic corpus is attributed</note> mean when he says, *Mind in reason, reason in soul, soul in spirit, and spirit in body?* What indeed is that thing in this world which attributes life to every creature and nourishes the same? And many more such doubts, by no means to be explained by the common crowd, from which we can easily extricate ourselves by this experiment of common Alchemy, if only we consider this substance of the heavens with due diligence and attention. To the first question, therefore, we say: the vital Soul is a splendid light emanating from God, which in a clear spirit...

# On the Exact Anatomy of Bread or Wheat.

Desire <note>original: *cupido*</note> is carried as if by a shining vehicle, by the rowing of whose wings it flies, and by whose presence it sometimes appears to the eyes. Under this form, golden-haired **Desire** was discovered lying in the embrace of the beautiful and radiant **Psyche**, as Apuleius fashioned in his enigmatic fable. In such a hermaphroditic subject, the clear spirit is the female or passive principle, while the light, with rays expanded everywhere within it, is the male or active principle. By the power and office of both these gathered into one, all things live. In this same way, we explain the second doubt: namely, where we affirm that a thin, clear, and transparent matter, similar to bright crystal, is the vehicle of the soul; for we say the soul is the splendid light, and the spirit is the radiant white. By these reasons, we can discern how the soul is said to be "all in all," and in any part of any thing. Likewise, the solution to the third question is drawn from the same demonstration, since this very soul in the spirit (which two are often joined together under the name of "soul" alone) is infused into the body.

Regarding the opinion of **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure associated with alchemy and hermetic philosophy.</note>, we shall explain it in the following chapter. As for the opinion of the Platonists—that there exists such a sphere called the "sphere of equality" or the "sphere of the soul"—this very object teaches us that it is that very orb in which the sun revolves. For the very matter which descends downward to give life to animals, vegetables, and minerals teaches us this by its composition; indeed, in it we observe so exact a proportion between spirit and light that light cannot, by any act or violence, hold dominion over the spirit. From this, it happens that the substance, as if by a certain power of **Medusa's** head, seems to be fixed and converted into a crystalline stone. Yet, on the other hand, the spirit does not so abound that it obscures the equal splendor of the light with its density, or shadows it with any darkness, or blunts the life-giving power in the light or the action of the celestial fire. For this reason, they are so equally proportioned to one another that neither can be hindered or oppressed by the other; on the contrary, one strengthens and animates the other in a perfect and absolute temperament. Thus, the spirit nourishes, sustains, and carries the light as if in a chariot, while the light (or its formal part) gives essence, life, and motion to the spiritual part, dispels the darkness of shadows from it, and promotes it first to the giving of life, and then to vegetation.

This, therefore, is the reason why that place from which this spirit flows is called the "sphere of equality" or "of the soul." This clear composition is nothing other than that central sun of every creature, whether animal, vegetable, or mineral, drawing its origin from that sun which inhabits the middle point of heaven and is continually revolved in the orb or sphere of equality. There, the formal light and the material spirit are weighed in the equal scales of nature, so that each in its kind completely pleases the desire of the other. Thus, their action extends perpetually toward life because of the lack of contrariety between them; for on account of the equal portion between them, they always act toward peace and never toward discord or contention, and for this reason, they are the authors of life and the enemies of death.

These two natures, reduced to such mutual reciprocation and friendship by means of a symphonic proportion, most aptly delineate and demonstrate the intersections made by the mutual meeting of two pyramids of the same dimensions. One of these pyramids shall be formal, the other material. By their contrary positions, I have attempted to delineate and uncover the disposition of the entire worldly nature in the physical history of my macrocosm. For the material pyramid (from which this bright spirit emanates) has its base or foundation in the lowest earth, being the hieroglyphic image of those waters which originally gushed and emanated from the darkness or the abyss, the principal part of which is the receptacle of this celestial light. The formal pyramid, however, has its base or foundation in the highest heaven, and its apex <note>original: *conum*</note> in the center of the earth, bearing the icon of that flame—

—or light which, in the first creation, descended from the circumference of the world downward toward the center. Through the material pyramid with its apex from the earth toward heaven, the water ascending from the earth toward the circumference of heaven is shown to be gradually thinner and thinner. Conversely, the light or fiery form descending from the circumference of heaven toward the earth is rendered weaker and thinner the more it declines from its source toward the center of the earth. This is no different than what we see in the geometric figure of a pyramid, which abounds more in weight, substance, and strength the further it proceeds from its apex toward its base.

A demonstration follows here of these two pyramids disposed in an opposite manner where they intersect each other. However, I have made more extensive mention of them in our booklet assigned to pyramids and annexed to the end of the technical history of our microcosm, to which I would most gladly refer you so that you may more exactly understand what is thought of pyramids there. Here, I would also wish the reader to be advised that although this "fifth essence" <term>Quintessence: The purest, fifth element in ancient philosophy, thought to compose the celestial bodies.</term> of ours is not that true one of the Philosophers in its purity, yet it stands to that one as the human soul stands to its spirit. Whence we say that since the spirit is the image of the soul, so also this fifth essence of ours is the image of that invisible and hidden one; and consequently, the latter is indicated by the former through this kind of external demonstration.

# Section I. Portion III. Part I. Book II.

Here **A** denotes the Earth, **b, c** the base of the material pyramid, and **m** its cone <note>the apex or point</note>. Indeed, **m** and **B** together represent the sun, the sole source of light and smoke <note>original: *fumus*, likely referring to the "fumes" or emanations of light</note>. **d, e** is the base of the formal pyramid, created by the emanation from the source **B**. The cone of said formal pyramid is **A**. The intersection made by these two, where the portion of one pyramid is equal to that of the other, is **f, g**; and therefore this orbit permeating the heavens is distinguished by the name **Sphere of Equality**. From this kind of matter and form, the celestial sun was procreated, and for this very reason, it is called the **Sphere of the Soul of the World** by the Platonists. Thus, it is clearly declared from the drawing of the pyramids placed here how each pyramid claims dominance for itself in every heaven. For example, in **K. L.**, the proportion of the formal pyramid is triple to one part of the material pyramid, and therefore it is called the **Empyrean Heaven**, or the **Fiery Heaven**, because the splendor of fire dominates there absolutely. Conversely, in the space **o. n.**, we likewise find three parts of the material pyramid to one of the formal pyramid, because it is called the **Elementary Heaven**, inasmuch as matter has its dominion there. But the middle heaven, through which the Sphere of Equality passes—inasmuch as the parts of the said pyramids of light and spirit are found distributed equally—is called **Ether**, as if it were *Aeth-aer*, that is, **Fiery Air** <note>A folk etymology: *Aether* from the Greek *aithein* (to burn) and *aer* (air)</note>, imparting by this reasoning an equal naming of the nature of both pyramids, which dominate in equal parts within it.

But if I wished to apply my mind and study to exploring the adaptation of these two pyramids, I call God to witness that I could fill an entire volume with the thread of this narration and the explanation of the mysteries contained in this subject of ours; but because I have already explained those things more diffusely in my twofold *History of Both Worlds* <note>Referring to Fludd's *Utriusque Cosmi Historia*</note>, I thought it sufficient to have set forth for you in this place the true and natural cause drawn from reason: namely, that by which I was led to discover the two pyramids—that equal proportion of spirit and light which concurs in the composition of my **Fifth Essence** <term>Quintessence: the purest, fifth element beyond earth, water, air, and fire</term> named a little earlier in this chapter. Now, however, we shall proceed to the final doubt, namely: **What is that thing in the world which imparts life first, and then, through its continuous succession, preserves life in each of these three kingdoms of nature—namely, the animal, vegetable, and mineral?** To which I respond: it is that very most subtle and simple Fifth Essence inhabiting this, our coarse and unpolished Fifth Essence, which we mentioned in this chapter. For the sake of confirming this, I will bring forth an experiment for you from this coarse substance of the Fifth Essence, so that I may make you certain along with me (provided you have faith in the truth) that a life-giving virtue exists exactly within this pure element.

### The first experiment proving the true agent of life is contained in this fifth element.

When I was occupied one day with the extraction of this **Celestial Balsam** <note>A medicinal or alchemical substance believed to have life-giving properties</note>, prepared in the common chemical manner, I was somewhat frustrated; for, treating the "earthly chaos" more severely than was right, I perceived a portion of this celestial flower to be burnt and consequently useless. I therefore washed the glass vessel in which the failing matter had been stored in a certain larger vessel, constructed of thick square stones, designed to receive rainwater from the eaves of the buildings. But behold! After a few days had elapsed, I found the water swarming with worms of marvelous form and length; for they were of unusual length, but somewhat slender or thin in width, and whitish in color, and all of one kind and shape. I immediately observed that this proceeded from this life-giving nature, since before that time not even one of these little animals appeared in this receiving vessel. Hence, therefore, it is manifest that the vital nature is one and the same in vegetables and in animals; the only diversity is in the vessel or body containing this celestial virtue. Whence it happens that it is called the **Vegetable Soul** in plants, but the **Vital Soul** in animals. This is indeed confirmed by the fact that bread nourishes the vital soul and even converts itself into animal nature. 

Hence also one may clearly and evidently see the ignorance of certain people in this world, who attribute nutrition, the preservation of life, the multiplication of blood, and the increase of every humor to the external bread and similar foods; but in every way, they are ignorant of the peculiar parts, their internal workings, or their natural offices—hardly different from how the blind common folk of this world are accustomed to assert foolishly and ignorantly that they know a man best, of whom they nevertheless have knowledge only of the exterior appearance. But how few (good God!) are there who rightly perceive the **Internal Man**, the understanding of which is the principal goal of all human life, toward which one ought primarily to strive: namely, to know and uncover the **Light in the Darkness**. For to the "Sons of Earth," all things are darkness, just as the things appearing sensibly in the world truly are; but conversely, it is given to the "Sons of Light" 

<margin>The hand of the philosopher or chemist interacting with the "chaos" or matter in a furnace.</margin>

to look into the darkness itself, and to behold with spiritual eyes that hidden light lurking in the center, which is the true and most ancient honor and dignity of every creature communicated to them by the Creator at creation. And although I by no means profess to have aspired to the summit of such great perfection, I nevertheless rejoice and congratulate myself that at least some spark of that light glimmers in me, which renders any soul secure and immune from the foolish anxieties of earthly things, for which the world burns with greed and desire. I conclude, therefore, that since we see by daily experience (which does not deceive even the peasants) that the presence of the sun is the author of both life and multiplication, it follows that this Fifth Essence of mine is the closest relative to the Sun—or to the true and simple Fifth Essence—and joined to it by the closest bond of blood; indeed, it is of the proper substance of the celestial sphere, insofar as it contains such a property of life within itself.

## The second experiment concerning the excellence of this fifth essence in Medicine.

I confess that I have used this natural balsam in the practice of Medicine only once; and then indeed (as was said before) I experienced its power upon myself. For when I was once afflicted with great trouble and pain in the hump <note>likely the carpus or back of the hand</note> of my hand, and suffered from a weakness of the nerves (which indeed used to happen to me quite often at that time of year when the cold companions of the harsh air are accustomed to rush in), I took a very small amount of this golden balsam and immediately anointed the ill-affected hand. I solemnly testify that from then until this very day (thanks be to GOD) I have scarcely felt any pain or torment. From this it is clearly to be gathered how friendly that substance is to nature, and how greatly it resists its impediments. Something lies hidden here which will not be open to everyone: if, therefore, the internal parts of this essence can be drawn out a little more exactly while its garments are still cast off, there is no doubt that it could perform far greater things yet.

## *The third experiment teaches how this fifth element differs manifestly from the other four inferior elements by sense or smell.*

The EARTH in this Chaos <note>The "Chaos" refers to the raw, unrefined matter at the start of the alchemical process</note>, due to the foul disposition caused by the element of fire, breathed out a heavy odor; the WATER breathed an unpleasant aura, proceeding partly from the earth and partly indeed from the air, which smelled only a little of the nature of a fiery odor. But truly, this [the air] was different and much more pleasing than either that of the earth or the fire. The FIRE breathed out a most foul stench, affecting the sense suddenly and heavily, by which it sufficiently proved that it was the cause of putrefaction. But the ETHER, or fifth essence, although it is close to fire in respect to both its composition and its simplicity, was nevertheless in its own peculiar and proper nature sweetly fragrant and wonderfully pleasant to my sense. It embraced such efficacy and power within itself that if I only touched it, I would still perceive its fragrance two or three days later, so penetrating and effective was it. And certainly (saving the judgment of others), to speak for myself, I prefer the power of this uncooked balsam of life to all other fragrant things that I have ever applied to my sense. From this it seems established that, as to its substance, this first essence has a nature far different from that of the four inferior substances which differ from one another.

# CHAPTER IX.

## *A certain transcendent inquiry, which can be performed and presented through the speculation of the higher natures of the human soul, the aforementioned visible foundations having first been observed and placed.*

JUST AS in that pyramidal half-proportion delineated above, which tends from the sphere of the sun downward, we find the entire composition of both the external man and the material world in a hieroglyphic manner—inasmuch as its base is the earth, in which the watery humor visibly dominates, but the airy spirit is invisibly contained, as is the element of fire, and finally that central gift or food of life which is enclosed in it—so that the external visible circumference of the human world is earth, while water possesses the next sphere, followed by air, and with it fire. To this visible orb, the life-giving ray of the sun or fifth essence stands as the center or internal principle, to give essence to the rest of the aforementioned things, not otherwise than the celestial sun is accustomed to provide its lucid power to the individual stars of heaven. In the same way, the rays of the sun or the ethereal splendor are the base or foundation of the internal, spiritual, and invisible man, whose center is GOD himself. For this reason, with premeditated logic, St. John calls Him the *light of man* <note>original: "lucem hominis"</note>; he who has once received this into the innermost chambers of his heart can say with the best right that he not only knows himself, but also understands how to sincerely venerate his GOD dwelling within himself (as becomes an upright and just man). For with this kind of self-knowledge leading the way, it is estimated by Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurio Trismegisto"</note> to be by no means impossible either to know GOD or to revere Him as is fitting for us; for in a certain passage he speaks in these words: *Think that the word of the Lord sees and hears in you.* Whence he also infers elsewhere: *you moreover, to whom a portion of mind has been granted, recognize your race, and consider your immortal nature.* For which reason he designates to us elsewhere, saying: *God is Light and Life, and the Father, from whom man was born.* If therefore you comprehend yourself as composed of life and light, you transcend back to life and light; from which the same author elsewhere infers and concludes: *He who knows himself, passes into God,* as the word of God has handed down. And in these things he seems to differ not at all from St. John, who affirms that *God is the word, and that all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made; in him was life, and the life was the light of men, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.* This, therefore, is the external man who meets the eyes, whose foundation is earth, for *God had formed man from the dust of the earth, Gen. 3.* GOD created man, whose base, foundation, or internal principle is the spirit; and this celestial spirit was breathed by GOD himself into the face of the muddy man, according to that: *And he had breathed into his face the breath of life, and man was made into a living soul, Gen. ibid.* So that we see here the foundation of both the internal and external man, and that the summit or apex of the structure of the external man is the base of the existence of the internal. And just as we see the sun, filled with that breath of life which GOD breathed on the first day of creation into the universal watery mass of the world, so that by its power the world might live, magnificently and with a most excellent appearance throughout the whole circle of the lands...

...be seen, so also is that sun the purest and highest thing in the world that can be discerned by human senses, so much so that the sharpness of human sight can scarcely, if at all, reach it. Upon this same spiritual basis, therefore, the internal man has placed his beginning, or his fundamental stone, so that the circumference of the spiritual man’s substance serves to contain the outermost embrace of the internal man, just as the earth performs this same function in the external man. The next sphere from the spiritual circumference is that light which, fluctuating in this spirit, imparts life to all creatures, not otherwise than how water flows around the earth; and then afterwards, in that sphere, the rational [spirit] moves, just as air is enclosed in water; then, in that rational spirit, the lucid spirit of the mind wanders, as if emanating immediately from the center in which **GOD** himself resides, clothed in his own glory—not, however, by inclusion, or, to speak with **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus and alchemy.</note>: *Inasmuch as he is the divine center of man, whose circumference is nowhere; that is, whose property it is to be within and without all things.* From the center of the internal man, therefore, **GOD** emits the rays of his grace, or restrains them from the entire composition according to his divine pleasure, according to that saying of the royal psalmist: *When God gives to the creatures, they gather; when he opens his hand, they are filled with good; when he hides his face, they are troubled; when he takes away their spirit, they expire and return to their dust* <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 104:28-29.</note>. By these words, the Prophet seems clearly to declare the varied action of **GOD** reigning in the center of the internal man, inclining either toward punishment or toward the benevolence of life. We see, therefore, that he approaches somewhat the center of the quintessence <note>The "fifth element" or purest essence beyond the four terrestrial elements.</note>, in which **GOD** himself primarily acts and presides. Hence it is said, *he placed his tabernacle in the sun*, which the same **Hermes Trismegistus** tells us, saying: *Mind in reason, reason in soul, soul in spirit, and spirit with all these in the body.* Moreover, he describes the motion of the spirit in the body elsewhere: *The spirit, diffused through the veins, arteries, and blood, moves the animal everywhere, and contains and carries about the suspended mass of the body.* Thus, therefore, we see that there is no element in corporeal or visible matter which is not referred to a spiritual substance of the same kind looking toward it; nor is there any proportion or ratio in the material or formal pyramid beneath the sphere of the sun tending toward the nature of a cubic body, which does not also have that same image or form in the part rising above the sun, according to that saying of the Apostle to the Hebrews: *By faith we know that it has always been so done with the world through the word of God, so that from those things which could not be seen, those things which can be seen are made.* The most wise **Rabbis** and **Cabalists** also say that all lower things are representative of higher things, and as it is below, so it is acted above, on which opinion all the sages of both the Hebrews and the Egyptians agree. Truly the difference (if there be any) consists only in this: that the part of the world lower than the sun is material, while the higher part is spiritual. Whence it evidently appears that just as the soul is the spiritual image of the King, so also the body is the image of the soul, as if a tabernacle or palace ordained to receive it; the only difference between the soul and the body is that the latter is visible and gross, while the former is spiritual, invisible, and subtle. Hence **Hermes Trismegistus** teaches us *that that which is thick is like that very thing which is subtle, and vice versa, that which is subtle is as if it were that very thing which is thick.* And so we have heaven in earth, and vice versa, earth in heaven; and in turn we possess heaven enclosed in earth, and earth in heaven, and by consequence earth and heaven are nothing but one and the same thing, namely water, as St. Peter testifies, saying: *that there were long ago heaven and earth from water and through water, consisting by the word of God.* The brightness of the divine word, therefore, is the basis of the formal pyramid, just as water is the basis of the material one; the light from the shining word is therefore the life of the waters, circling the watery mass from the center everywhere, according to that saying of John: *In him was life, and the life was the light.* We conclude, therefore, that the progression from visible thickness to invisible subtlety made through the steps of nature—namely from earth to water, air, fire, and ether—demonstrates to us the progress from the ethereal sphere, or the light of equality, or the highest point of visibility, upwards or inwards toward the very point of unity, beyond which no progression is given. The ascent from the sun toward **GOD** is of this kind: namely, the ethereal spirit as the receiving basis, then the light or soul swimming in that spirit, then the Empyrean or rational spirit included in the soul or vital light, then afterwards the mind lurking in that intellectual spirit, in whose center is **GOD** himself, the first actor and first mover, where the ethereal spirit is to the soul as air is to the elementary fire;

# On the Exact Anatomy of Bread or Wheat.

Thus we see how we must occupy ourselves and work around the invisible parts of man with the eyes of contemplation alone; for with that alone leading the way, we climb toward the blessed cone of unity by that central and most hidden scale of the pyramid. From this we learn at the same time that all these five particles, or orbs, at the base are reduced to a single point in the cone. This is the unity drawn and extended from the base of the center through its own axis to the cone, where all things coincide into one nature. Infinite is the scope of this and the remaining pyramidal mysteries, upon whose bases it will not be difficult to establish the entire structure or fabric of nature, both visible and invisible. But because an exact epitome <note>A summary or condensed version.</note> of all those things which can be proposed by me concerning these matters is provided in my larger volumes, I will pass over them here with a light step, so that I may bring an end to this book with a description of the Earth, as it is the foundation of the visible world, both the greater <note>The Macrocosm or universe.</note> and the lesser <note>The Microcosm or man.</note>.

# CHAPTER X.

->The final appearance concerns the element of earth, which is the basis of all the rest.<-

In the first place, therefore, before we gird ourselves for the description of the element of earth, it must be known that it may seem likely that the greater spirit of the sun—which began to exercise its kingdom in heaven on the fourth day of creation—was the last of all to have set forth and been extracted from the earth. This occurred, surely, after the remaining four elements were segregated from it. For it was said by Moses *that the earth was created on the third day, and a proper place was assigned to the sublunary water to encompass it, which was given the name Sea.* Consequently, air and fire were finished on that very day and produced out of the dark chaos. From this it seems probable that, the earth having been first situated and founded, the bright substance of the sun proceeded from Chaos in order and series after the other three transparent elements. By the power of its own light, it was elevated to the center of the middle heaven on the fourth day of creation.

In plainly the same way, we perceive in this our ocular demonstration <note>A visual experiment or diagrammatic proof.</note> that, in imitation of the course of that nature, the central sun of our matter emerged from the earth after the separation and arrangement of the remaining four sublunary elements. This separation was indeed made by the power of that thick and terrestrial fire, which receives its action from the God who presides over light and fire, and consequently it must necessarily imitate Him in its action, according to that philosophical axiom: *That which makes a thing such, is itself more such.* <note>original: "Quod facit tale magis est tale" — a logical principle meaning the cause of a quality must possess that quality in a higher degree.</note> Therefore, since by the power of that act (which, although it be terrestrial, is nevertheless the true and hidden act of God Himself) a certain central sun clearly results and emerges from the earth or dark chaos after the appearance of the four elements, it can be seen—according to the probability of nature in producing her actions—that the Sun of the greater world was produced from the mass of terrestrial chaos on the fourth day in exactly the same way, immediately after the other elements were reduced to order according to the metric and symphonic law of Nature.

But to return to our purpose: once the quintessence <note>The "fifth essence" or purest spiritual component extracted from matter.</note> has been separated, we find a dark mass, a *caput mortuum* <note>literally "dead head"; the useless residue left after distillation.</note>, the earth, condemned in the opinion of men to be of no effect. For as it was said, the earth was "void" before the creation of the greater world, because there was no sign or effect, nor any vivifying light manifest in the darkness before creation. Hence those shadows were called *Hyle* <note>Greek term for primordial matter.</note>, which afterwards, through the mediation of the appearance of light and the act existing in it, became *Chaos*, and was afterwards called *Earth*. Thus, at the end of the creation of the world, these dregs or muds of the waters were converted into a fruitful and fertile earth; for immediately after it was placed in the center of this universe (as we read in Genesis 1), it brought forth most abundantly both vegetables and minerals, and finally animals.

We assert, therefore, that we have found a certain central heat naturally implanted in this earth of ours, which is the true act and primitive seed of every plant, mineral, and vegetable. It is, in a way, a fixed salt, participating in those four volatile natures which fled from this terrestrial chaos by the force of fire. And for that reason, in creation, plants and minerals were produced containing the natures of different elements within themselves: the hotter and subtler of them proceeded from the fixed salt of the fiery element; the temperate from the fixed salt of the air; the phlegmatic, cold, and watery from the salty portion of the water; and finally those which were most thick and dry from the earth. Because something of the vivifying moisture of the sun remained in these (which the thick spirits of the earth constrained and embraced so tightly that it could not ascend together with the solar body), it now struggles to ascend, with a desire to see its universal nature reigning in heaven and to join itself with it. So much so, that it drags along with it various thick spirits that retain it, and thus they are converted into vegetables, whose roots are fixed to the earth for reasons demonstrated in the first book.

I have found, therefore, all these vivifying but also fixed salts in my terrestrial mass, which, according to their moderation or firmness in fixation, produce either vegetables or minerals. For the animal participates in a more volatile substance of the elements, which is therefore not bound or fixed to the earth like the vegetable or mineral, but is mobile from one place to another, seeing as much in the earth as in the water or air. However, the residue of my Chaos, overflowing with condemned shadows and now destitute of almost all virtue, I compare to Lucifer, or the prince of darkness, who, despoiled of his splendor, was cast down headlong toward the shadows, an exile from all light and grace. For this reason, it is called by some "condemned earth" <note>original: "terra damnata"</note>, void of every good quality for preserving its own subsistence. And if the reader has understood me rightly in these things which have now been said, he will perceive that under this type of my discourse, I have, in a mystical manner, hidden the truly condemned earth and the fall of Lucifer, and under a sensible veil, explained a matter of great importance.

### First experiment by which it is proved that the mineral nature can participate with the vegetable.

I attempt to prove this by a twofold experiment. For first of all, I cut away a fungus or "wick" from this dark and dreg-filled earth so that I might burn it with oil; but I discovered it to be of such great hardness that, although it burned continuously, it was nevertheless not consumed in the manner of other vegetables. Thus, it might not undeservedly be called an "incombustible wick" <note>original: "lichnus incombustibilis"</note> and is distinguished by some with such a name. Afterwards, having taken pieces of it, I cast them into a glowing fire, and they took on a color exactly like that of a living coal; yet when they were later withdrawn from the fire and cooled, they turned out similar to steel or iron, taking on a quasi-metallic disposition.

### Second experiment expressing the internal heat of this earth proceeding from the salt fixed within it.

After my final distillation, I removed this "dead head" <note>term: "caput mortuum" - the useless solid residue left over after a chemical distillation or sublimation</note> from the vessel. I found it to be somewhat cold and, as it seemed to me, destitute of the heat of the fire. However, when this dreg-filled earth was placed upon wooden boards and began drawing the air to itself, after five hours had elapsed, it began to burn anew so fiercely that, had its flame not been detected and extinguished with vigilant care, it would have set fire to the place and the house.

And so I have briefly subjected the anatomy of this most excellent vegetable to your eyes for inspection, with each element elicited from its "chaos" <note>The author refers to the raw, unrefined state of matter before chemical separation</note> by comparing them to their likenesses in the Macrocosm and Microcosm <note>term: "Macro and Microcosm" - the Renaissance theory that the universe (macro) and the human being (micro) reflect one another in structure and essence</note>. And although I could write a full volume regarding the explanation of this subject, I have instead proposed in this treatise of ours to lay open and explain to you the very base and foundation upon which I have constructed my volumes on the Macrocosm and Microcosm. 

Because of this work, some—either choked by ignorance or puffed up with envy—think a window has been opened for them to interpret my actions, to judge my religion, and to accuse me of the crime of introducing recent and new opinions. These people condemn my teaching according to their own whim and say that I foster I know not what sects, and especially that of the **Brothers of the Rosy Cross** <note>original: "fratrum Roseæ crucis" - the Rosicrucians, a mysterious and controversial secret society of the era</note>. It has seemed to me, therefore, to be of primary and necessary importance to my fame and reputation to declare the unblemished truth to sincere men—those who, with all prejudice far removed, weigh the matter with an equal scale—lest perhaps by giving credence to such idle and wicked babblers, they themselves might be circumvented and induced to carp at my actions. 

But I cherish a firm hope that they will easily discern the truth from these things I have proposed in this treatise and will come around to my opinion, having considered the sensible demonstrations brought forward by me here. I adjure and witness, moreover, that if they refuse to give credit to these things I have recited, I shall choose four or five men of grave judgment and reputation, in whose sight I will demonstrate anew the things I have committed to writing here. But if any spiritual matters lie hidden beneath this corporeal and visible demonstration of mine, they are by no means seen by the ignorant; they condemn not me, but the blindness of their own intellect, for those submerged in earthly darkness cannot judge the colors of heaven. For those things which are spiritual or celestial are accustomed to be seen by the intuition of the mind, and not of the flesh.

Now indeed I shall proceed to the final book of this treatise, in which I have resolved to apply each of these mysteries to the "engines" of my Macrocosm and Microcosm, both interior and exterior.
