# Section I. Portion III. Part I. Book III.

...is understood as the eternal form of my chaos, which is conceived as a thing destitute of all action, embracing no actual element within itself—that is, a thing existing simply in potentiality alone, and therefore nothing in actuality. And hence it was that in the third chapter of my first book on the **Macrocosm** <note>The "Macrocosm" refers to the universe or "great world," a central concept in Fludd's Hermetic philosophy</note>, I determined that this first matter—this **Hyle** <note>original: "Hylam"; from the Greek *hyle*, meaning wood or raw matter</note>, I say—was by no means created. Because of this opinion or assertion of ours, I have felt myself unjustly and falsely accused by certain ignorant people or those overwhelmed by envy, without my cause being heard at all. They act as if I had concluded from this that some thing was originally uncreated, and consequently that something was co-eternal with God, even though Scripture nevertheless teaches us that God created all things primordially out of nothing. But indeed, such detractors, while they do not understand my meaning, deceive and trick themselves in this censure of theirs; for far be it from me to say that any thing is uncreated except God alone. Rather, I say that this **Hyle** is a mere "nothing" in actuality, inasmuch as it is called "something" only in potentiality and power. Conversely, we find that a thing existing in potentiality or "possibility" alone differs greatly from that which exists as a thing in actuality. From this it follows that since first matter is something in potentiality—that is, a thing conceived by the mind in potentiality alone—it is simply and absolutely nothing in actuality.

Now, since every creation is the bringing into actuality of that thing which never before really existed (for the presence of God gave form to all things which before were nothing), it is gathered by the force of inevitable consequence that creation is nothing other than the "actuation" or reduction of a "nothing" (that is, a thing in potentiality) into something actual. But truly, since **Hyle** or first matter did not exist as such a thing before the Spirit of the Lord shone out of the darkness and was carried over the waters, it follows that it was nothing, being devoid of all form and essence by which any specific thing is named. Hence it was that it seemed to **Plato** that this matter could be compared to no other thing than a phantom shown to someone in a dream, which, once he has awakened, is known to have been a mere fantasy; and **Saint Augustine** compares it to silence, which in respect to speech is mere nothingness.

Others truly have estimated it to be so remote from every truly existing thing that they define it as a thing which can scarcely, or not even scarcely, be imagined. Furthermore, to comprehend it in one word: it was a certain "imaginative something" which in the truth of the matter was nothing, until God, appearing out of the darkness—as one who out of His grace willed to hide Himself no longer—dispelled the dark deformity (which was the form of nothingness) by the power of His splendor, and put on the actual form of the waters as they now appear. Thus He drew them out of the opaque whirlpool of potentiality and brought them forth into that clear splendor of light which informs all things and illuminates all things, by whose power they were cleansed and purified. This also the Sacred Scriptures seem to argue in express words, where according to the translation of **Pagninus** <note>Sante Pagnini (1470–1541), a Dominican friar and leading Hebraist of the Renaissance</note> we read: *The hand of the Almighty made the world out of unformed matter.* According to the exposition of **Tremellius** <note>Immanuel Tremellius (1510–1580), a Jewish convert and leading Reformed theologian</note>: *Your hand created the world out of unformed matter.* But **Jerome** says: *Your hand created the orb of the earth out of invisible matter.* From this we conclude, first, that this deformed matter existed before the creation of the world; secondly, it is clear that it was not "created" [in the formal sense], because it was deformed, whereas all creation is "information" <note>The act of giving form to matter</note>.

I depicted the type or image of this **Hyle** in the fourth chapter of my first book on the **Macrocosm**, namely in the form of an infinite mass or thick cloud, black like pitch, without any consideration of a bright spark being enclosed in it. However, as pertains to the full resolution of that question—whether first matter or **Hyle** be created or not—I advise those of you who have a full desire for resolving this doubt to refer to Section 1, Portion 1, Part 2, Book 1, Chapter 5 of the *History of the Preternatural of Both Worlds*, as it is the place in which you can see the complete opinion of my mind and the authorities firmly establishing it.

# CHAPTER II.

->The Author's Chaos aptly applied to that of the Greater World.<-

Immediately after the appearance of God out of the darkness, the viscous spirits enclosed in the darkness embraced an infinite number of sparks or rays of light. These rays, penetrating into the dark abyss, changed that mass—whether **Hyle** or first matter—into the obscure **Chaos**, which is raw and undigested matter. Whence it is said that in its innermost parts or marrow, the five elements <note>Fludd often adds a fifth element or "ether" to the traditional four</note> were enclosed in such a confused manner that they struggled and contended with one another with great impetus; not otherwise than happens in a dark and vast abyss collected in the middle region of the air, where a thundering cloud is observed to resist the action of the most rapacious lightning bolt enclosed in its belly, which indeed does not cease to attack it until it breaks out from its prisons into liberty. To this chaos, therefore, which on the second day of creation fluctuated in the deformed region of the third day, I apply the model of my own chaos, from which I extorted my five elements by the violence of terrestrial fire, in imitation of that Almighty Craftsman who by His power originally extracted those four elements of the world from that universal chaos by means of His celestial fire. Hence it is that in the 10th chapter of the 1st book of the *Physical History of the Macrocosm*, I expressed a double image or figure of chaos: the first I formed according to the intention and mind of the philosophers, but the second I delineated according to my own invention and the appearances which showed themselves to my eyes from this model of mine.

# On the Exact Anatomy of Bread or Wheat.

### CHAPTER III.

->*Concerning the appearance of the divine spirit which moved upon the waters out of the darkness, and the allusion of our experiment to it, as well as the creation of the first three days.*<-

It must be gathered from the discourse of Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurij Trismeg." - Hermes Trismegistus was the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical and hermetic texts were attributed.</note> that when the spirit of the Lord moved upon the waters, those waters were like a gathered or disturbed smoke or vapor; whence he himself calls them a moist nature, agitated by an ineffable countenance. He says that in this moist nature—so disturbed by the sight and aspect of this immense light and splendor of the spirit of God—a terrible shadow or a certain immense darkness fell downward into the disturbed moist nature in a spiral or oblique revolution. Now, indeed, so that we may apply these things to our present work in a way that is not unfitting, we find in our first appearance <note>Referring to the first stage of the alchemical distillation of the wheat.</note> the thick and cloudy appearance just reported by us; and in it, a black and opaque shadow precipitating itself downward toward the bottom of the water or moist nature by the power of fire or a certain reverberating light. This light, in its operation, imitated that divine splendor, inasmuch as it derived its origin from it.

The image of this darkness reflected downward is expressed generally and quite clearly in Chapter 6, Book 1 of the *History of the Physics of the Macrocosm* <note>original: "Physicæ Macrocosmi Historiæ" - This refers to Fludd's own massive encyclopedia of the universe published in 1617.</note>, just as the spirit moved upon the waters proceeding from the word *Fiat* <note>Latin: "Let it be done."</note>, together with the decline of darkness progressing downward toward the center, along with the formation of the waters (which were the vehicle of that operating light), is depicted to the life by the figure on page 49 of the same book.

And since in Moses <note>The Book of Genesis.</note> mention is made of three days before the creation of the world was completed—of which on the first, the highest fiery or luminous heaven was made; on the second, the middle region or ethereal heaven; and on the third, the lowest or elementary region—it necessarily follows that since only the first heaven was made on the first day of creation, then indeed the containing cavity of the second or middle heaven was still formless and overwhelmed by darkness, and consequently that space of the lowest heaven as well. From this it follows that if the darkness, which before the existence of any things would erase and deprive the form of the first heaven, was put to flight by the presence of reflected light and not driven downward toward the center, this shadow of darkness so thrust down and depressed was mixed with those shadows which denied all form to the middle heaven (or the operation of the second day) through the space of the first day. Thus, the darkness of this middle heaven was now doubled or duplicated; and consequently, for the same reason, the darkness of the lowest region was tripled after the perfection of the second heaven.

From this, therefore, arose that **Chaos** which contained the three elements within itself: namely, the sphere of fire, that of moisture, and the globe of earth. From this, therefore, proceeds that triple kingdom in the composition of nature: namely, the **Animal, Vegetable, and Mineral**. And from here proceed those three complete regions in the earth or the kingdom of darkness, each of which has respect to one of these elements. From here (I say), first of all, we have the **Earth**, which is cold and dry like a certain thick or cold and dry water, since almost all moisture is drawn out of it. Next to this follows the **sphere of moisture**, which is either cold (the element commonly called **Water**) or hot and moist (which we commonly call **Air**). Then afterward follows the **sphere of fire**, which is like a hot and dry water, so that this hot and dry water is nothing other than a certain dross of the spirits of the fiery or empyrean heaven. The sphere of moisture, however, is a thicker portion of the spirits of the ethereal or middle heaven which were enclosed in darkness; and the hot and moist part of this sphere is the basis of the ethereal part which is above the sphere of the sun, and its cold and moist portion is the denser part of the spirit which floats between the sun and the sphere of water. For this reason, in the creation of the first, second, and third days, I have expressed the figures reported on pages 55, 88, 63, 66, and 69, from which the degrees of darkness shine forth—namely, to what extent in measure and proportion they descended toward the center of the world, where they were established in that place where they even now remain, on the third day when the name of "Earth" was bestowed upon them.

The celestial light, springing immediately from the spirit of GOD, produced the five elements of the greater world out of a triple chaos through a circulating and reverberating power. However, the manner in which each of these four sublunary elements was separated from the dark mass and from the remaining elements, along with the true method of operation in their partitioning, you will find in the second book of my volume on *Macrocosmic Physics*, chapter 11, page 63. Among these, the element of fire is seen to enjoy the highest place, which nevertheless, beyond all doubt, was the last to flash out and emerge from the black mass of the earth, as has been demonstrated by us both in our experiment of extracting fire from our "chaos" <note>The author refers to his laboratory matter from which he extracts essences</note> and also in chapter 12, pages 64 and 66, declaring the position of the dark earth. Therefore, this passage expresses those elements as somewhat confused, disturbed, and impure in their first appearance; but indeed, the figure on page 69 depicts the same elements purified and completely distinguished and arranged in their natural seat by means of the bond of the <term>quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth element" or purest essence that binds the other four</note>. Furthermore, beyond all these things, just as in our small-scale operation we observed the quintessence—or the spark of the grain—leap out last of all from the sphere of our central sun of chaos, so also it is likely and probable that the fiery and spiritual globe of the sun in the greater world finally emerged after the chaos was established in the center of the universal machine or structure, and was sublimated into the heaven. Experience in this operation of ours confirms this, in which we find the first element, namely water, was first liberated from the dark prison; afterwards the second, which was air; then fire, which was the third; finally the quintessence, the fourth; and lastly the earth, which was the external foundation of all the aforesaid. Thus we find that the quintessence or fifth element (whose chief habitation is in the center or heart of the middle heaven) was extracted last from the womb of the great and general chaos.

And truly, if we now note how the Sun of the greater world is said to have been made by Moses—easily the prince and father of prelates and wise men—after the positioning of the earth and the limitation of the waters, we shall perceive most clearly that this mystery of his tends toward my same goal. For I am compelled to reason thus: Since the creatures of the first heaven were created on the first day, and the creatures of the lowest heaven, such as minerals and vegetables, were made on the third day, what was the reason why the creatures of the middle heaven—namely the Sun, Moon, and remaining stars—were only procreated on the fourth day? I answer: it seemed so to the supernatural GOD, that this earthly chaos, according to its natural position, should bring forth or give birth to a "natural GOD," or the splendid light of nature hidden in the dark chaos to vivify the world in a temporal way and to produce multiplication in sublunary compounds; which light was raised into heaven at the beginning of the fourth day.

Nor should this seem impossible to us worldly folk, since from the earth springs the supernatural and spiritual GOD himself, by whom invisible souls and spirits are preserved in their essence. For in the sacred text this is found: *The earth shall be opened and bring forth a savior* <note>original: "Aperietur terra & pariet saluatorem" - a Latin rendering of Isaiah 45:8</note>. And this spiritual and supernatural GOD, the invisible son of GOD the Father (just as the worldly Sun is called by Plato the "visible son of God"), directs and governs from the Sun upward through a spiritual and invisible <term>Diapason</term> <note>An octave or harmonic interval representing universal order</note> harmony, just as the visible sun works downward through a similar visible and material one. He who immerses himself in our worldly harmony in Book 3, Chapter 3 of our *History of Physics* will find things pertaining to this matter. And as for the figure of the formal and material Diapason, see page 90. Furthermore, I have explained this matter more at length in chapters 6 and 7 of the first book of my *Macrocosm*, where sufficiently valid reasons with figures confirming the matter are brought forward; whence I have proposed to myself to persevere in this mind and opinion until rigid and violent rejectors of such demonstrative opinions bring forward sounder reasons, supported by stronger experience than has been produced by me.

Now, therefore, as far as the body of the Sun of the greater world is concerned, we find it to be nothing other than condensed spirit—whence the philosophers defined it as *the denser part of its orb*. We all see it is also illuminated on all sides by lucid flames, whose rays are like agents that generally work in the spirit of this visible world. And because we see that lucid body placed in the very center of the middle heaven, and GOD himself—the source and origin of all forms—is said by the prophet David to dwell in the highest heaven (that is, in the purity of light), while on the opposite side the infected earth (which is the thick and great mass or mother of matter) is placed in the lowest center, so that the source of form differs from that of matter by the opposition of diametrical space, in the middle of which the Sun is established; it follows infallibly, therefore, that the Sun participates equally in form and matter. It looks downward toward material spirit and gazes upward toward formal light.

And this is the reason why the ancient philosophers spoke so many words about the "sphere of equality" in which the Sun revolves, and others about the sphere of the <term>World Soul</term> <note>Anima Mundi: the spirit connecting all living things to the divine</note>, which I have approved by the reasons of wise philosophers in Book 4, Chapter 10 of the *Macrocosm*, and I have demonstrated their truth with figures and conclusions explained on pages 81, 89, 90, and 165. Whence it happens that such a substance is marked by immortality and contributes to the sustenance of life. # On the Exact Anatomy of Bread or Wheat.

...I might investigate the [proportions] of the excellent action and passion of life. Therefore, by a geometric method of inquiry, I discovered that the earth is the source of matter and passion <note>In this context, "passion" refers to the capacity to be acted upon or shaped, the opposite of "action."</note>, because I perceived it to be the thickest foundation of material substance. I perceived the truth of this matter all the more clearly because I observed that Water—the element closest to it in place and nature—is thinner, lighter, and more transparent than it; then Air is thinner than water, and Fire thinner than air. Finally, by logical consequence, I gathered that the ether, or the substance of the starry heavens, was thinner than elementary fire by the same proportion. Lastly, I concluded that the intellectual or Empyrean heaven was the thinnest of all, since its substance, due to the immediate presence of God, is nothing other than the thinnest spirit of the world turned into fire and light; for in this heaven, light was created on the first day. 

Now, since no created matter or spirit can exist within God, we have freely and sincerely asserted that matter in this place—necessarily being contiguous to God—ends and is terminated as if in a unity or a material point, as if one were to say *No further beyond*. Wherefore, it is clear that the material progress from the opaque source of the earth, moving upwards, is like a flame of fire, which the higher it ascends, the more it is sharpened and reduced to a point. And this is the reason why we have reduced the entire scope or foundation of matter lying in the earth into the form of a pyramid, whose base is placed in the earth as the thicker portion of matter, while its cone <note>The apex or tip of the pyramid.</note> touches the very throne of God; and this pyramid we call the material, watery, and passive pyramid. 

Now, because the seat of God is said to be at the summit of the heavens, in the highest heaven, or the heaven of heavens—namely where the point of the earth's radius or the point opposite the center terminates at the circumference of the world—and perceiving moreover that the act of God in creation is proportioned and relates equally to the passion of moist matter, we fashioned another pyramid contrary in position to that material one. For its base is as if continuous or contiguous to the presence of God, namely in the circumference of the fabric [of the universe], while its cone points downwards toward the base of the material pyramid, or the center and middle of the macrocosmic fabric, just as the material cone reached the base of that formal one above. 

And that this is so in reason, I deduced in this way: because God is said to be the source of all light; then the heaven placed nearest to Him, in which He shines immediately from His splendor, is called the Empyrean or fiery; then the middle heaven is called Ether, as if "fiery air," because air and fire are equally proportioned. Afterward, we perceive by experience that the effect of light in the lower heaven is weak, so that the appetite of matter is never satisfied, whence it constantly desires to change its old form into a new one; and this is the cause of alterations in the lower heaven. Hence we see the effect of light gradually and step by step diminish its power in its descent and decrease in its act, and this is due to the dominion of the lower matter, which extinguishes and restrains its force—no differently than light, the more it raised itself on high, mutilated the thickness and resistance of matter by its efficacy and the power of its dominion in the upper region. 

It follows, therefore, that just as the mass of moist matter can be reduced to a pyramidal form, which is called the material pyramid, so also the mass of light emanating in the world from the presence of God—shining out of darkness or potentiality into act—can be reduced to a formal pyramid. In its descent, this is seen to cut and divide that ascending material pyramid in equal proportion, so that where their meeting and intersection occurs, there appears to be the sphere of equality, or the seat of the soul of the greater world <term>Anima Mundi: the "World Soul" that animates the universe</term>, in which the sun completes its daily course. The diagrams and reasons for these two pyramids meeting each other, along with their intersections, are expressed to the life in my said book on pages 105, 18, 84, 89, and 90. And how these two pyramids are to be understood not geometrically but physically is sufficiently declared with reasons and demonstrations on page 76. 

And to make this pyramidal doctrine of mine easier for you, I have explained my entire intention regarding them in a special book, which you will find inscribed at the end of the history of my technical microcosm, *On the Speculative Pyramid of Metaphysical and Physical Science*. We gathered this entire doctrine which we found concerning these two pyramids from the speculation of that middle substance, as it is exactly and completely tempered in light and spirit. And just as reason itself dictates to us, no one can imagine a middle point for himself unless regard is had for the two extremes—no differently than we see in Arithmetic that the number two cannot be given unless its two extremes, namely one and three, are weighed—therefore, finding the mean in the radius of the orb of Nature, I immediately measured its extremes, making the mathematical radius the axis or central line of each of these pyramids of nature, both the material and the formal. 

Upon these reasons, therefore, as the most stable and safe foundations, I have placed the structure of my philosophy, to refute those rumors which have scattered the idea that the foundations of my doctrine are erroneous because they are new—doing so everywhere but thoughtlessly, in the manner of the ignorant common people. But I would urge these insolent censors to put hand to pen and refute those things proposed by me, so that all, leaning on the wings of justice, may perceive both them and me for what we are, and thereby learn to judge more rightly of us and our errors.

Lastly, the reason for the growth and multiplication of plants described by me in the first book of my macrocosm, as also of the sensible and vital spirits in animals expressed in the next following chapter, is fully demonstrated in the second chapter of the first book of this treatise and the fourth chapter of the second book, and especially in its third experiment. # CONCERNING THE MICROCOSM.

### CHAPTER I.
### Concerning Man.

Now, so that we may apply this experimental conclusion of ours to man and his parts—that is, first to his external and visible part, and then afterwards to the internal—we say that the human body, which is his external part, is to be compared to the dark and opaque earth. This is because, without the infusion of spiritual parts into it—namely the soul (which derives its origin and essence from heaven)—the body is of no greater esteem or strength than that lifeless earth we mentioned before, namely the "dead head" <note>original: "caput mortuum," a term from alchemy referring to the useless residue left after distillation</note> or the dreg-like remains of our chaos. How this human body may rightly be called "earth," I have shown in the second chapter of my fifth book on the history of the microcosm, page 100; there I proved at the same time that although it is called earth, it also contains within itself the elements of water, air, and fire, which are entirely necessary for its composition. Furthermore, just as we asserted in this very treatise (Book 2, Chapter 9) that the Platonists established that the soul is in the spirit, and the spirit is in the body; so also in our "fifth essence" <term>Quintessence: the purest, highest element that permeates all nature</term> we see the manner in which the life-giving rays of light (which is that true soul the Platonists understood) are introduced into the body by means of a clear and bright spirit, acting as a vehicle or vessel perfectly adapted to it by Nature. And for this reason, the spirit of man was called the "vehicle" or "chariot" of the soul by the wisest philosophers; and because the spirit is bound so closely to the soul by the invisible joints of nature, it is frequently taken for the vital soul itself. Hence it was said by the Apostle: *The sword of GOD is powerful, a sword acting even to the division of the soul from the spirit* <note>A reference to Hebrews 4:12</note>; for no one except GOD alone can separate these two from one another. Regarding this soul and spirit, along with their union and division, we have made mention at length in Book 13 of my history of the physics of the macrocosm (Chapters 1 and 2), as well as in Book 12 (Chapter 14) and various other places pertaining to this. Now, however, as to how the spirit works within the body—carrying the vital light within itself like the oil of a lamp carries its flame—I have sufficiently expressed in Book 8, Chapter 8. There I demonstrated in the first place that this spirit is the true "radical moisture" <term>Humidum radicale: the fundamental fluid or "fuel" believed to sustain life and bodily heat</term> of every creature, both animal and vegetable, and that its principal seat is in the heart. For this reason, the heart hangs downward like a formal pyramid, because of the shape of the life-giving light hiding and working invisibly within it. In that same place, I describe the method by which the spirit is carried into the body, based on the authority of *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with alchemy and philosophy</note>, who speaks in these words: *The spirit, diffused into the veins and arteries and the blood, moves the living creature on all sides, and holds up and carries about the mass of the body; the soul is in the spirit, reason is in the soul, and mind is in reason.* Then, in the chapter immediately following, we reported what the life-giving soul is: namely, *a spark, as it were, of celestial light, which is nourished by its own spiritual crystalline liquor.* Concerning the operation of this soul and the degrees of its power in the body of every living creature, we have dealt abundantly in Chapter 5 of the said book, where I indicated that the abundance of vital light in this spirit is the cause of the body's agility. So also in Chapter 3 of the said book, I declared this soul (which I imagined floating in an ethereal spirit, as it were) to be like a "middle soul" or the middle region of the human soul. In this mixture conducive to life, just as the light acts benevolently toward life, so the spirit receives its passions with a sweet and natural embrace.

## CHAPTER II.
### On the Natural faculty, and that all vegetation proceeds from the Liver; likewise concerning the seed or the Liver of man.

I have told you in my experimental operation—namely in the second book and second chapter of this present treatise—that the principal and immediate cause of vegetation <note>The power of growth and life</note> proceeds from the air, where I brought an experiment to light for the sake of proving this very thing to you. Thus it is also evident that the airy part itself procreates blood within the nourishment, by the virtue of which the entire mass of the human body is vegetated and increased; whereas, when that part is lacking, the body wastes away and becomes flaccid. From this it is manifest that the natural faculty is principally fostered and sustained by this element, mixed with a portion of the soul’s quintessence <note>The "fifth essence," a celestial substance above the four earthly elements</note> which I cited above. Concerning this vegetable or airy essence, I have spoken sufficiently in the seventh chapter of the ninth book of my *History of the Macrocosm*, where I aptly applied the airy part of my experiment to this business and clearly explained all actions within this natural faculty. And although it is established by some that the seed <note>original: "sperma"</note> is a foamy and superfluous part of the third digestion, I am nevertheless certain and instructed by faithful experience that the central and principal part of the spermatic mass consists of an ethereal and vital nature. We have spoken some words of this before, and what can be said regarding this point of the subject we have discussed more fully and even more lucidly in the *Mystical Anatomy* in chapters three, four, and five of Book 11 of my *History of the Macrocosm*. We conclude, therefore, that this natural faculty is that act in the airy spirit which we mentioned in chapter 7, book 3 of that same *History of my Microcosm*; where, not without just reason, I called it the "elementary ray" and the subject of the sensitive soul, or the basis of the entire fabric of the human soul.

## CHAPTER III.
### That the invisible or spiritual parts of the human soul are built upon those visible parts as corporeal foundations and bases; the Reason for the descent of the soul into the human body is also discussed here.

Just as in our experimental demonstration we beheld with bodily eyes the visible portions of the vegetable and animal soul consisting in the subtle substance of that whole spirit—which exists between the sun of heaven and the dark earth from which the body is formed—so it is fitting for us to contemplate the spiritual and invisible parts of the soul with the eyes of the intellect. These parts ascend from the visible body of the sun even unto the point where their matter is contiguous with God Himself. Wherefore, just as the ethereal spirit is carried in the air as if in its own vehicle, and the luminous soul is carried in this ethereal spirit as if in a vehicle—the foundation of all of which is the opaque earth—so the soul of man is the basis or vehicle of the rational or intellectual spirit, in which the rays of the Mind rejoice to bathe and wash themselves invisibly. Furthermore, the essence of God dwells in the center of the Mind. And this is that very thing which Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius Trismegistus," the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with alchemy and hermetic philosophy</note> inculcates in us with these words: *The Word into the mind, the mind into reason, reason into the soul, the soul into the spirit, and this into the air; and then all these things, gliding downward through the golden sea, are transferred into the body with that and in that as the final vehicle.* I have described the entire method of this descent into the human body in the third book, eighth chapter of my *History of the Microcosm*, where these things are contained: *By what vehicles or through what media the lights of each heaven, constituting the human soul, are joined to the body*; and in the third chapter of the fourth book of the same, which contains this: *By what virtue of worldly harmony is the Mind attracted to its opaque body?* At the end of that chapter, a hieroglyphic demonstration with harmony is expressed, showing the descent of the soul into the body. And in the fourth chapter of the said book, where these things are read: *How the mind and intellect, penetrating from the superior through the whole world toward the inferior even to the center, may notice the mysteries of each heaven, participate in the nature and disposition of each heaven, and bring their virtues with itself into the worldly man?* So also in chapter 2, book 8, the sense of which is this: *How the middle soul with its mistress, the Mind, is infused into the body by means of the ethereal spirit?* This, therefore, is that Mind, from the possession of which man is rightly called the "image of God," as you find described at greater length in chapter 5 of the third book of my *Macrocosm*. As far as pertains to this excellent head of the human soul, we have placed it in the fourth chapter of the third book of the aforesaid history, where I call it the "super-celestial ray" and the "act of God," as also in the whole seventh book of the same subject, and in various places of my Microcosmic work, where it is demonstrated that the mental part is the unity of the internal man. And although Hermes Trismegistus affirms that the Word <note>original: "Verbum"</note> is in this mental ray, it is nevertheless my opinion that this mental ray is the Word itself, since it is an immediate emanation from the fountain of unity and light. I have proved in the book cited above that this can in no way suffer within itself; whence, and because it is also the first emanation from the Father, I have demonstrated it to be the Messiah or the power of the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH</note>, which seems to be confirmed by that saying of St. John: *In him was life, and this life was the light of men, and this light shone in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.* But this is explained more clearly in our *Cabalistic History*. I could bring forth and commit to letters infinite matters concerning this subject, but this is not the goal of my intention, which strives to declare to the world how, raised by the rowing of the movement of my own wings, I have reached this point, and what remains in my power for each thing written by me...

# Section I. Portion III. Part I. Book III. On the Exact Preparation of Bread or the Anatomy of Wheat.

The things alleged in my writings, concerning both the Macrocosm <note>The "Great World" or the universe at large</note> and the Microcosm <note>The "Little World," referring to the human being as a reflection of the universe</note>, provide experimental testimony; for what is more certain than ocular demonstration <note>Proof seen with one's own eyes</note>? And so I shall bring an end to this brief treatise. Although at first glance it might perhaps seem ridiculous—due to the commonness of the subject matter—to those who lack understanding, those clouded by ignorance, or even to critics <note>original: "momis," referring to Momus, the Greek god of mockery and unfair criticism</note> and certain "mercurial" wits prone to rash judgment, I nevertheless deem it wise to warn my readers not to pass over obvious and common things with a "light foot" (as they say). For although they are able to recognize and distinguish the external coverings of these things, it will seem very difficult to uncover the treasures hidden within them and to behold them with open eyes. 

This is the reason why fools turn up their noses at things they have never seen, judging them to be impossible—as if, forsooth, all things were so stretched to the limit of their own capacity that they must, by right, either be made manifest to their own brutish senses or else be utterly denied the possibility of existing in the nature of things. Hidden mysteries are suited to the wise alone; manifest and vulgar things are for the fools as well as those intoxicated by worldly wisdom. The former, since they are truly learned and well-versed in the mysteries of God and their own nature, are held by the world to be simpletons, inasmuch as they do not wish to reveal themselves to the world. The latter, though they are in truth overwhelmed by mere foolishness, are falsely held by the common crowd to be learned and wise; for in their deceptive manner they appear prudent when in truth they are the most dull-witted of all. Thus, in vanity, passes the glory of the world <note>original: "sic enim in vanitate transit gloria mundi"</note>; for whatever is under the sun, except for the true knowledge of God, is vanity, according to that saying of the wise man: 

->*Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.*<-

# PREFACE.

## CHAPTER I.

### *In which the various formulas of speech used by Anatomists, before they arrive at the direct sequence of their practice, are discussed; and also the Author's method in this matter, its reasoning, and its model are explained.*

It is the custom and a sufficiently laudable habit of almost all Physicians that, before they enter upon the path of a public Anatomy <note>A public dissection, often held for students and the public</note>, they deliver a certain oration, both to render the minds of the listeners more attentive and prepared, and so that the subject to be handled—preceded by a refined speech of this kind—might be made more pleasing. But truly, the artists differ wonderfully from one another in the subject of their orations; for some turn their speech only to the structure of the human body, others to the praises of the body's perfections and symmetry, others to the antiquity and excellence of the anatomical art, and finally others delight in celebrating the encomiums of both ancient and modern Anatomists with elegant words. 

Yet (as it seems to me), nothing is more suited to the prelude of the anatomical art, and nothing more honorable or glorious can happen to the cadaver about to be dissected, than that the lineage, essence, governance, or properties of its mistress—namely, the soul <note>Latin: *anima*</note> that once inhabited it—and finally the reason for its flight and liberation, be revealed to the minds and ears of the listeners with the highest oratorical wit and in sufficiently ornate words. For who, I ask, well-versed in philosophy, would desire to look upon or affect the effects of a natural thing while the intrinsic acting causes of those things remain unknown? Since the former are familiar to the senses and consequently to the beasts, while the latter are subject to the internal intellect, which is the inner principle of man. And who, passing through some noble palace and admiring its wonderful craftsmanship, would not inquire after the master of such a great building, though he be absent, and labor to know his status, condition, and lineage? 

Therefore, we think it a matter to be chastised with the whip of ignorance if anyone should rashly plunge into the sea of bodily Anatomy, or the external man, without making any mention of the internal man. For the soul alone (by Divine will) is the architect of this microcosmic lodging; by its fingers the organs of such a most noble palace were most skillfully fashioned, and this whole visible house was fabricated with admirable art according to the invisible pattern of its spirit. 

As for the praises of the body and its parts, and their exact and symmetrical proportion, as well as the excellence and dignity of Anatomy and Anatomists: what need is there, I ask, for commendation in the preface? Since the practice itself will clearly enough exhibit to the spectators the most worthy excellence of the parts of the human body, their admirable joining in the body, their harmonious arrangement and position, and finally their utility in performing the functions of the soul, their mistress. Furthermore, through the exquisite skill of the expert Anatomist, the science will sufficiently extol itself with praises; for the parts of the human body, being equally divided and demonstrated, will speak for themselves, as will that anatomical art by whose direction the dissection of such parts is performed. 

Therefore, the formula of the Soul's descent into the muddy body <note>A reference to the body being made of "clay" or earth</note>, the conditions of its dwelling in that lodging, and finally the reason for its separation and departure from its tabernacle, I have narrated in the sequence of the oration preceding the Anatomy (performing the office of anatomical lecturer in the London College of Physicians in the Year 1620) in the context of a speech of this kind.

## T H E  O R A T I O N.

Just as the insolence of the envious and malevolent is not to be borne—from whose number, may God grant me better than that anyone should have crept today into this solemn congregation of wise men secretly and without our knowledge—so I ask and beseech you (Mr. President, holding the highest rank of dignity and command in the Medical magistracy; Doctors and colleagues most skilled in the art of medicine; Nobles, for whom the foundations of a famous origin have created glory; and all listeners in general, most adorned with both learning and benevolence) by the common law of humanity, that you remain in the duty of your holy goodness. 

And although you may rightly feel that I am by no means to be equaled to my predecessors in this art—who, having approached the anatomical mystery with toilsome labor and the daily experience of others going before them, have diligently cultivated it—nevertheless, so that something may be produced today upon this medical stage before you, by which your thirsty ears and eyes, perhaps greedy for novelty, might be in some way soothed, the famous custom of this College (which we celebrate publicly before this most pleasing assembly of Doctors through annual returns) commands and warns me, and your sweet gentleness toward me urges and persuades me.

Lo, therefore, and behold, we pray for pardon if, in this administration of anatomy, either some manifest error, or...

# Common Anatomy

The traces of a limping science <note>original: "scientiæ claudicantis vestigia" — likely referring to the imperfect state of human knowledge compared to divine truth</note> may have reached the sharp gaze or the refined ears of some among you. But before we draw back the tragic curtain of this desolate palace (though it be white in color), or fold away the theatrical veil of this same ghostly image, I begin thus: to render clear to you the proofs of reason, as if they were documents of untainted truth, concerning that divine lady <note>The Soul</note> who once inhabited it—her lineage, her essence, the order of her descent into such a lodging, the economy of laws within it, and finally her flight, now that the palace has been violated by the blow of the executioner.

The Mind is a holy breath of God, a noble offspring of divine parents, adorned with every beauty, made in the likeness of the Holy Trinity, equal to eternal glory, ordained within itself for blessedness, and the lawful heir of salvation. This most beautiful of creatures (I say), reclining sweetly upon a bed of thin and dewy spirit above the high peaks of the world, and surrounded by every choir of graces and the service of angels; the North Wind <note>original: "Zephyri" — though usually the West Wind, here used for a gentle breeze</note> of a mild, softly breathing air, carrying her downward by its tranquil spirit; she reclines, having glided gently down little by little through the slopes of the high worldly valley into the most pleasant garden of the earthly paradise. In the very center of this, planted with tall and vast trees of wonderful condition; where likewise among other pleasing herbs the Virgin Roses flowed with morning dew; this winged offspring of the eternal Creator, the sweet and honeyed soul of the microcosm <note>term: Microcosm — the "little world," referring to the human being as a reflection of the entire universe</note>, looked out upon a peaceful fountain of the crystalline liquid of the vital spirit. Near its flow, a certain royal house was built, not by human hands, but by divine arts: I mean a noble palace, made from the precious clay of the earth into a human image, which you would say at first sight was the bright and pleasant lodging of some God. And certainly, by the testimony of Holy Scripture, this was the temple of the Holy Spirit. The arrangement of this wonderful earthly Tabernacle greatly pleased the heavenly Soul, and she was immediately captivated by its beautiful appearance.

And now that heavenly inhabitant confidently enters it, by whose presence even the inner chambers, arranged far and wide—a house precious beyond price—so gleam with her own splendor that the house creates its own spiritual day for itself, even if the sun of the macrocosm <note>The physical sun of the universe</note> were unwilling. Thus the color of the shining rooms of the dwelling flashes against the life-giving edge of this internal sun; thus the bright clarity of its walls shines back (while the soul governs within it). Nor do the other parts respond less to the majesty of this animate house, so that it rightly seems an earthly palace built for a great deity after a heavenly model, for the conversation of a divine and incorruptible nature with a corruptible human one. Now they long for the breast to be raised by the swelling of the earthen image, now for the healthy vein to pulse, now for the body to be filled with spirit. Now the mass is suffused everywhere with a bloody redness and native heat. The face, previously deformed by earthly paleness, now seems to turn purple as if from virginal modesty and shame in its beautiful habit, and is decorated in a wonderful manner with flashing eyes, reddening cheeks, and open eyes. The head shines with resisting hair, and the breast is most accurately adorned with white breasts and glowing nipples. And so the entire earthen work of the eternal Signifier is converted into a true and entirely beautiful youth. And now, testing himself, he tries to move his limbs little by little, and at last the first Adam rises, who, snatched up by the contemplation of his own divine form, emerges joyful and brisk, suffused with the quite deceptive and fragile joy of earthly things.

By this means (I say), the soul—once free and flashing with holy splendor—is now bound by the long-lasting shackles of love to a dark body. I speak of a Bright Heaven, corrupted by the love of lower things, which unexpectedly plunges itself into the dark prisons of the earth, plucking a taste both sweet and bitter. For by this heavy bond she herself has obtained an earthly disposition, and thus separated from her heavenly lineage, she has miserably brought upon herself a long-lasting forgetfulness. Indeed, being now lulled to sleep by bodily passions, and led outside herself through the sensible forms of her palace, she has forgotten what she is or was; since she remembers having existed as nothing else, she believes for certain that she is nothing except what she is seen to be.

Therefore, she burns with such a vehement love for her prison that she seems to be sharply afflicted by its pains, she who by herself knows not how to grieve or suffer; she dreads destruction who knows not how to perish; she fears deficiency, whose divine nature cannot fail. She feeds on the speculation of the eyes; she is soothed by sonorous hearings; she is delighted by the sweetest odors; she is refreshed by large feasting. And although she herself in no way uses all these things—on account of the simplicity of her nature—she is nevertheless affected by heavy sadness, and her sorrow is doubled, if the necessities of this house of hers are withdrawn. From here, therefore, vices contrary to reason creep in, while the soul, by indulging too leniently in the delighted body, is known to give place to sin. But by a secret decree of the immense Creator of things, a fatal commerce was made between these two; He, noticing that a specimen of divine likeness might neglect gross things and flash very little with the desire for earthly things, willed it to be covered with a black garment, or an earthly house. For this reason, He ordained that man, the most noble creature, be fashioned from a heavenly soul and an earthly body—as if from an eternal and a mortal nature—so that a rational animal thus conformed could satisfy both its origins: both to wonder at and pray to heavenly things, and to inhabit and govern earthly things.

And now the soul thus enclosed is rightly defined as the internal image of the external man, for whom the supreme wisdom is taste, intelligence is vision, the mind is the eye, reason is the gaze, and reasoning itself is the investigation of the object. There are three powers by which she works: the concupiscible, the irascible, and the rational <note>term: Concupiscible/Irascible — medieval psychological terms for the "desiring" and "spirited/angry" parts of the soul</note>; by the first she desires and loves, by the middle she despises and hates, and by the last she discerns between the two former ones. There are four affections, the foundations of every virtue as well as vice: Joy and Hope, which are derived from the concupiscible; Grief and Fear from the irascible. Finally, the steps through which she shows herself both upward and downward are her five powers: for by means of sense she observes bodies; by imagination, the likenesses of bodies; by reason, their natures; by intellect, created spirit; and by intelligence, that which is uncreated. For sense informs imagination, imagination informs reason and creates knowledge.

knowledge, which is also called prudence; next, the divine presence instructs the reason and brings forth wisdom. From this, two actions of the mind’s life are reckoned: by the virtue of one, it regards things falling and transitory, and is inclined toward the flesh by means of the senses; by the effort of the other, it is sublimated on high, and with full wings flies away to God, dwelling in and around Him. And this is that divine <term>economy</term><note>In this context, "economy" refers to the management or internal organization of the soul's functions.</note> of the soul governing in its lodging; these are the admirable laws of its <term>polity</term><note>The "polity" or "civil government" of the soul within the body.</note> in the human body, by which it expands itself at will to things lower and higher, and is divinely illuminated to know and contemplate God above itself, itself within itself, the Angels beside itself, and whatever is contained within the circuit of heaven beneath itself.

The corporeal ship, therefore, thus furnished with all necessities, running to and fro through the vast ocean of the world (with the soul as mistress and leader), either completes the ways of the sea peacefully and is gently vibrated in a light wave (a life indeed known to very few), or is endangered, shaken by various whirlwinds of storms. Nay, indeed, the ship itself (the guidance of the governess being lost or at least neglected), thrust to the margin of further unhappiness, is accustomed for the most part to be submerged headlong and overwhelmed by unexpected death; nor can that agile and illustrious effort of so divine a leader precede the severity of human fortune.

Behold, you have before your eyes a tragic and ghost-like object of such a condition: the former carnal lodging of the soul, in which she for a long time instituted and administered the laws of her economy. But now, destined at last for the shipwreck of the cross or the gallows by the grimness of fate, and fixed there by the cruel hand of the executioner (placing the snare upon the neck, and by that tightened at the throat, shutting off the offices of the spirit), the soul has emerged by secret paths, leaving behind its hearth and deprived of all earthly things; and in a moment (carried on ethereal wings) fleeing away on high, it has left this its earthly palace—destitute of life and action, but not of the perfection of its fabric—in this our custody and power.

Behold therefore (most distinguished spectators, who pursue the pleasure of this sufficiently celebrated spectacle), I, the public minister of this day’s exercise, bring forth into the middle of the stage this mournful subject, everywhere suffused with a boxwood color <note>original: "colore buxeo" - likely referring to the yellowish, pale hue of a corpse.</note>, like a certain victim to be offered to your eyes, so that I may satisfy your curious zeal for seeing and my duty toward you in this matter. Behold (I say) the ghost-like likeness, deformed by the penal fury of death and the wretched squalor of deprivation; consider (I say) the external man by himself alone, the internal man being eternally lost and slipped away, with curious but also pious and Christian eyes. While I, the principal—though unwilling—actor of this tragedy, or rather the involuntary author of so great a butchery (not so much inhuman as necessary) now to be performed in this enclosed pit, prepare myself confidently to reveal with a dutiful hand this most wretched but, in its intuition, admirable example of human fragility, covered in linen cloths; so that with the knife or scalpel, plunged deep into the cadaver even to the core, you may recognize, under the judgment of one or two days' light, the secret chambers of the same, which once served the soul inhabiting it.

# I HAVE SPOKEN.

Indeed, I have not produced this form of peroration for you in this place for the sake of teaching (as one whose success in Latin elegance was never so great), but to indicate that the subject of the Anatomy to be prefaced ought to be the internal and spiritual part of man, which is to be dissected by living words rather than by a scalpel, however dexterous or sharp, and consequently is to be directed and explained only by the thread of a discourse. As the field of this subject is ampler and more spacious than others, so also students in Anatomy will never find it sterile but most fruitful, so much so that it is permitted for anyone to bring forth various orations or sermons concerning this subject in his own manner.

# CHAPTER II.

## Concerning human Anatomy in general.

The more skillful of the Philosophers, and those best versed in medicine, were accustomed to warn their auditors that they should not indeed place certain faith in books treating of Anatomy, but that they should rather gaze frequently and diligently upon that [book] inscribed by Nature herself, with the reason of the eye as guide, whereby they might more rightly judge concerning individual things or members in the human body not well perceived or understood before, and might diligently notice their sites and positions.

Moreover, they seem to suggest to us that this observation of human parts is to be explained by a manifold description, explaining their names, origins, substances, compositions, or actions and the diseases commonly happening to them, and even the constellation presiding over each part.

The word "Anatomy" (as we find among some) is derived from *Ana* (which is "equal") and *tomia* (that is, "division"), as if one were to say Anatomy is as it were an "equal division" <note>The author provides a folk etymology here; "Anatomy" actually comes from the Greek *ana-* (up/throughout) and *temnein* (to cut).</note>, whence it is defined by some that Anatomy is the right and equal division especially of the internal and external parts.

The effect of this kind of operation is employed either in living bodies or in dead cadavers, whence Galen himself instituted several books both concerning the Anatomy of the living and of the dead.

The ancients indeed were accustomed to divide the practice of this matter into four species, according to the number of the principal members: one of which pertained to the brain, to which the **animal virtue** <note>The "animal" faculty (from *anima*, soul) related to sensation and motion.</note> is referred; another regarded the heart, which serves the **vital virtue**; the third embraced the liver, attributed to the **natural faculty**; and the last looked with strict inquiry at the testicles, which greatly regard the **generative power**. Concerning which we shall speak (God willing) in their order and methodically.

# BOOK I. OF THE LOWER REGION.

## CHAPTER III.

->*On the general division of man into three regions, corresponding to those of the greater world.*<-

The general relationship between this fabric of the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "Little World," referring to the human body as a reflection of the universe.</note> and that of the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The "Greater World" or the universe at large.</note> consists either in a mathematical similarity of shapes or in a clearly physical respect for both. And although by geometric consideration the body may appear irregular, we shall very easily perceive that in truth it is spherical and possesses a fixed center no differently than its own world [the universe] does, if we mark out circles with a compass from the point of generation—whether male or female—or the seat of the private parts (with the radii extended equally from there to the head). Indeed, this location corresponds perfectly with the Earth of the Macrocosm, the womb of the elements, which contains their seeds and the procreative influences of the higher powers. From this, the error of those who placed the navel as the center of the body is clear, since its radii are unequal, as can be seen by experience and has been demonstrated elsewhere in my *History of the Microcosm*. Furthermore, by physical comparison, the head of the Microcosm (being the lodging of the divine mind and reason) regards the intellectual world or the <term>Empyrean Heaven</term> <note>The highest heaven in ancient and medieval cosmology, believed to be the home of pure fire or light and the dwelling place of God.</note>. Likewise, its chest or middle region—from whose center the heart, the greater light of the Microcosm, is accustomed to dart rays of life to every member of the entire fabric—corresponds to the starry heaven of the Macrocosm, from whose middle <term>Apollo</term> <note>Used here as a metaphor for the Sun.</note> disperses and emits the thinnest waves of vital spirits in every direction. Finally, the <term>yellow bile, blood, phlegm, and black bile</term> <note>original: "Cholera, sanguis, pituita, & melancholia." These are the four humors of ancient medicine.</note> of this same lowest region are held in close relation to the four elements of fire, air, water, and earth in the sublunary world.

In the specific description of this body, I shall begin my discourse from its lowest region (as it is more liable to putrefaction), and thus gradually and little by little I shall strive toward the higher parts, God assisting.

# On the Common Containing Parts

In the abdomen, four things are primarily to be considered, namely its:

*   **Name**, which is used among the:
    *   Greeks: *Epigastrion* <note>original: "ἐπιγάϛριον"</note>.
    *   Latins: *Abdomen* and *lower belly*.
    *   Arabs: *Mirach* <note>A medieval anatomical term derived from Arabic, referring to the abdominal wall.</note>.
    *   English: *The paunch or belly.*
*   **Composition**, which we consider either in respect to:
    *   **Site or position**, by which it is divided into the following portions:
        *   **Epigastric**, of which there are three parts, namely:
            *   Right hypochondrium <note>The upper lateral region of the abdomen, located under the ribs.</note>.
            *   Epigastrium <note>The upper middle region of the abdomen.</note>.
            *   Left hypochondrium.
        *   **Umbilical**, of which there are three parts:
            *   Right lumbar region.
            *   Umbilical region <note>The central area around the navel.</note>.
            *   Left lumbar region.
        *   **Hypogastric**, of which there are three regions:
            *   Right.
            *   Middle.
            *   Left.
    *   **The parts constituting it**, of which some are:
        *   **Containing**, from which that integral part of the abdomen called the *Mirach* is composed, and they are either:
            *   **Common**, which are 5 in number, namely:
                *   Cuticle <note>The outermost layer of skin; the epidermis.</note>.
                *   Skin.
                *   Fat.
                *   Fleshy panniculus <note>A layer of muscle or tissue just beneath the skin.</note>.
                *   Common membrane.
            *   **Proper**, of which there are two types, namely:
                *   The 8 muscles of the abdomen.
                *   Peritoneum <note>The lining of the abdominal cavity.</note>.
        *   **Contained**, which are everywhere enfolded and, as it were, grasped by the simple membrane of the Peritoneum; and of these, some:
            *   **Serve digestion**, and are:
                *   Omentum <note>A fold of fatty tissue hanging over the intestines.</note>.
                *   Stomach <note>original: "Ventriculus"</note>.
                *   Small intestines.
                *   Portal vein.
                *   Liver <note>original: "Hepar"</note>.
                *   Part of the vena cava.
            *   **Are dedicated to excretion**, namely:
                *   Large intestines.
                *   Gallbladder.
                *   Spleen. Kidneys.
                *   Ureters, Bladder.
            *   **Adapted for generation**, namely:
                *   Seminal vessels.
                *   Testes.
*   **Site**, since it extends from the pubic bone to that of the pointed cartilage <note>The xiphoid process at the base of the breastbone.</note>.
*   **Use**, so that it may be a common receptacle for the organs of both nutrition and generation.

# Book I of the Lower Region.

### CHAPTER I.

### Concerning the Epidermis or little skin.

*Starting from the surface of this lower belly and moving toward its center, we shall begin by descending little by little and step by step; first, we will treat the cuticle, which is the first thing to present itself to our eyes.*

<margin>
This part of the common coverings is the first to present itself to the eyes.
</margin>

It is named:
- In Greek, <note>original: "ἐπιδερμίδα & ἐπιδερμίς"</note> epidermis.
- In Latin, <note>original: "Cuticula"</note> Cuticle.
- In English, the scarf skin or chaff skin <note>The "scarf skin" is an archaic term for the epidermis; "chaff skin" refers to its tendency to flake like grain husks.</note> by way of similarity.

It seems to have an origin (according to almost everyone's opinion) that is waste-based <note>original: "excrementitiam"</note> and not derived from the primary seed. Authors vary regarding this, for:
- Some will have it that it arises from the "flowering" of the blood.
- Others say it is born from the excess of the true skin.
- My own opinion in this matter, however, is that it is produced by a denser and drier portion of the air breathed in through the pores, adhering to the external surface of the body or the true skin.

It has a substance that is very thin, delicate, and porous.

It possesses a form very similar to a spider's web, or (as we have observed) to the husk of wheat: For as the true skin is to the flesh, so we perceive the bran of the wheat to be to its flour; similarly, the cuticle is observed to adhere to the skin no differently than the wheat husk to its bran. It is divided from the true skin, and is gradually brought to the eyes or subjected to treatment by blistering medications, or a glowing iron, or other such means, and is thus lifted away.

It is entirely destitute of sensation, since it falls away without feeling or pain both in those afflicted by sickness and those endowed with health (from whom it is sometimes removed for the sake of beauty through the ingenious mystery of decoration <note>Likely a reference to cosmetic peeling or skin treatments of the era.</note>).

In temperament, it is cold and dry.

It has a twofold use:
- First, it defends the true skin (which is very sensitive) from the cold injuries of the external air.
- Second, it retains the watery <term>serous: relating to thin, watery fluids like sweat or serum</term> humors, which without such an obstacle would very easily penetrate through the true skin, as is clearly demonstrated in those who have been flayed.

It is afflicted by many various diseases, such as Spots, Purple fever, Scurf <note>original: "Morphea"</note>, Jaundice, Dandruff, Pimples, and Shingles <note>original: "Herpes miliaris"</note>, etc.

It has a <term>Saturnine: influenced by the planet Saturn, associated in medical astrology with coldness, dryness, and the outermost boundaries</term> constellation.

# CHAPTER II.

### Concerning the True Skin.

<margin>
The second of these parts of the common containers.
</margin>

*The Name* —
* The Greek is *derma* <note>original: "δέρμα"</note>.
* The Latin is *cutis vera*.
* The English is The Hide or skin.

*The Origin* is derived from a denser or thicker substance of the seed <note>The author refers to the "spermatic" theory of embryology, where certain tissues were thought to form directly from the father's seed</note>, or (as others will have it) from the very *periosteum* <note>the membrane covering the bones</note>.
*The Substance* is compacted from fibers of all kinds, so that it may dilate itself more easily; and fibers of this sort are derived from the thin threads of the nerves, from which it happens that this part claims for itself such exquisite sensation. It is extremely porous, for through those passages, vapors, sweats, and humors are accustomed to flow out.
*The Composition* is nervous <note>meaning fibrous or sinewy</note>, and it acquires for itself tiny little veins and even capillary arteries.
*The Figure* is likened to the bran in wheat, just as we not improperly compared its cuticle <note>the epidermis</note> to the chaff of the same above.
*The Quantity* is so ample and spacious that it involves the entire body, with only the perforated places (such as the mouth, ears, etc.) excepted. In *Density*, however, it is unequal, since it is thicker in the head than in the face.
*Observation* regarding a continuous break <note>a wound</note>: it is not regenerated, inasmuch as it is a "spermatic" part <note>Early modern medicine held that tissues formed from seed, like bone or skin, could not regrow once destroyed</note>; but indeed, a certain scar, brought on either by art or by nature, supplies this defect, by means of which the lips of the wound are glued together.
*Sensibility* is very apparent on account of its nervous composition (as has been said), although Aristotle seems to attribute that property to the flesh quite unadvisedly.
*The Temperament* is cold and dry, as are all other nervous members.

---

*Connections* are made by —
* The mode of union, as in the head and face.
* Communion, as in the hands, feet, and back.
* Hanging or placement against, as in the remaining members. And the instruments by which connections of this sort are made are the nerves, veins, and arteries.

*The Use* is twofold, namely for —
* Fortifying the fat and the flesh against the cold attacks of the external air.
* Receiving and retaining serous vapors, lest those exhaling from the center should suddenly vanish.

*Ailments* or the most familiar diseases are itching, the mange <note>scabies</note>, ringworm <note>serpigo</note>, scabs <note>impetigo</note>, <unclear>sphora</unclear> <note>likely a skin eruption or psoriasis</note>, leprosy, smallpox <note>variolae</note>, and others of this kind.
*The Constellation* <note>The astrological ruler</note> is Saturn ♄, who has power over hides.

# CHAPTER III.
## Concerning Fat.

<margin>
This third part of the common containing parts <note>The "containing parts" are the outer layers of the body that enclose the internal organs.</note>
</margin>

<image-desc>The following text is organized into branching logical divisions using decorative braces to categorize the names, origins, and properties of fat (Pinguedo).</image-desc>

It is named:
- In Latin:
    - *Pinguedo* <note>General term for fat.</note>
    - *Adeps* <note>Often refers to harder animal fat or suet.</note>
- In English: fat or Grease.

It has its origin, as some wish to claim, from thick blood; nevertheless (as it seems to me), it is derived as much from the oily vapor of the external air itself inhaled through the pores, as from the fattier juice of nourishment. This vapor is condensed by external cold and congealed between the skin and the flesh; in this state of congealment, it is strengthened everywhere within the veins and membranous fibers (for the sake of better durability).

It is located between the true skin and the fleshy membrane.

It is found more abundant in respect to quantity in phlegmatic bodies <note>Refers to the Four Humors; those with a "phlegmatic" temperament were thought to be prone to moisture and weight.</note>, but more scarce in choleric ones.

It is entirely destitute of sensation.

It has an airy temperament, that is, hot and moist.

It has a twofold use, for:
- Like a double-layered garment, it defends internal heat against external cold.
- It is accustomed to preserve those consumed by extreme hunger for a long time by its own moisture.

It is sometimes affected by diseases, of which those that happen to it most frequently are sweats and preternatural <note>Abnormal or unnatural.</note> wasting away, and these are for the most part symptomatic.

It holds a Constellation:
- Common, which is Jupiter ♃ and Venus ♀.
- Proper to this region:
    - From the planets: Venus ♀.
    - From the signs: Virgo ♍.

# CHAPTER IV.
## Concerning the Fleshy Membrane.

<margin>
This part, filling the fourth place of the common containing parts
</margin>

It is called:
- By the ancients, as they were for the most part engaged in the anatomy of infants and beasts: the Membranous Membrane <note>original: "Panniculus membranosus"</note>.
- By more recent authors: because in adult humans it is seen to be such: the Fleshy Membrane <note>original: "Panniculus carnosus"; a layer of tissue often associated with muscle movement in the skin.</note>.

It is said to arise from liquefied fat.

It has a membranous substance in infants and brutes, but truly a fleshy one in humans (as has been said).

Its composition requires veins and arteries interwoven everywhere.

It is located between the fat and the common tunic of the muscles, to which it strongly adheres; between this membrane and the true skin, the superficial veins are observed to be scattered and sown about, except in the head, forehead, scrotum, penis, and similar parts.

It has a shape like the thinnest parchment.

It has its connection with the underlying muscles through fibers, and with the skin through the fat.

It has this use: that it defends the muscles and interior veins against external cold like a pelt or tunic.

It has a Constellation:
- Common: Saturn ♄.
- Proper to this region:
    - From the planets: Venus ♀.
    - From the signs: Virgo ♍ and Libra ♎.

# ON THE PROPER CONTAINING PARTS OF THE ABDOMEN.

### CHAPTER V.

#### Concerning the Common Tunic of the Muscles.

<margin>The last of the common containing parts</margin>
*Name: It is the common tunic <note>A "tunic" in this context refers to a thin covering or sheath of tissue.</note> of the muscles.*
*Origin: Derived from the Periosteum <note>The membrane covering the surface of bones.</note> as some maintain, or rather (as it seems to me) it is derived from the fibers of the muscles.*
*Substance: It is nervous and membranous.*
*Composition: It receives nerves, veins, arteries, and its own specific flesh.*
*Position: It is located between the bare and simple substance of the muscle and the fleshy layer <note>original: "panniculum carnosum," a layer of muscle or tissue just beneath the skin.</note>.*
*Use: Its purpose is twofold:*
*1. One is to hold the muscles in their natural site and position.*
*2. The other is to preserve them from decay, as without it, pus-like matter from neighboring parts would flow and drip into the empty cavities of the muscles.*

# Book II of the Lowest Region

The muscle <note>original: "musculus"</note> is so named because, when dried, it has a head or beginning, a body or middle, and a tail or end, appearing very similar in its boundaries to a mouse <note>The word "muscle" derives from the Latin "musculus," meaning "little mouse," as the movement of muscles under the skin was thought to resemble a mouse running.</note>. However, we nonetheless find a clear exception in this species of muscle against that general rule, insofar as it seems to deviate from that standard description of muscles.

<margin>This organic part of the body is (according to Galen in Book 1 of *On the Movement of Muscles*) the instrument of that motion which occurs according to impulse.</margin>

**It is composed of parts:**

- **Similar parts, which are five:**
    - Fibrous flesh, which is formed most aptly for receiving the influences of the motor faculty.
    - The nerve, which exists as the instrument of motion itself; because it directs the muscle in its action as a hand directs a pen.
    - The tendon or ligament, by whose office strength or power is usually conferred upon the muscle.
    - The vein and artery, whose role is to nourish that muscular substance and preserve it in its natural condition.
    - The common sheath of the muscles, which we mentioned above.
- **Dissimilar parts, which are three:**
    - The head or beginning, which is usually composed of ligaments originating from the bones, and these are for the most part nervous in nature.
    - The belly or middle, which is always fleshy, except in the diaphragm.
    - The tail or end, which is a nerve or tendon constituted of many fibers of membranous substance; however, these ends or tails are not always tendinous, but only in those muscles which are naturally disposed to move the bones.

**It is moved by means of a triple organ, namely:**

- **By a twofold motion, specifically:**
    - **Voluntary, from the animal faculty as its internal principle or agent, and is of this kind:**
        - **Simple, which is performed in six ways, namely:**
            - Upward.
            - Downward.
            - To the right.
            - To the left.
            - Forward.
            - Backward.
        - **Composite, performed in only one way, namely in a circle.**
    - **Involuntary, which is of a violent and forced nature.**
- **The brain, which commands like a king in his kingdom; for its duty is to judge the desired object—namely, is it useful? Is it to be pursued with hatred? Or the opposite—by means of reason, which sits like a judge on a raised tribunal seat in the middle of a theater. From here, therefore, arises the principle of voluntary motion.**
- **The nerve, which, in the place of a messenger or immediate servant, hastens to carry the brain's commands downward; this organ works by the power of the animal spirits <note>In early modern medicine, "animal spirits" were believed to be a subtle fluid or gas that traveled through hollow nerves to transmit sensation and motion.</note>, through which it is accustomed to communicate the brain's commands to the muscle.**
- **The muscle, which, illuminated by the animal spirits as if by divine rays, contracts itself and moves in various ways according to the demands of the matter to carry out the commands of its king. Thus, the judge is accustomed to give the sentence of death, the intermediate servant leads the condemned criminal to the cross, and the executioner, in the final place, executes the judge's sentence.**

I believe I have said enough regarding these matters; therefore, I shall descend briefly, and with a light leap, to the particular description of the five pairs of abdominal muscles.

## A Passing Note to the Reader.

Lest it should perhaps seem irregular or dishonest to you (kind reader and diligent observer of the images engraved in this treatise) that I have used figures of human parts that are not my own in this—

# Concerning the Proper Containing Parts of the Abdomen.

I have deemed it worthwhile and not at all inconvenient to inform you that you find these anatomical figures expressed in my work not by my own choice, but through the prayers and insistence of Johann Theodor de Bry, our engraver <note>Johann Theodor de Bry (1561–1623) was a famous Flemish-German engraver and publisher known for his high-quality scientific illustrations.</note>; indeed, I want it known that this was carried out against my own desire. He provided a twofold reason for his wish, as explained so many times in his letters: first, that I might relieve him of the loss of expense and fruitless labor through this service of mine; and second, so that by reducing such expenses, he might be able to sell this work of ours at a cheaper price, more affordable for scholars. Moved by this consideration, I am forced—contrary to the goal of my own invention and the inclination of my will—to be restricted to those figures of the most renowned Caspar Bauhin <note>Caspar Bauhin (1560–1624) was a Swiss botanist and anatomist whose "Theatrum Anatomicum" became a standard reference.</note>, seeing as they were engraved in copper at the expense of the said Theodor de Bry in the year 1605, and are ready at hand with him without further cost or the weariness of storage.
