## CHAPTER III.
### Concerning the oblique ascending muscles.

<margin>The oblique ascending muscle has its</margin>
Name, both
> From its motion, which is carried upwards.
> Because its flesh is composed of oblique fibers stretching upwards, as is demonstrated in Plate 2 by the letters H H.

Substance, which is partly nervous <note>In this period, "nervous" often referred to sinewy or ligamentous tissue</note>, partly fleshy, and partly tendinous, as was just said.
Size, which is sufficiently large and spacious.
Shape, in respect to the position of its fibers, which, together with those of the oblique descending muscle, imitate this intersection. For this, observe the X in Plate 2 at fiber I, intersecting fiber H, so that the fibers seem to intersect themselves in a center. And indeed, if we explore the matter a little more accurately, we will find that all the fibers of all these four muscles coincide in the same center, as if Nature herself wished to contract the entire power of these muscles into a single point, so that the forces thus united might perform the function destined by Nature for this part more expeditiously and powerfully. Therefore, the position of the fibers of the four muscles intersecting themselves in the center is of this sort:

<image-desc>A circular diagram with a dotted perimeter. Inside the circle, four straight lines intersect at a central point, resembling a compass rose or a wheel with spokes. The lines are labeled with lowercase letters: a vertical line from 'a' (top) to 'f' (bottom), a horizontal line from 'g' (left) to 'h' (right), and two diagonal lines from 'e' to 'b' and 'c' to 'd'.</image-desc>

a. b. and c. d. represent the intersection made by the fibers of the descending and ascending muscles. e. f. is the fiber of the <term>rectus muscle</term> <note>The "straight" abdominal muscle, known today as the rectus abdominis</note> meeting with the others in unity at the center. And also fiber g. h. is that of the transverse muscle, which meets with the rest at the central point. This is explained from the observation of the fibers of the oblique descending muscle (A. or I.), the oblique ascending (H.), the transverse (K.), and the rectus (E.), showing precisely how they intersect one another. See Plate 2.

Various connections, for its parts are bound to:
> The Origin: the attachment of the <term>ilium</term> <note>The uppermost and largest bone of the pelvis</note>.
> The Side: the <term>apophyses</term> <note>bony outgrowths or processes</note> of the vertebrae of the back.
> Above: its fleshy part to the 4 lower false ribs.
> The membranous Tail: (after its tendinous embrace of the rectus muscle) to the substance of the <term>linea alba</term> <note>Latin: "white line"; the fibrous structure that runs down the midline of the abdomen</note>, see Plate 2, letters H H. D.

A double utility, namely for:
> The compression of the intestines, for the sake of excretion.
> The pulling down of the <term>thorax</term> <note>The chest</note>, both straight and obliquely, so that respiration may be better and more easily achieved.

Fixed Constellation <note>The astrological correspondence assigned to this body part</note>, which is Virgo ♍ and Libra ♎.

# CHAPTER VI.
## Concerning the Pyramidal muscles, and those which are called the cremasters.

<margin>The Pyramidal Muscle</margin>
It is said to take its name from its likeness, since it displays the shape of a pyramid.
Its substance is fleshy, and in this regard it seems to differ from the property and definition of a true muscle (according to the opinion of Columbus <note>Realdo Colombo (c. 1515–1559), a famous Italian anatomist and surgeon</note>).
They are numbered as right and left.
Its position is above the pubic bone, where its fleshy base takes its beginning, while its cone rises directly within the hollow of the rectus muscle. As is indicated by the letter F in the following Table 2.
Its base is connected to the pubic bone, upon which it is braced as if on its own foundation; however, its cone, reaching into the hollow of the rectus muscle, is attached there with a more tendinous flesh. As is shown by F in Table 2.
It is useful (contrary to the opinion of Columbus, who denies that a part of this kind possesses either the definition or property of a muscle) for achieving the erection of the penis, as seems probable from its position.
It has a fixed constellation, which is Leo <note>original: ♌</note> according to the judgment of the astrologers.

Furthermore, as pertains to those muscles which are called the Cremasters <term>Cremaster: from the Greek 'to hang'; the muscles that support the testicles</term> and the "suspenders" (inasmuch as the testicles of both man and woman are suspended by them), they are not properly numbered among those of the abdomen, as they belong only improperly to that region, although Cabrollius <note>André du Laurens or Barthélemy Cabrol, noted 16th-century surgeons</note> seems to support this opinion.

---

# CHAPTER VII.
## Concerning the White Line.

The name is attributed to it by likeness, since it displays the appearance of a white and somewhat broad line <note>original: Linea Alba</note>.
Its substance is tendinous or membranous.
Its composition is formed from the meeting of the tendinous ends of the eight aforementioned muscles of the abdomen into a unity of essence.
Its size is unequal, as it is larger and wider above the navel, but below it, it is much narrower and tighter.
<margin>Of which</margin>
Its shape is compared to the Milky Way in the heavens in respect to its color; but in respect to its direct passage, it can best be compared in the Microcosm <note>The human body viewed as a miniature reflection of the universe</note> to the meridian circle of the Macrocosmic <note>The universe or Great World</note> sky. For since the belly is round, it can be compared with the hemisphere of the world, of which we imagine the navel to be the arctic pole, through which this meridian of ours seems to pass, just as the cosmic one passes through the polar star of the world.
Its position is in the middle of the belly, which it intersects into two equal parts, like the artificial meridian of the world's hemisphere. This is delineated by ddd in Table 2.
Its action and use is that, by the gathering of the said extremities into one line, both the Peritoneum itself and the umbilical vessels are strengthened by it.
Constellation:
* From the Planets, it is referred to Saturn <note>original: ♄</note> and Venus <note>original: ♀</note>.
* From the fixed stars, it has regard for those looking upon the particular members of this region.

### CONCLUSION.

The diseases of these muscles are wounds, bruises, abscesses <note>original: Apostemata</note>, inflammations, gangrenes, tumors, and others of this kind.

# BOOK THREE.

# Book III of the Lower Region.

## CHAPTER I.

### Concerning the Peritoneum.

**I**n the second or preceding portion of our study regarding the parts contained within this region, we have methodically, and in proper succession, stripped away first the "double cloak"—namely the skin and the cuticle; then their "double-layered lining," which is the fat; and finally their "multi-layered garment" composed of the muscles. Now, indeed, we have arrived at its final and most internal clothing, or thin undershirt: that is, the membrane called the **peritoneum**, which immediately encompasses beneath itself and wraps within itself all the parts or members included in this region. We shall, therefore, speak of it in this place, so that once its history and description are thus completed, we may proceed slowly toward the revelation and explanation of the parts contained under it.

It is called:
* In Greek, *peritonaion* <note>original: "περιτόναιον"</note>, because it circles around all the internal organs on every side, and seems, as it were, to swim both above and below them.
* In Arabic, *Syphach* <note>A term used in medieval anatomy derived from Arabic 'sifāq' for a membrane.</note>.
* In Latin, the membrane containing the internal organs.

<margin>The membrane immediately encompassing the internal organs</margin>

*It arises, according to the opinion of Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, the influential 2nd-century Greek physician.</note>, from the extremities of the transverse muscles, specifically in that very place where they meet with the fleshy portion of the Diaphragm—that is, around its circumference; namely around A.A. and K.K. in Plate 3.*

*It has a spermatic substance <note>In early modern medicine, "spermatic" referred to tissues believed to originate from the primary reproductive fluid, characterized by being white, cold, and dry, such as membranes or bones.</note>, which in its nature is simple and thin, yet nevertheless quite firm and sinewy, the better to retain natural heat within the center.*

*It appears to be composed of two tunics (although only a single one is attributed to it by Galen). Furthermore, nerves, fibrous membranes, as well as small veins and some small arteries also concur in its composition. For the Arteries and veins, see II. and KK. in Plate 3.*

*It enjoys a quantity so ample and spacious that it extends itself over all the vessels of nutrition: for it embraces all those parts which are contained between the diaphragm and the legs themselves, and it even wraps itself inward near the loins, in which part it is also observed to be thickest. Its extension is demonstrated by the letters A.A. B. C. D. in Plate 3.*

*It possesses a nearly oval shape, if it were stretched out entirely as it is, and in its form it imitates that sack in which the oil of almonds or olives is usually pressed out. On the outside, it is observed to be rough, so that it may adhere better and more firmly to the muscles; but on the inside it is quite smooth and free from roughness, lest it bring any discomfort by its inequality to the intestines situated beneath it.*

*It is found to be perforated in many places, yet these holes are not in it in vain, but each of them is destined for its own use and office. Its openings are marked in Plate 3 by the \*\* signs.*

*It claims for itself a position immediately beneath the transverse muscles: and the "white line" <note>The linea alba, the fibrous structure running down the midline of the abdomen.</note> passes through its middle, as seen by E.E. in Plate 3. And it lies over the omentum <note>The fatty apron covering the intestines</note>: see Plate 4. a. AA. BB. and Plate 5. BB. where it is divided.*

*It is connected to the transverse muscles by tendons; and also to all the common parts, insofar as it is observed to provide them with a common tunic; and at the top it is attached to the pointed cartilage <note>The xiphoid process at the base of the breastbone.</note> F. in Plate 3: and in Plate 4. a. its connection to the base of the bladder is indicated.*

It has a manifold use, for:
* It gives a common tunic <note>A covering layer or membrane.</note> to all the contained members of this region, namely those pertaining to nutrition and generation as well as to excretion. As is shown by A.A. B. C. D. in Plate 3.
* It contributes to the excretory faculty of the intestines. How it brings forth the intestines from Plate 3 can be seen by its position.
* It strengthens the intestines in their natural position. As is explained by the same plate.
* It preserves the stomach <note>original: "ventriculum"</note>, and stands in place of a defense for it, lest it be suffocated by flatulent vapors.
* It retains the innate heat in its center, for it defends it so that it does not escape or fly away: and it appears to provide this because of its firm compaction. For this, see Plate 3.

# On the Peritoneum and the Parts Contained Immediately Beneath It.

Relaxation, which occurs for the most part from excessive moisture, from which the following diseases arise:

For these types of diseases, I have known craftsmen highly skilled in surgery to use an incision both in the lower <term>Mirach</term> <note>An Arabic term referring to the abdominal wall or the soft parts of the belly</note> or part of the abdomen, as well as toward its upper part, in safer locations and removed from the membranes of the muscles. At the same time, I saw them employing a variety of ligatures, sometimes made of hemp thread, silk, and occasionally of pure gold (which they praised above all others), though I confess with varying success.

**Dropsy** <note>original: "Hydropisis"; an old term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid</note>, which is accustomed to gather around this tunic; and this is the reason why Paul of Aegina <note>A 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician</note> taught, not inaptly, that the incision for Dropsy ought to be made a little above the navel, namely toward the side opposite to the side in which the principal organ is affected. For example, if the cause of the dropsy lies in a disordered condition of the liver, let the incision or perforation be made toward the left; if from that of the Spleen, toward the right. Nevertheless, more recent authors, taught indeed by daily experience, were accustomed to perforate the navel itself for this malady, a practice which I myself have observed many times. Here, however, it should be noted in passing that I am not referring to two types of Dropsy, namely <term>Anasarca</term> <note>General swelling of the whole body</note> and <term>Tympanites</term> <note>Swelling due to gas in the abdominal cavity</note>, but to <term>Ascites</term> <note>Fluid accumulation specifically in the peritoneal cavity</note> and its treatment in this place.

### TABLE

# On the Peritoneum and the Members contained beneath it.

## CHAPTER II.
### Concerning the Navel and the Umbilical Vessels.

Regarding the member located in the center of the belly:
*   **The Name,**
    *   Commonly, it is the Navel <note>original: "Umbilicus"</note>.
    *   Ancient, and used by the elders, it is called the "little old woman" <note>original: "vetula"</note>, on account of its wrinkles; for the navel is wrinkled like an old woman.
*   **The Shape,** is similar to the orifice of an intestine contracted in the manner of a purse.
*   **The Position,** is in the very midpoint of the belly, and in its placement it relates to the rounded belly as the North Star <note>original: "stella polaris"</note> relates to its hemisphere; and we have also previously compared the "white line" <note>the *linea alba* of the abdomen</note> of the same to the meridian circle of the world, not inaptly.
*   **It is illustrated** by the letter C in Table 4, specifically where it is divided from the Peritoneum.
*   **The Vessels,** are various, in the consideration of which two things must be observed, namely their:
    *   **Number or distinction,** for there are four, namely:
        *   **One Vein,** called the umbilical vein, of which the:
            *   **Origin,** is from the womb <note>original: "matrice"</note>.
            *   **Termination,** is in the center, as it were, of the liver itself, and it enters almost at the root of the *vena cava* itself. See B in Table 4, and D. B. & A. B. in Figure 2.
        *   **Two Arteries,** also called umbilical, which, seeking a path downward through the doubling of the Peritoneum, are carried near the bladder, and end there where the great artery <note>the aorta</note> divides itself into branches.
        *   **A single vessel** called the Urachus <note>term: Urachus; a duct connecting the bladder to the umbilical cord in the fetus</note>, which, taking its origin from the bottom of the bladder, is said to draw urine from the fetus and return it through the passage of the navel. See H. and b. in Table 4.
    *   **The Use,** which is of importance:
        *   **Significant,** while the fetus remains in the womb. For by means of these, through the navel:
            *   The fetus is nourished in the womb.
            *   Urinary excrements are expelled.
        *   **Of no use,** once the infant is brought forth into the light, except that the umbilical vein stretches and pulls the substance of the liver downward, and that strongly; it is believed that unless nature had provided a ligament of this kind, a sudden suffocation would occur.
*   **Astrological Correspondence.**
    *   From the planets: Venus <note>original: ♀</note>.
    *   From the signs: Libra <note>original: ♎</note>.

# CHAPTER III.
->Concerning the Omentum.<-

<margin>The Name, among:</margin>
*   The Greeks, is *epiploon* <note>original: ἐπίπλοον</note>, as if "floating upon the intestines."
*   The Arabs, is *Girbe* or *Zirbus*.
*   The Latins, is *Omentum*, and it is called by Aristotle the "serous" or "fatty membrane."
*   The English, is *The cale or quayf* <note>Modern English: the caul or coif, referring to a hood or net-like covering</note>.

**Origin**, comes partly from the peritoneum <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note>, and partly from oily blood.
**Substance**, is spermatic <note>meaning white and membranous</note> or membranous, interspersed with fat.
**Composition**, consists of a double membrane interwoven with fat, which also requires for its completion veins, arteries, and nerves springing from the sixth conjugation <note>In early anatomy, the "sixth conjugation" referred to what we now identify as the Vagus nerve and others</note>. Regarding this, see *Plate a. 4. Q Q Q Q. & Plate b. 4. ll. mm. & Plate b. 4. figure 2.* A notable vein is shown at C. And also B. C. D. And g. in figure 1.
**Quantity**, is larger and deeper in women, on account of their giving birth, than in men.
**Figure**, is like a pouch or a travel-bag. See *Plate b. 4. a a a a. b b b b. And I. I.* where the shape is indicated.
**Placement**, is above the intestines. See *Plates 4. K K K K. And Plate b 4. HHH. And CCC.*
**Temperament**, in respect to the disposition of the membrane, it is earthy or cold and dry; but truly, insofar as it is mixed with fat, it is seen to claim an airy or hot and moist faculty for itself.
**Connection**, it is connected with the Colon intestine, for the omentum is present for this intestine in place of the Mesentery <note>the membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</note>. Concerning this, see *Plate b. 4. G. G.* It is also bound to the vessels of the spleen, as in *Plate b. 13. B. B. C C.*

<margin>The Use, that it may contribute to:</margin>
*   The concoction <note>digestion</note> of the stomach and the small intestines, because it retains heat within, and for that reason preserves the natural heat by which digestion is completed. See *Plate b. 4. G G.* where it is shown to pass across the bottom of the stomach.
*   The supporting of the branch of the portal vein proceeding from the liver and tending toward the spleen, as shown at *G. Plate b. 4.*
*   The defending of the intestines from external cold, for its fat together with the veins and arteries warm the belly and also the stomach. See *Plate a. 4. K K K K.* for it covers the intestines.

<margin>To which belong:</margin>
<margin>The more common diseases</margin>
**Rupture**, that which is called *Epiplocele*, which occurs when the omentum descends into the lower coverings of the testicles.
**Precipitation**, namely when the substance of the omentum falls into the bottom of the belly. I knew a certain "golden knight" <note>a knight bachelor or titled gentleman</note> nearly 80 years of age affected by a disease of this kind, who, because of an evident defect of the Omentum, was troubled by a sensible coldness of the intestines. From this it also happened that he used to suffer from a frequent slipperiness of the belly <note>diarrhea</note> and catarrh descending from the head. To counter these evils, he was forced day and night to fortify his viscera against the assaults of external cold with the skins of swans and foxes. Nevertheless, a certain menstrual-like matter <note>referring here to a monthly discharge rather than female menstruation</note> used to sweat out and gush forth every month through the region of the groin and the pubic bone, tending toward a yellow color; I judged this to have come from the fatty matter of the fallen substance, which could be felt and discerned by the hands from the outside.
**Consumption**, for I saw a boy suffering from this evil, for whom, as this member was affected, a rebellious catarrh with a vehement cough came upon him, so that a significant thinness occupied his entire body in a short time. I judged him to be affected by wasting <note>tabes</note> and consumption <note>phthisis</note>, not indeed without the agreement of others. But indeed, when our patient died and the corpse was carefully examined internally by a skilled surgeon, we found the omentum destroyed, the intestines as if frozen with cold, and the brain filled with a phlegmatic and icy humor, which used to drip steadily and copiously into the lungs. The lungs were healthy enough beyond expectation, except that their convex surface had taken on a somewhat bluish color due to the abundance of catarrh. The small veins appearing on the surface of the heart were swollen; the blood contained in them was frozen into fixed blue-colored branches by the copious catarrh and fluid. Finally, I concluded the cause of the disease was the failure of the Omentum, by which the intestines, serving digestion, were weakened by cold and could not perform their work due to the lack of natural heat. The liver, however, due to the lack of chyle <note>nutritive juice from digestion</note>—which the mesenteric veins ought to have steadily supplied to it—began to burn with unnatural heat because of the lack of its usual humor. It greedily raised the spirit of the raw chyle into the region of the brain, which in that region froze into water or rheum, and steadily threw itself downward into the cavity of the lungs, excited a vehement cough, and at length, with the abundance of watery matter suffocating the life-giving spirits and the blood being frozen and thus deprived of natural motion, I perceived it as necessary that the patient exchange life for death, even while the lungs remained whole.

<margin>The Constellation, from:</margin>
*   The Planets: Venus.
*   The signs of the Zodiac: Virgo.

# CHAPTER IV.
## On the Intestines in General.

The intestines are considered either in:
- **General**, and thus we consider the entire intestinal tube, of which we note:
    - **The Name** among the:
        - Greeks: <term>entera</term> <note>original: ἔντϵϱα; the root of the modern word "enteric"</note>.
        - Latins: *Intestina*.
        - English: <term>The guts, or bowels, or trips</term> <note>"Trips" is an archaic term for tripe or intestines</note>.
    - **The Origin**
        - **Of the Tunics** <note>The layers or membranes of the intestinal wall</note>:
            - Of the two interior ones, it is from the "dura mater" <note>original: dura matre; early anatomists often believed the internal membranes of the body were continuous with the protective layers of the brain</note>.
            - Of the single exterior one, it is derived from the <term>peritoneum</term> <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note>.
        - Of the veins, which are innumerable, they are derived from the trunk of the <term>portal vein</term> and the mesenteric branch.
    - **The Substance**, which is <term>spermatic</term> <note>original: spermatica; in early medicine, this referred to white, fibrous tissues (like nerves and membranes) thought to be formed from the "seed" in the womb</note> and nervous for the sake of greater expansion.
    - **The Composition**, which is made of three tunics, consisting of:
        - Two internal ones proper to themselves, of which:
            - The innermost is dense, fleshy, and fatty, woven from transverse and circular fibers. See letter g. in Plate 6, Figure 4.
            - The outer is thin and nervous, composed of oblique and straight fibers. See Plate 6, Figure 4, letters ff.
        - One external layer common to them, as it is derived from the Peritoneum, which usually provides a covering to every part contained in this region. This tunic is designed by nature so that if the two internal tunics are perforated by a sharp humor <note>an acidic or irritating bodily fluid</note>—which often happens in **Dysentery**—the waste may still be retained by the strength of this very strong and firm tunic, preventing it from flowing into the cavity of the belly. Look at ee. in Plate 6, Figure 4.
        - Moreover, the inner of these tunics differs from that of the stomach, because the stomach’s is thick and fleshy, while this one is thin and nervous.
        - For a demonstration of these tunics, see Plate 6, Figure 4, namely ee, ff, g, and hh.
    - **The Quantity** (size), either in:
        - **Length**, according to:
            - The experience of André Laurent <note>André du Laurens (1558–1609), a prominent French royal physician</note>, the measurement is observed to equal seven times the length of the body, provided the intestines are dried and extended by blowing air into them (as is usually done).
            - But indeed, in my own practice, I found a body of 1 and 1/2 <term>ells</term> <note>original: ulnæ; a traditional unit of measurement</note> whose intestinal length did not exceed 9 ells, and of this dimension, the <term>colon</term> <note>the large intestine</note> claimed 1 ell for itself.
        - **Width**, which varies according to the arrangement of the particular intestines; for example, the "thick" intestines (large intestines) are wider than the "thin" ones (small intestines).
    - **The Shape**, which is likened to a horn or a trumpet, whose orifice and neck and entire anterior part are observed to be thinner and narrower, while its posterior part is larger and wider; likewise, its slender portion is narrow, while the thicker portion is spacious. However, its shape as it lies in the body is winding <note>original: anfractuosa; full of twists and turns</note>, as seen in Plate 5, where A, BB, CC, D, E, and FF signify the surrounding neighboring members, and H, I, K, N, O, R, S, and T designate the seats of the specific intestines.
    - **General Connection**, which is made by the <term>mesentery</term> <note>the fold of membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</note>, which is also firmly bound to the back.
    - **Position**, which is below the navel and in the hypogastric region <note>the lower abdomen</note>, stretching from the bottom of the stomach all the way to the anus; in its upper part, it is covered by the <term>Epiploon</term> or <term>Omentum</term> <note>the fatty apron of the belly</note>. For the positioning, see Figure 5, which follows.
    - **Sensibility**, which is apparent and arises because this part is nervous; however, this sensitivity is not very exquisite, but rather somewhat dulled due to the abundance of fat adhering to it and the viscous fluid involved with it.
    - **General Use**, which is partly for digestion, and partly for receiving, retaining, and—at the proper time—expelling the waste of the first digestion.
    - **General Diseases**, which are flux, constipation, gas, worms, diarrhea, <term>lientery</term> <note>a type of diarrhea where food is passed undigested</note>, dysentery, piercing pain, rumbling, growling, etc.
- **Species** (specific types), concerning which see the following chapter.

# CHAPTER V.
## Concerning the Intestines in Detail.

<image-desc>The page consists of a large, complex ramified diagram (synoptic table) using hierarchical braces to classify the characteristics of the small intestines. A primary brace on the left groups the entire contents under a descriptive preamble. This then branches into five main categories: Name, Quantity, Connection, Use, and Diseases.</image-desc>

The upper part is called the slender and thin intestine, which is divided into three parts, each of which has the name of a specific intestine; and in all of them these things are to be considered, namely:

*   **Name, for that of the**
    *   First part,
        *   In Greek, it is { **Twelve-fingers-long** <note>original: "Dodecadactilos"</note>. / **Gatekeeper** <note>original: "Pylorus"</note>. / **Outgrowth** <note>original: "Ecphysis"</note>.
        *   In Latin, it is { **Duodenum**, because it equals 12 fingers in length. / **Doorkeeper** <note>original: "Ianitor"</note> / **Gate-bearer** <note>original: "Portanarius"</note> { Inasmuch as it is continuous with the lower orifice of the stomach.
    *   Second part, is the **empty intestine** <note>original: "ieiunum"</note> because, when an incision is made, it is always found empty and destitute of <term>chyle</term> <note>the milky fluid of digested food</note>.
    *   Third part, is called the **Ileon**, since its end terminates around the <term>ilium bone</term> <note>the large bone forming the upper part of each half of the pelvis</note>.

*   **Quantity, namely**
    *   Length
        *   Of the first, it extends from the lowest orifice of the stomach to the beginning of the jejunum, for it ends in that place where the duct of the gall bladder penetrates into the intestines. You will see this in Table 6, Figure 1, where H. is the <term>Pylorus</term> <note>the opening from the stomach into the duodenum</note>, and H. to K. measures the duodenum; L. is the bile duct.
        *   Of the second, it stretches from the end of the duodenum to the beginning of the ileum intestine.
        *   Of the third, it is measured from the end of the jejunum all the way to the <term>blind intestine</term> <note>original: "caecum"</note>. In Table 6, N. is the end of the thin intestines.
    *   The width of all is narrow, and they are observed not to differ much from one another in this regard.

*   **Connection, namely**
    *   Of the Duodenum, it is with the stomach.
    *   Of the Jejunum }
    *   Of the Ileum } with the <term>Mesentery</term> <note>the fold of membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</note>. Concerning which see Table 8, letters L M M M.
    *   Their natural position can be determined from Table 5, where K. S. T. denote the portion of them below the navel.

*   **Use, which is**, that they serve for the discharge and completion of <term>concoction</term> <note>an ancient physiological term for the "cooking" or digestion of food by bodily heat</note>. Just as concoction occurs in the stomach, in the liver, and in the solid parts, so also three stages are found in each of those concoctions; for in the
    *   First Digestion, there is { Preparation in the mouth. / Cooking in the stomach. / Discharge or perfection in the thin intestines.
    *   Second Digestion, there is { Preparation in the <term>mesaraic veins</term> <note>veins of the mesentery</note>. / Cooking in the liver. / Discharge or perfection in the larger veins.
    *   Third Digestion, there is { Preparation in the capillary veins. / Cooking by application and union in the fleshy habit. / Discharge by assimilation and "flesh-making" <note>original: "carnificationem"</note>.

*   **Diseases, for those of the**
    *   Upper part, include the regurgitation of bile into the stomach, outgrowth, slipperiness, etc.
    *   Middle or jejunum, include either the too slow or too rapid attraction or "devouring" of the chylous matter.
    *   Last or Ileum, include that suffering which, from the affected place, is called the <term>iliac passion</term> <note>a painful and dangerous intestinal obstruction</note>.

Note that the particular demonstration of these slender intestines is found in Figure 1 of Table 6 immediately following, where H. etc. appear.

<margin>
The general intestine, or its continuous tube, is divided into two parts differing in kind, of which:
</margin>

The **lower thick part** is also distinguished into three sections, regarding which several things should be observed:

*   **Name**
    *   Of the first part, which is the:
        *   **One-eyed** <note>original: "Monoculus"</note>, named for its single opening.
        *   **Sack** <note>original: "Saccus"</note>, from its likeness to one.
        *   **Blind intestine** <note>original: "Cæcum intestinum"</note>, because in it there is no direct passage of waste, but rather a turning back or "regurgitation."
    *   Of the second part, the **Colon**.
    *   Of the third part, the:
        *   **Straight intestine** <note>original: "Intestinum rectum"</note>, named for its physical position.
        *   **Longaon** <note>An archaic term for the rectum, derived from its length in certain animals</note>.

*   **Substance: It is thick, and possesses these features:**
    *   In the first (the **blind intestine**), a small appendage like an **earthworm** <note>original: "lumbricus"; this refers to the appendix</note>. See Table 6, figures 1 and 2, at point P.
    *   In the second (the **colon**), **semi-globes** <note>known today as haustra</note> protruding from what are like its ribs, which are not inappropriately called **cells**. Likewise, it has a valve inside which is found at the entrance to the blind intestine. See Table 6, figure 3, where the valve is marked with a † and the protrusions with R.
    *   In the third (the **rectum**), its structure is smooth and uniform, though it is somewhat wider at the end.

*   **Quantity**
    *   Of the **blind intestine**: it is very small and seems to be nothing other than the beginning of the colon. See O and P in Table 6, figures 1, 2, and 3.
    *   Of the **colon**: it is the most spacious of all and very wide in its breadth. See Table 6, figure 2, points O, Q, R, S, T, V.
    *   Of the **rectum**: it is shorter and more truncated than the colon, and is observed to be wider at its end.
    *   The shape of the colon and the blind intestine is shown in Table 6, figures 2 and 3.

*   **Position**
    *   Of the **blind intestine**: it is on the right side above the **iliac bone** <note>the "hip bone"</note>. In Table 5, it is marked with H. In Table 6, figure 1, O is the beginning of the thick intestines and figure 2, P is the blind intestine. In Table 5, its site is described by D.
    *   Of the **colon**: its path is varied, for it moves from the blind intestine to the right kidney, to which it is tied; then, passing under the hollow of the liver along the length of the bottom of the stomach, it crosses toward the spleen. Heading downward under the spleen, it inclines toward the left kidney and is also attached to it by a ligament. Finally, descending and turning toward the back, it makes two turns in an **S-shape** <note>the sigmoid colon</note>, and thus joins with the start of the rectum. In Table 5, the path from I to K denotes the movement of the colon from the right kidney to the liver, etc.
    *   Of the **rectum**: it begins at the **sacrum** <note>the large triangular bone at the base of the spine</note> and extends all the way to the very end of the hip bone, terminating in the anus. In women, this lies beneath the uterus, and in both sexes, it is adjacent to the bladder. <note>The author uses the term "sympathy" or "consensus" to describe how one organ's condition affects another.</note> Because of this connection, when the bladder is affected, the **Longaon** <note>rectum</note> also suffers, and vice versa. For the start of the rectum, see Table 5, letter O.
    *   In general, the start of these is indicated by the number 1 in the preceding Table 5.

*   **It should be noted in passing that there are three muscles of the anus:**
    *   One is circular, called the **sphincter**, which is placed at the end of the rectum; it is wider than it is thick and consists of transverse fibers. Its use is to keep the feces in the intestines by contracting like a **purse string** <note>original: "instar burse"</note>.
    *   Two are wide but thin; they begin at the ligaments of the sacrum and iliac bones and end in the area of the sphincter. Their use is to hold the rectum up so it does not fall downward <note>this describes the levator ani muscles</note>.

*   **Connection**
    *   The **blind intestine** is, for the most part, not tied to the **mesentery** <note>the fold of membrane attaching the organs to the body wall</note>.
    *   The **colon** is tied:
        *   To the **mesentery** by a general connection. See Table 8, figure 1.
        *   To the **omentum** <note>a fatty apron of tissue</note> or **epiploon**. See Table 4.b, figure 2, letters E, G, G, F.
        *   To the **kidneys** (see Table 6, figure 2, letter O) and the **bottom of the stomach** (as in Table 5, letters K and O).
        *   <gloss>And from this connection arises the vomiting in those suffering from a **stone** <note>kidney or gallstone</note>, and also in those with **colic** <note>severe abdominal pain</note>.</gloss>
    *   The head of the **rectum** is strongly tied to the sacrum, but at its end, it is squeezed by the muscles surrounding it in a circle, called sphincters, to which it is attached with a firm bond. See Table 6, figure 4, which shows the portion of the mesentery connecting the rectum to the sacrum; and from R to S in Table 8, figure 2, it indicates the part that binds this intestine to the back.

# On the Organs Immediately Contained Beneath the Peritoneum.

Their use is to receive and retain, at the proper time, the waste products of the first digestion. In this way, if any good and useful juice still remains in them, it may be drawn and lifted as much as possible toward the liver by means of the mesenteric vessels <term>messeraicis: veins that carry nutrients from the intestines to the liver</term>. Subsequently, they serve to expel and secrete these wastes for the sake of relieving the whole body.

---

### Tree of Intestinal Conditions and Influences

*   **Diseases which are —**
    *   Excessive dilation of the cecum <term>cæcum: the 'blind' pouch where the large and small intestines meet</term>, by which it happens that not only are the excrements of the colon usually vomited up, but sometimes even the substance of an enema <term>clysteris: a liquid injected into the rectum</term> administered through the anus; this is for the most part fatal.
    *   I believe also that various dangerous diseases are produced by the obstruction of this part.
    *   Of the colon: the colic passion <note>severe, cramping abdominal pain</note>.
    *   Of the rectum:
        *   Tenesmus <note>the painful and constant urge to evacuate the bowels, even when they are empty</note>.
        *   Relaxation of the sphincter.
        *   Fistula, etc.

*   **Astrological configuration from —**
    *   **Planets**
        *   By themselves: Jupiter [♃] and the Moon [☾].
        *   With the fixed stars, namely:
            *   | Saturn [♄] | | Aries [♈︎] and Libra [♎︎] |
            *   | Jupiter [♃] | | Taurus [♉︎] and Scorpio [♏︎] |
            *   | Mars [♂] | | Gemini [♊︎] and Sagittarius [♐︎] |
            *   | Sun [☉] | In | Cancer [♋︎] and Capricorn [♑︎] |
            *   | Venus [♀] | | Leo [♌︎] and Aquarius [♒︎] |
            *   | Mercury [☿] | | Virgo [♍︎] and Pisces [♓︎] |
            *   | Moon [☾] | | |
    *   **Fixed stars in**
        *   The thin [intestines]: Virgo [♍︎].
        *   The thick [intestines]: Libra [♎︎].

---

Note that wherever I make mention of the planets with the fixed stars, such as Saturn [♄] in Libra [♎︎], etc., it should be understood as the beginning of the disease. This occurs when the planet which is the ruler of the sixth house <note>In traditional medical astrology, the sixth house of a birth chart or a diagnostic chart governs health and illness</note> is found outside the sixth house in one of these signs. For example, if Saturn—who is the ruler of Saturn’s house—is found at the cusp of the sixth house (the significator of disease), but is located elsewhere in Gemini [♊︎], it denotes that the disease was produced in the belly, and so on for the others.

At this point, we think it would not be useless to propose a double question pertaining to these parts along with their solutions. The first is: **Can enemas [clysteres] injected through the anus ascend to the stomach?** We affirm this, as Rhazes <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi, a highly influential 9th-century Persian physician</note> affirms it in the 9th book of the *Continens*. However, Galen in the 5th book of *On the Method of Medicine* denies it. Yet, in the 3rd book of *On the Causes of Symptoms*, Galen himself seems to admit the same. We say, therefore, that it is one thing to speak of a stomach that is healthy, and another to discuss one that is diseased. Furthermore, a poor condition of the valves and of the blind intestine—whose job is to prevent liquids injected through the anus from moving upward into the small intestines, and from there into the stomach, whose lower opening, called the Gatekeeper [Portonarius] <note>the pylorus</note>, is weak and has feeble retention—is the primary cause of such an abnormal <note>original: "praeternaturalis," meaning a condition outside the natural state of health</note> occurrence.

The second question is: **Can enemas injected through the anus provide nourishment?** We say that the substance of an enema can nourish the body by reason of the small branches of the portal vein inserted into the rectum and the colon by means of the mesentery. However, we acknowledge that the administration of this kind of nourishment contributes only a little to the body, both because of the smallness of the branches and because they are quite few in number.

## CHAPTER VI.
### Concerning the portal vein with its branches.

Even before we proceed further to the other parts enclosed centrally within the corpse, we first consider it worthwhile to bring to light the description of the <term>portal vein</term> <note>original: "venæ portæ"; the large vein carrying blood from the digestive organs to the liver</note> itself. This is because it is usually demonstrated and placed before the eyes of the spectators more clearly before the removal of the intestines or viscera and their extraction from the cavity of the belly. We especially note here its <term>splenic branch</term> <note>the vein leading to the spleen</note>, which is said to carry the <term>melancholic juice</term> <note>original: "succum melancholicum"; black bile, one of the four humors believed to cause melancholy</note> from the liver to the spleen. Its trunk is indicated by B in Table 7.

**Name:** It is called the portal vein from its function, since the juice <note>chyle</note> transferred from the intestines by the mesenteric veins to the liver is observed to enter and be introduced through the small branches of this vein as if through a gate.
**Origin:** It originates in the liver, in which its thinner roots are scattered and spread out. See Table 4, Figure 1, g. And Table 7, 1. 2. 3. 4.

<margin>
Of this vein: The branches are eight, of which
</margin>
**The First** climbs to the top of the stomach, where it circles the stomach like a crown, whence it is also called the **coronal vein**. See P. Q. R. of Table 7.
**The Second** creeps along the length through the bottom or lowest part of the stomach. The use of these two branches is to nourish the substance of the stomach, contrary to the opinion of those who think it is nourished by <term>chyle</term> <note>the milky fluid of digested food</note>. See N. and OO. and D. as well as Y. Z. in the said Table.
**The Third** is assigned to the nutrition of the <term>omentum</term> <note>the fatty "apron" hanging over the intestines</note>, through which it is observed to be dispersed everywhere. See Table 7, H. L. S. V.
**The Fourth** proceeds to the spleen, and its duty is to carry the blood or melancholic juice from the liver into the spleen (as a place destined for this by nature). From this kind of branch arises that vein ascending upwards between the tunics of the stomach as far as its orifice, which is also usually called the **short vessel** <note>original: "vas breue"</note> by practitioners. Its duty is to raise the acid humor created in the spleen upward to the orifice of the stomach; they say the property of this humor is to excite appetite and hunger. See T. Table 7.
**The Fifth** reaches out to that large intestine called the **Colon**. See e e. Table 7, and a a a a.
**The Sixth** (and this is larger than the others) it sends out to the small intestines; however, its small branches are more prominent and visible in the <term>jejunum</term> <note>the middle part of the small intestine</note>, but the <term>ileum</term> <note>the final part of the small intestine</note> also seems to abound with a plenty of these. See Table 7, d d d d.
**The Seventh** passes to the **rectum** intestine. These last three branches, springing from the large trunk, immediately enter the substance of the **Mesentery**, where they distinguish themselves into infinite tiny veins which are called from this the **Mesaraic** <note>mesenteric</note> veins. The use and action of these three is thought to be to attract chyle from the intestines to the liver, so that it might be transmuted into blood by the **true Alchemy of nature**—that is, as if white chyle <note>likened to silver</note> were turned into red blood <note>likened to gold</note>. See ff. Table 7.
**The Last** (according to the opinion of <insert>Realdo</insert> Colombo) is that which is assigned to the spleen; he asserts that this branch, descending through the mesentery on the left side, seeks the end of the rectum, and there creates the **hemorrhoidal veins**. For this reason, we are advised by him and others that we should evacuate melancholic blood from the spleen through those veins using blood-letters <note>leeches or lancets</note>. But with their permission, let us be allowed to doubt this for a moment: for if we consider the origin of the veins or branches, which is mesenteric (marked by **c.** in the following demonstration, the extremity of which is **g. g.** indicating the hemorrhoidal veins), we will find that this duct by no means leads directly from the spleen. Thus, the whole bloody juice can be drawn out from the mesenteric branches of the Portal vein rather than the splenic dregs being extracted through this passage. Therefore, I would wish that Anatomists far more skilled than I in this matter would diligently investigate and notice this; for in my experience, I have noticed the stomach and intestines to be more weakened by excessive evacuation of blood from this part than the spleen to be unburdened of its fecal impurity. I would wish, therefore, that the Reader observe with a diligent gaze the Table depicted below, where he will most easily perceive the truth of this matter. For this, see gg. Table 7.

<margin>
Uses:
</margin>
**The First** is for preparing, carrying, and transferring the chyle elaborated in the stomach and distilled down through the small intestines to the Liver, so that it may be changed there into blood.
**The Second** is for distributing the chyle, now reduced into blood, here and there to nourish and preserve the natural parts (such as the stomach, Omentum, Spleen, intestines, and mesentery).

# CHAPTER I.
## On the Mesentery.

<image-desc>A large synoptic diagram (Ramist table) organized with brackets that analyzes the mesentery across several categories: name, origin, substance, composition, position, connection, division, temperament, use, diseases, and astrological associations.</image-desc>

*   **Name,**
    *   *In Greek, it is Messaraion.*
    *   *In Latin, Messenterium.*
*   **Origin,** as to its substance, it comes from those ligaments which connect the lumbar vertebrae <note>the bones of the lower back</note> together; hence the great <term>sympathy</term> <note>a shared physiological connection or shared pain</note> arising between the lower back and the intestines.
*   **Substance,** is membranous, and is almost nothing other than a doubling of the peritoneum.
*   **Composition,** it is composed of two membranes together with innumerable veins and arteries, and is also packed with abundant fat. However, we think it should be noted above all that very many <term>glands</term> <note>specifically lymph nodes</note> are found in it, which seem to be created there by nature so that its small veins—which because of their location are called <term>meseraic</term> <note>now commonly called mesenteric veins</note>—would not be pressed upon by the intestines. *For this, see Table 7. b. b. & c. & d d d. where the veins are shown. And I I. & KK. mark the glands.*
*   **Position,** is in the middle of the intestines. *For this, see Table 8. figure 1. and its center is shown by H.*
*   **Connection,** is made with:
    *   The intestines and principal parts, through its whole substance, regarding which see *Table 8. CCCC. & D. & EEEE. & F.*
    *   The back and kidneys, through ligaments.
*   **Of this there is**
    *   **A division into two portions, namely:**
        *   The Mesaraeum, to which the small intestines are attached and bound. *See L.MMM. Table 8. fig. 2.*
        *   The <term>Mesocolon</term> <note>the fold of the peritoneum that attaches the colon to the back abdominal wall</note>, so named because the colon intestine is attached to and inserted into it. *And regarding this, see fig. 2. Table 8. N. to O. & O. to P. & P. to Q.*
    *   **Temperament,** <note>the balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, wet, dry—believed to govern health</note>
        *   With respect to its fatness, it is hot and moist.
        *   With respect to its own membranous substance, it is cold and dry.
    *   **Use, either for:**
        *   Retaining and gathering the intestines in their natural position. *To see how this happens, look at Table 8.*
        *   Attracting and conducting <term>chyle</term> <note>a milky fluid containing digested fats</note> to the liver <note>original: hepar</note> through those organs called the meseraic veins.
        *   Transferring blood-based nourishment from the liver to the intestines, as if the liver intended to compensate the laborious duties of the intestines with a kind of honest food, like a payment.
*   **Diseases,** tumors, <term>abscesses</term> <note>original: Apostemata; inflammatory swellings</note>, imbalances of temperament, etc.
*   **Astrological association from the stars**
    *   Practical stars <note>The seven classical planets which "act" upon the body</note>
        *   By themselves. <insert>Saturn ♄, Jupiter ♃, Mars ♂, Sun ☉, Venus ♀, Mercury ☿, Moon ☽</insert>
        *   In the signs of the Zodiac Aries ♈︎, Taurus ♉︎. <insert>Aries ♈︎, Taurus ♉︎, Cancer ♋︎, Leo ♌︎, Libra ♎︎, Scorpio ♏︎, Capricorn ♑︎</insert>
    *   Fixed stars or signs of the Zodiac Virgo ♍︎.

# CHAPTER II.

## The Pancreas and its description.

<image-desc>The following anatomical details are structured under the heading "Of which," grouped by a large vertical curly bracket on the left side of the page.</image-desc>

**Name**
*   *Greek: Pancreas.* <note>original: "παγκρέας"; literally "all flesh," referring to its consistent texture.</note>
*   *Latin: Affusio or lactes.* <note>The term "lactes" was often used in early anatomy to refer to the pancreas or the small intestines due to their milky appearance or function.</note>
*   *English: The Sweetbread.* <note>A common historical and culinary term for the pancreas or thymus gland.</note>

**Substance**: It is quite *glandular and flesh-like*, for it possesses the appearance and likeness of flesh on all sides.

**Position**: It is located beneath the cavity of the liver and the back part of the stomach, for it lies directly under the <term>duodenum</term> <note>the first part of the small intestine</note> and the vessels. See *Table b.4. figure 1. aaa.*

**Connection**: It is joined to the cavity of the liver by a strong ligament.

**Use**: It serves to
*   Support and prop up those branches of the <term>portal vein</term> <note>original: "venæ portæ"; the large vein that carries blood from the digestive organs to the liver</note> which extend to the stomach and the <term>spleen</term> <note>original: "lienem"</note>.
*   Protect the substance of the stomach from the hardness of the spine, serving as a cushion.

**Diseases**: For the most part, these are *abscesses*. <note>original: "apostemata"; a localized collection of pus.</note>

**Astrological Influence**: It is governed
*   By the planets: Venus <note>original symbol: ♀</note>.
*   By the signs of the Zodiac: Leo <note>original symbol: ♌</note> and Virgo <note>original symbol: ♍</note>.

---

It should be noted here in passing that a glandular substance is a simple part of the body, and is either:
*   Soft and spongy, such as the <term>tonsils</term> <note>original: "Amigdalæ oris"; literally "almonds of the mouth"</note>, the Pancreas, and the Testicles.
*   Hard and dense, such as the <term>parotid glands</term> <note>original: "Parotides"; the large salivary glands located in front of the ears</note> and other such parts.

# CHAPTER III.

## Concerning the Esophagus of the Stomach.

In the observation of the stomach (which is nature’s primary organ for digestion), two parts are considered, namely:
- Its **Gullet**, which:
    - Is Called:
        - In Greek, *Esophagus*. <note>original: "Οἰσοφάγος"</note>
        - In Latin:
            - *Stomachus*. <note>In early modern medicine, "stomachus" often referred specifically to the gullet/throat, while "ventriculus" referred to the stomach organ itself.</note>
            - *Gula*. <note>The gullet or throat.</note>
        - In Arabic, *Meri*. <note>original: "Mērī"; a traditional Arabic anatomical term for the esophagus.</note>
        - In English, The Gullet.
    - Has a substance that is *membranous or sinewy*, and is by its nature entirely bloodless.
    - At its very top, two tonsils hang down, as seen in Table 9, E. E.
    - Is Composed of:
        - **Two tunics** <note>layers or coats of tissue</note>, of which:
            - The **interior** is denser and has straight fibers in its makeup, a type of texture ordained by nature to pull food prepared in the mouth downward.
            - The **exterior** truly enjoys transverse <note>crosswise</note> fibers, intended for compressing the food thus drawn into the esophagus further downward.
        - The two tonsils mentioned above.
        - A **glandular substance** sitting upon the fifth vertebra of the chest (thorax), the use of which seems to be for defending its sensitive and tender substance from the vertebrae of the back. For this, see F. in figures 1 and 2 of Table 9.
    - Has a varied Position, for its:
        - **Beginning** is behind the larynx, or in the lowest cavity of the larynx, to which it is partly attached. This is indicated by A. in Table 9, figures 1 and 2.
        - **End** is continuous with the upper orifice of the stomach, just as the <term>duodenum</term> <note>the first part of the small intestine</note> is to its lower part. For this, see G. in figures 1 and 2 of Table 9.
        - **Path**, in its descent from the beginning toward the end, is as follows: It stretches downward between the <term>trachea</term> <note>original: "asperam arteriam" or "rough artery," the historical term for the windpipe</note> and the vertebrae of the back, and this passage is quite direct; but truly, as it approaches the heart, it seems to incline to the right, as if commanded by natural instinct to give place to the heart. After this, approaching the <term>diaphragm</term> <note>original: "diaphragmati"</note>, it leans back again to the left, lest in its passage it should bring any harm to the **Liver**; indeed, so that it may perform this more easily, it makes its passage at the end beneath the ascending <term>vena cava</term> and above the descending <term>aorta</term>. When this is finally accomplished, it pierces the <term>midriff</term> <note>original: "septum transversum"; the diaphragm</note> and, immediately penetrating into the lowest region of the <term>microcosm</term> <note>A philosophical term for the human body, viewed as a miniature version of the universe.</note>, it is fixed into the upper orifice of the stomach. This path can be discerned from its shape explained above. For this, see A. and B. and G. in Table 9, figures 1 and 2; its inclination is indicated by C. and D.
    - Obtains the Shape depicted in the image below: Table 9, which can also be observed from the descriptions above.
    - Has the Use of conducting food and drink into the stomach.
    - Is afflicted by Diseases, such as difficulty in swallowing, ulcers of the esophagus, abscesses, and the spitting of blood.
    - Claims for itself a Constellation:
        - From the planets, **Jupiter** (♃).
        - From the stars of the Zodiac, **Cancer** (♋).
- The **Stomach** itself, concerning which see below.

### CHAPTER IV.

#### Concerning the Stomach.

<image-desc>
A large-scale hierarchical diagram (Ramist chart) categorizing the anatomical and physiological properties of the stomach (Ventriculus). The subject "Ventriculi" is placed on the left, with a tall vertical line branching into seven primary categories: Name (Nomen), Substance (Substantia), Composition (Compositio), Quantity (Quantitas), Figure (Figura), Temperament (Temperamentum), and Site (Situs). Each category is further detailed with brackets, particularly the "Compositio" branch, which includes detailed descriptions of the three tunics (layers), nerves, and veins.
</image-desc>

**The Stomach**

* **Name**
    * In Greek, it is { *Gaster* <note>original: "γαστήρ"</note> / *Koilia* <note>original: "κοιλία"; literally "cavity" or "belly"</note>. }
    * In Latin, { The Proper name is the ventricle <note>original: "ventriculus"</note> / The Common name is the stomach <note>original: "stomachus"</note>. }
    * In English, *The stomak*.
* **Substance**, is more seminal <note>original: "spermatica"; meaning white, fibrous, or membranous tissue, then believed to be derived from seed</note>, membranous, or sinewy than bloody or fleshy; consequently, it is bloodless.
* **Composition**, consists of
    * **Three Tunics <note>layers or coats of tissue</note>, of which**
        * **The First, or Inner**, is more membranous or sinewy and extremely thin; its:
            * **Origin** arises from the membranes of the brain springing from the *dura mater* <note>the tough outermost membrane of the brain</note>; it first descends to the mouth with the nerves derived from the third and fourth pairings. There, it clothes the entire mouth and is said to form the uvula through its various foldings; then, afterward, it descends to the stomach itself, where it is observed to weave together the inner tunic by a wonderful industry and texture of nature. This is the reason why there is such a great "sympathy" <note>original: "consensus"</note> between the stomach, the mouth, and the head, so that when the head or the *dura mater* is wounded, vomiting follows, and those things which are offensive to the stomach are rejected and spat out from the mouth.
            * **Fibers** from which it is woven are straight; by the power of these, the stomach performs its duty of drawing food into itself from the Esophagus. For these, see Figure 3, Table 9, K, and this Figure 1.
        * **The Second, which is the Middle**, is more fleshy and dense than the first. Its fabric:
            * **Arises** from the *pericranium* <note>the membrane covering the skull</note>, which, as soon as it descends to the Esophagus, takes on fleshy fibers for itself.
            * **Is constructed** from oblique fibers for the sake of retention, which results in it assisting with digestion <note>original: "concoctioni"</note>. See Figure 3, Table 9, I.
        * **One is Common <note>the outer layer shared with other organs</note>**, and this:
            * **Arises** from the *Peritoneum*, which provides a common tunic to all parts of this region; hence it is called "common."
            * **Is fabricated** from transverse fibers, to which the power of expulsion is attributed. For these, inspect hhh in Figure 3, Table 9.
    * **Nerves from the sixth pair** <note>the Vagus nerve</note> which are two, namely the right and the left, embracing the Esophagus and the uppermost orifice of the stomach. For these, see T. V. in Table 9.
    * **Veins from the gastric, splenic, and coronary veins** from the 1st, 2nd, and 4th branches of the portal vein. For these, see a., b., dd., etc.
* **Quantity**, is either larger or smaller according to the proportion of the body and the gluttony <note>original: "gulositatem"</note> of the person.
* **Figure**, is like a small gourd, a chemical retort <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note>, or a bagpipe <note>original: "cornu musæ"; literally "horn of the muse," a term often used for a bagpipe's drone or a curved horn</note>. See Figures 1 and 2, Table 9.
* **Temperament**, with respect to its position which is between the liver and the spleen, it is tempered <note>balanced in its "humoral" qualities of heat and cold</note>.
* **Site** is between the spleen and the cavity of the liver. In its wonderful position, a specific proportion in nature's arrangement must be observed: she placed the narrower portion of the stomach in that part of the body where the principal organ contained is more ample and vast—namely, the mass of the liver. But truly, where the narrower part—the spleen—has its site, there the more vast region of the stomach claims its station. Thus, the stomach seems to be weighed in the scales of nature, so that it is not felt to be more burdensome or troublesome to the right side than to the left. Its natural position is indicated in Table 5, FF, showing that it lies between the hollow of the liver and the intestines.

<margin>There are three similar <term>similar: in Galenic medicine, "similar" parts are those made of a single substance, like bone or membrane, rather than organs made of multiple tissues</term> parts.</margin>

The first is its upper opening, which is called the **Heart-entry** <note>original: "Cardia"; the name reflects the historical belief that the upper stomach opening and the heart were closely linked in sensation</note>. When this part is affected, that affliction often occurs which is therefore called the **Cardiac passion** <note>likely referring to severe heartburn or stomach-related chest pain</note>. This location is the seat of hunger and appetite because it is exquisitely sensitive; this is because both the right and left branches of the **recurrent nerves** <note>original: "recurrentibus"; referring to branches of the vagus nerve</note>—also known as the **sixth pair** <note>in early anatomy, the vagus nerve was classified as the sixth pair of cranial nerves</note>—descend to this part and wrap all around this opening. See G. and I. K. in Table 9, and also the letter m.

The second is its lowest opening, which is like a door suited for retaining the nourishment within the stomach until the perfection of **concoction** <note>original: "concoctio"; the process of digestion, then thought of as a "cooking" of food by internal heat</note>. For this reason, it is called the **Gatekeeper**, the **Porter**, and the **Doorkeeper** <note>original: "ianitor & Portanarius & ostiarius"; all referring to what we now call the *pylorus*</note>. See H. in Table 9, where the letter P shows how it attaches to the **duodenum** <note>the first part of the small intestine</note>; the bile passage is also indicated by Q. R.

The third is its **bottom** <note>original: "fundum"</note>, in which concoction and **chylification** <note>the process of turning food into a milky fluid called chyle</note> are usually completed and brought toward the exit.

n. Is the interior surface of the stomach.

# Book IV of the Lower Region. CHAPTER V. Concerning the Liver.

It is called in Latin: *Hepar* or *Iecur*; in English: The Liver.

It is a most noble organ, for according to Galen in his book *On the Formation of the Fetus*: "This is the first of the organs to be completed in its development; furthermore, it is the author of the natural spirit, and the source and seat of blood, and of love," according to that verse of the Poet:
->The heart feels wisdom, the lungs speak, the bile contains anger,<-
->The spleen makes one laugh, the liver compels one to love.<-

It arises from blood and is nourished by the same. —

It has a simple substance, which seems to be nothing other than blood, as if clotted. It is divided into two or three lobes, contrary to the opinion of Colombo <note>Realdo Colombo (c. 1515–1559), an influential Italian anatomist who argued the liver had only one lobe in humans</note>. It is also divided into two parts according to its surface, namely into the convex (outer) and the concave (inner) parts. For the convex side, see *Table 5, CC and Table 10, AA, CC.*

For its composition, it requires:
- A single coat or membrane, surrounding it from the outside, which is derived from the peritoneum <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note>.
- Its own flesh, called *parenchyma* <note>original: "paneuchima"; a common early modern spelling for the functional tissue of an organ</note>.
- The roots of the Vena Cava and the Vena Porta, whose junctions <term>anastomosis</term> are marked by PP in Table 10; and "ggg" are the roots of the portal vein, and "cccc" and "dddd" are the roots of the vena cava.
- Several small arteries from the celiac artery, and the umbilical vein, for which see *B. Table 10.*
- Nerves, namely a small branch originating from the sixth pair <note>referring to the vagus nerve in the old numbering system</note>, which is inserted only superficially and immediately under its coat. Hence it happens that the liver is sensitive only on its surface. How this nerve passes from the left part of the stomach to the liver is shown to us by *X, Y in Table 9.*

In its size, it is observed to be larger in humans than in beasts of the same dimension. However, it is found to be vaster and larger in timid and lazy men than in the courageous.

Its shape is not exactly spherical, but like that of a split horse's hoof. Its outer part is convex and smooth, while the interior is concave and rough. In the posterior part, it has two protruding bumps, which are adapted by nature so that the vena cava is not compressed by the vertebrae. For this, see *Table 9.*

It has a hot and moist temperament <note>In the system of the four humors, the liver was considered the source of blood, which shared these qualities</note>.

<margin>This is a principal organ</margin>
It is connected:
- Above, namely to the diaphragm <term>septo transuerso</term> by a membranous ligament; see *H. Table 10 and D. Table 5.*
- To the false ribs on the left side, to keep it proportionally in its place. See *I. Table 10.*
- To the intestines, by the veins; see *Table 7 where the Portal Vein is indicated.*
- To the peritoneum, by the coat attached to it from the outside.
- To the navel, by the umbilical vein, as shown in *B. Table 10 and B. Table 4.*

It is useful for converting chyle <note>the milky fluid produced from digested food</note> into blood, for such a transformation happens nowhere else. It is indeed nature's wonderful laboratory, adorned with many distilling vessels of various arrangements, as will be taught more extensively in its "mystical anatomy." Furthermore, the liver is the seat of both the concupiscible <note>desiring</note> and natural faculties.

It has very many diseases, such as:
- Imbalances: hot, moist, cold, and dry.
- Smallness, concerning which see *Rhazes, book 17 of the Continens, treatise 1, chapter 1.*
- Obstruction <term>oppilatio</term>, namely in its veins.
- Pain, concerning which see *Galen, book 5 On the Affected Parts, 7; Avicenna, chapter 7.*
- Weakness in digestion, followed by: Cachexia <note>general wasting of the body</note> or dyscrasia; Atrophy.
- Inflammation.
- Flatulence.
- Ulcers <term>exitura</term>.
- Swellings <term>apostemata</term>, such as: Phlegmon <note>acute, localized inflammation</note>; Erysipelas <note>a bacterial skin infection</note>; Oedema <note>swelling from fluid</note>; Scirrhus <note>a hard, cancerous tumor</note>.
- Hepatic flux <note>a type of chronic diarrhea attributed to liver failure</note>.
- Corruption of the liver's digestive faculty, followed by: Hyposarca <note>a form of dropsy or swelling</note>; Ascites <note>fluid accumulation in the abdomen</note>; Tympanites <note>distension from gas</note>; Leucophlegmatia <note>a pale swelling or dropsy</note>.
- Pain in the hypochondria <note>the upper abdomen below the ribs</note>.
- Rupture of the liver.

It is subject to the constellation of:
- The planets on its own: Jupiter (♃).
- The signs of the Zodiac: Leo (♌).

The thick and large roots of the Vena Cava extend into the substance of the liver from its summit all the way to the bottom. Moreover, this vein is the mother of all veins, which is observed to have its origin from the convex <note>original: "gibbosa"</note> part of the liver, just as the portal vein does from its concave <note>original: "caua"</note> part. From its general trunk, infinite branches—and from those again, little branches—are observed to sprout, just as branches with their divisions have a relation to the trunk, and rivulets to the great river from whence they emanate.

# Book IV of the Lowest Region.

### CHAPTER VII.
### Concerning the gallbladder.

<image-desc>A complex, tree-like diagram with text nodes connected by lines and curly braces, illustrating the anatomical and physiological description of the "vesicula fellis" (gallbladder). The diagram branches out from the main topic into categories such as its names, substance, composition, shape, temperament, ducts, connections, utility, associated diseases, and astrological constellations. **It is called**
*In Latin,* *Vesicula fellis* <note>original: "Vesicula fellis"</note>, *Bursacholer* <note>A medieval term meaning "bile-purse"</note>, & *citrina* <note>referring to its yellowish color</note>.
*In English,* *Cista fellis* <note>The chest of the bile</note>, *The gall* <note>original: "The gauld"</note>.

**It has a substance, of which the part**
That contains is nervous or membranous.
That is contained is the sharper part of the blood: or its bilious excrement <note>In early medicine, "excrement" referred to any byproduct of the body's "cooking" or digestion of blood</note>.

**It is composed of**
One [part] is specific to itself.
*Two tunics <note>layers of tissue</note>, of which*
One is common, and this is derived from the Peritoneum <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note>.
*Veins & arteries, which are indicated by figure 1, Table 12.*
*A small nerve common to it and the Liver: which is indicated by O. Table 12. fig. 1.*

It possesses a shape that is round at the bottom, but in its total dimension it is oblong like a pear. See A fig. 1. Table 12. & fig. 2. r.

**It enjoys a temperament <note>the balance of primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, dry</note> regarding its**
Containing part, cold & dry, as it is membranous.
Contained part, namely the bilious humor, hot & dry.

**It has two passages <note>ducts</note>, of which**
<margin>A small vessel hanging beneath the Liver</margin>
One receives the bilious matter from the liver, and this one is simple, which is indicated by DDD. Table 12. & E & H.
One is common to all, and has an exit into the bottom of the Duodenum, or the beginning of the Jejunum <note>parts of the small intestine</note>. See Q. R. Table 9. And 11. Table 12. aaaaa. fig. 2.
The other is observed in very few [people], and this is said to penetrate to the bottom of the stomach; Galen <note>A famous Greek physician of the 2nd century</note> makes mention of an affliction of this kind, whom he relates was troubled by a continuous and bilious vomiting of matter.
The other sends out bile from the small vessel of the gall into the intestines, and of this, two branches are counted, of which

It holds its site under the right cavity of the liver, from which several thin roots of the portal and caval veins descend, through which the bilious juice is observed to distill into this kind of receiver. All of which is explained through fig. 2. Table 12.

**It is connected**
*To the Liver, by a natural union and binding, as explained in Table 12. fig. 2.*
*With other parts through veins, arteries, and nerves.*

It has this utility: that it receives the bile or the choleric excrement of the blood, and pours it gradually into the intestines, by which they are made more lubricated for the sake of better excretion, and by its sharpness they are rendered more fit for expelling excrements.

It is affected by its own diseases, such as the obstruction of the passages (which yellow jaundice, the regurgitation of bile into the mass of the blood, and bilious fevers follow) and also the stone <note>gallstones</note>. For I remember that I opened the gallbladder of a certain wine-merchant <note>original: "Oenopolae"</note>, and found in it over a hundred small black stones like peppercorns, which I perceived to have been procreated from thick bile scorched <note>or "adust," a medical term for humors dried by excessive heat</note> in its own vessel.

**It has a constellation**
*From the planets, Mars <note>original: "♂"</note>.*
*From the stars of the Zodiac, Leo <note>original: "♌"</note>.*

### CHAPTER VIII.
## Concerning the Spleen.

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Name | In Latin, it is *Lien* or *Splen*. <note>The author provides both common Latin terms for the organ.</note> |
| | In English, The spleen. |

The substance *is soft, thin, and spongy, so that the melancholic and earthy parts of the blood mass may be more easily separated; it draws these from the Liver through the portal vein before the blood-making matter enters the vena cava.* <note>Early modern medicine taught that the spleen acted as a filter for "black bile" or melancholic humors.</note> *For its dissected substance, see Table 13, letters I and K.*

Its composition consists of:
*A thin membrane derived from the Peritoneum.* <note>The lining of the abdominal cavity.</note>
*Its own flesh, originating from dreggy or thick blood.*
*Veins, springing from the fourth branch of the portal vein, which are inserted into it along with the arteries for its sake. See Table 13, letter N and H; furthermore, for the splenic branch, see Table 7, letter T and aaaa.*
*Arteries, derived from the first branch of the aorta or great artery. Letter N in Table 13 indicates these and the veins.*
*A nerve, emerging from the left side.*

The shape *is very similar to an ox's tongue: it is convex (hunched) toward the diaphragm, and concave in that part where the veins, arteries, and nerves are inserted into it. For its upper and lower positions, see Table 13, letters D and E. For the right and left sides, see F and G. For its vessel, see H. And LL for its convex part and the furrows impressed by the ribs. And MM for the end without furrows.*
The color *is like that of muddy blood, but indeed it is accustomed to differ in some individuals.*
The quantity <note>meaning size</note> *is quite notable, and according to the constitution of the body, it is larger and more ample in some than others. I myself have observed in a certain priest that the spleen was increased beyond nature, on the convex surface of which I noticed several horns newly rising up, as it were; their substance was endowed with such hardness that they could scarcely be scratched or lightly scraped away by scalpels.* The natural position *is designated by G in Table 5, on the left side.*

The connection is made through—
*Veins, arteries, and nerves with the liver, heart, and brain, and other parts.*
*Its convex part, with the diaphragm.*
*The membrane, with the Peritoneum.*
*The short vessel <term>vas breve: a small vein connecting the spleen and stomach</term>, with the Stomach.*
*The Omentum <note>original: "Epiploon"</note>, with the other parts of the body. See CC and DE in Table 13.*

The small veins *are many, among which there is one unique one which is short, and which rises from it and penetrates between the membrane of the stomach at its upper orifice; it is said to carry an acid humor <note>original: "humorem acidum"</note> from the spleen, by means of which hunger and appetite are excited, the stomach is strengthened by the sharp sensation, and digestion is aided. It should be noted, however, that where this vessel is wider, hunger is delayed or tolerated with difficulty beyond the appointed time; hence it happens that some so affected are frequently seized by the passion called "cardiac" <note>likely referring to heartburn or stomach distress</note> for this reason. But where a vessel of this kind is narrower, hunger is said to be tolerated for a long time, and the appetite is observed to be weaker.*

<margin>Of this member—</margin>
<insert>*Erasistratus <note>Ancient Greek anatomist</note> had asserted in vain that the spleen was created for no purpose.*
*Aristotle (in Book 3 of "On the Parts of Animals") thought it was necessary only by chance.*</insert>
<insert>Alexander of Aphrodisias and Aretaeus conclude that the spleen is an instrument of blood-making <note>original: "sanguificationis"</note>.</insert>
<insert>*Randoleius utterly denies that the spleen is the receptacle of the melancholic humor.*
*Plinius of Poitiers, a physician (in his book on the spleen), contends with many arguments that the spleen prepares the vital spirit, a most powerful blood, as the material for the vital spirit. He says that from there, through its arteries, that blood so prepared is transported to the left chamber of the heart.*</insert>
<insert>*Galen (whom more recent physicians follow) in Book 1 of "On the Preservation of Health," the book "On the Formation of the Fetus," the sixth book of "On the Affected Parts," and the book "On Black Bile," says the spleen [contributes] to the blood...*</insert>
