# ->On the Parts Appearing in the Center.<-

It seems to be affirmed that this organ was ordained by nature for the purpose of receiving dregs of blood <note>original: "sanguinem faculentum," referring to the thick, sediment-like waste products of the blood</note>, and he proceeds to support this with various arguments or reasons.

<margin>Its use seems to be uncertain, for</margin> Pliny, in the 11th book of his *Natural History*, says that a peculiar hindrance to running consists in the spleen. For this reason, he says that in certain cases, and as men are taught, it has been removed from some animals through a wound or incision, which animals he asserts were nevertheless accustomed to live. I myself have known of a dog's spleen being removed by a skilled surgeon through an incision while the dog was still living; and Leonardo Fioravanti <note>A famous 16th-century Neapolitan physician known for his bold surgical experiments</note>, a Neapolitan physician, confidently relates that a most noble woman—who was gravely, indeed lethally, afflicted in her spleen and abandoned by all other doctors—committed herself into his and a most experienced surgeon's hands; after the spleen was removed by the power of the incision, she recovered her former health.

André du Laurens <note>original: "Andreas Laurentius," a prominent French anatomist and physician to Henry IV</note>, in the 6th book of his *Anatomical History*, affirms that certain perfect animals in which there is little dreggy blood are destitute of a spleen, and that a certain youth was dissected in Paris <note>original: "Lutetiae," the Latin name for Paris</note> who lacked a spleen entirely. However, what my own opinion is regarding the utility and proper action of the spleen, I shall state elsewhere outside of this treatise, since I have proposed to myself to discuss in this place only matters commonly acted upon and known.

<margin>Diseases in it and those arising from it are:</margin>
Distemper <note>An imbalance of the four humors</note>: hot, cold, moist, or dry.
Abscesses: such as Scirrhus <note>A hard, cancerous tumor</note> and swelling.
Pain.
Black Jaundice <note>Associated with an excess of "black bile," which the spleen was thought to regulate</note>.
Windiness and inflation <note>Bloating or gas</note>.
Splenetic flux.
Spleen too large or too small.

<margin>Its constellation is from:</margin>
The Planets: Saturn ♄.
The Stars of the Zodiac: Leo ♌.

## CHAPTER I.
## Concerning the Emulgent Veins.

They are called "Emulgent" <note>From the Latin *emulgere*, meaning "to milk out," referring to the historical belief that these veins strained or "milked" the urine from the blood.</note> by name, and this is derived from their function.
They are two in number:
- The Right,
- The Left,
- Which rise out from the body of the *vena cava* <term>vena cava: the large central vein returning blood to the heart</term> like two wings. See a.b. Table 15.a.
- The Left passes from the trunk of the *vena cava* over the vertebrae and the Aorta, and thus enters into the middle of the cavity of the left Kidney; this is also generally higher in its position than the right, because the spleen <note>original: "lien"</note> occupies less space than the Liver <note>original: "Hepar"</note>: But truly, this rule is not always observed to be constant.
- The Right passes from the same vein directly above the Aorta, and penetrates into the curved center of the right kidney in the same manner as the left; and this is for the most part lower in its position than the left on account of the size of the Liver. However, as soon as both of these enter the substance of the kidneys, they divide into infinite little branches, which for this reason are called capillary veins. For their position, see Table 15.a.b. and Table 15.b. h.

Their position is not varied, for the vein:
- First, is continuous with the trunk of the *vena cava*. As a. & b. Table 15.a.
- Afterward, they extend and disperse into many capillary venules (as has been said) as soon as they have entered the kidneys, which are scattered thinly through the substance of the kidneys. As appears to the eye near T. & V. Table 15.a. And for the openings through which they enter, see e. Table 15.b.

These venules
Are connected:
- First, to the trunk of the *vena cava* to which they are continuous. As a. & b. Table 15.a.
- Afterward, to the kidneys, into which as soon as they have entered, they extend and disperse into many capillary venules (as has been said), which are scattered thinly through the substance of the kidneys. As appears to the eye near T. & V. Table 15.a. And for the openings through which they enter, see e. Table 15.b.

They are used to carry both the serum of the blood and the blood itself for the purpose of nourishing the kidneys; the Kidneys, moreover, separate the blood from the serosity <note>The watery part of the blood, destined to become urine.</note> and soak up the former for nourishment, but truly they send the useless serosity through the ureters into the bladder.

### CHAPTER III.
Concerning the Ureters.

They are named:
In Greek, *Ureteres*. <note>original: "Ureteres"</note>
In Latin:
Urinary vessels. <note>original: "Vasa urinaria"</note>
The white vein, according to Celsus. <note>original: "Vena alba"; Aulus Cornelius Celsus was a 1st-century Roman encyclopedist known for his medical compendium.</note>

**They originate** from the concavity or the "snub-nosed" <note>The term "fima" refers to the recessed, curved part of the organ.</note> part of the kidneys. As shown in Table 14, figure 1, C and D; and Table 15.a. near T and V. It is also indicated at m and n in Table 15.b.

**They have a substance** that is membranous and fibrous. <note>original: "nervosam"; in early modern anatomy, this often referred to a sinewy or tough texture rather than just nerves.</note>

**In quantity**, they appear narrow at first glance, but if they are distended with air, they are found to be quite wide and spacious, especially toward the upper ends. For this, one may see Table 18, book 1, page 158, by Caspar Bauhin. <note>Caspar Bauhin (1560–1624) was a Swiss botanist and anatomist famous for his anatomical tables.</note>

<margin>These oblong vessels</margin>
**In number**, they are said to be two, as appears through T and V in Table 15.a.

**They are positioned** along the length of the long muscles <note>Likely referring to the psoas muscles of the back.</note>, as is evident through Table 15.a. They move from the kidneys to the bladder. See Table 15.a.c. and d.d.

**They have a shape** that is oblong and hollow in the manner of veins, as can be seen from the kidneys to the bladder in Table 15.b.

**They have an insertion** into the substance of the bladder, specifically in its sides; in these places, penetrating between both tunics <note>layers of tissue</note> of the bladder, they travel and stretch almost toward the neck of the bladder, and from there they are reflected into the innermost cavity of the bladder. By this winding and reflection, the lower layer of the bladder seems to serve in the place of a valve, so that the urine does not flow back or regurgitate out of the bladder. For this, see Table 15.b.d.

**They have a use**, serving in the place of channels or tubes, so that through them the urine or serous matter—separated from the blood by the power of the kidneys—may be carried down into the bladder.

**They are affected by diseases**, such as obstruction and corrosion; indeed, I knew a certain nobleman for whom one of these had been perforated by an ill-shaped stone. <note>original: "calculo"; a kidney or bladder stone.</note>

# Concerning the Parts Contained within its Depths.
### CHAPTER IV.
### Concerning the Bladder.

<margin>The Name</margin>
The Latin name is *Vesica*.
Aristotle, in the first book of *The History of Animals*, defines it as the "receptacle for liquid waste." <note>original: "Humidi excrementi receptaculum"</note>
In English: The bladder.

The substance of the bladder is the same as that of the ureters, namely nervous and membranous, so that it may more easily dilate and extend itself whenever necessity requires it.

The body of the bladder is unique; it is quite thick and dense, and is woven from three types of fibers, namely:
*   **Straight fibers**, intended for drawing the urine into the bladder; these are arranged in the inner part of the bladder.
*   **Oblique fibers**, which are the instruments of the retentive faculty <term>retentive faculty: the biological power to hold or retain substances</term>, by which urine is held in its receptacle until the proper time, so that a person is not constantly forced to emit urine; these have their place in the middle of the membrane.
*   **Transverse fibers**, and these are ordained for expelling the serous matter <note>serous matter: here referring to the watery component of urine</note> contained within the bladder; they are located in its outer part.

<summary>This page describes the anatomy and physiological function of the human bladder, detailing its membranous composition and the three types of fibers—straight, oblique, and transverse—that allow for the collection, retention, and expulsion of urine.</summary>

## CHAPTER VI.
### Concerning the preparatory vessels. <note>Latin: *vasa praeparantia*, the spermatic veins and arteries thought to "prepare" the blood before it reaches the testes.</note>

<margin>The number is 4, namely</margin>
Two veins from the trunk of the hollow vein <note>The vena cava</note>.
Two arteries from the trunk of the Great Artery <note>The Aorta</note>.
Flowing forth. For the trunks of both from which these emerge, see Table 15. b. f. & gg. and Table 15. a. q. & R.

<margin>The origin, namely</margin>
Of the veins, descending from the hollow vein:
The left is from the left emulgent <note>renal</note> vein, see g. Table 15. b.
The right is from the trunk of the hollow vein below the right kidney. See O. Table 15. b.
Of the arteries, emerging from the great artery near the kidneys, which are demonstrated through Table 15. b. r.

<margin>The preparatory vessels, of which the</margin>
Substance or composition is similar to common veins or arteries, except that nature provides these with another tunic derived from the peritoneum.
The movement toward the testes is indicated by e. f. Table 15. a.
The length is greater in men than in women, because in men the testicles hang outside the belly. For the length, see Table 15. b. o. & r.
The marvelous plexus or union, net-like, called <term>Anastomosis</term> <note>A connection between vessels</note> by the Greeks, in which the vein embraces the artery and conversely the artery the vein, like the branches of ivy creeping upward through an ancient wall; and an embrace or entanglement of this kind occurs in the middle of the path of descent of these vessels toward the testicles, and they cling to one another until they reach them. These plexuses last from y. to x. Table 15. b.
The use is for filtering and preparing the material of the seed for the generation of sperm: and also (and this especially) for mixing in a specific manner the invisible seed with the visible sperm, as we shall declare below in its proper place.

<margin>The seminal vessels are 13, of which some are</margin>
The Elaborating and Ripening vessels, called the <term>Epididymides</term> <note>The coiled tubes behind the testes</note>, and these are 2 in number.
The Purifying vessels, which grant the seed a prolific power by removing superfluous watery moisture, of which kind are the two Testicles.
The Carrying vessels <note>The vas deferens</note>, likewise two in number, whose role is to transfer the sperm, thus purged of its superfluities, into their own vessels called the "out-flowings."
The Receiving vessels, two in number, called the <term>proflates</term> <note>likely referring to the seminal vesicles</note>.
The Ejaculating vessel, one in number, which is the tube <note>Latin: *syringa*</note> that usually ejaculates the sperm into the cavity of the womb, and this is called the penis or the male member.

## CHAPTER VII.
### Concerning the elaborating vessels.

<margin>They are called</margin>
Paraflates.
Epididymides.
Variform <note>vessel-like</note> structures.

<margin>The elaborating vessels</margin>
Are two in number. See Table 15. b. n.
They have a nearly pyramidal shape. For the varicose pyramidal vessel, see Table 15. b. where it is demonstrated.
They claim their position in the upper part or head and summit of the testicles, and they lie in the middle between the end of the preparatory vessels and the testicles. See Table 15. b. n.
They are connected to the preparatory vessels (which are entangled together) and to the testicles by a strong adhesion; indeed, they seem to be continuous with the proper tunics of the testicles themselves. See Table 15. b. i.
Their use (as some wish) is for ripening the prepared seed or sperm.

### CHAPTER VIII.
### Concerning the Cleansing or Purifying Vessels.

<image-desc>A tree-like diagram visually organizes information about the "Cleansing or Purifying vessels". The main branches are "Name", "Substance", "Of these vessels", and "Use". "Name" further branches into "Greek", "Latin", and "English". "Of these vessels" branches into "Tunics [coverings], which are in" which then splits into "Men (three, namely)" and "Women". "Men (three, namely)" lists three types. "Use, is according to" branches into "Some authors" and "Cabrol and Aristotle".</image-desc>

*The Name,*
*   Greek, is *Didymoi* <note>original: "Δυδυμοι"</note> meaning "the Twins."
*   Witnesses <note>The Latin term "testes" literally means witnesses, as they "testify" to virility.</note>.
*   Latin, *Testiculi*.
*   English, the *stones*, or Cods <note>An archaic term for the scrotum or testicles.</note>.
*The Substance,* is a soft and loose flesh. It is shown by X. in Table 15. b. insofar as it is still clothed in its innermost tunic.

*Of these vessels*
*   *The Tunics [coverings], are in*
    *   *Men, three, namely:*
        *   The *Erythroid* <note>original: "Erythroeide"</note>, arising from the thin membrane of the muscles descending obliquely. This is interwoven with fleshy fibers and is believed to form the muscle of the testes <note>The cremaster muscle.</note>.
        *   The *Dartos*, arising from the Peritoneum; it is white in color and is attached to the *Epididymis* vessels.
        *   The *Epididymis* <note>The author here uses the term for the covering itself</note>, so named by Columbus <note>Matteo Realdo Colombo (1516–1559), a famous Italian anatomist.</note> because (as I think) the *Epididymides* are continuous with these types of tunics. And this species of tunic immediately covers the substance of the testes.
    *   *Women,* there is only one, which is wrapped by the peritoneum. The shape is somewhat round. See Table 15. b. X.
*   *The Use, is according to*
    *   Some, who attribute the prolific power of the seeds to them.
    *   Cabrol <note>Barthélemy Cabrol (1529–1603), a French anatomist.</note> and Aristotle (whom I follow), for the purpose of purifying and cleansing superfluous moisture, and for the refinement of the seed. For no semen is found in the testes, but only a watery and useless humor.

That common vessel containing the testicles is called the Scrotum, which is composed of the cuticle, the skin, and a fleshy membrane (so that it might be more fit for expanding itself); its use is to contain the tender testes and to defend them against the injuries of external cold.

### CHAPTER IX.
### Concerning the Carrying Vessels <term>Vasa Deferentia: the ducts that transport sperm</term>.

<image-desc>A tree-like diagram visually organizes information about the "Carrying vessels". The main branches are "Name", "Origin", "Number", "Position", and "Use".</image-desc>

*Of these*
*   *The Name,* is the carrying vessels (*vasa deferentia*), named from their office or use.
*   *The Origin,* is derived from the *Epididymis*, for each of them begins from it: it is described by y. in Table 15. b. and by q. in Table 15. a.
*   *The Number,* is two, namely the right and the left.
*   *The Position,* is located between the testicle and the prominent glandular body <note>The prostate</note> which is joined to the neck of the bladder. Its measure is shown by y. n. in Table 51. b.
*   *The Use,* is to carry the seed or sperm, which has been matured in the *parastatae* <note>An old term for the epididymis</note> or *Epididymides*, to the prominent glandular bodies.

### THE MIDDLE REGION.
## A description of the CHEST, OR THE MIDDLE RE-
gion of the Microcosm <note>The "Microcosm" or "little world" is a Renaissance concept viewing the human body as a miniature reflection of the universe.</note>, divided into five books.

{ The Name
    { Greek, derived from *thorax* <note>original: "θώραξ"</note> which means to leap; perhaps because in its very center the heart is known to move rhythmically and to lead the measures of life with a symphonic beat: hence this region is called the Thorax.
    Latin, *pectus*.
    English, The breast.

<margin>Regarding the Thorax</margin>
{ All its features are considered
    { Position, which in this part is
        { Anterior, located between the collarbones and the pointed cartilage <note>The xiphoid process at the base of the breastbone.</note> or the Diaphragm.
        Posterior, seen to be measured from the twelve vertebrae of the back.
        Lateral, surrounded by the true and false ribs and the intercostal muscles.

Shape, which is round or oblong; it is not sharply hunched or keel-shaped like that of brute animals, but rather more flat.
Use, since it serves as a bulwark or a fortification for the heart and for the parts of life and its adapted organs.

Parts, concerning which see the following chapter.

->### CHAPTER I.<-
->Concerning the Clavicles <note>The collarbones</note>.<-

<margin>Of which the</margin>
Name is derived from their function, inasmuch as they strengthen and support this region as if with keys <note>original: "clauibus"; the author links the Latin 'clavicula' (little key) to the bone's role in locking the shoulder to the breastbone</note>.
Substance is hard, solid, and not at all hollow.
Shape is curved, that is, like the letter ~. See Table 2.
Number is twofold, for a single one corresponds to each side.
Connection is made firmly with the cartilage of the breast.
Position is on both sides of the throat, for the member placed between these two bones is called the jugulum <note>The hollow of the throat</note>.
Use is for the strengthening of this region.
Diseases are fracture and dislocation. For these clavicles, see Table 2 from A to T.

->### CHAPTER II.<-
->Concerning the bone of the breast called the sternum.<-

<margin>The name is the bone sternon.</margin>
Substance is uncertain, for sometimes it is:
  As if bony.
  Spongy and porous.
  Cartilaginous.
  However, it is in any case softer than that of the clavicles. See figure IX, Table 2.
Composition is either:
  From 4, 5, 6, 7, or more bones.
  Entirely a continuous and undivided bone, and at its base appears that small bone which is named from its resemblance:
    The bone of the pointed cartilage. See figure 9.
    The sword-shaped bone <note>original: "Os ensiforme"; the xiphoid process</note>. Table 2, K. &
    The Pomegranate <note>original: "Malum granatum"; a historical anatomical term for the xiphoid process due to its shape</note>. S, Table 4.
<margin>Of this bone the</margin>
Quantity, or its magnitude, is wider and thicker at the top toward the clavicles, but indeed in its depth or bottom it is observed to be far narrower. As is evident from figure IX, Table 2, h.e.i.k.
Position is in the middle of the front part of the Thorax, and it extends in length from the clavicles (to which it is bound by a firm connection) all the way to the Diaphragm or the top of the stomach. See Figure IX, h.e.i.k. and for the internal part of the sternum see AAA, Table 4.

The **Connection** is varied, for:
{ **Internally**, it adheres strongly to the mediastinum <note>The central compartment of the thoracic cavity between the lungs.</note>.
**Above**, it is fastened to the clavicles <note>collarbones</note> by a tight insertion. Namely in *g.* of figure IX, Table 1.

The **Sides** of the same are united by a cartilaginous connection to the ends of the true ribs. Namely in *c.* of figure IX, Table 2, and see *A.* Table 4.

The **Use** is that it serves as a kind of shield or buckler, by which the heart and vital organs are fortified and defended against external injuries.
**Diseases** include rupture, etc.

### CHAPTER III.
### Concerning the Ribs.

They are named **ribs** <note>original: "costæ"</note>, inasmuch as they fortify the sides.
They have a **substance** that is partly bony and partly cartilaginous.

In **Number** they are 24, namely:
{ 12 on the right side.
{ 12 on the left side.
} See figures 9 and 10, Table 2, from 1, 2, 3, 4, up to 12.

These lateral bones
} are **Divided** into:
{ **True ribs**, which are 7 in number on each side, occupying the uppermost position; and these are called "true" because, by joining themselves to the sternum, they complete the circumference of a circle. See figure 9, Table 2, up to 7.
{ **False ribs**, which are five in number on each side, and these are called "false" because they do not complete a circular course, but fail, as it were, along the way. See from *a. 7* in figure 9 to 12.

They are clothed by a **double membrane**, of which:
{ **One** is derived from the periosteum <note>The dense layer of vascular connective tissue enveloping the bones</note>, and this adheres firmly to the ribs.
{ **The other** arises from the pleura <note>The membrane lining the thorax and enveloping the lungs</note>, and this covers that tunic derived from the periosteum.

They provide this **Use**: to laterally defend the spiritual organs <note>The "vital" organs of the chest, such as the heart and lungs, associated with the "vital spirits" in early medicine</note> from external injuries or violence.
They are subject to **Diseases** such as fracture, dislocation, and loosening <note>original: "relaxationi"</note>.

### BOOK II.
Concerning the
## SPECIFIC COMPONENTS OF THE MUSCULAR
### SUBSTANCE.
### CHAPTER I.
Concerning the intercostal muscles. <note>The muscles located between the ribs.</note>

<image-desc>A tree-like diagram with curly braces categorizes information about intercostal muscles, detailing their name, substance, number, use, diseases, and astrological influences.</image-desc>
The Name is "Intercostal Muscles" from their location or position.
The Substance is partly nervous <note>meaning fibrous or sinewy in this period</note>, partly fleshy, and partly cartilaginous, as was previously reported regarding the nature of muscles.
The Number is 22. Vesalius <note>Andreas Vesalius (1514–1564), the foundational figure of modern human anatomy</note> maintains that the lower ones serve inspiration, while the outer ones serve expiration; for those of the first two ribs dilate the upper part of the chest, just as those two of the lowest ribs contract it, occupying a significant place in respiration. But concerning this in its own place. See Table 1. AB. & CC. & D. but especially See T.T. for the intercostal muscles.
<margin>Of these muscles</margin> The Use is chiefly occupied in the action of breathing.
Diseases are tumors, ulcers, abscesses <note>original: "apostemata"</note>; indeed, I remember that in my childhood I was afflicted with an almost lethal carbuncle <note>a severe, painful cluster of boils</note> toward the left part of the chest. From which danger (thanks be to God), through the industry of a certain skilled and learned surgeon, I finally emerged healthy.
The Constellation is:
  From the planets: Saturn ♄
  From the fixed signs: Cancer ☍ <note>The symbol ☍ here refers to the zodiac sign Cancer, which traditionally governs the chest.</note>

### CHAPTER II.
Concerning the Breasts.

<image-desc>A tree-like diagram with curly braces categorizes information about the mammae (breasts), detailing their nomenclature, composition, quantity, shape, temperament, use, diseases of milk and substance, and astrological influences.</image-desc>
They are named:
  Mammae.
  Mammilla.
  Teats <note>original: "Vbera"</note>.
They have a varied composition: For the breasts
  Of the Male consist of skin, fat, and nipples; but they lack glands, as there is no necessity for them to generate milk.
  Of Females, however, besides the skin, fat, and nipples, they have many glandular bodies; they consist therefore of skin, fat, the fleshy membrane <note>panniculus carnosus</note>, and glands, nerves, veins, and arteries. For the movement of the mammary vein see Table 4. B. C. For the mammary arteries see DE. & LL. Table 6. b.
They enjoy a varied Quantity, according to the disposition of the person's body.
They have a round Shape, and the breast is like a hemisphere whose pole is the nipple.
They have a cold and moist Temperament <note>In Galenic medicine, "temperament" refers to the balance of bodily humors</note>.
They provide Use:
  For the adornment of the human body.
  For the generation of milk (intended for the nutrition of the infant).
<margin>Which</margin>
Are oppressed by various diseases, namely either due to the indisposition
  Of the Milk, such as its:
    Excess or diminution.
    Blindness <note>blockage</note> and curdling.
    Putrefaction and freezing <note>coagulation</note>.
    Excessive thickness or thinness.
  Of the Substance, such as:
    Abscess.
    Greatness or swelling.
    Erosion <note>corrosio</note>.
    Ulcer.
    Cancer.
    Inflammation.
    Hardness.
They have a Constellation:
  From the planets: Saturn ♄
  From the Signs of the Zodiac: Cancer ☍

## BOOK THREE.
### CHAPTER I.
### On the Diaphragm.

<margin>The name is</margin>
Diaphragm <note>From the Greek *diaphragma*, meaning a partition wall.</note>.
*Phrenas* <note>Greek: *phrenes*</note>, not because it participates in wisdom <note>The ancients sometimes associated the diaphragm with the seat of the mind or soul.</note>, but because when it is inflamed, it induces a continuous "phrensy" <note>original: *phrenitidem*; a state of delirium or brain fever.</note>. However, this species of phrensy differs from that called "idiopathic" <note>meaning a primary disease of the organ itself.</note>, which happens from an inflammation of the membranes of the brain: because in this case [the diaphragm], the voice is hoarse and breathing is frequent and difficult.

<margin>Substance</margin>
The middle part is membranous and nervous <note>meaning full of sinews or tendons</note>, and in this it differs from the common property of a muscle, and is therefore unique.
The outer part is fleshy and somewhat tendinous. For its complete description, see Table 3, letters a, b, c, d, e.

<margin>The composition is made of</margin>
The membranous part is composed of two coats, of which:
} The lower arises from the peritoneum <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note>.
} The upper is derived from the subcostal membrane <note>the pleura, which lines the chest</note>.
Regarding this, see Table 3, b, c, d, e.
It also has its own nerves, for which see Illustration II, Figure 1, Table 5.
The fleshy part is that which consists of simple flesh. This is denoted by f and g in Table 3.
Veins and arteries also concur in its composition, as seen in Table 1, n and o.

<margin>The quantity in—</margin>
Width is so ample that it fills the entire lower circumference of the chest <note>original: *Thoracis*</note>, as is evident through m and o, l in Table 1.
Length extends from the sword-shaped cartilage <note>the xiphoid process at the base of the breastbone</note> to the second vertebra of the loins.
The aforementioned Table also notes this.

<margin>Of this membranous muscle</margin>
In height, its fleshy part is lower and more depressed where it turns at its circumference than the nervous part which appears in the center. And this is declared by the raised letter "a" in Table 1.
The position is between the vital and natural parts <note>The "vital" parts (heart/lungs) are in the chest; the "natural" parts (stomach/liver) are in the belly.</note>, for by it they are distinguished from one another; see Table 1, Book 2, a.
For the Diaphragm in its seat, see RR, Table 4. For the partition free from the breastbone <note>original: *sterno*</note> and the sword-shaped cartilage.
The shape is round, but yet it verges more toward an oblong figure; and in this figure or image, it is seen to differ from all other muscles. But truly, its shape was so ordained by nature that it might most aptly bound the lowest region of the chest. For this, see Table 3. It has, moreover, two fleshy "twists" <note>the crura of the diaphragm</note> which are signified in Table 1 and Table 3 by h and i.

<margin>There are three openings, of which</margin>
{ Two are on the left: } One is destined for the Esophagus, the other for the trunk of the Aorta.
{ One is on the right, and this is proper to the trunk of the *vena cava* <note>the main vein returning blood to the heart</note>. For these, see Table 1, e and m, and Table 3, k, l, and m.

<margin>The connection is made</margin>
{ At the front part, with the breastbone; see Table 1, u.
{ At the sides, with the ends of the lower ribs. And it is indicated by X, Table 1.
{ At the back part, with the first two vertebrae of the loins. As is shown near o o, Table 1.
{ Also, from its surface, it has a closeness with the heart. As in F, G, Figure 2, Table 5.

<margin>Use</margin>
{ The first is to provide the duties of breathing; for it is the principal organ of respiration.
{ The second is for expelling the dregs of the belly <note>assisting in bowel movements</note>, for it is observed to perform this work especially.

Diseases are inflammation, phrensy, flatulent distension (as in those suffering from hypochondria <note>pain/distress in the upper abdomen</note> and Scurvy).

<header>CONCERNING THE SPECIFIC PARTS OF THE MEMBRANOUS SUBSTANCE THAT ACT AS CONTAINERS.</header>

## CHAPTER II.
### Concerning the Pleura.

<margin>Its name is</margin>{ The Pleura <note>From the Greek word for "side" or "rib."</note>.
The membrane lining the ribs.
The subcostal tunic <note>Literally the "under-the-ribs" coat.</note>.
**Origin:** It proceeds from several small fibers descending from the *dura mater* <note>The tough outermost membrane of the brain.</note> or the *pericranium* <note>The membrane covering the skull.</note> through those openings through which the intercostal nerves descend.
**Substance:** It is membranous and spermatic <note>In early anatomy, "spermatic" referred to white, firm tissues like tendons or membranes, believed to originate from the same "seed" as the embryo.</note>, and in its composition it is doubled so that it may more firmly hold and support the veins diffused everywhere through this region.
**Quantity:** It is so large that it encompasses the contents of this region in the same way as the peritoneum <note>The lining of the abdominal cavity.</note> encompasses those of the lowest region.
<margin>The membrane of this</margin>**Position:** It is located throughout the entire middle venter <note>The thorax or chest cavity.</note>. Moreover, this membrane grants a tunic <note>A covering layer.</note> to every part enclosed in this middle region, just as the peritoneum is seen to provide the same in the lowest region. Furthermore, just as the rib is immediately invested by the periosteum <note>The membrane covering the bone.</note> which adheres firmly to it, so also the Pleura rests upon this periosteum; for this reason, it is called the membrane "girding the ribs."
**Connection:** It has a firm connection with all the vertebrae, the ribs, and even the breastbone <note>original: "osse sternon"</note>, so that it can hardly be separated from them without the danger of rupture.
**Use:** In every respect, its function is similar to the action of the Peritoneum; namely, that it covers the parts contained in the Thorax in the same way that the peritoneum surrounds those of the lower belly.
**Diseases:** These include pleurisy <note>original: "pleuritis"</note>, pneumonia <note>original: "peripneumonia"</note>, etc.

---

## CHAPTER III.
### Concerning the Mediastinum.

<margin>{ Its name is the mediastinum, by reason of its office, inasmuch as it is seen to divide the region of the Thorax into two equal parts along its length. See Table 4.</margin>
**Order:** It is the first among the contents, although we name it here among the "containers" because it is formed by a doubling of the pleura, which is a containing part.
**Origin:** It is from the pleura itself, for this is nothing other than the pleura folded back.
**Substance:** Therefore, it is the same as that of the pleura and other membranes.
**Composition:** It is made of two membranes which (as was said) arise from the pleura, and it appears to be nothing other than the pleura doubled over.
**Quantity:** It extends from the collarbones <note>original: "clauiculis"</note> all the way to the xiphoid cartilage <note>original: "mucronatam Cartilaginem," the pointed tip of the breastbone.</note>; that is, it passes through the entire length of this region, as appears through F. G. and HH. in Table 4.
<margin>Whose</margin>**Shape:** It is thin and subtle, very much like a spider's web.
**Number:** It is one, without a mate or pair.
**Temperament:** It is cold and dry, like the rest of the membranes.
**Connection:** It is made at the lower part of the breastbone, and from there it descends perpendicularly to the vertebrae of the back themselves, to which it is also attached with a firm bond. See Table 4. L. G. and HH.
**Position:** It is in the middle region of the thorax, for it divides the vital parts <note>The heart and lungs.</note> into two equal parts along their length, and appears to bisect the lower belly. But in the left side, it leaves a space aptly arranged for containing the pericardium <note>The sac surrounding the heart.</note>. For its natural position on the right and left, see GG. HH. and I. K. and LL. in Table 4.
**Use:** It is to distinguish the left side from the right, which work nature ordained for this purpose: so that if one part of the vital organs should be injured, the other might remain whole and unharmed.
**Diseases:** These are abscesses <note>original: "Apostemata"</note> and ulcers. I remember, moreover, that in a certain deceased nobleman I found a severe abscess in the lowest portion of this membrane, by which the entire pericardium was consumed and the substance of the heart was putrid.

### BOOK IV.
Concerning the
## PARTICLES CONTAINED
### WITHIN IT.
### CHAPTER I.
Concerning the Pericardium <note>The membrane or "sac" that surrounds the heart.</note>.

<margin>Name</margin>
{ In Greek, it is *perikardion*.
{ In Latin, the heart's
{ Envelope.
{ House.
{ Capsule.
{ Little chest.
{ Sheath, according to Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note>.

**Origin:** It is derived from the base of the heart, and not from the ligaments of the vertebrae, as some quite thoughtlessly maintain.
**Substance:** It is hard, dense, and well-compacted, yet entirely devoid of fibers.

**Composition:** It consists of a double
tunic, namely:
{ The **Proper** <note>The inner layer</note>, which is seen to be composed of the nerves of the sixth conjugation <note>The vagus nerve</note>, arteries, and small veins (which are also
{ inserted into the transverse septum <note>The diaphragm</note>). See Table 5.c.
{ The **Common** <note>The outer layer</note>, and this is derived from the pleura <note>The membrane lining the thoracic cavity</note>.

**Quantity:** It is much larger and more spacious than the heart, so that the heart may move more freely in its motion and in the measure of its *Diastole* <note>expansion</note> and *Systole* <note>contraction</note>.
<margin>Of this envelope</margin>
**Figure:** It represents the likeness of the heart, of which it is the receptacle, just as a sheath is most certainly seen to be adapted to the shape of a sword. See Table 5.B.fig.1.
**Position:** It is everywhere around the substance of the heart. In Table 5.B. it indicates the beginning of the Pericardium. D.E.F. its face. fig. 2. BB. it is reflected to the sides and A. the vessels of the heart.
**Temperament:** It is cold and dry, in respect to its membranous substance.

**Connection:** It is made through
{ Membranes, with the base of the heart. See B.fig.1.Table 5.
{ Its own vessels, with the origin of the lungs, with the liver, with the heart, and also by grace of its
{ nerves it has a relationship to the head. See fig.1. & 2. Table 5. where it is shown how it is connected
{ to the lungs by itself and to the Liver through the vena cava A.

**Use:** It is
{ To defend and fortify the heart from external vapors and other injuries.
{ To contain within itself a watery moisture, which (as some maintain) serves for the cooling of the heart.

**Diseases:** These are Abscesses <note>original: *Apostema*</note>, ulcers, consumption, etc. I inspected the corpse of a certain soldier named James Cromer, opened by incision, whose entire pericardium had been consumed by an abscess; indeed, we even found the heart itself deeply ulcerated.

## CHAPTER II.
### Concerning the ascending vena cava.

In passing, I wish the *reader* to observe in this place that, although we have previously spoken of the nature of the entire <term>vena cava</term> <note>The "hollow vein," the primary vein carrying deoxygenated blood to the heart</note> in a succinct manner, nevertheless, in our public administration of <term>Anatomy</term>, we specify the <term>ascending vena cava</term> in this section. We shall clearly demonstrate the trunk emerging from the hump of the <term>Liver</term> <note>original: "Hepatis"</note>, and also its entry into the right <term>ventricle of the heart</term>, along with its individual branches—both those tending directly upward and those inclining laterally—since we could not conveniently reach a genuine and visual description of it before the removal of the <term>pericardium</term> <note>The sac surrounding the heart</note>.

## CHAPTER III.
### Concerning the Heart.

<margin>It is named, { In Greek, kardia. In Latin, Cor.</margin>
In dignity it is the most noble, being the first thing living in man and the last to die.
It is ordained by nature (as some will have it) both in time and in place, before the other principal members.
But <term>Galen</term> <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medical science for 1,300 years</note> seems to assert that the brain is more ancient than the heart. Others, taught by experience, say that the <term>Brain</term> is brought into the light at the same time, affirming that in the space of seven days after the injection of the seed into the womb, three bubbles are smeared within its mass, each of which corresponds to one of these principal members. And again, they assert that within 15 days these are reduced into members of that kind, so that one can be distinguished from the other in some way. Concerning these matters, we propose to dispute more widely in our mystical <term>Anatomy</term>, by divine permission.

> If the straight [fibers] are contracted, then while the other types of fibers are relaxed, the heart is dilated; this action is called *Diastole*. And in the time of this motion, the heart is accustomed to draw air from the lungs through the <term>venous artery</term> <note>original: "arteriam venosam"; historically referring to the pulmonary vein</note> into the left <term>ventricle</term> for its own cooling and for the nourishment of the vital spirits. And also by this same action, the heart draws blood from the trunk of the ascending <term>vena cava</term> through the valves of its right ventricle—which are open on the outside but closed on the inside, and very similar to the points of arrows—and this for the sake of nourishing the substance of the <term>lungs</term>.

<margin>It enjoys a substance of dense and solid flesh woven from three kinds of fibers, of which:</margin>
> If the transverse [fibers] are contracted, the straight ones are again relaxed, and the heart is indeed contracted and repressed; this action is called *Systole*. In the time of this motion, the smoky wastes of the air are expelled from the left <term>ventricle of the heart</term>, partly through the venous artery, and partly through the great <term>artery</term> <note>The aorta</note> into other parts, as some will have it. But my opinion does not agree with this at all: for that which is partial and separated from the air in its superfluity, I believe is thrust into the portal and stored in it; but that which is superfluous and useless, I believe is sent out through the windpipe by expiration. Also in the space of this motion, that blood drawn from the <term>vena cava</term> by the preceding motion, and prepared and elaborated in the right <term>ventricle of the heart</term>, is introduced through the <term>arterial vein</term> <note>original: "venam arteriosam"; historically referring to the pulmonary artery</note>, fitted with semilunar valves, to nourish the <term>lungs</term>. For a light nourishment is required for the substance of the <term>lungs</term>. It is necessary that the blood be rectified again by a vessel of a less pure nature, so that it might be rendered lighter and more subtle to perform this function of its own.
> The oblique [fibers] produce that rest which intervenes between *Diastole* and *Systole*.

<margin>It is composed of parts</margin>
<margin>Similar, such as:</margin>
> Its own flesh, as mentioned before.
> Two <term>coronary veins</term>, which contribute to the nourishment of the heart. For these, see L. fig. 2. Tab. 5. and LL.
> Two <term>coronary arteries</term>, restoring its substance with vital fibers. And for these, see L. fig. 2. Tab. 5. and LL.
> A <term>nerve</term> arising from the sixth conjugation <note>The vagus nerve</note>, and <term>Fat</term> <note>original: "Pinguedo"</note>, which contributes to its moistening.

<margin>Organic, concerning which see below at sign A.</margin>
<margin>It has a shape like a pine nut.</margin>

During that time, the entire cavity of the chest was filled with thick and foul water, like urine or thick lye. Thus, in the midst of his illness, there was an error in the calling and consultation of many physicians, who all felt differently than I (who said he suffered from an abscess in the chest cavity along with a quantity of water). They unanimously felt his disease was composed of flatulent matter enclosed in the venous artery or the arterial vein. But the outcome of the matter proved their consensus to be false.

The substance of the lung is lighter and more airy than other parts of the body; for if it were nourished by the same blood as the other parts, it would be less fit to perform its required duty, which consists of continuous motion. Hence, a light substance requires light nourishment, since we are taught that like is most aptly nourished by its like, and nature rejoices in its own likeness. *See A. fig.1. Table 5.*

<margin>The **Right** [chamber], which is so named for the blood, since it contributes to the purification and thinning of the blood; and in this we observe four things, namely:</margin>
<margin>The organic parts of the heart are examined in the chamber of the heart, either:</margin>
Six valves or small membranes, namely:
(Three in the orifice of the auricular vein, closed on the inside. Three in the orifice of the arterial vein, open on the inside and closed on the outside, so that blood does not return into the heart. And these are called **semilunar** <note>Half-moon shaped</note> from their appearance. The **venous artery** <note>The pulmonary vein</note>, through which air is introduced by inhalation to the left ventricle of the heart for the sustenance of life and the cooling of the heart and arterial blood; its waste part is expelled again through exhalation. *For this see fig.2. Two vessels, namely:
Seven more internal parts, namely:

And these are ordained by nature so that the vital spirits, forged in the left laboratory of the heart and placed into the great artery (destined to receive them), should not return again into the laboratory. *For these see Bauhin in the place cited before.*

Five valves placed in the said vessels, of which:
Two are placed in the orifice of the venous artery, open on the outside and closed on the inside; these are called **Mitral** because they are very similar to the mitres of Bishops. Their duty is both to receive the air introduced by inhalation and to emit the useless part of it.

### CHAPTER IV.
## Concerning the Great Artery. <note>The Aorta.</note>

The difference, namely between it and a vein, for
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;A **Vein** has only a single tunic <note>layer or coat</note>, and that one is thin and porous, which is composed of straight fibers and some moderately oblique ones.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;An **Artery** is endowed with a double tunic, of which
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The **Exterior** is very similar to that of the vein, being of the same substance and composed of the same or similar fibers.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The **Interior** is five times denser or thicker in proportion, and woven from transverse fibers: so that it might better contain the subtle spirits of life. <note>The "vital spirits" were believed to be carried in the arterial blood to animate the body.</note>

The **Name**, which is
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Aortes* in Greek, and commonly called the **Aorta**.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The **Great Artery** in Latin.

The **Origin**, which is from the left ventricle of the heart. For this, see *a.* in Table 6.a. and *A.* in Table 6.b. And *aa.* in figure 2 of Table 8 denotes its orifice <note>opening</note> cut away from the heart.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**Offshoots** of this kind are the Arteries:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**Coronary**, proceeding from the aorta before its trunk exits from the left cavity of the heart. And a circular cluster of small arteries of this kind is intended for the preservation of the heart, just as the coronal veins are for its nourishment. For these, see *B.* in Table 6.b. and *aa.* in figure 2 of Table 8.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**Intercostal**, produced from the *Azygos* <note>The "unpaired" vein/vessel system</note>, whose duty is to assign vital power to the muscles of that place. For these, see *I.* in Table 6.b. and *H.*

which is also depicted in the description of the <term>vena cava</term> <note>The "hollow vein," the primary vein returning blood to the heart</note>, as it is found within the body.

## CHAPTER V.
### Concerning the Lungs.

<image-desc>A hierarchical diagram illustrating the classification and properties of the lungs. The main topic "Concerning the Lungs" branches into several categories like "Before we come to the description of the lungs...", "Name", "Substance", "Composition, made of", "Size", "Temperament", "Number", "Position", "Connections made with", "Use is", "Diseases are", and "Constellation, from". Each category further branches into sub-categories, often grouped by large curly braces. The "Constellation, from" section includes astrological symbols for planets (Sun ☉, Moon ☽, Saturn ♄, Jupiter ♃, Mars ♂, Venus ♀, Mercury ☿) and zodiac signs (Aries ♈, Taurus ♉, Gemini ♊, Cancer ♋, Leo ♌, Virgo ♍, Libra ♎, Scorpio ♏, Sagittarius ♐, Capricorn ♑, Aquarius ♒, Pisces ♓).</image-desc>

Before we come to the description of the lungs, it must be
known that there are three kinds of respiratory organs, for
some are:
    Moving, such as the 65 muscles of the Chest <note>original: "Thoracis"</note>.
    Carrying air to the lungs and to the left chamber of the heart, such as
    the windpipe <note>original: "aspera arteria"</note> and the Larynx.
    Receiving, and of this kind are the lungs, which we
    shall treat here.

Name,
    In Latin,
        By the Philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle.</note>, it is the fan of the heart.
        By Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician (980–1037 AD) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard text.</note>, the knives of the heart.
        By physicians in general, *pulmo*.
    In English, it is The Lungs.
Substance, is soft, rare, and spongy.
Composition, is made of:
    Its own flesh, which is called Parenchyma <note>The functional tissue of an organ as distinguished from the connective framework.</note>.
    Nerves descending from the sixth pair <note>original: "sexta coniugatione"; in historical anatomy, the "sixth pair" of cranial nerves often referred to what we now call the Vagus nerve.</note>.
    The arterial vein <note>The pulmonary artery.</note>, concerning which see figure 2, Table [X].
        Branches. Concerning these, see C. & D. figure 1, Table 7, and figures 3 & 4
    abundantly.
    The venous artery <note>The pulmonary vein.</note>, concerning which see figure 4,
    Table 7.
    A single tunic <note>A covering membrane.</note>, which it receives from the Pleura.
    The Windpipe <note>original: "Trachea Arteria"</note>, whose bifurcated trunk plunges into the substance of the lungs, as in
    Table 9.
Size, it fills the cavity of the Chest.
Shape, it is likened to an ox's foot. As appears in figure 2, Table 7.
Temperament, is more hot than cold by reason of its airy and light flesh; for this reason nature formed it light
and spongy so that they might provide pure blood and perform their natural office with less labor. And because of this
composition from its own substance and air, nature [provides] pure and thin [blood] in the right chamber of the heart,
elaborated from thick blood as was declared above.
Number, it is judged to be two-fold, whence they are called "lungs" <note>The Latin "pulmones" is plural.</note>, since that whole mass is divided into a right and left
part by the mediastinum, as in figure 2, Table 7. Each of these is observed to have its own lobes, but in truth
their substance is continuous, wherefore they are accustomed to be called both "lung" and "lungs." For the upper and lower
lobe, see P. Q. Table 4, and N. O.; and in Table 5, L. M. N. O. are its 4 lobes, which are more clearly indicated by E. F. G. H. in figures 1 & 2, Table 7.
Position, is in the middle of the chest, where they also surround the pericardium. Their front face is denoted by Table 7,
figure 1; the back by figure 2.
Connections are made with:
    The Heart, by the arterial vein and the venous artery: which is indicated by A. B. of figures
    3 & 4, Table 7.
    The Brain, by the nerve from the sixth pair. See q q. Table 8.
    The Vertebrae and ribs, by membranes from the Pleura.
    The Windpipe or Trachea, by a strong union. As is indicated by B. Table 7, figure 1.
    Respiration and voice, and also built for the cooling of the heart.
Use is, that it be an organ for:
    Not absolutely necessary for life, seeing as some animals such as
    fish and reptiles can and usually do live without it.
Diseases are:
    Dyspnea, or difficulty breathing.
    Asthma.
    Cough <note>original: "Tussis"</note>.
    Damaged voice or hoarseness.
    Pleurisy <note>Inflammation of the pleura.</note>.
    Empyema, the spitting of blood with a cough.
    Phthisis <note>A progressive wasting disease, usually tuberculosis.</note>.
    Pneumonia <note>original: "Peripneumonia"</note>.
Constellation, from:
    The Planets,
        The Sun ☉
        Whose signs are ☽ <note>The Moon</note>

### CHAPTER VI.
### Concerning the Recurrent Nerves.

They received their name from their flexible movement <note>original: "à motu fuo flexibili"; these are now known as the recurrent laryngeal nerves because they loop backward</note>.
They arise from the sixth conjugation of nerves <note>In early modern anatomy, the vagus nerve was often classified as the sixth pair; today it is the tenth cranial nerve</note>. As appears by *ee* in Figure 1, Table 8.

<margin>It has movement,</margin>Downward, together with the carotid arteries (by which they are stabilized and supported) through the neck into the cavity of the Chest. For this, see *OO* in Figure 2, Table 8. And *HH* indicates the carotids from *GG*.

Upward, while a branch of each of them returns again from the depths of the chest by the same path by which it previously descended; and in its return or backward step, one of them adhering to one artery and the other to the other, it seeks those six muscles by which the larynx is usually opened and closed. And these nerves are attached for the sake of activating the muscles. For this, observe the adherence of *OO*, *HH*, and *GG* to the artery in Figure 2, Table 8. For the location of the revolution of the right branch, see *P* in Figure 2, Table 8; as for the left, the right ascending one is *QQ* in Figure 2, and the left ascending one is *SS*.

The Right [nerve] reflects or loops under the collarbone <note>original: "clauiculo"</note>, around the branch of the great artery that leads to the right armpit, as if wound around a certain small pulley <note>original: "carotulam"</note>, and it runs back upward until it disperses into the three parts of the muscles of the larynx. For this, see *P* in Figure 2, Table 8 for the place of reflection, and *S*, *N*, and *M* for the location of the larynx.

<margin>They obtain a varied position or site after their descent, for</margin>The Left [nerve], submerged much further and more deeply, is wound around the greatest artery <note>the aorta</note> near the heart, especially at that part where it reflects itself toward the spine from the emerging part, and then afterwards returns to the larynx, and is distributed into the remaining three muscles of the left part of the larynx and the hyoid bone of the tongue, as shown by *π* in Figure 1, Table 8; and see *r* in Figure 2 and Table 8 for the place of reflection, and *N* and *S* for the place of insertion into the larynx muscles; see also *n* in Figure 1 and *l*, *m*, and *o*, *p*.

In Number, there are two. See *OO* and *QQ* for the right, and *HH* and *SS* for the left.

Branches from their "presses" <note>original: "torcularibus"; likely referring to nerve plexuses or junctions</note>.

They are useful for producing the voice, whence when these nerves are injured, the voice is either corrupted or entirely destroyed.

    *   The Right [part of the omentum]: regarding which small branch, see *y* in Figure 1.

# BOOK FIVE.
### Concerning the
## ROUGH ARTERY AND THE PARTS
## CONNECTED TO IT OUTSIDE
### THE THORAX.

### CHAPTER I.
### Concerning the Rough Artery <note>original: "Aspera Arteria"; this is the historical term for the trachea or windpipe, so named because of its ridged, cartilaginous texture compared to the "smooth" arteries that carry blood.</note>.

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Name is | Trachea |
| | Rough |
| | Artery. |

**Substance**, is cartilaginous, which makes it more suitable for producing the voice; for by this kind of composition, it is moderately disposed between hard and soft.
**Composition**, is firm, toward which the veins coming from the external jugulars, the carotid arteries, the recurrent nerves from the sixth conjugation <note>The "sixth conjugation" refers to the vagus nerve in the historical numbering system of Galen.</note>, and a double membrane all converge.
**Quantity**, is spacious and ample enough for the measure of respiration or the proportion necessary for the body.
**Figure**, is round and ringed with joints and imperfect circles, especially in the posterior part which presses against the Esophagus; this was indeed so ordained by nature so that it would not impede the passage of food to the stomach. For the anterior part of this, see Table 9, figure 1. For the posterior, figure 2.
**Position**, begins immediately below the Larynx and extends all the way to the lungs, and in its extension, it passes over the gullet. After it has reached the lungs, it divides itself into two branches, namely the right and the left, and each <margin>Of which</margin> of these is subdivided into several others. For the division, see figure 2; for the rings or semicircular cartilages, see dd. figure 2, Table 8, C. D. and bb. figure 1, Table 9. For its subdivision into branches, see CCC. figure 1, Table 9. For the pipe <note>original: "fistula"</note>, see aa. figure 1, Table 9. Furthermore, for the cartilages of the larynx, see mm. and nn. figure 2, Table 9.
**Temperament**, is cold and dry, inasmuch as it is a spermatic part <note>In humoral theory, "spermatic" parts were tissues believed to originate from the father's seed, such as bone and cartilage, characterized by being cold and dry.</note>.
**Connection**, is with the aforementioned extreme parts, namely the Larynx and the lungs; specifically with the Larynx at kk. figure 1 and mm. nn. figure 2, Table 9.
**Use**, is twofold, namely:
1. For conducting air into the lungs and the left chamber of the heart, and also for expelling the smoky wastes <note>original: "fuliginosa"; refers to the "sooty" vapors believed to be produced by the heart's heat.</note> of the same.
2. That it may be the proper and principal organ of the voice.

## CHAPTER II.
Concerning the Larynx.

**Name:** Larynx. For a detailed description of it and its appendages, see Plate 10, the second Plate after 10, and Plate 3 after that.

**Substance or composition:** It is made of three large cartilages, of which:
The **Anterior** is the largest in size; it is convex on the outside and hollowed out on the inside in the shape of a shield, which is why it is called *thyreoeidēs* <note>original: "θυρεοειδὴς"; the thyroid cartilage</note>. For this, see F. in figures 2 and 3, and aa. in figure 1 of Plate 10, and n.n. in the second Plate, figures 3, 4, and 5.
The **Second** is smaller than the first and larger than the third; it is positioned in the esophagus <note>The author likely refers here to the proximity to the gullet</note> and is called *krikoeidēs* <note>original: "κρικοειδὴς"; the cricoid or ring-shaped cartilage</note>. See figure 2 of Plate 9, n.n.
The **Third** is the smallest and ends in a sharp angle, hence it is called *arytainoeidēs* <note>original: "ἀρυταινοειδὴς"; the arytenoid or ladle-shaped cartilage</note>, from the shape of a vessel. See c.c. in figure 1 of Plate 10, and c.c. in figure 5 of the second Plate.

**Muscles serving it:** There are 20, of which:
Twelve are its own [intrinsic]. For some of these, see fig. 1.e.e., fig. 2.f.f., g., l., and m., and f.g. in fig. 3 of the second Plate, and f.f.g.s., g., and l. in fig. 7.
Eight are common [extrinsic] to it.
**Mercury** <note>The symbol ☿ denotes the astrological influence of the planet Mercury over these muscles</note> alone governs them.

**Location:** It is situated at the very top of the rough artery <note>term: rough artery (arteria aspera); the historical name for the trachea or windpipe</note>. As seen in figures 1 and 2 of Plate 9, k in figure 4 of the second Plate, figure 6, and 2 in Plate 3 after 10.
**Nerves:** These proceed from the sixth pair <note>The vagus nerve, historically classified as the sixth cranial nerve</note> and especially those called the "recurrent" nerves. See m. in figure 3 of the second Plate after 10.
**Use and action:** It is to form the voice, for it expands and compresses greatly, and opens and closes.
**Diseases:** These are attributed to the Artery, since the Larynx is the summit of the rough artery.
**Associations:**
From the planets: **Mercury**
From the signs: **Mercury**
With the planets: Those recited in the section on the rough artery.

---

## CHAPTER III.
Concerning the Epiglottis.

**Name:**
Greek: *Epiglotta*.
Latin: *Lingua laringis* (The tongue of the larynx).

**Substance:** It is membranous, like a thin and fatty cartilage; however, it pertains to the esophagus and adheres to the root of the tongue and the cartilage of the larynx. For this, see fig. 2, Plate 10.
**Shape:** It is in the form or likeness of the reed of a pipe <note>referring to a musical instrument's mouthpiece</note>, namely round and slightly larger in size. For this, see b. in figures 4, 5, and 6 of the second and third Plates after 10, fig. 1 of Plate 10, and n.λ. in fig. 10 of Plate 3 after 10; n.n. describes its base and apex.
**Location:** It is situated opposite the Arytenoid cartilage and originates from the root of the tongue, as Galen teaches us in *On the Use of the Parts*. See b. in fig. 1, Plate 10, O. in figures 1 and 2 of Plate 9, and b. in the second Plate, figures 4, 5, 6, and 7.
**Humor:**
**Temperament:** It is clearly moist and viscous.
**Connection:** It is joined to the root of the tongue and is continuous with the shield-shaped [thyroid] cartilage. See Plate 3 after 10, fig. 10, and N. and b. in fig. 4 of the second Plate after 10, where *it explains its origin*.
**Use:** It serves as a lid or stopper for the opening of the larynx, so that when any nourishment is swallowed through the esophagus, none of it accidentally or suddenly falls or creeps into the rough artery. For this organ is raised during respiration, but in swallowing it falls and is pressed downward, covering the passage leading to the lungs through the trachea artery—that is, the passage through which we draw in the airy spirit.

### CHAPTER IV.
### Concerning the Tonsils.

<margin>These small portions or glands</margin>
Are called,
*   In Greek, *Parishmia*.
*   *Tonsils*.
*   In Latin, *Amygdalae* <note>Literally "almonds".</note>.
*   In English, *The Almonds of the throat*.
They have a glandular substance.
The shape is like a grain, similar to fleshy or *spongy* glands. For these, see Table 9 of the *Lowest Region*, E. E.
The position is naturally placed on each side of the larynx.
They have a connection with the uppermost opening of the *Esophagus*, as seen at E. E. in the place previously cited, and F. Table 12 following.
They are useful for receiving and soaking up the moisture descending from the brain, with which they moisten the tongue and all the surrounding members in the mouth; this action is especially necessary in burning fevers where the humor is exhausted.
They are affected by diseases, namely:
*   *Abscesses*.
*   *Inflammation*.
*   *Tumors*.
*   *Wounds*.
According to their constellation, they claim for themselves:
*   From the *Planets of the Sun*, ☾ <note>The Moon symbol is used here, perhaps indicating a lunar influence despite the text saying "Planets of the Sun".</note>
*   From the *Signs of the Sun*, ☋ <note>The symbol for the Descending Node/Dragon's Tail.</note>

### CHAPTER V.
### Concerning the Uvula.

<margin>Whose</margin>
Name,
*   In Greek, is *Gargareon*.
*   In Latin, is
    *   *Columna* <note>Column</note>
    *   *Columella* <note>Little column</note>
    <note>The preceding two terms are described as:</note> when it is found to be misshapen. And then it is seen to be diseased.
    *   *Uvula* <note>Little grape</note>, when it presents an image like that, and then it is also unhealthy and in an unnatural state.
    *   *Gurgulio* <note>Windpipe/Gullet</note>, commonly (as found in Rufeus) insofar as it is found within the limits of health: although *Gurgulio* is most often taken for the *Trachea Artery*.
*   In English, *The pallet of the throat*.
The origin is from the *dura mater* <note>The tough outermost membrane enveloping the brain</note>, of which it is a portion; for after that membrane has exited the upper skull, it spreads out and grows, becoming almost fleshy. Then it descends to the bone, whose entire "heaven" or roof—indeed the whole mouth, both lower and upper—it clothes. At the extremity of the palate, it flies toward it double, and being somewhat long, it produces by its entanglements an oblong particle distinguished by various names, namely this which we call the *Gurgulio*. Then this membrane, plunging itself downward as far as the stomach, is said to weave its internal tunic there. And from this comes such a great sympathy between the stomach and the mouth, that one is accustomed to reject that which is not pleasing to the other.
The substance is membranous and spermatic <note>In early medicine, "spermatic" referred to tissues derived from the primary "seeds" of the embryo, like membranes or nerves.</note>. P.
The quantity is only small, but its dimension is long.
The position is shown by E. Table 12.
The shape is like a drop of ice hanging from a house <note>An icicle.</note>, of which the upper part is *naturally longer*, and the lower part more narrow.

## CHAPTER VI.
### Concerning the Tongue.

<margin>It is called,</margin>
<p>In Greek, *glotta*.</p>
<p>In Latin, *Lingua*.</p>
<p>In English, *The Arcunge* <note>likely a corruption of "arch-tongue" or a specific regional anatomical term</note>.</p>

<p>It has a substance that is large and strong at the root, into which the Hyoid bone is fixed. However, it is thin at its extremity for the sake of greater speed <note>referring to the agility required for speech</note>.</p>

<margin>It is composed of,</margin>
<p>A membrane <note>original: "Tunica"</note>, common to the mouth. For this, see figure 1. AAA. Table 11. and BB. and C.</p>
<p>Two ligaments, attached to its lowest parts.</p>
<p>A bone situated at its root, called the Hyoid <note>original: "Voedes," a variation of Hyoides</note>, because it is shaped like the Greek letter upsilon (~). The uses of this are various.</p>
<p>Several muscles, some of which are inserted into the upper part of the same, and the action of these is to lift the tongue to the palate; others attached to its sides move it laterally; others inserted into the lowest part of the same carry it downward and incline it. For its muscles, see D.E.F.G. figure Table 1.</p>
<p>Two arteries woven into it.</p>
<p>Two veins appearing in its lowest part; and these we are accustomed to cut <note>referring to bloodletting</note> in hot afflictions of the tongue and throat.</p>
<p>Two pairs of nerves dispersed into it, of which one is soft, which extends from the third conjugation <note>the historical classification of cranial nerves</note> into its furthest trunk, intended for discerning flavors. The other is hard, and derived from the third conjugation, and is disseminated through the muscles of the tongue itself, so that it may serve its voluntary movement.</p>

<margin>This member</margin>
<p>Is placed in the mouth as if in a cave of its own and prepared by nature, but truly at its base it is attached to the bone (~). For the tongue with the epiglottis, see the following Table 12.</p>

<margin>It is useful, both for</margin>
<p>Discerning flavors <note>the sense of taste</note>.</p>
<p>Performing the duty of speaking.</p>

<margin>It is afflicted by various diseases, such as</margin>
<p>Diminution, loss, and corruption of Taste.</p>
<p>Softening and heaviness of the tongue.</p>
<p>Spasm of the tongue.</p>
<p>Greatness <note>enlargement</note> and shortness of the tongue.</p>
<p>Lisping and Stammering, of which mention is made by</p>
<p>Avicenna <note>Persian physician Ibn Sina</note>, Book 3, Fen 6, Chapter 16.</p>
<p>Ranula <note>a cyst under the tongue</note> of the tongue, concerning which Aetius <note>Greek medical writer</note> writes in Book 2, Sermon 4, Chapter 37; Avicenna, Book 3, Fen 6, Chapter 17.</p>
<p>Abscesses of the tongue.</p>
<p>Burning <note>inflammation</note> of the tongue.</p>
<p>Suffusion of the tongue, concerning which Rhazes <note>Persian physician Al-Razi</note> writes in the Book of Divisions, Chapter 50, and Aetius, Chapter 20, Book 2, Sermon 4.</p>
<p>Bothor <note>an Arabic term for small swellings or pustules</note>, concerning which Rhazes writes in the 7th book of the Continens, treatise 2, chapter 2, 76.</p>
<p>Avicenna, Chapter 22, as predicted.</p>

<p>The planets alone: Mercury ☿</p>

### CHAPTER VII.
Concerning the Teeth.

->**Teeth**<-
*   **Name**
    *   Greek, is *odontes* <note>original: ὀδόντες</note>.
    *   Latin, *Dentes*.
*   **Substance**
    *   is bony.
*   **Number**, is 32. For there are:
    *   Eight **Anterior** <note>front teeth/incisors</note> namely in part:
        *   Upper, four.
        *   Lower, four.
    *   **Canines**, specifically:
        *   Upper, two.
        *   Lower, the same number.
    *   **Molars** <note>literally "jaw-teeth"</note>, 10 [per jaw]. Of which five are:
        *   Upper.
        *   Lower.
*   **Regarding these**:
    *   The **Nerves** proceed from the third conjugation <note>the third pair of cranial nerves in the historical numbering system</note>, and these are inserted into their roots; hence comes their so prompt and easy faculty of sensation.
    *   The **Principal Utility** is to prepare the food to be sent into the stomach so that it may be more easily digested.
*   **Diseases**: there are not a few when they are affected by:
    *   Difficulty of their emergence <note>teething</note>.
    *   Pain.
    *   Decay and perforation <note>cavities</note>.
    *   Worms <note>a common historical belief that tooth decay was caused by "tooth worms"</note>.
    *   Loosening.
    *   Numbness from cold <note>literally "congealing"</note>.
    *   Alteration of color.
    *   Grinding at night.

### CHAPTER VIII.
Concerning the Lips.

->**Lips**<-
*   **They are called**:
    *   In Greek, *cheile* <note>original: χείλη</note>.
    *   In Latin, *labia*.
*   **Substance**:
    *   They have a muscular substance, for they consist of four muscles, as we shall immediately declare.
*   **They are moved**:
    *   by voluntary motion.
*   **Muscles**: <margin>These members</margin> they have various ones, in which these things must be observed:
    *   **Number**, which is 4. For:
        *   Two proceed from the furthest edge of the lower jaw.
        *   Two pairs arise under the cheeks.
    *   **Motion**, which is like a gatekeeper, specifically:
        *   **Oblique**, which are four; for two are present for each lip, one tending to the right, the other to the left.
        *   **Straight**, the same number; of which two are entirely straight, and of the remaining two, one pulls the upper lip downward, and the other carries the lower lip upward.
    *   **Composition**, which embraces, besides the muscles, the veins, arteries, and nerves.
*   **Utility**: they are useful both for:
    *   Retaining the food until it is well prepared by the teeth.
    *   The ornament and decoration of the countenance or face.
*   **Diseases**: they are afflicted by various ones, such as:
    *   Clefts <note>cracked lips</note>.
    *   Tumors and abscesses. <insert>Concerning all of which Avicenna treats in Book 3, Fen 3, Chapters 11, 12, 13, 14, 15.</insert>
    *   Ulcers.
    *   Trembling.

### CHAPTER IX.
### Concerning the Mouth.

<margin>In the composition of the mouth, we observe two things especially, namely its</margin>Common membrane, with which it is clothed everywhere both below and above; of which we made fuller mention in the chapter concerning the Uvula, namely regarding its origin, which we said was from the *dura mater* <note>The tough outermost membrane enveloping the brain and spinal cord</note>, and also regarding its progression.
<margin>Three kinds of muscles, of which</margin>
> Two close [the mouth], namely those which lift the hanging lower jaw, for which reason it is required that they be large and quite strong to perform that work. These muscles are called the temporal muscles; if these are harmed or wounded, a convulsion follows—and that quite often—or indeed sometimes fever, *Caros* <note>A state of deep stupor or lethargy</note>, or delirium supervene, which for the most part are lethal signs.
> Two others are opposite to the aforementioned two, and these open the mouth itself, and they are far smaller than the aforementioned.
> Two others, which are intermediate in respect to the rest, both in length and position, are ordained by nature so that they may move the mouth in various directions.
> For the description of the mouth, see the following Table.

## THE THIRD REGION.

### DESCRIPTION OF THE HEAD, OR THE HIGHEST REGION OF THE MICROCOSM, Divided into four books.

- <margin>In the highest region of the microcosm, the following are considered:</margin>
    - The Name, which is the head <note>original: "caput"</note>, acting as the beginning and the summit of the entire human structure.
        - The front portion, devoid of hair, is named the forehead.
        - The upper, forward part is the <term>sinciput</term> <note>the front of the skull</note>.
        - <margin>Position and number</margin> The summit between the sinciput and the <term>occiput</term> <note>the back of the head</note> is called the <term>vertex</term> <note>the crown</note>, named as if it were the center of a circle.

        - The face is everything that extends from the whole forehead down to the chin.

        - Containing parts, and these are:

                - The fat.

            - The cerebrum <note>the main part of the brain</note>.
            - The cerebellum <note>the "little brain" at the back of the skull</note>.
            - The seven pairs of nerves.
            - The eye and its parts:
                - Membranous parts.

    - The Use, which is to contain the animal spirits <note>in early medicine, these were subtle fluids responsible for sensation and movement</note> and to serve their faculties.
    - Disease, which is either:
        - Of the whole:
            - Called <term>Cephalea</term> <note>a chronic or general headache</note>.
        - Of a part:
            - Called <term>Hemicranea</term> <note>a migraine or pain affecting one side of the head</note>.
    - The Constellation <note>astrological influences</note>:

# CHAPTER II.
## Concerning the Pericranium.

It is called,
  Pericranium <note>The membrane that wraps the skull.</note>
  Periosteum <note>Literally "around the bone."</note>

<margin>Specifically, it is that membrane which wraps the skull beneath the skin of the head, and this</margin>
Arises from thin fibers originating from the *dura mater* <note>The "tough mother," the outermost thick membrane surrounding the brain.</note>, emerging from the hollow of the skull through the sutures. In this emergence, the said fibers are formed into the membrane called the periosteum. For its appearance, see Table 2, figure 1, letter N; letter M indicates the skull.

It is connected with the *dura mater* by means of the fibers beneath the skull. See GGG in Table 2, figure 1, and HH, II.

<margin>This is either taken</margin>
It is useful for clothing the skull and for containment, so that the animal spirits <note>In early modern medicine, these were subtle fluids believed to carry sensation and movement.</note> and also vapors do not escape in too great a quantity through the cracks of the sutures.

Generally, and in this way, every membrane or tunic immediately clothing all bones is called periosteum; for those also are derived from the *dura mater* or the thick meninges.

The diseases are fracture, splitting, and bruising.

And of this,
  The constellation is Aries <note>original: "V." (symbol for Aries)</note> among the signs, and Saturn <note>original: "h." (symbol for Saturn)</note> among the planets.

# CHAPTER III.
## Concerning the Skull.

The name, it is called
  In Greek, *Cranion* <note>original: "κρανιον"</note>.
  In Latin,
    *Calvaria*.
    *Cranium*.

Of which
  <margin>Truly, in which two things we achieve, namely</margin>
  The number [of sutures] are
    <margin>of them</margin>
    Two are transverse, namely:
      The Coronal, so named from the crown of kings; see A.B. Table 1.
      The Lambdoid, from its likeness to the Greek letter Lambda (λ); see C.D. Table 1.
    One is direct, the Sagittal, named from its arrow-like shape; see E. Table 1.
  <margin>There are five sutures, of which some are</margin>
  Various functions:
    The Coronal: its function is to distinguish the "stern-bone" <note>The frontal bone, likened here to the front of a ship.</note> from the others.
    The Lambdoid: it divides the "box-bone" <note>The occipital bone</note>, also called the bone of praise or memory, from the others.
    The Sagittal: it separates the two parietal bones from one another.
  <margin>Two are false or spurious, of which</margin>
  The names:
    Squamous <note>Scale-like</note>, so called from its likeness.
    *Mendosa* <note>False or deceptive</note>, by the common people.
    Temporal, by Galen <note>A famous 2nd-century Greek physician</note>. For these, see F.G.H. Table 1.
  Use or function: so that they may distinguish the petrous <note>stony/hard</note> bones, and so that they may release vapors laterally from the brain.
  <margin>The peculiar bones are four, namely:</margin>
  Two of the temples, which the sagittal suture divides; and they are called the parietal bones. See N. Table 1 following; and for the bones of the vertex <note>the top of the head</note>, see I.K. Table 1.
  One of the forehead, divided from the others by the coronal suture; and this is called the "stern-bone," the coronal bone, and the common bone of the forehead. See L. Table 1.
  One of the occiput <note>back of the head</note>, divided from the others by the Lambdoid suture; and this is called the "box-bone" or the bone of memory. See M. Table 1.

The function or use is to fortify both "mothers" of the brain—namely the *dura* and the *pia mater*—and even the brain itself against accidents and external injuries, defending them like a helmet.

The diseases are:
  Fracture.
  Fissure.
  Incision.
  Caries <note>Decay or rot of the bone.</note>.

The constellation, in common, is Aries <note>original: "V."</note>.
