For the **Boreal** (North) wind, which is cold and dry, meeting the **Auster** (South) wind, which is hot and moist, produces sperm and blood in the <term>microcosm</term> <note>The "small world"—the human being seen as a reflection of the universe.</note>, just as they produce clouds and thick air in the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>The "great world"—the universe.</note>. From such things they create mixtures, and the physical constitution will lean or incline toward that "quarter" which holds dominion in the region of the air—that is, whichever wind seems to stand more strongly and with greater power. For example, if the South wind prevails, it creates a more moist disposition tending toward "salty" or "burnt" phlegm. If the North wind prevails, then it renders the nature of the seed or the "cloud" inclined toward a drier and colder blast, yet mixed with a certain moisture which is all the more viscous, icy, or glassy as it has a greater force of the North wind over the South. And this is exactly how things behave in the human world. Thus, various degrees of this physical constitution are observed to arise from the opposition of these two winds, according to the greater or lesser dominion of one over the other.

From this it originates that if demons—or evil spirits of a lowly wind—invade the spirit of the wind that was exultant at a person's birth, and they hold dominion over the natural spirit of the newborn, then they indeed convert that natural habit (which is suited to a healthy life) into a morbid disposition which physicians call "preternatural" <note>Outside the natural order; in medical terms, a state of disease.</note>. Do we not see this same thing happen in the air of the world? For instance, when sometimes the Boreal or North wind, or the Northwest wind, drives clouds from the North toward the South, we see in the opposite point of the horizon a contrary South wind—carrying the clouds as vehicles or chariots for contrary demons—being snatched up and carried with a violent motion against the clouds and blasts of the North wind that dominates the hemisphere. Whereupon the air, which a moment before was peaceful enough and not covered by great storms or clouds, is now suddenly disturbed by darkness, thunder, and lightning, and the entire nature of the hemisphere seems to be disturbed preternaturally and to fall "sick."

We say, therefore, that the natural state of the winds in the composition of the seed—or rather, at the time when that air is drawn in through breathing, which is later converted into seed—will be the disposition of the newborn according to nature while he lives. Every wind contrary to this disposition will burden the spirit of the newborn and struggle with it, not otherwise than a wind struggles with its opposite in the greater world; and within these winds are demons, who are accustomed to move them back and forth. We could bring forth infinite demonstrations of these things here, but a fuller discourse on this matter is destined for the second section of this work.

But truly, I will say now in a single word that the truth of this matter is proven by the effect. For the nature of the North wind (as was said before) is accustomed to cure the sickly effects of the South wind's blasts; it corrects its putrid breath, dries its moisture, moderates its heat with cold, and whatever the South wind has attempted to dissolve, the North wind immediately binds and freezes with a contrary breath. And thus the matter stands regarding the breaths of the **Spleen** and **Liver** in the lesser world.

Furthermore, because the natural spirit of a person belongs to the nature of the prevailing wind at their birth, if some demon of the opposite wind inhabits them, it vexes that person and strongly attacks their internal spirits. This is why, if someone is afflicted by **Epilepsy**, that malignant spirit is observed to afflict the human spirit more when that wind blows which belongs to its own regime and society. This is also why, in the time of a plague, many escape untouched: namely, those whose natural spirit is of the same nature as the wind bringing the disease. Since the harmful demons are "familiar" or similar to them, they do not strike. Thus that woman (according to the history of <term>Galen</term> <note>The famous Greek physician of the 2nd century AD whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a thousand years.</note>) who used to drink the juice of **Hemlock** from her infancy, was in the end unable to be poisoned by it, even though all other men would feel the madness of the contrary blasts of these pestilential demons until their final breath.

On Mystical Anatomy.

In the macrocosm <note>The universe or "great world."</note> there are clouds and vapors ordained to sustain the life of animals and plants. Just as blood and sperm are produced in the microcosm <note>The human being, viewed as a miniature reflection of the universe.</note>, and consequently the flesh and fetus are created from them, they are also buffeted by the attacks of contrary winds. Thus arise diseases and passions of both the body and the mind, just as, conversely, animals are refreshed and usually recover when a naturally balanced wind blows. This was the basis for the observations of Hippocrates and Galen regarding the winds; being taught by the outcomes of these blasts, they predicted that such diseases would occur, even though they were nevertheless ignorant of the internal reasons or causes of these diseases and winds.

As God is a living spirit (from "breathing" <note>original: *a spirando*</note>), so He also breathes life and essence into His spirits. Insofar as He is God, He holds dominion in the light (where He is called the "Open God" <note>original: *Deus patens*</note> and the "Bright Aleph" <note>Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, used here to represent the primary source of all things.</note>) as well as in the darkness (as the "Hidden God" and the "Dark Aleph"). He is the God breathing through the latter toward generation, life, and health—both temporary and eternal, which is called salvation—just as through the former He leads toward the weakness, deprivation, and languor of creatures. In His latter property, He is called *Chesed* (that is, Mercy) by the wise Hebrew Rabbis. Over this presides the name of God full of kindness, *El*, and *Tiphereth* (or Grace/Beauty), in respect to which property He is called *Eloah*. The first of these titles precedes the commission of error or sin—namely, the mercy that was always with God before all time. Furthermore, He is called *Iesod* (that is, Redemption/Foundation), over which presides the name *Sadai* <note>Shaddai, often translated as Almighty.</note>, through which the effect of divine mercy and grace is proven; this last is brought into effect after the commission of sin. But indeed, in His first property He is called *Geburath* (that is, Punishment/Severity), over which presides *Elohim Gibor* <note>God of Might.</note>, signifying severity. Also *Netzeth* (Triumph) and *Malchut* (Kingdom). From the first He takes vengeance on His enemies or rebels; through the second, having gained victory, He sets up the trophy of His victory; and through the last, having conquered the malignant spirits, He reigns forever and ever over His subjects or creatures. Just as He is a spirit wandering in darkness, so He hides His face from creatures, and then, because of the absence of that face, He breathes blasts of weakness, death, or deprivation from the region of darkness; but when He shows His face, health and life are restored. According to the Prophet: "When God hides His face, creatures are troubled; when He sends forth His spirit, they breathe again." But from the beginning of the world—namely, the divine breathing in the world and in creatures, both toward life and death, and toward health and disease—we prove this through instances from the Holy Bible, and I shall now begin first with the testimony of the blessed, merciful, and benevolent breath.

There is also another state of the soul, which is more moderate, closer to the internal being, and devoted to the human will. And in this manner Job said: <margin>Job 19:17; Job 15</margin> *My spirit has become a stranger to my wife;* <note>original: "Spiritus meus alienus est factus vxori meae"</note> and in this sense the saying is understood: *the wicked man turns his spirit against the mighty God.* <margin>1 Samuel 28:14</margin> Sometimes the spirit is also taken in the abstract and not in the concrete, and so it is written: *The spirit of Samuel ascended from the earth, and spoke to Saul;* and elsewhere: *Man knows not how to bring back the spirit that has departed from the body.* <margin>Wisdom 16; Ecclesiastes 11:5</margin>

And thus we gather the infinite actions of breathing and their various effects in the **microcosm** <note>The "small world," referring to the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note>, all of which certainly proceed from the properties of the **macrocosmic** <note>The "great world" or the universe.</note> winds, or the natures of the blasts and their effects. Although it is most difficult for man to explain all these things (according to that saying of the wise man, *man is ignorant of the way of the spirit, just as he is ignorant of how the bones grow in the womb of a pregnant woman: so he is ignorant of the work of God himself, who makes all these things*), yet it is very easy to draw from the sacred fountain the fact that God is the source of the winds and **meteors** <note>In this period, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note>, both natural and supernatural.

We also learn that his breathing ministers are the angels themselves, to whom are subjected infinite legions of demons—both the good for doing good, and the evil for doing harm and punishment. These angels breathe the commands of God into the heavens, the Elements, and the earth. To every region of the world and its Cardinal wind, a certain angelic intelligence presides. By the impulse of the winds (which receive their power from the angelic spirit), the meteors—fiery, airy, watery, and earthy—are produced in the world. Such meteors bring alterations to the microcosm that are either favorable to health and generation, or conducive to disease and corruption. The blasts of the microcosmic spirit follow the pattern of those in the macrocosm, both in the procreation of natural meteors and the production of supernatural ones. The origin and beginning of all these breathings proceed from the blast of the spirit of the nostrils of **Jehovah**: as the Prophet Samuel testifies, speaking in these words: <margin>2 Samuel 22:8</margin>

*And the earth was shaken and moved, the foundations of the heavens were disturbed; they were shaken when his anger was kindled, whose smoke descended through his nose, and fire from his mouth consumed, glowing coals were kindled by him; and bowing the heavens, he descended with darkness under his feet. And he sits upon the Cherubim, and flies and is visible upon the wings of the wind, and he puts around himself a hut of darkness, the blackness of waters, the densities of the higher clouds; from the splendor that is before him, coals of fire burn. Jehovah thunders from the heavens, and the Most High utters his voice, and sends out arrows by which he scatters the enemies, lightning by which he routs them; and the lowest channels of the sea are seen, the foundations of the habitable world are revealed by the rebuke of Jehovah, from the blast of the spirit of his nostrils.*

From which it is gathered that from the blast of the spirit of the nostrils of Jehovah in his anger, first comes the earthquake and the vibration and disturbance of the entire air. Then the winds or smoke through his nose, and thereafter the consuming or flashing fire is breathed out from his mouth, as well as burning coals or thunderbolts. Then the darkness or thick and black clouds under his feet; and that God himself, sitting upon the Cherubim or his aerial angels, flies in and upon the wings of the wind; and that the black clouds arising from the smoke in his nostrils surround him—which are nothing other than the black density of the thinner air. Whence they are called blackness and density of the waters of the upper clouds, that is, of the pure aerial heaven. Then he also produces thunders, with his arrows and lightning. And finally, deep gaps in the earth.

From this it is clear that the primary power is attributed to the breath of Jehovah; the secondary to the Cherubim or angels upon whom he sits; the third to the winds, which are the smoke of Jehovah's nostrils, upon whose wings he himself flies. Hence it is clear that the power of God is immediate in himself and in his angels; the angels are in the winds and produce the winds; the clouds contain the angels, God, and the winds (or spirits of a lower nature); the winds produce clouds by thickening them, and the clouds send forth flashes and rains; and the flashes produce thunders which accompany the lightning; and finally, by the sight of the Lord in his fury, the heaven and earth are moved, and the foundations of the earth and sea are revealed. By these things, the steps of the progression of actions are notably explained, starting from God himself—the Act of acts and Fountain of Light—moving from simplicity toward those mixed compositions called meteors, which are immediately converted into perfectly mixed substances.

<margin>Psalm 90:14; Psalm 106:4; Deuteronomy 28</margin> But here, reader, I wish to explain an admirable mystery to you: I want you to consider that man himself is nothing other than such a dense cloud in which Jehovah sits upon the Cherubim, and flies upon the wings of the wind—that is, the vital spirit—or kindly breathes the breath of life into our nostrils (whence he is called by the Prophet) *the sun giving life and glory;* and elsewhere, *the prolongation of life is the kindness of God.* And elsewhere, *God follows his people with benevolence and with his salvation.* And elsewhere, *he whom God has visited with his salvation shall enjoy good.*

Or, he speaks and breathes in us in wrath and in rebuke, whence it is said: *Jehovah will make the pestilence cling to you until you are consumed; Jehovah will strike you with a hot and burning wasting.* And Job says: *You lift me up into the wind, you set me upon it, and you make my substance melt away;* that is, so that my bodily cloud may be converted by dissolution into air or wind, from which it arose through thickening.

We conclude, therefore, that God inspires the angels, the angels inspire the demons, the demons inform the winds, and the winds produce meteors—both healthy and unhealthy. The meteors, by a certain inseparable kinship, infect the air. The air is the fuel and food of the spirits, both vital and natural, by which man is nourished. This air is continually introduced into the body both through breathing and by means of nourishment. Once introduced, it fills the body either with good juice or with contagious seeds, according to the kindness or severity of the wind blowing from the quarters of heaven. Both of these qualities are derived from the properties of the names of God, which are attributed to Him based on His actions in the world.

For in His nature, insofar as He is **Chefed** <note>original: "Chefed" i.e., Chesed, the Hebrew Sephirah of Mercy or Loving-kindness.</note> or Clemency, through the Angels **Raphael** and **Zadkiel**, He breathes health from the West or from the temperate spring; just as in the nature of **Tiphereth** <note>The Sephirah of Beauty or Balance.</note> or Grace, through the Angel **Michael**, He breathes the benefit and benevolence of life. But indeed, in His property of **Geburah** <note>The Sephirah of Severity or Judgment.</note> or Punishment, through **Samael** and his subject **Meririm**, He breathes plagues and contagious diseases and burning fevers from the South. And in the disposition of **Malchut** <note>The Sephirah of the Kingdom, the physical world.</note> (that is, the Kingdom and the "Tree of Cutting" among the **Kabbalists**), through **Gabriel**—because (according to the testimony of **Tedaco Levi** <note>Likely Zadok the Levite.</note>) he proves severity in the North. From this, cold and numbing diseases are introduced. But concerning these matters, we shall discuss effectively and clearly in the book on the causes of supernatural diseases, God willing.

The circle functions as a compass with ORIENS (East) at the top, OCCID (West) at the bottom, MERIDIES (South) at the right, and SEPTENT (North) at the left. The **Microcosmic East Wind** <note>original: "Subsolanus microcosmicus"</note>, or the **Heart** (for the Heart is the principle of life, just as the sun is the principle of the day), breathes the vital spirits through the **Aorta** <term>Aorta: the main artery of the body, here seen as a conduit for "vital spirit" rather than just blood.</term> toward the West. This Aorta disperses its rays laterally through its branches to the South and the North; this blast of life is the very wind that God breathed into Adam. The **Microcosmic West Wind** <note>original: "Favonius Microcosmicus"</note> breathes fairly benevolent vapors from the seminal vessels toward the East. Indeed, the seminal vessels are most rightly likened to the Western region because the seed remains within them; unless it is "corrupted" <note>In the alchemical and biological sense of the time, "corruption" or breaking down was a necessary stage for new life to grow, like a seed rotting in the earth before sprouting.</note>, it does not take on a new form or rise again. This is just as the setting sun appears to die and be extinguished, yet it would not be said to rise in the East unless it had first set. Furthermore, we shall declare below that the bright form of the seed originates from the Heart, just as Western splendor or lightning originates from the East. Moreover, the West Wind blows a benevolent vapor from the intestines, which it sends through its winding passages—mediated by the **mesenteric vessels**—partly to the Liver and partly into the Stomach, by which the stomach is gently expanded and ventilated.

The **Microcosmic North Wind** <note>original: "Septentrio microcosmicus"</note>, or the **Spleen**, sends its dry blasts to the Liver (the South) by means of the splenic branch, and into the stomach by means of the first and second branches of the **Portal Vein** <term>Portal Vein: a major vein carrying blood from the digestive organs to the liver; here thought to transport "windy humors."</term> and the "short vessel" <note>original: "vasi breui," likely referring to the gastric veins.</note>. By this, the stomach is distended, and here the North wind freezes and thickens the **humors** <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that governed health.</note>. It also sends blasts into the **Colon** <note>The large intestine.</note> via the fifth branch, and into the small intestines via the sixth. For this reason, these intestines are subject to "windy diseases," namely **Colic** in the colon and the **Iliac passion** <term>Iliac passion: a historical term for a painful and often fatal intestinal obstruction.</term> in the small intestine. The **South Wind** <note>original: "Meridies"</note>, or the **Liver**, which is the source of the **natural spirit** <term>Natural Spirit: in traditional medicine, the spirit responsible for nutrition and metabolism, centered in the liver.</term>, blows directly toward the North or the Spleen. It drives dark blood before it into that region, not unlike how the macrocosmic South Wind blows dark, murky clouds toward the North—which the North wind is then accustomed to dissipate and purify with its contrary blast, as Isidore says. The Liver also blows its moist vapors into the stomach through the first and second branches of the portal vein, and into the **Omentum** <note>The fatty tissue layer covering the stomach and intestines.</note> through the third branch (where it sometimes produces **dropsy** <term>Dropsy: an old term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid.</term>), into the colon through the fifth, and into the small intestines through the sixth. When a blast of this kind is dense and thick, it generates a **hepatic flux** <note>A chronic discharge or diarrhea attributed to liver dysfunction.</note>.

The **Northwest Wind** <note>original: "Corus"</note> participates in both the North and the West. It is produced partly from the motion of the intestines and the seminal vessels—for in widows and virgins, "corrupted" seed produces a **hysterical wind** <note>Referring to "hysteria" or "the vapors," which early modern medicine believed was caused by toxic gases or "winds" rising from the reproductive organs.</note>—and partly from the North, because of the windiness expired from the spleen into the intestines through the fifth and sixth branches of the portal vein. Because this blast blows against the **Southeast Wind** <note>original: "Eurus"</note>—that is, toward the region where the gallbladder is located—it induces **hypochondriac** <term>Hypochondriac: relating to the upper abdomen (the hypochondrium), which was thought to be the site of "melancholy" and "windy" vapors.</term> suffering, Colic, the Iliac passion, and other such ailments. Due to the repercussion of the Southeast Wind (or the hot, fiery vapor of the gallbladder), it affects the area around the diaphragm and the viscera with heat. ## CHAPTER VII.

### Concerning the positioning of man according to the doctrine of Pythagoras, Plato, and Aristotle, and concerning the Cardinal winds of the same according to that system.

But perhaps this discourse of ours might seem harsh and "new" to someone, wherein we made the **Spleen** the North of the microcosm and the **Liver** (positioned opposite it) its South—especially since the seat of the **Heart** (being above the region of the elementary world) is hardly to be believed as the starting point of the **East wind**. Furthermore, critics might reply that I am too arrogant in this discussion of mine, daring to refute men of such great fame and authority as **Pythagoras, Plato, and Aristotle** in their opinions, and refusing their doctrine which establishes the Eastern quarter of the world as the right side of the body.

But indeed, I respond to those who object in this way: I have followed the sentiment of **Sacred Scripture** regarding the position of man in relation to the world, rather than my own or a merely rational one, as was explained in the preceding pages. I did so even more because, since the Spleen partakes in **melancholy**, what could be more fitly compared to the Northern quarter in man than the Spleen? For that quarter is cold and moist <note>Typically the North is cold/dry, but here Fludd links it to the moistness of the "mundane melancholy" seat.</note>, and consequently the seat of worldly melancholy, just as the South is hot and moist, like the mass of the **Liver**. However, this much is certain and proven by experience: the microcosm enjoys its own quarters and cardinal winds no differently than the macrocosm does its own, and those cardinal winds of man are governed by the blasts of the world, and are affected—either by health or by sickness—according to their properties.

For if we were to admit the positioning of the microcosm in relation to the macrocosm according to the opinions of the aforementioned philosophers, we would find that they do not differ much from our stated intention. Let the **East**, therefore, be the right side of man; consequently, his left side must be the **West**, his front the **North**, and his back the **South**. When it stands this way, it follows that the **Liver** corresponds to the Eastern quarter, the **Spleen** to the Western, the **Stomach** to the Northern, and the **viscera** (or intestines), the "salty sea" of the **bladder**, and the **womb** in women correspond to the Southern quarter.

For first, the **Liver** (which is the source of the natural spirit leading to life and growth) can be quite aptly compared to the **rising sun**, which restores the creatures of the earth by its appearance, and tints the hemisphere, the waters, and the land with its rays. Even so, the liver breathes its tinted and reddish rays into the whole body by means of the veins, giving it life and growth. Just as the East wind blows directly into the quarter of the West wind, so also the liver sends out its spirits through the **splenic branch** into the Spleen (which is the quarter of the microcosm opposite to it). Furthermore, the **Spleen** is clearly of a Western nature: namely, dark, cold, and muddy. Yet it does lead to life, as it is said by some to "purify" the thick, bloody humor, and thus contribute to life and nutrition; hence it can be considered the Western quarter.

We can also quite clearly relate the **Stomach** to the **North**, since raw, viscous, and thick humors abound in it, and coldness has dominion in it of itself—even if heat works within it due to the warmth of the surrounding organs. And this is why, although the Liver is very hot and glowing, we nevertheless observe the stomach to be mostly affected by cold. Furthermore, we have noted—and this in almost everyone—that after the administration of an emetic medicine <note>vomitorii: a substance used to induce vomiting.</note>, the matter that rises and is carried upward is very viscous and like water "congealed by cold." From this, it is argued that this part of the microcosm can be not improperly referred to the North.

Or, if not the stomach, let us propose the substance of the **Brain** itself. For in the brain, the southern vapors (rising from the internal organs) are condensed into icy and viscous humors, as is evident in **Epilepsy**, **catarrh** <note>coriza: a cold or nasal congestion.</note>, and other diseases of this kind. Finally, we can adapt the **viscera**, the **intestines**, as well as the **Bladder** and the **Womb** in women to the Southern quarter, for moist vapors constantly rise from them. Indeed, we observe "storms" arising from that part, just as the clouds, whirlwinds, and thunders of the macrocosm are usually produced from the South by its glowing and raging "demon" <note>dæmone: here used in a Neo-Platonic sense as a guiding or animating force/spirit of a direction.</note>. Hence come **Colic** and **Iliac** sufferings; hence the stones of the kidneys and bladder, which are compared to **thunderbolts** <note>fulminaribus: literally "lightning stones" or "thunderbolts."</note>. Hence those "demonic" diseases that are stirred up by the womb, whose habit is to suffocate the microcosm or to deprive it of its natural motion for some space of time—as if some malignant demon were raging from the South. Indeed, even in men, the "demon" of **Epilepsy** attempts to produce this same effect or worse, and for the most part, it aligns with the demon of the womb. Furthermore, just as we see that the position of the Southern wind in the macrocosm is "below the earth" and consequently its blasts are carried upward (as **Isidore** says), so the matter stands with this Southern quarter of the body.

By these things, one can see that even with this positioning of the philosophers, the quarters of the "lesser world" (man) can be quite properly adapted to those of the "greater world." And yet, if we look at the matter with sharper eyes, some doubts are to be found even in this comparison—namely, whether the nature of the stomach is cold and dry, like that...

## EPILOGUE OR CONCLUSION.

Truly, the air or **worldly spirit** <note>original: "spiritus mundanus"</note> is a wondrous thing, hidden beyond human grasp. Although philosophers placed it as the middle of the **Elements** <note>Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note>, the Hebrew doctors (who are very well-versed in formal mysteries) refused to count air among the Elements. Instead, they maintained it is something greater and more secret in the nature of things, seeing as it is like a medium and a "glue," connecting higher forms with lower matter—that is, heaven with earth, or the soul with the body. For this reason, they made it the resounding instrument of the world's spirit, since it receives all the mysteries of the super-celestial region and the influences of the heavens—like a common lap or womb for all sublunary nature—and strives to impart portions of these to the rest of the elements and elemental things. It is also that most polished mirror in which the wise have glimpsed the divine image of creating nature, the substances of angels and demons, and all things hidden in nature. Indeed, through this very spirit, the souls of men living in far-distant places can confer with one another and converse in spiritual speech; for the spirit of living things joins itself most easily with it, since they first emanated from its fountain, and differ in substance from it no differently than a drop of water differs from its mass. Therefore, in this kind of spirit—or "spiritual sea of the world"—angels, demons, and spirits both malignant and benevolent swim, no differently than little fish visible in the material sea. By their violent motion, they disturb and agitate this invisible sea as they swim constantly from one quarter of the world or another; and this movement of the air is called "wind." Thus, the primary agent in the winds is an angel, a prince and leader having dominion over this or that quarter of the world, who (to speak with the poets) opens the **prison of Aeolus** <note>The mythical cave where the winds were kept.</note> in that quarter and sends out the spirits retained within to execute the will of God, by whose motion the air is violently driven toward the opposite part of the world. From this, a noise—either greater or lesser according to the violence of the motion—is emitted, as may be observed in the precipice of a river. Likewise, in the movement of a multitude of herring or other fish in the sea, waves arise, and an agitation of water is stirred up in that part of the sea. Furthermore, just as the **celestial Mercury** <note>The planet Mercury.</note> is observed by Astrologers to be a "shapeshifter" <note>original: "versipellis," literally skin-changer.</note> and of a mutable nature—whence he is ready to appropriate to himself the nature of any planet with which he is joined or which he regards—so indeed is this air of ours, which should truly be called our **sublunary Mercury**. It changes its nature according to the disposition of the planet or **Intelligence** <note>A guiding angelic spirit associated with a planet.</note> predominating in the heaven. Hence, sometimes it grows hot and adheres to the fiery element—indeed, once inflamed, it is nothing other than fire or the fiery element—and then it draws this kind of property from an **Eastern demon**. At other times it is air, and then it remains in its spiritual nature, which it draws from the **apothecary of Raphael** <term>Raphael's apothecary: A poetic reference to the Archangel Raphael, traditionally the healer, associated with the West.</term> in the West. Sometimes it turns itself into a watery nature, nevertheless not setting aside its fiery heat, and thus it condenses into clouds and thins and consumes itself into rains and tears—namely, when **Uriel** blows from the South and the raging **Meriri** <note>A demon of pestilence or the "midday devil" mentioned in Hebrew traditions.</note>, that tumultuous demon, emits fiery sighs and a thundering voice from his damp breast; in which case it participates in two natures, namely **Martial** <note>Related to Mars.</note> and **Lunar** <note>Related to the Moon.</note>. Furthermore, when **Saturn** reigns with the **Moon**, or when **Gabriel** blows from the North, it is turned into earthy, hard, and dry matter, whence it converts its substance into ice, hail, snow, and frost. From these things it is right to see that the air, with its demons, turns itself according to the pleasure of the stars, and the stars with their angels are subject to the commands of the **Archangels** who stand before God. It is their part to perform or execute nothing in this world that is not first ordained by God the supreme Creator, the "Act of Acts," and the beginning of motion and life.

It is also prepared to participate in the healthy nature of **Jupiter** <note>In medical astrology, Jupiter rules the liver and governs growth and the production of blood.</note> (which gives growth to the entire body and produces bright and red clouds through the natural blood), as well as in the morbid and supernatural disposition of **Mercury** and **Mars**. For just as there is no quarter in the air of the **macrocosm** <note>The "greater world" or universe.</note> that is more sufficient for imbalance—both watery and fiery—and for contagious seeds, so also no region is found in the **microcosm** <note>The "lesser world," meaning the human body.</note> that brings more diseases to the human body than the Liver. This blood is afterwards disseminated by the Liver through the entire human "earth" by means of the veins, where, through application, union, and assimilation, it is converted into flesh; thus the external part of man is sustained and continued in its being.

Finally, what in man is more similar to the **Northern part** of the world than the **Spleen** <note>original: "Lien"</note> itself? For just as that Northern region is cold and dry, terrestrial, constrictive, and full of raw things, so also the Spleen is observed to be the most terrestrial part of the internal organs, cold and dry in complexion, the seat of **melancholy** <note>Black bile, the humor associated with the earth and cold/dryness.</note>, and the receptacle of a thick and muddy substance. By their violence—like the northern winds pressing upon the middle region of the air—they distend the diaphragm in a painful manner and disturb the microcosmic heaven, as if terrestrial demons were conspiring against the God of the Heavens and his creatures in the manner of the **Titans** <note>In Greek mythology, the Titans warred against the Olympian gods.</note>. And by these kinds of breathings, the thin wateriness of the stomach is frozen and contracted into a viscous and glassy matter. Furthermore, just as the North wind is accustomed to stir up dark and thick clouds in which fiery demons mix, and are perceived to stir up horrendous thunders, so also the winds emitted by the Spleen are sometimes mixed with a fiery and burning heat. From this follow burning hypochondriacal passions with intense central heat, the effects of which are **Mania**, **Lycanthropy** <note>A form of madness where a person believes they have turned into a wolf.</note>, and fiery and melancholic furies, accompanied by roaring, murmuring, and continuous belching. This was the case with that demoniac whom Christ finally liberated by casting out that raging demon, of whom it is written: *two men possessed by demons met him, coming out of the tombs, so fierce that no one could pass that way.*

Whether through food or through breathing, this spirit mixes itself with the spirit of the blood (for in the blood is the soul or life, as the Sacred Scriptures testify) and alienates it from its natural obedience and duty. It leads it against the movement of its natural **Genius** <note>A protective or guiding spirit inherent to a person or organ.</note>, deceives it with its illusions, and bends it according to its own malevolent appetite and against life. It sows its contagious seeds in the spirit, from which nothing is harvested but supernatural fruits and corrupt effects, unless its assaults are driven back by a stronger spirit, and this natural spirit, thus seduced, is brought back to its former balance by the power of a contrary wind. ### Section I. Portion III. Part III. Book I.

...it happens that when the obstructing **phlegm** <note>original: "pituita," one of the four bodily humors, associated with cold and moisture.</note> is removed by purges or vomiting medicines, and the **mesenteric passages** <note>original: "meatibus messeraicis," the veins carrying nutrients from the intestines to the liver.</note> are opened, the patient immediately seems to feel better for a short while. And the nature and property of this **evil demon** <note>original: "cacodæmonis."</note> is recognized by the fact that it directs the disposition of its actions more toward the elements of **fire**, **air**, **water**, or **earth**—from which it is also possible to determine the nature of the wind that produced it. For the **East** sends forth fiery spirits, the **West** aerial ones, the **North** earthy ones, and the **South** watery ones; the humors—**Choler**, **Blood**, **Melancholy**, and **Phlegm**—obey these spirits. 

But if the humor predominating in a disease is observed to participate in a dual nature, it must be believed that the spirit causing the illness comes from a collateral wind, or one positioned between the cardinal points. For example:
* If from **burnt phlegm and choler**, it comes from the **South-East wind** <note>original: "Euro-austro."</note>.
* If from **raw but thick phlegm and burnt choler**, it comes from the **East-North-East wind** <note>original: "Vulturnio."</note>; that is, one in which there is one part of the Northern blast, which is cold, and another of the East wind, which is hot.
* If **raw phlegm**, but not diffused, occurs with a little unnatural heat, it is attributed to the **South-West wind** <note>original: "Affrico," which participates in the blasts of the South and West winds.</note>. 
* Furthermore, if **melancholy is joined with phlegm**, we attribute it to the **North-West wind** <note>original: "Coro."</note>.

Thus we see that the harmful spirit appears to participate in a dual nature. And here, finally, we must observe what the nature of these malignant spirits is: to reduce all the juice of nourishment—both liquid and solid—into humors that more closely match their own nature. This can be seen and noticed in **putrid fevers**, **epilepsy**, and other diseases of this kind. This is why, if a portion of the burdensome or "sinning" matter is removed today by medicines, we find the stomach and hidden passages overflowing with the same humor tomorrow, as if no part of it had been diminished the day before. ### *On the Anatomy of the world spirit, and that the mystical nature of the blood—both natural and vital as well as animal—is drawn from the aerial spirit.*

SINCE it is a well-worn and proven truth, poured forth not unwisely from the mouth of **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: "Mercurii Trismeg." A legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the author of the Hermetic Corpus, a series of sacred texts on philosophy, alchemy, and magic.</note>: namely, that **Man is the son of the world**, just as the world is the offspring of God; it follows not absurdly that man himself is procreated from the **spermatic parts** of the world, or from its purest elements mixed together. We believe it escapes no one, however foolish, that a son takes his origin from the seed or sperm of his parents. Now, this sperm, which is the more visible part of the seed, is nothing other than purified **venous blood** <note>original: "sanguis venalis." In the physiology of this era, venous blood was "natural" blood, produced in the liver to provide nutrition to the body.</note>, just as the seed (which is the more invisible part of the sperm, relating to the sperm as the soul does to the body) is originally poured out from the **arterial blood** <note>original: "sanguine arteriali." Arterial blood was considered "vital" blood, carrying the vital spirit from the heart.</note>. This has been discussed elsewhere, and we will announce it in broader speech below, God willing.

And since the very simple humor of the blood is nothing other than the **element of air** in the **macrocosm** <note>original: "mundo maiori," the Great World or universe.</note> transmuted by various concoctions into animal blood, we think it worth the effort to speak of the secret disposition of the world's air. We shall establish a "verbal anatomy" of its secret parts, so that by knowing the principle—the source—we may reach a better understanding of that which is derived from it. Regarding the air and the origin of the other elements, and how they were produced in their being by means of the **Divine Word** <note>original: "verbo diuino."</note>, I believe I have explained this more than enough in our *History of the Macrocosm*. Similarly, concerning the difference between sperm and seed, their origin, and their action in generation, we have made quite a copious mention in our treatise on the **microcosm** <note>The human being viewed as a miniature reflection of the universe.</note>. However, in this place I will add something pertaining to our current undertaking and especially necessary, so that the origin of blood, its secret nature, and the admirable mysteries contained within it may be better drawn out.

We say, therefore, that there is a very strict relationship between the air of the macrocosm and the venous or natural blood, since both are elements contained within the sublunary region of each world, and insofar as the blood is produced from the air no differently than a son from a father, as we shall declare below. We say also that the same relationship exists regarding arterial or vital blood, as both exist from the middle or celestial region of each world, and also insofar as the father of that blood is the **ethereal spirit**, just as the father of the lower blood was the **aerial spirit**. The certainty of this our opinion is confirmed both by our doctrine on the element of air and the **quintessence** <note>original: "quinta essentia," the "fifth element" or purest part of a substance.</note> in bread or wheat, as is evident from those things which we have sufficiently explained in Book Three, *On the Anatomy of the Nutritive Power of Bread*. 

And certainly, if you explore the matter a little more accurately, you will find that the air itself, or the sublunary heaven, differs from the **ether** or superlunary heaven in nothing at all except in thickness or thinness, or mixture and purity; for the entire **world-spirit** <note>original: "spiritus vniuersus mundanus."</note> is the same in essence, but truly it is divided in itself as far as we are concerned, or in what we perceive, because it is observed to be thicker in one place and thinner and purer in another. This is indeed said to come from this, and is confirmed by us elsewhere: namely, because the presence of light (of which...

## CHAPTER II.

### *Whether it is probable that the substance of thick air is transformed into venous blood, ether combined with air into arterial blood, and that portion of the intellectual spirit with ether into the [animal] spirits; and in what manner this may be performed.*

<margin>Exodus 7.
Psalm 103, 29.</margin>
That the transformation of air into blood (through condensation) is possible in the nature of things is clear from this: we find among trustworthy authors that blood has been poured down from the middle region of the air in the manner of rain, and that waters have been transformed into blood. This is even testified to in the Holy Scriptures, from which it is certain that it is within the power of nature to bring this very thing to its height and conclusion. But what is more evident in this matter than our daily experience, by which we are taught that the very effect of the first digestion—namely, the chyle <note>The milky fluid produced from digested food in the stomach and intestines.</note>—is changed into blood by the mystical and hidden property of the Liver <note>original: "Hepatis"</note>. Furthermore, by that same observation, we notice that when air is drawn into the left chamber of the heart, it leaves there the specific nature of the ethereal heaven and the most subtle portion of the aerial spirit. The heart, through its own organs, strives to draw this to itself, and expels the useless and watery smoke of the air as a superfluity through exhalation. This ethereal nature, which is utterly necessary for the life of the creature, the heart hungers for and attracts to itself at every moment; without it, neither man nor any other animal could endure for even a moment of time. 

Zeno did not hesitate to call this ethereal substance, or "food of life," the "natural fire," and he made the heart its receptacle. For this reason, Prometheus called the heart the vessel of celestial fire—that fire which he is fabled to have stolen from the heavens so that he might enrich man with a long life. For this matter is the food of the vital soul; because the heart is the common receptacle for it, it is called the seat of the soul by Plato. This, I say, is that nature which is the invisible fire, present everywhere in the world, from which Zoroaster taught that all things were brought forth. Heraclitus of Ephesus seems to agree with this; and because Democritus, Orpheus, and many of the Pythagoreans observed a certain soul presiding over every creature by the virtue of this fiery quintessence, they confidently affirmed that "all things are full of Gods." To these they assigned divine honors and dedicated prayers and sacrifices. But truly, reconsidering the matter again and again, they reduced all these souls to the single Soul of the World, or referred those Gods back to the one Jove <note>Jupiter, the king of the gods, here used as a philosophical term for the supreme governing principle.</note>. 

By "Jove," therefore, they seem to hint at the Word or the emanation of the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, often used in mystical texts to represent the source of all life.</note>, which is the fountain of man; and by "Gods" or "souls," they understood the divine rays spread everywhere into the world spirit, offering life to every creature. These rays are no more separated from the uncreated Word than the rays of the sun are from the sun: but we shall deal with these matters more extensively in the treatise on the heart. Finally, that the intellectual spirit dwells in the center of that celestial fire, and how that happens, has been said in the preceding sections. Thus, that spirit, carrying itself upward through the trunk of the Aorta and leaping out through the narrow orifices of the choroid plexuses <note>A network of blood vessels in the brain where cerebrospinal fluid is produced.</note>, mixes itself with the sensitive spirits made from the venous blood; and from this, it happens that the rational soul, by the mediation of the internal senses, operates with the intellect in the human race.

But let us return to the reasoning by which air is reduced into natural, vital, and animal blood, and see how nature can perform this work of transformation. First, therefore, we wish it to be observed that just as there are two parts to the human composition—namely, body and spirit—so also there is a twofold reasoning for nourishing each of them. For since "like is usually nourished by its like," it must be considered that the invisible man <note>The spiritual or vital aspect of a human being.</note> must be nourished immediately by the spirit of the thinner blood, namely the arterial (which is the vehicle of the vital spirits), just as that spirit is refreshed and multiplied by the ethereal spirit of the macrocosm <note>The "great world" or the universe.</note> through the successive motion of exhalation and inhalation. 

But it is certain that the external and visible man (being composed of thickened elements) is preserved and continued in his being by the successive administration and application of such nutrients, in a more remote way, and immediately from the venous and thick blood produced from the juice of foods. Nutrients, however, are of various kinds according to the diversity of the kingdoms of composed things (which are mineral, vegetable, and animal). From these kingdoms, the vegetable and animal contribute chiefly to human nourishment, and not the mineral (as its parts are so compact and difficult to digest that they scarcely obey the violence of fire, much less human heat). ...the spirit is indeed resolved. Bread is the prince of vegetables, both because it is quickly reduced to a chylous pulp <note>Chyle is the milky fluid produced in the small intestine during digestion.</note> without any labor of nature, and because it is very rich in an aerial nature and most full of natural growth. It was offered by God to our ancient ancestors as the primary and royal nourishment, whence God said <margin>Gen. 3:19.</margin>: *In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread.* Therefore, whether the matter of nourishment is animal or vegetable, it is reduced to chyle by the **chemistry of nature**—as if in Nature’s own bath. Once the subtle parts of all the elements are separated from the coarse dregs through the filtration of the mesenteric veins <note>Veins that carry nutrients from the intestines to the liver.</note>, it is "cooked" in the hollow region of the **Liver**. In this digestion, the less thin "earth"—or melancholy—which is least suited for nutrition, is divided from the aerial mass by a second separation and transferred through the splenic branch into the spleen. The superfluous "fiery" matter, useless for nourishment, is poured into the gallbladder. The phlegm, or "watery" element (comparable to seawater), is sent downward through the kidneys into the "sea" of the bladder. Finally, the "aerial" element or humor is contained in the vessels or trunks of the Vena Cava and the Portal Vein. However, we do not say this is purely aerial, because it still contains within it the subtle parts of every element—namely fire, water, and earth. (In the composition of the body, these elements belong to their own members: it is the duty of the more "earthy" part to look after the bones, cartilages, membranes, and ligaments; the "watery" part creates fat; and "fire" works with the "air" regarding the generation of flesh.) Nevertheless, it is referred to as air because air holds the predominance in its mass. Here, a question may arise that is not easily discussed, and in the resolution of which even many of the most learned men have hesitated:

<margin>From whence comes the red color of the blood.</margin> Namely, from where does that blood-making power arise, by which the pale chyle, verging on white, is so promptly reduced into a red tincture <note>In this context, "tincture" refers to a deep, transformative color or essence.</note>? Some wish this multiplicative staining power to come from the nature of the Liver (since its substance is intensely red), as if the redness of the liver were so infinite that it could stain an infinite proportion of aerial chyle without any decrease in its own redness. Furthermore, if this were granted, it would not be absurd if we consequently asked: from where did the liver itself receive this red tincture, adorned with such multiplicative power? For it is certain and proven that the substance of the liver itself takes its origin from the blood. Thus it is clear that the "thing created" cannot have an innate quality that its "creator" is said to lack; yet blood is not observed to be so abundant in multiplication that it could attribute an infinite tincture to something similar to itself. Others say this is a "hidden property of nature," but with such an answer, we only gather the unknown through the more unknown, and thus remain entirely ignorant of the essence of the matter. To this question, we—taught by better experience—respond that this power of staining consists neither in the liver nor in any part of the human body, but lies hidden in the center or "occult" part of the **air**, introduced into the body either through breathing or by means of the juice of nourishment.

For in *Book 2 of the Anatomy of Bread*, the reason for the growth and multiplication of plants is most clearly explained: namely, because its aerial part (which seems to be nothing other than a certain volatile salt) is clearly white and transparent in its liquid substance, even though in its "occult" center it is greatly stained with redness. Indeed, by a certain magnetic virtue born within it centrally, such a substance is ready to attract to itself the **solar form** <note>The life-giving, "golden" spiritual energy associated with the sun.</note> lurking invisibly everywhere in the vast spirit of the world, and to gather it into itself, as if it were a feminine matter in nature that greedily desires the form of light and rapidly draws it to itself. An experiment of this matter was demonstrated in the place cited above, where we declared that the clear and aerial matter of wheat or bread, in its white nature, was converted into a sufficiently intense redness within the space of a few hours when exposed to the sun. From this, I concluded that the property of multiplication and growth, in both vegetables and animals, flows from such an aerial substance—not, I say, from its own power (as it is not infinite or "more-than-perfect"), but from its internal magnetic disposition. By this, it draws to itself the formal rays from the **Soul of the World** <note>The *Anima Mundi*, an intrinsic spirit believed by alchemists to animate all nature.</note> present everywhere, and progressively contracts the "radical moisture" from its likeness expanded throughout the world. In no other way do we say that this air—once hidden in the chyle, but now stripped of heterogeneous nature and purged in the liver—ceases to attract to itself the rays of the **microcosmic sun** <note>The heart or the vital spirit within the human "small world."</note> or the life-giving soul of the microcosm. It could not have performed this in its chylous state, insofar as its magnetic force was partly submerged in a watery or phlegmatic nature and partly hindered by coarse and earthy dregs. But now, partly by the power of the mesenteric veins and partly by the power of the liver, having cast off these hindrances of foreign elements, it enters vigorously upon that work of transformation and is observed to bring it to a happy conclusion.

And certainly, examining this matter a little more accurately with the "glowing knife of fire" <note>A metaphorical or literal reference to intense heat used in chemical distillation.</note>, I perceived that this matter, by slow heat—indeed by the dew of the bath itself—was sublimated into the cap of the **alembic** <note>A chemical apparatus used for distillation, consisting of a gourd-like container and a cap.</note> in the form of the whitest snow or hail. When a glowing coal was applied to it, I saw the matter suddenly melt like honey or butter and change into a golden or hyacinth color, thus denoting to us that although the manifest and external part of this aerial substance is white, its hidden and internal part is marked with the tincture of blood.

But as for arterial blood, the reason for its tincture is the same as that of the thick and venous blood, except that the aerial substance of that blood is far thinner and more subtle than the venous or "natural" blood. Thus, there is as much difference between the substance of one and the other as there is between the lowest and highest regions of the air. For just as the lowest region of the air participates more in earth and water, and is consequently thicker and less hot than the highest region (which participates in ethereal fire), so also the blood of the lowest region of the body is denser and colder than that of the vital region, which is very thin and abounds in heat. ->Of the Mystical Anatomy of the Blood.<-

It has its origin in the heart, which, according to Zeno <note>Zeno of Citium (c. 334 – c. 262 BC), the founder of Stoicism, who viewed the soul as a "fiery breath."</note>, is the *receptacle of natural fire*, or as Prometheus would have it, the vessel of *celestial fire*. Second, because that heat is more effective and natural in its operation, which is naturally present in the subtler and purer spirit; for celestial heat is far stronger and more powerful in its action than any elemental heat, since it is the source and origin of the latter. Third, because the heart is recognized by the most excellent of the philosophers to be the origin of the blood, as the place from which the beginning of life is drawn. Therefore, the substance of arterial or <term>vital blood</term><note>In pre-modern medicine, arterial blood was believed to carry "vital spirits" and was distinct from the "natural" blood of the veins.</note> is thinner and more spiritual than <term>venous blood</term>, and stands in relation to it as the visible and purest spirit of wine <note>original: "spiritus vini"; ethanol or high-proof alcohol.</note> stands to the "water of life" <note>original: "aquam vitæ"; a medicinal brandy or distilled spirit.</note> in which the other elements are mixed with the true spirit. In the same way, the blood of the animal relates to the vital blood as the spirit of wine—which, due to its purity, vanishes into the air and renders itself invisible—for it is fitting for invisible spirits to be nourished by things similar to themselves. 

We say, therefore, that the subtlest air is the vehicle for the invisible substance of the <term>ether</term>, which, containing the "food of life," is introduced with its contents into the left chamber of the heart. From there, once the thicker substance of the air—participating in exotic and foreign elements—is expelled by the action of the heart and the internal attraction of the pure air (which arises from celestial power), it partly reveals its internal "tincture" and partly gathers and contracts the rays of the internal <term>microcosm</term> <note>The "small world" of the human body, reflecting the "macrocosm" of the universe.</note> into the spirit. In this way, it drinks in a full portion of the blood's tincture. However, by what method, art, or industry nature is accustomed to perform its dissolutions, its separations of pure from impure, its changes from form to form and color to color, and its transmutations from a liquid, thick substance into a more liquid and thin one within this human house, temple, or rather Laboratory and workshop—this you shall have demonstrated in the following chapter.

# CHAPTER III.

### *On the wonderful alchemy of nature in the human body, the layout of that same laboratory, the vessels differing from one another, and finally on the remarkable formula for operating, purifying, refining, and moving toward perfection within this, its laboratory.*

How empty-headed and void of reason are those men—and with what unworthiness they should be rejected by nature itself—who mock, despise, and hate the chemical art, whether applied to medicine or to the transmutation of one metal into another. The industry of nature, so sagacious and skilled in its actions, its constant practice, and its virtue in purifying and preserving the human body—engaged day and night—seems to testify and declare this brilliantly. For what invention of distilling or preparing, or any method of separating the subtle from the gross and thick, is there in the art of common chemistry—whether in the skill of circulating and digesting, or the artifice of distilling by descent, ascent, filtration, sideways, or through sifting—that nature has not already tasted? And this was so long before any science reigned among men, before Adam or any of his successors devised any art. 

If, therefore, we wish to explore the matter a little more accurately, we shall perceive with open eyes that man himself has stolen the entire science of Alchemy from nature herself. Its laboratory or distillery is the human body; the vessels contained in it and required for such an operation are the organic members contained therein, among which four are especially eminent, which we call the "principals": namely, the liver, the <term>seminal vessels</term>, the Heart, and the Brain. 

The Alchemist, therefore, is furnished and fortified in his laboratory with <term>Alembics</term>, Retorts, Recipients, <term>Mary’s Baths</term> <note>The "Bain-marie," a water bath used for gentle, even heating.</note>, wind furnaces, reverberatory furnaces, and furnaces of Sand, Ash, and <term>Antenor</term> <note>A type of furnace designed for constant, moderate heat, often used in long-term digestions.</note>, and such things he has ready at hand in every task, so that he might better lead the matter to be distilled, little by little and step by step, toward exact purification—that is, from a corporal nature toward a spiritual one. Does not nature seem to provide the very same thing in its operations, in which it is constantly observed hurrying toward the goal of perfection? Let us proceed, then, in the exploration of the mysteries of nature’s laboratory, and see if there is anything an Alchemist, however skilled and remarkable in his art, can do that nature does not seem to know, or for which she has not already provided him with the patterns of her own craftsmanship.

The Alchemist, therefore, desiring to bring a thing or matter to the perfect goal of subtlety and thinness, first chooses to handle it with his hands, breaking it into smaller parts, whether by pulverizing it, dividing it into small portions by cutting, or grinding it with filings. Then, once a preparation of this kind is made, he is accustomed (in imitation of nature) to commit it to some suitable "monster" <note>Likely referring to a specific vessel or chemical environment; "monstro" here might also imply a potent or unusual substance.</note>, by the virtue of which he makes the first entrance or penetration into the body to be dissolved. To perform this work better, more effectively, and more quickly, he attempts to place that circulatory vessel, with its <term>menstruum</term> <note>A solvent used in alchemy to dissolve solids.</note> and the subject to be dissolved, into a Mary’s Bath or a <term>horse’s belly</term> <note>original: "ventrem equi"; a method of using the heat from fermenting horse manure to provide a steady, low temperature for digestion.</note> (which he also calls the heat of horse dung). Has the Alchemist not imitated nature in the very beginning of this operation? Nature first approaches the task by preparing coarse food through the grinding of the teeth, and then, through the long neck of her circulatory vessel (namely, the Esophagus), she pushes that which has been thus broken and ground-downward.

into the stomach, no differently than a person skilled in chemistry—following the example of nature—introduces his material into the belly of an oblong matrass <note>original: "matracei"; a long-necked glass flask used for distillation or digestion.</note> through its neck so that it may be refined (following an initial breaking and grinding). Then, nature’s intention—for the better completion of its first operation—is to visit and penetrate the center of the prepared matter and to make the body porous, so that the subtler spirits trapped within may more easily flow out. To ensure this happens, it is necessary for a certain liquid to be mixed with it; hence nature grows thirsty and makes the eater desire a drink, so that a better entry into the dry substance may be achieved, the dry may melt into the moist, and thus the first stage of dissolution may be perfected. And so that this operation may be carried out more quickly, nature seems to seal this "circulatory vessel" <note>The author views the stomach as a vessel where matter is moved in cycles, similar to an alchemical circulatory vessel.</note> both above and below, lest the spirits exhaling from the center of the matter break out of their vessel and fly away in vain. Thus, the stomach is said to be closed during the time of the first <term>concoction</term><note>A traditional medical term for digestion, viewed as a process of "cooking" or "ripening" food through bodily heat.</note>; then, with the heat of the liver and viscera surrounding it everywhere—which is moist and warm—it intends to circulate the matter in its own time, namely until the entire substance, along with its liquid, is reduced to a pulp or <term>chyle</term><note>original: "chilum"; the milky fluid consisting of lymph and emulsified fats formed in the small intestine during digestion.</note>. In exactly the same way, the Alchemist, always imitating nature in his operations, firmly plugs his matrass (or "arm-pipes," or "pelican" <note>A "pelican" was a specific alchemical vessel with two curved necks that returned distilled liquid back into the base, symbolizing continuous refinement.</note>) during the time of digestion and circulation of the matter, so that the spirits do not evaporate and vanish. He delights in adapting it to horse manure or a <term>Bain-marie</term><note>original: "balneo Mariæ"; a water bath used to provide gentle, consistent heat.</note>—that is, a warm and moist heat—so that by this kind of operation, his first intention of dissolution may be fulfilled. And thus the coarse medicine, now subject to putrefaction and dissolution, is ready to receive a new form; or, as the "lead of the philosophers" casts off its filth—by which I mean the pale chyle, turning away from useless dregs as if from its own leprosy—it is now, in a way, prepared for a true transmutation into gold.

Therefore, we must inquire further into the laboratory of both the Alchemist and Nature, and hasten toward the second stage of their operation. We see, therefore, that nature itself—once the time of circulation or concoction is complete and the lower orifice of the stomach is dilated and opened—pours all that dissolved matter (the useful mixed with the useless, the chyle with the dregs) into the receiving vessels, namely the thin intestines: the Duodenum, Jejunum, and Ileum. It does this by a second type of distillation (which is usually done "by descent" <note>Distillation *per descensum* involves heating the substance from above so the refined liquid flows downward into a receiver.</note>), so that in these vessels, it may labor to distinguish the coarse from the subtle, the useful from the useless, the necessary from the superfluous, and the pure from the impure. In this operation, the Alchemist, following nature’s example, either pours off the digested matter by tilting or allows it to flow into another vessel placed beneath it, by means of which the subtle is distinguished from the thick and the pure from the impure. Here, then, we arrive at a third kind of distilling: that which is called "through a filter." For the practitioner of Chemistry perceives that nature itself—by the power of the <term>mesenteric veins</term><note>original: "venarum meseraicarum"; the veins that transport nutrients from the intestines to the liver.</note>, with which the thin intestines are most abundantly filled—attracts and lifts the thinner portion of the first concoction (that is, the matter circulated in the stomach) upward to the region of the Liver. By this path, nature separates the subtle from the thick—that is, the pure, whitening chyle from its coarse dregs. The more earthy part, or the dregs remaining at the bottom of these intestines, is cast out into another, lowlier vessel, namely the colon, where they are kept so that the spirits that are still more fixed and share in its salt may be drawn out by the heat of the place and raised on high through certain filaments of that same "filter" to the region of the Liver. Here (I say), the Alchemist—this "ape of nature"—endeavors to undertake this same thing in his artificial operations. In place of the mesenteric veins inserted everywhere into the intestinal vessels, he chooses either a cloth made of wool or cotton, or a piece of thick and porous paper, and divides and cuts it into various sections in a manner very well known to chemists. Each of these sections is meant to correspond to a mesenteric vein. He then dips this cloth, thus divided into small portions, into the vessel receiving that matter circulated in the Heat-bath, so that, in the manner of the mesenteric veins, it might separate the subtle from the thick and lift it high into another clean vessel, so that it may be brought to the third level of perfection. And this mode of distilling is called "filtration" by the Alchemists.

But now, at last, we approach that organ in nature’s laboratory, or that "furnace of digestion," in which nature herself rectifies and matures the pure matter prepared in the first digestion by a still further distillation. In an operation of this kind, the chylous nourishment, pale and weak, is transmuted into red blood by a marvelous power. The "animal lead" (I say), somewhat pale and now cleansed of its leprosy, is now transmuted into true gold, or into a golden nature and disposition. Here, therefore, we have the first order of circulation and cooking in the furnace, in which coarse gold is melted down through the first degree of Alchemy. How coarse, then, are those men, and how submerged in ignorance, or how overwhelmed and rebellious in their vain opinions, who believe that a transmutation from one species into another cannot be done? And yet, in this very place, one may behold the whitening chyle itself habitually converted into the reddest blood by the industry of nature. Nor certainly (if we look at the matter with just eyes) will we perceive that raw lead and imperfect metal differ more in substance and nature from gold than chyle does from blood. For just as the beginning or principle of blood was nothing but chylous water—that is, a watery humor, imperfect and raw in its chylous nature—it is nonetheless reduced to a mature perfection in its bloody form. So also gold in the beginning was Mercury, or a thick, immature, and raw water; its first degree toward concoction is lead itself, but the last and the goal of its perfection is gold. Is this to be believed impossible, when we see even greater miracles in nature? Namely, that we may observe vegetable nature itself converted into animal nature, as in the flesh and blood of creatures, in which herbs, grasses, and fruits are transformed into the substance of the one nourished. And yet, that these effects of nature happen daily is manifest even to the senses of fools—

# On the Mystical Anatomy of the Blood.

it is clearly declared and demonstrated; however, that the substance of an irrational animal migrates into that of a rational one, and vice versa, is something I know escapes no one and is doubted by none, since it is a fact known to all and proven by experience. From this, therefore, the foundations of the most excellent contemplations can be drawn, and very difficult questions and doubts can be raised—such as: Can the substance of a beast (indeed, even that of vegetables) be converted into human body and substance? Will there be a resurrection of the beastly or vegetable body on the last day, since by the operation of nature they have now become the same, namely the same flesh and bones as the human body, for which a resurrection from death to eternal life is certain? If that follows, it is asked: Is it in the power of nature to so prepare irrational animals, and indeed even vegetables themselves, that through their conversion into the human body they may be able to live forever through the resurrection? 

This stands against the opinion of those who, with a hardened mouth and full of lies, exclude God from the works of nature, and say that operations of this kind exist outside the power of nature—as if God worked outside of nature in this world, when he is essentially here and everywhere; as if (I say) the internal soul of <term>passive nature</term><note>The material world that receives the action of the divine; in this context, the "passive" elements that God acts upon.</note>, inhabiting its most exact center, could be distinguished from the substance of God himself. Therefore, those scoundrels should be relegated to eternal exile who do not hesitate to pronounce with unheard-of audacity that Physicians are for the most part Atheists, as they are those who contemplate nature so deeply that they usually reject God himself and his worship entirely, nor do they wish to acknowledge any God besides nature. 

To these people, I do not hesitate to respond with a serene face and full of confidence: that he is rather the Atheist—indeed, he should be considered an irrational brute—who seeks and tries to find God outside of nature, and who is ignorant that God is found within and inhabits the hiding places of nature. For insofar as He is outside of all things, what mortal can find Him, or comprehend Him with even the thinnest eyes of the intellect? Hence it is said that Moses *saw the back parts of God, and not the front* <note>original: "Dei posteriora viderit, & non priora"; a reference to Exodus 33:23, implying humans see God's effects in the world, not His pure essence.</note>, that is, not God in His essence, but clothed in the garments of nature, that is, in His creatures, in whose center He is said to be moved by the spirit. For in the word (according to that of Saint John) *was life*, and the Psalm says, *By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the spirit of his mouth.* From this it is clear that the power of any creature (which consists in the power of the soul) proceeds immediately from the spirit. 

Furthermore, it is said that *God is clothed in light*, which light is the thinnest of His natural garments; then *God placed His tabernacle in the sun.* Afterward, He is adorned with a garment still thicker and denser, whence it is said, *A thick cloud is His hut*, and elsewhere, *You are the temple of the Holy Spirit*, and elsewhere, *The earth shall bring forth the Savior.* From these it is clear that God is in passive nature just as an agent is in the patient, or a soul in a body, or rather, the Divine Mind in the soul itself, for the mind is the center of the soul. And this agrees with that definition of Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure to whom various mystical and alchemical texts were attributed.</note>: *God is a circle,* he says, *whose center is everywhere, but whose circumference is nowhere.* 

We conclude, therefore, this side-discourse of ours against such adversaries and despisers of nature, by affirming that Nature itself is God—I do not say the passive and numbered or created nature, or the universal waters, but the active, numbering or creating nature, or the virtual active nature, informing the shapeless universal waters, and emanating immediately from the Throne and being of creation. Therefore, let the fools be silent if they cannot comprehend these things, since they are agreeable not only to the opinion of the divine philosophers, but also of the Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles, among whom Saint Peter fell into an opinion of this kind, namely: *that the heaven and the earth were founded through the waters, and in the waters by means of the word.* Let such men know, then—nor is this said by us without consideration—that whoever cannot inspect the mysteries of nature with <term>Lyncean eyes</term><note>Eyes as sharp as those of the lynx, or referencing Lynceus, the Argonaut with supernatural sight.</note>, and does not know how to penetrate into the depths of her perfume-box <note>original: "myrothecium"; a container for ointments or perfumes, here used metaphorically for nature's hidden secrets.</note>, it is certain that they wander as far from the knowledge of God and true Theology as darkness is from the height of light, the Devil from God, or truth from falsehood. These are the kind of people who dwell in the "letter" or the outer bark, or the surface, which are said to kill; they reject the living spirit and the creating light dwelling in the center, where life is present, so that they tread the broad path leading to perdition, while few acknowledge and enter the path of God and nature. But about these things I have disputed more widely elsewhere; therefore, I will turn the thread of my discourse back to the matter at hand, and I will now say what else is done in the laboratory of nature.

The furnace (I say) <term>Antenor</term><note>Likely a corruption or variation of "Athanor," the self-feeding furnace used by alchemists to maintain a steady heat over long periods.</note>, or the secret furnace of the first degree or operation in this laboratory of nature, is the **Liver**. Its role is to smelt the **animal gold** of the first order—namely, the thicker and elementary blood—in which the four elements are still mixed in a confused manner. I mean the four humors corresponding to the four elements. For although this secret furnace, by means of its airy heat, strives as much as it can toward the separation of the superfluous elements (which it attacks with a triple purification), it cannot yet fully purify its golden and ruddy material. 

This purification is done partly through a distillation of the fifth kind, which is called "to the side," by which action it divides the earthy or <term>melancholy</term><note>Black bile, associated with the element of Earth.</note> dregs from the blood mass, and pours and drops them laterally through the splenic branch into the **spleen**. Partly it is done through a "gentle descent," by which way the yellow bile or fiery superfluity is sent into the vehicle of the **gallbladder**. And partly it is done through a "deeper descent," by which distillation the matter of the false phlegm is sent into the sea of the **bladder** through the kidneys and ureters. 

Nevertheless, the Liver cannot so purify its golden and ruddy material that it is not still somewhat contaminated by some useless dregs of the elements; thus, this mass is most rightly compared to the air of the sublunary world, which because of its impurity seems to claim for itself the title of imperfection. Whence it happens that the elementary air is subject to changes; so also this blood mass, and the solid and fleshy parts that arise and are nourished by it, are subject to diseases and changes. Therefore, the property of this secret vessel corresponds to the nature of the sublunary world, as it is ordained for nourishing and sustaining the elementary parts of the body. For this reason, this animal gold, although it is thick and of the first order, nevertheless seems sufficient for cherishing the less noble and thicker parts of the body. Here, therefore, we have the principal actor of the sublunary or Elementary world, whose...
