Section I. Portion III. Part III. Book II.

The still-imperfect passive substance—if it is treated again in the even more noble <term>Antenor</term><note>Original: "Antenore." In this context, the author uses "Antenor" as a metaphorical name for a specialized alchemical furnace or digestive vessel within the body.</note> and digested by its heat, which is of the second degree—is accustomed to forge a blood, or rather a gold, that is more inclined toward a celestial disposition. This substance is far purer and more subtle than the first, and is destined by nature to restore the lighter and more dignified members of the body with nourishment. Nature, therefore, takes a portion of that blood which was prepared by heat in the first Antenor (namely, of the Liver) and sublimates it through "ascent" (which is the sixth species of distillation). It rises from the bottom of the <term>cucurbit</term><note>A gourd-shaped chemical vessel used in distillation; here, the author compares the cavity of the liver to the base of a still.</note>—that is, the cavity of the liver—through its narrow neck (which is the <term>vena cava</term><note>The large vein that carries blood into the heart.</note>) to the right chamber of the heart. This acts as an <term>Alembic</term><note>The cap or "head" of a still where vapors condense.</note> or head; once its joints and openings are well-sealed, this bloody matter is reduced through circulation into a substance far purer than before.

This is the secret furnace of the "second order" of nature, whose heat is very temperate and is likened to the celestial sun. The arrangement of this furnace is wondrous, since in it not only elemental gold is digested, but also that which is celestial. For as this vessel is double, having a binary cavity, the right side is adapted for the elemental blood sublimated from the Liver through the vena cava. This blood circulates and is digested there until it is reduced to the nature of the highest region of the air, so that it is now made into food ready to nourish the light substance of the lungs. The left side, however, is in its nature so subtle and of such mystical property that, like <term>Prometheus</term><note>The Titan from Greek mythology who stole fire from the gods to give to humanity.</note> himself, it constantly snatches celestial fire. Furthermore, once digestion is complete and the pure is separated from the impure, it dispenses this fire of life through the arteries throughout the entire body. It imparts innate heat to every member of the body; for the duty of this smooth, double-ventricled furnace is to attract to itself the hidden rays of the sun and heavens—the invisible fire of <note>Zoroaster and Heraclitus were ancient philosophers associated with the sacred or primary nature of fire.</note> Zoroaster and Heraclitus—to prepare what is attracted, to separate the pure from the impure and the useful from the useless, and finally to administer what has been separated to the whole body. For fire of this kind is the food of the <term>radical moisture</term><note>In medieval medicine, "radical moisture" was the essential fluid thought to sustain life and vital heat, similar to the oil in a lamp.</note>.

In this fire, therefore, gold is purified—both the elemental and gross (or earthly and passive) kind, and that which is celestial, subtle, ignited, and active. The former is effective for the nourishment and preservation of the body, while the latter is ordained for the rectification and continuation of the spirits, both "animal" and "vital." Therefore, the heat of this Antenor or secret furnace is the second degree in the purification of blood (or Elemental gold), but it is the first degree in the digestion and preparation of the blood (or celestial gold). From this we see a process like that of wine: first it is circulated in the stomach, then its tartareous dregs are separated (as if by a filter) from the pure or more liquid part through the mesenteric veins; then later, the <term>aqua vitae</term><note>Literally "water of life," referring here to a highly concentrated or distilled essence, like pure alcohol.</note> is drawn out with the other elements in the liver or another vessel. Next, a pure but visible spirit of wine is created, and finally, the last degree of refinement occurs in the ventricles of the brain. There, those spirits are so exactly refined and rectified that they pass invisibly into a "spiritual smoke," which, because of its purity, is made fit to receive the impressions of Reason itself, and indeed, of the Intellect.

We shall proceed, then, to the final degree of the blood's digestion, which takes place in the "animal" Antenor—that is, the brain—just as the middle degree was completed in the "vital" one, the heart. This degree of animal fire in the brain (which we compared to the super-celestial fire, just as we compared the middle or vital fire in the heart to celestial fire, and the first or natural degree in the liver to elemental fire) is perfected in a vessel adorned with a triple ventricle. In the first two of these, certain organs woven from tiny veins and arteries in a <term>Daedalean</term><note>Complex or labyrinthine, named after Daedalus, the mythical builder of the Cretan Labyrinth.</note> or labyrinthine fashion—called the <term>choroid plexus</term><note>A network of blood vessels in the brain that produces cerebrospinal fluid.</note>—convert the fluid in the veins into a smoke or highly subtle air through secret digestion. This is the "subject" of <term>fantasy</term><note>In historical psychology, "fantasy" or "phantasia" was the mental faculty that gathered and processed sensory images.</note>, into which the impressions of the rational soul are introduced. It changes the fluid contained in the tiny arteries into an invisible spirit and a light of intellectual nature, which hides within this spirit. This acts upon the airy or "fantastic" smoke no differently than the soul acts upon the body, or heaven upon the earth, or the sun's rays upon the air. But the vehicle of the acting divine light is that vital or arterial spirit, which these choroid plexuses, by an admirable art or property, are accustomed to render invisible. Thus, in this subtle and invisible form, it is now as fit to perform the duties of the rational soul as it was in its visible form (when it was arterial blood) to perform the duties of the vital soul. So also we see that the spirit of wine, or its <term>quintessence</term><note>The "fifth essence," the purest and most concentrated extraction of a substance.</note> (which we can compare to arterial blood), is rendered invisible by repeated rectifications, so that it is usually converted entirely into air or an invisible spirit and vanishes into the atmosphere.

In this way, these spirits—both venous and arterial—existing in the first two ventricles are prepared, cooked, and thinned; they are still gross "animal spirits" like smokes before they reach the natural sense. The perfection of this entire work is finished in the third ventricle of the brain (or the third-degree Antenor), and then these spirits, having been made invisible, migrate into the fourth ventricle. There, they begin to carry out the will of Reason—as invisibly through sense and imagination as they do visibly through motion.

Therefore, the first Antenor (the Liver) administers the elemental region in the <term>microcosm</term><note>The "little world," i.e., the human body as a reflection of the universe.</note> and consequently corresponds to the sublunary heaven of the <term>macrocosm</term><note>The "great world," the universe at large.</note>, where the work of growth and generation is done. The second (the Heart) is related to the Sun in the celestial macrocosm. The third (the Brain) looks toward the <term>Empyrean</term><note>The highest, most spiritual part of heaven, associated with pure light and fire.</note> or intellectual heaven. I will remain silent here regarding the admirable craftsmanship of "natural chemistry" performed in the seminal vessels, as I have proposed to mention that elsewhere. From these things, therefore, one may see how many mysteries of natural chemistry are observed in the various dispositions and operations of the human body, and how subtly and sagaciously Nature brings her affairs to a conclusion in the Microcosm. Consequently, how worthy of hatred and contempt are those men who mock Alchemists! For the true chemist attempts to undertake nothing that nature has not already outlined in the human body. For example, in the composition and preparation of medicines, nature teaches him first to dissolve them in a proper <term>menstruum</term><note>An alchemical solvent.</note>. Then, to separate the impure dregs from the pure juice. Then later, through the first degree of digestion, which mimics the nature of the Liver...

# CHAPTER IV.

->On the Anatomy of human blood, dissected by artificial chemistry.<-

Having completed the description of natural chemistry and the power of blood through its various preparations, we shall proceed quickly to its artificial explanation—by which the elements of blood are distinguished from one another—so that we may then move on to the wonders of blood brought to light by art.

I have seen many chemical operations on human blood in my time and have been an eyewitness to their effects. However, I truly confess that I have only valued one, which was put into practice by a certain German very skilled in common chemistry and very familiar to me, named La Pierre, who performed this experiment many times in Paris <note>Original: "Lutetiæ," the Roman name for Paris.</note>. He said he received this secret from the Bishop of Noyon through a certain nobleman called Menanton. He said, or at least believed, that its goal was finally to reach the <term>Philosopher's Stone</term><note>The legendary alchemical substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting immortality.</note> (so long sought by sophisticated and false philosophers but never found) by means of a preceding "philosophical cooking." I will say nothing of the desired effect of such a secret, nor is it truly my intention to give any credit to it. My intention here is to describe the division of the blood's elements in the common way, and to explain the medical mysteries of some of them; to perform this more clearly, I will follow the experiment of my friend in this matter.

He chose blood drawn from men between 25 and 30 years old, healthy of body and robust in habit. He let it putrefy in horse manure <note>A common source of steady, gentle heat in early chemistry.</note> or some other warm place. He took an excellent <term>retort</term><note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-curved neck used for distilling liquids.</note> and covered it on all sides (except for a round spot left at the top for peering inside) with well-tempered <term>lute</term><note>Original: "luto." A paste or cement used to seal joints or protect glass from the direct heat of a furnace.</note> so that it might better withstand the violence of the fire. He poured as much of the prepared putrefied material into that vessel as would fill it halfway. The shape of the luted retort is as follows, lest this seem difficult to understand for beginners in the chemical art.

When it was well-fixed to the furnace, he applied a sufficiently vast and large receiving vessel to its opening, in which the spirits leaping upward from the matter could play and circulate well. He sealed the joints with paper soaked in a glue made of flour and egg whites; once these were well-dried, he covered them a second time with the same papers smeared with that glue, and indeed even a third time. ### Section I. Portion III. Part III. Book II.

He finally arrived at the formula for distilling, which (by gradually increasing the fire) he extended over the space of 8 days, or an entire week, as if he were imitating the action or operation of nature itself in this matter. For up to the fourth day, he applied a heat very similar to the heat of the Sun in the month of June, so that any given drop followed the next only every quarter of an hour; for this kind of operation, the first two <term>degrees of fire</term><note>Alchemists used four "degrees" of heat, ranging from the warmth of a brooding hen to the intense heat of a furnace.</note> were required, during which time the element of water was accustomed to reveal itself as <term>phlegm</term><note>A watery, tasteless liquid produced during distillation, associated with the element of Water.</note>. Then he stirred a slightly stronger fire by the power of the third degree of fire, by whose action a certain cloudy air began to ascend into the receiving vessel; when this had completely exhaled from the <term>retort</term><note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances.</note> and was gathered in the receiving vessel, he proceeded to the fourth degree of fire. Finally, by its impulse, the Element of fire came forth, first under a yellow form, and then afterward tinged with a dark redness. This element was observed to participate in some way in the <term>Fifth Essence</term><note>Also known as the "quinta essentia" or ether; the purest, most incorruptible part of a substance.</note> itself because of its worthiness alongside the celestial spirit; once well-<term>rectified</term><note>Purified through repeated distillation.</note>, he affirmed that it shared in the nature of true <term>potable gold</term><note>Original: "auri potabilis." A legendary alchemical medicine consisting of gold dissolved in a liquid form, believed to have universal healing powers.</note>.

But truly, it must be observed here that (since that fifth essence is only drawn out last) the fire should be increased in every way on the final day, and even lit beneath the grate itself, because that glutinous matter (as was said regarding the fifth essence of bread) only exits by the violence of the fire and is raised from the earth. When it is noticed that nothing more distills, the fire is extinguished, and once the furnace has cooled, the retort is removed. As for what pertained to the investigation of the fourth element—namely, the Earth—he affirmed it must be drawn away from the <term>caput mortuum</term><note>Latin for "dead head." The solid, useless residue remaining in a vessel after all volatile components have been distilled off.</note> residing in the bottom of the retort. Regarding this sediment of matter, he told me a truly wonderful story, which I intend to declare to you in what follows, since we have decided now to treat the common and non-miraculous operations of nature. And so the first chemical preparation of this matter was completed, in which he himself observed various colors appearing in the hollow of the glass through a hole left in the top of the retort. He said that in the final degree, he covered this hole with ashes so that the heat of the fire would be more effective in its operation. We proceed thus to the second preparation or purification of this mystery.

All that which flowed from the retort into the receiving vessel during this first operation must be taken and replaced in a retort similar to the first, but not coated in <term>lute</term><note>A protective paste or clay used to seal joints or protect glass from direct heat.</note>. It should be placed in a pot filled with sifted ashes, well-fitted to the aforementioned furnace, and its beak should be connected to the glass <term>vesica</term><note>A bulbous glass adapter or "bladder" used to extend the path of the vapor.</note> described below, whose other orifice must enter the mouth of the receiving vessel. Small pieces of paper should be soaked with the lute or glue described above, and with these, the joints must be well-plugged so that the subtle matter does not escape. The order and shape of the vessels to be joined together follows here:

Therefore, through the first degree of fire, the phlegm or element of water is very easily drawn out, but this degree must be very slow, lest the cloudy air be sucked out together with the water. Once the water or phlegm has been extracted (which you will perceive from this: when that work is completed, cloudy air will gradually appear in the receiver), the receiving vessel must be changed. Then we will perceive a certain matter or almost invisible air ascending, which, by gradually thickening itself, will be converted into a substance or turbid and somewhat whitish smoke, and in the end will be transmuted into a lemon-colored liquor and condensed; when the smoke ceases, the receiver must immediately be changed again.

In the third place, you will wait for the element of fire, which will acquire a reddish color for itself, and that redness will be dark.

Finally, the fifth essence, or fifth element, rises with difficulty and diligent observation; for otherwise, it will suffocate itself in the neck of the retort and be burned.

It should be noted that for the production of each element, the space of one day is required, for this operation must be done slowly and step by step.

As for the element of the earth of the blood itself, it is to be drawn from the <term>caput mortuum</term> in this way after the breaking of the retort (in which our author first saw wonders, as we shall declare below): This must be taken not only from the first retort but also from that of the second distillation or operation, and reduced into a powder, then—

# On the Mystical Anatomy of Blood

...should be entrusted to an earthenware vessel, which must be very well sealed with its own lid. This cover should have a hole at its top through which the vapor rising from the material being <term>calcined</term><note>Calcination is the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to reduce it to ash or a friable powder.</note> can easily escape. It should be exposed to a violent fire for a period of 8 or 10 hours until it is perfectly calcined. Then, once the fire is extinguished and the vessel has cooled, the calcined material should be extracted, reduced to <term>alcohol</term><note>In early chemistry and alchemy, "alcohol" referred to any extremely fine, impalpable powder (from the Arabic "al-kuhl"), not specifically the liquid spirit we recognize today.</note> or a subtle powder, and reserved for the use described below.

We now approach the third operation, which is nothing other than the <term>rectification</term><note>The process of refining or purifying a substance by repeated distillation.</note> of the elements previously separated. First, therefore, the <term>phlegm</term><note>The watery, tasteless element produced during distillation.</note> must be rectified, and this is done with gentle heat by means of a <term>Bain-marie</term><note>A water bath used to provide steady, moderate heat.</note>, and you shall keep it aside.

Next, you shall also purge the "air" element in the Bain-marie, separating it from its watery and fiery additions. Our author himself distilled this material through oiled paper and reduced it into a substance like the purest snow or <term>manna</term><note>A substance described in the Bible as food from heaven; here it refers to a white, flaky crystalline sublimate.</note>; this material must also be saved for its own use.

After this, the oil (which is referred to as "fire") must be rectified seven times in small <term>retorts</term><note>Glass vessels with long, downward-pointing necks used for distilling liquids.</note> until it acquires the color of a <term>hyacinth</term><note>A reddish-orange or yellowish-brown gemstone; the "oil" of blood becomes a deep, clear red-orange liquid.</note>. With this, he also joined that essence which he called the "fifth," and this material, thus permitted and so many times rectified, he called his **Potable Gold**. He said that if this were applied or administered for dangerous diseases, it would bring stupendous utility. Whether his assertion is true or false is not for me to dispute in this place; I only wished to tell you what I found to be true and have proven by experience regarding the chemical "anatomization" of human blood and its dissection into its elements.

Finally, I took the calcined earth and placed it in a sufficiently large <term>alembic</term><note>A classic distillation apparatus consisting of a gourd-like bottom and a "head" (cap) with a beak.</note>, over which I poured at least a large portion of the rectified phlegm. I put on its head and <term>macerated</term><note>Soaked to extract soluble parts.</note> it in a gentle Bain-marie or in moderately warm ashes. In this kind of maceration or infusion, a receiving vessel should be attached to the beak of the alembic's head, and if anything distills into it during the process, it must be poured back over the whole mixture. This infusion must be continued for three full days, and in the interval, the material must be removed and shaken many times. Finally, when this work is finished, this macerated material is to be poured into a clean earthen vessel, and its clearer part, separated from the turbulent dregs by way of filtration, is to be extracted in a Bain-marie. Thus, I found a whitening salt at the bottom of the alembic, which I made white and clear like crystal by dissolving it in the recently extracted liquor, followed by filtration and a triple distillation.

That author of ours thought he could produce an excellent medicine by mixing some of these elements together, once a "philosophical decoction" had been performed. By this, he did not doubt he could not only purify impure metals, but even refresh and restore a human body languishing in sickness. Therefore, he mixed a single portion of that substance with three parts of his **Potable Gold** and two parts of "air," and he treated this composition for a long time over a <term>lamp of common alchemy</term><note>A specialized oil lamp designed to provide a constant, low heat for weeks or months.</note>. I do not believe the effect of this operation differed much from those of the "spurious" chemists, who, leaving the right path, dream of distorting and violently forcing the efforts of nature toward their own fantastic conceptions and inventions. 

As for me, I hope I have performed my duty toward you, Excellent Readers, skillfully and abundantly, in that I have brought before your eyes the anatomical division of the elements of human blood, performed by the ministry of the chemical art. And although some might perhaps object to my aforementioned assertions—claiming that according to my demonstration, only a very small portion of blood is found to participate in the element of "air"—I would nevertheless like them to remember that I did not say the entire mass of blood was simply "airy," but that the mass was compacted from the more subtle portions of the elements remaining after the first separation of the dregs. For which of the physicians or philosophers is ignorant of the fact that the <term>vena cava</term><note>The large vein carrying deoxygenated blood into the heart.</note> is never destitute of the serosity of the blood (which is water), or that the blood naturally lacks its own fibers, or is entirely free from its bilious or oily matter? Indeed, we read quite easily that the blood itself is converted into fat, for if it is "cooked" [in the body], tallow or fat can be made from it; that blood is endowed with these "dregs" of its own is hidden from no wise person. <margin>Aristotle, *On the Soul*, book 3</margin> But truly, blood is called "air" because it partakes more of air than of any other element. Nor is it unknown to physicians and philosophers experienced in nature that a purer blood is present in some, and a more impure blood in others, which happens according to a man’s <term>complexion</term><note>The "temperament" or balance of the four humors in an individual.</note> as well as his age. Hence, the author of the aforementioned secret seems to have regard for age. There is also a certain time in life in which the "balance of weight" is said to reign, in which without doubt the blood (which, according to the Sacred Scriptures, is the <note>original: "vita & anima sedes"</note> **"life and the seat of the soul"**) is most tempered and purest in the human body.

But now, lest you object that this experiment of ours brings you no utility beyond the "anatomization" of the mass itself (which alone pertains to our purpose), I desire to put forward some of the medicinal uses of its elements.

Its **Phlegm** is said to contribute wonderfully to itching and <term>scabies</term><note>A contagious skin disease caused by mites.</note>, and for this purpose it has indeed been tested.

The **Element of Air** and also of **Fire** are accustomed to mitigate the pains of <term>podagra</term><note>Gout of the foot.</note>, <term>gonagra</term><note>Gout of the knee.</note>, <term>sciatica</term><note>Pain affecting the back, hip, and outer side of the leg.</note>, and <term>chirogra</term><note>Gout of the hand.</note>—wonderfully so, and indeed in an instant.

Its **Salt**, dissolved into a liquor, is observed to restrain all pains and to perform many other things which we have not yet tested; but for the pains of gout, I have tested it many times.

And so, you have blood divided into its elementary parts by the chemical art. Now, however, I shall prepare myself to recite to you a remarkable story, confirmed by the testimonies of many, concerning a certain notable accident that happened to this author of ours during his first operation. But before I come to the declaration of it...

# CHAPTER V.

## *Concerning the mystical and occult disposition of the air, and that it is the vehicle and receptacle of souls, demons, Angels, and many other invisible mysteries; Likewise, that it is converted into blood through condensation.*

<margin>Tobit 12:15, Psalm 103:20</margin>
Just as the Empyrean spirit <note>The "Empyrean" refers to the highest heaven, traditionally thought to be occupied by the element of fire and the presence of God.</note> is said to be the medium between God and the celestial bodies—whence the Angels dwelling in that spirit are said to "stand before the face of God," and elsewhere, "the most powerful ministers of God in strength, performing his word, listening to his voice," that is, they are mediators between God and celestial creatures—so also the aerial spirit of the world is the medium between the celestial soul and the body. ### Of the Mystical Anatomy of Blood.

...and it is the sanctuary and storehouse of immense secrets of both the heavens and the earth, for it is one spirit and a single essence, covering the entire globe of the earth and the mass of the waters. This essence reaches from the earth all the way to the highest, most hidden heaven, and even ascends above it; for the ether is nothing other than moderately thin air, which is guided and moved by the Word of God (reigning in its center and outside its periphery). By the power of that Word, it shall remain until the very end. It embraces within itself the hidden mysteries of winds, lightning, and thunder, as well as comets, rain, snow, and hail. It is the worldly sea in which the specific forms of all inferior things and the <term>radical moisture</term><note>A term in medieval medicine referring to the essential fluid thought to sustain life and provide the "fuel" for the body's natural heat.</note> of every living thing swim. It is that common space into which the souls or spirits of the departed return. Finally, I believe it is hidden from no one even moderately versed in philosophy that this is the spirit which mixes itself with all sublunary things, acting as the vehicle for spirits or forms—both those that bring health and those that are malignant and composed of poison. 

Hence, air is defined by some as the vital spirit which penetrates all that exists and connects them to one another; it fills all things and moves all things by the power of its soul. For this reason, among certain Hebrew Doctors, this spirit is not numbered among the elements; rather, they regard it as a "glue" joining the elements and the things made from elements together. They call it the "resonant spirit of the world," which receives all influences and spirits into itself. This, therefore, is the spirit which transforms itself into human blood through the assistance of Nature—just like a second <note>original: "alter Protheus." Proteus was a Greek sea-god famous for changing his shape at will.</note> Proteus. In this visible form, it nevertheless contains its invisible mysteries, such as the Divine Mind. (And hence it is said that "man is the temple of the Holy Spirit.") It contains good Angels, such as the one of whom the prophet Zechariah speaks:

<margin>Zechariah 2:3</margin>
> *Behold, the Angel who spoke in me went forth, etc.*

And Iamblichus describes the office of such an angel thus: *This angel (he says) reconciles the soul to the body, communicates with it and cares for it, and directs the life proper to the soul, etc.* That it is also capable of containing wicked spirits and demons is taught to us not only by the testimony of the Holy Scriptures but also by daily experience in the case of the possessed and those obsessed by diabolical spirits. For wicked spirits are permitted to inhabit the lowest spirit of the world, since they cannot inhabit the ethereal or Empyrean spirit due to their impurity. 

Furthermore, the air contracted into blood is the seat of the soul, in the center of which (as was declared above) the Divine Mind has its seat within its own Empyrean spirit. This is confirmed by many passages of the Holy Scriptures. For God said:

<margin>Genesis 9:4</margin>
> *You shall not eat flesh with the blood; for I will require the blood of your souls from the hand of all beasts, and from the hand of man, and from the hand of his brother I will require the soul of man. Whoever sheds human blood, by man shall his blood be shed; for man was made in the image of God.*

And hence it is said in Job 24:12 that the soul of the wounded or the slain cries out, and God does not allow it to go unavenged. It is as if he were saying: "The soul cries out for the violation of itself and the pouring out of its tabernacle," etc. From these things, it is clear, first, that the soul or life is in the blood; second, that the likeness of God is in the blood, insofar as it is established by the Word in which there is life. For this reason, the severest punishment is ordained for those who attempt to violate the temple of nature and the sanctuary of the soul. For although blood is "visible air," invisible forms nevertheless seem to dwell in it—namely, the mind, the Angel, the soul, and the invisible spirit. The nearest receptacle for all these is the air; as blood is procreated from air, it is their remote and outer vehicle. But that the soul is in the blood is clear from this passage of the Holy Scriptures, where it is said:

<margin>Leviticus 17:10</margin>
> *If anyone eats blood, I will set my face against that soul and will cut him off from his people, because the soul of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you so that you may make atonement for your souls upon the altar; for the blood is for the expiation of the soul. Therefore I said to the children of Israel: No soul among you shall eat blood. If, therefore, anyone in hunting or fowling takes a wild beast or bird which it is lawful to eat, let him pour out its blood and cover it with earth, for the soul of all flesh is in the blood.*

But let us hear (I pray) what the ancient philosophers, distinguished by the title of divinity, have to say on this matter. Some hold that the vigor of life consists chiefly in the humors of <term>choler</term><note>Also known as yellow bile, one of the four humors of ancient medicine, associated with fire and heat.</note> and blood: in the blood, I say, so that it may be dispersed throughout the entire body, and in the choler so that it may be rendered more lively in its action. Hermes Trismegistus says that *blood is the chariot of life or the soul, so that when life moves, the vehicle is driven by its motion; but he says that fluid blood, when deprived of this life, coagulates and freezes and exists as if dead.* Empedocles placed the chief power of life or the soul in the heart, and this by way of the blood. But the Epicureans deny this, because they observed that when the heart was extracted from crocodiles, life nevertheless remained in them for a long time. The Stoics recognize that life is in the heart, but they entirely deny that it is present in the heart by reason of blood, but rather by the power of spirit; Chrysippus seems to demonstrate this clearly. Others, agreeing with Moses in this, affirm that it is forbidden and prohibited by the Oracles to eat the blood of a creature, as its soul is within it. 

Truly, in my opinion, it is very easy to produce peace and concord among all these philosophers and to reconcile them with one another. For he who said the soul is in the heart by means of the blood spoke the truth; nor did he lie who asserted it is in the heart by reason of the spirit. For just as a portion of the ethereal spirit or the celestial soul is in the worldly spirit, so also is that spirit within the blood, the vessels of which are the heart and the liver. Nor does the reasoning of the Epicureans follow—that an animal dies immediately when the heart of a crocodile is removed—because the power of life is diffused through the veins and arteries into the entire body. For it does not follow that a green tree dies immediately because it is deprived of its root; for as long as blood is perceived to move in the parts of the animal, life is said to remain in it. We conclude, therefore, from these things that have been said, that the Word is the center of every thing, without which nothing can endure; and that the Divine Mind in man is within the angelic spirit, and that intellectual spirit is in the celestial soul, and the celestial soul is in the invisible air, and the invisible air is in the visible air, which is the blood.

...and blood is in the heart and liver, and by this reasoning the soul can be said to be in the heart both by reason of the blood (in which it exists mediately) and by reason of the spirit (in which it exists immediately). <note>The author distinguishes between "mediate" (indirectly through a medium) and "immediate" (directly) presence.</note> In this same way, God can be said to exist within the human spirit, the blood, and the heart, and consequently, He is present everywhere in the <term>Microcosm</term><note>Man, viewed as a miniature summary of the entire universe.</note> just as He is in the <term>Macrocosm</term><note>The universe or the great world.</note>. Whence by the Apostle, man was not unwisely called the *Temple of the Holy Spirit*.

These things being so, it is evident that the soul—without its ethereal spirit (which is, as it were, the <term>radical moisture</term><note>The essential fluid believed to sustain life and bodily heat.</note> of life), and that spirit without its own course (which is the mundane air), and that air without its vehicle (which is the visibly condensed human element, namely the blood)—could neither enter into the body, nor move within it, nor finally depart from it by the violence of death. This is because blood is bound to air, air to ether, and ether to the radiant or vital soul by the chains of nature in such a way that one cannot move without the other in this elementary region. Indeed, every part of the blood has such a relationship to its whole while the soul acts in the body, that it is also regarded by its whole. For the airy spirit can no more be divided from its like (as is clearly enough declared in the effect of the <term>weapon salve</term><note>original: "unguenti armarii." A 17th-century medicinal theory where an ointment was applied to the weapon that caused a wound rather than the wound itself, acting through "sympathetic" spirits.</note>, of which more below) than a part of the soul can be divided from its whole. Thus, when it is said that *the souls of the slain cry out*, 

<margin>Job 24:12</margin> it is not understood as a "maimed" soul, but an entire one, along with its invisible vehicles, both airy and <term>superlunar</term><note>Belonging to the realm above the moon; celestial.</note>, which are bound by a wondrous link to their final vehicle, namely the blood. And from this it happens that if someone passes through a place where a man was killed, or where the corpse of a dead or murdered man is newly hidden, he is sometimes affected by stupor and fear. This is because the air—which is now the final vehicle in which the soul of the slain is carried—is perturbed by such a slaughter and is surrounded on all sides by horrible and tremendous specters. Thus, joining itself with the internal spirit of the passing man, it affects him with similar invisible shapes, from which fear is struck into him. For the spirit of nature is so tender that it most easily receives external impressions, even invisible ones. From this it arises that if the spirit's sense of vision becomes weak due to long sickness, and the air is dense enough to serve as a mirror for it, a person may perceive the image of his own face in it. This is not only written of by Aristotle and Albert <note>Albertus Magnus, the medieval polymath.</note>, but was also found to be true by me myself when I was laboring under a certain dangerous fever. From these things it is clearly manifest that the air, which is the seat and chariot of the slain man's soul, has an inseparable connection to the blood still remaining in the body of the deceased. Is this not clearly demonstrated in the case of accused criminals? For in the presence of those conscious of the murder, the corpse is often known to pour out fresh blood; but if they are not at all guilty, no blood will exit the corpse. This would never happen unless the airy spirit, the receptacle of the soul, held such a relationship to the corpse. For this spirit, not yet totally separated from the blood of the corpse, is moved as if struck by fear, and by such a sudden motion it liquefies the congealed blood with the heat of its own movement. <note>This refers to "cruentation," a historical forensic practice based on the belief that a victim's wounds would bleed in the presence of their murderer.</note>

Furthermore, there is a struggle and contention, as it were, between the spirits of the slain and the slayer, such as there was between the spirits of Eteocles and Polynices. <note>In Greek mythology, these brothers killed each other in battle; it was said that even the flames of their funeral pyre split in two, refusing to mix.</note> When they killed each other in battle, even their spirits mixed with the fire's flame seemed to distinguish flame from flame. For without doubt, the soul of the departed is accustomed to inhabit the airy spirit as its vehicle, even when separated from the corpse. Whence it is affected by similar passions after its separation from the body, because the passions of man do not arise from the body (which is immobile of itself), but from the sublunary spirit, by which it is moved turbidly and perversely by the soul as a passive thing driven by an agent. In its motion, it stirs up the passions, governed by fatal influences. For the soul is so pure in itself that, unless it is affected by such a rebellious spirit, it acts sweetly and benignly. For it is the sublunary spirit, and not the ethereal one, which is ready to receive spirits both malignant and benevolent, by which the soul is either perturbed or pacified. For the heaven is not naturally subject to changes, because it acts mercifully in its spirit; but where its actions are poorly received, their effects will be perverse. But to proceed further still in this inquiry of ours, Hermes Trismegistus says: 

<margin>Pimander 10</margin> *that when the soul returns into itself, the spirit is contracted into the blood and the soul into the spirit.* Furthermore, he says *that the soul is the receptacle of the Mind, and that the spirit is the clothing of the soul; but he makes the blood the receptacle of the spirits.* For the spirit, by means of its internal essences, acts upon the blood in no different a way than the soul acts upon the body, or the heaven upon the earth. *A similar relationship is held between the soul and the spirit, and between the mind and the soul.* Whence he concludes that *the spirit, diffused through the body through the veins and arteries and blood, stirs the animal on all sides, and sustains and carries about the suspended mass of the body.* And elsewhere he concludes that *just as the soul could not penetrate the body except by the mediation of the spirit, so also it cannot exit the body except by the mediation of the same spiritual vehicle.* Nor indeed can that spirit be so separated from the blood that it does not have a relationship to the blood as its vehicle, which even upon dissolution will be converted into its own invisible and spiritual nature. And this is the reason that the souls of the deceased sometimes appear to men, and then again vanish from sight as if in a moment. For just as a visible cloud is nothing other than condensed and contracted air, which when expanded again is converted into its invisible being (even when dissolved with no rain appearing), so also that spirit, the vehicle of the soul, joins with the spirit of the blood (which has already been thinned by putrefaction and reduced to invisible air) in the vast cavity of the world. Floating here and there in the mundane spirit, it is accustomed to suddenly contract itself, and by that contraction to appear visibly to men in the same form and likeness that the body had while it enjoyed the "breath of life." <note>original: "vescali fruebatur aura."</note> For it is certain and confirmed by philosophers that there is no figure in corporeal things that was not first in spiritual things, nor is there any likeness of a creature here on earth that was not first formed in the heavens. Thus also the spirit of Samuel appeared—true and not a deceptive trick—to King Saul, namely by the condensation of his invisible spirit into a visible appearance, which suddenly through expansion was made invisible again. So also the body of Elijah, made spiritual by transfiguration, appeared with that of Moses to Christ and the Apostles on Mount Tabor. And also that...

# On the Mystical Anatomy of Blood.

...that of Christ after the resurrection, who appeared in the midst of the Apostles by contracting his subtle form and making it visible through condensation. However, when they <note>Referring to spiritual bodies or the resurrected</note> wished to vanish, they did so suddenly through expansion and thinning. For according to the words of St. Paul, they rose from corruption to incorruption, and from a bodily state to an incorporeal and spiritual one. Thus, it happens that the spirits of the dead—especially when the corpses are deprived of proper funeral rites, or when their blood is treated in a violent or extraordinary manner—are sometimes observed to appear visibly. We could cite innumerable examples of such apparitions here, but because other matters call for my attention, I shall reveal to you this single account of a similar event which occurred when our previously mentioned author was performing the secret operation described before.

## CHAPTER VI.

->*Concerning the wondrous history demonstrating the mystical connection of blood after someone's death with their spirit and soul.*<-

Whether the cause of this event was some celestial constellation, a particular method of working, the specific hour chosen at the start of the work, or whether it was due to the deaths of some of those from whom the blood had been drawn, or even the long putrefaction of the blood-matter—both the Practitioner himself and I, as well as many other witnesses who saw and heard it, remain in ignorance. However, our previously cited author, in the city of Paris <note>Original: "Lutetia"</note> near the place called The Temple <note>A district in Paris originally belonging to the Knights Templar</note>, steadily undertook this work—the chemical anatomy of human blood—at the urging of his many friends. He received the blood from a friend; it had undergone putrefaction in a well-sealed jar for two years and had been drawn from the arms of various people. He began his work on a certain Saturday <note>The "day of Saturn," often associated with heavy, earthly, or transformative alchemical processes</note> around the ninth hour, which is the time when the common Mass is celebrated. For an entire week, by observing various degrees of fire (as explained above), he pursued his intention with a continuous flame.

Meanwhile, on the following Friday around midnight, while our practitioner was lying in bed in a room adjacent to his laboratory, between sleep and waking, the brightness of the full moon illuminated the room (which was in the upper part of the house). Behold! Suddenly there arose a horrible lowing, like the bellowing of oxen or the roaring of a lion. Hearing this, the practitioner was struck with astonishment and stupor; flowing with cold sweat, he remained still and motionless in his bed. When that sound in the laboratory ceased, he suddenly saw between himself and the window a certain cloud condensed into an oval shape, which gradually seemed to take on a complete human likeness; then, letting out another sharp cry, it suddenly vanished.

Certainly, although this may seem incredible to some, not only the noblemen in the neighboring rooms, but even the host himself with his wife (lying in the lower part of the house), and even neighbors living on the opposite side of the street, distinctly heard both the roar and the voice; some were even awakened by its vehemence. The practitioner said he found solace in this: the Bishop from whom he had received this prepared blood and the secret of its use had forewarned him that if any of those from whom the blood was extracted should die during the time of putrefaction, their spirit would often appear in the practitioner’s work-area with great disturbance.

Furthermore, on the following day (Saturday), he removed the <term>retort</term><note>A glass vessel with a long neck used for distilling substances</note> from his furnace and broke it with a light tap of a key. In it, he found the <term>caput mortuum</term><note>Latin for "dead head"; a term in alchemy for the useless residue left after distillation. Here, the author implies it took a literal shape.</note> of the blood. I say "head," but it should not be called an inert or dead thing, for in every feature—face, eyes, nostrils, mouth, and hair (which was somewhat thin and golden in color)—it represented a human head. There are many eyewitnesses to this: my dearest friend and a nobleman of the highest trust, Lord de Bourdallone, first secretary to the Duke of Guise. He sent letters to me in England regarding this matter, which was partly why I traveled to Paris—to learn the certainty of this event and to attend to other private business. There, I heard this history confirmed and proven by grave and honest men: by Monsieur Menanton, who lived in that house at the time, by a certain Doctor of Medicine, by the host of the house, and many others. From this, it is clear that the entire spirit of that dead man regarded the spirit of that small amount of blood extracted during his life with an indivisible connection. Thus, when that portion of his blood was tortured by fire, his spirit, exhaled from the body, was disturbed and vexed due to the "symphonic" or harmonious continuation of one to the other. This is also best explained by the following experiments.

From this kind of observation and experience, others whose noses had been shortened by some accident began to wound their own arms and apply their own mutilated noses to them. Although they could only achieve this with extreme labor and the greatest weariness, the expectation of a twofold advantage instilled great patience in them: namely, not only the rebuilding and restoration of the defective limb, but also its continuation in that same state until death. From this sort of experiment, we have a clear enough explanation of how great a relationship exists between the blood of one person and another—and much more so between the entire mass of the same blood and a small portion divided from it, just as is abundantly explained in the mystery of the Weapon Salve <term>Weapon Salve: Also known as the "Magnetic Ointment" (unguentum Armarii), this was a controversial 17th-century remedy believed to heal wounds by applying the ointment to the weapon that caused the injury rather than the wound itself.</term> or magnetic ointment (of which we shall say something below). ### CHAPTER VIII.

->*Concerning a certain Experiment depending on the occult sympathy of blood with its like, by means of which the senses of two men distant from each other by a long interval can be very easily discerned (without any letters or messengers mediating between them).*<-

The preceding experiment (as I said) was the foundation for this subsequent one. For when some of the more acute minds perceived such a great sympathy between the flesh of one man and that of another (the origin and nourishment of which was blood), they noticed that this proceeded from the occult spirit of the blood of both. For if the seat of the soul is the spirit, and the seat or vehicle of the spirit is the blood, it is necessary that this kind of sympathy in nature proceeds primarily from the first Actor or Agent <note>The "first Actor" refers to God or the universal creative force</note>, whose mediated chariot and receptacle is the blood, and whose immediate receptacle is the spirit, wandering invisibly through the mass of the blood.

Hence, they approach the matter in this way: they either wound the arm or some other place with an incision, or pierce it with cauterization. Once the wound is thoroughly cleansed of its own blood or mucous matter and begins to form new flesh, a companion of the man thus wounded must extract some drops of blood, either by incision or a prick, from his own finger or some other place. He must pour these into the other man's wound so that, the hole being closed with a plaster, this infused blood can ferment and finally unite with the blood of the wounded man. But if anyone should object that the infused blood, being outside its own proper place, would become rotten, we acknowledge that the *substance* of the blood can contribute nothing to our Sympathetic work, but only the *occult spirit* in that blood, by means of which the soul of one seems to communicate with the soul of the other. For spirit is very easily joined to spirit by the "glue of nature," since nature delights and rejoices in nature—just as we see in a drop of water or beads of quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, which usually join inseparably to their whole mass. Once the wound is healed in the usual manner, they say a secret lies hidden in this: namely, if the scar of the wound is pricked with a needle or pin, the place or part of the other person from whom the blood was extracted—no matter how far distant from the wounded person—will immediately feel the same prick through the wonderful sympathy of the spirits. Since this is the case, they conclude it is a very easy thing, by means of a certain Alphabet, to communicate anything of any nature or condition between themselves. For example, let one prick be imprinted for the letter A, two for B, three for C, and so on for the rest. Indeed, I have heard that the consensus and bond of this kind of blood communication is so strong between the spirit of one and that of the other, that when the man from whom the blood was extracted dies, it is necessary that the nature of the blood infused in the wound also be rooted out by incision, lest the place rot; and then afterwards the wound must be healed in the former manner. Finally, this kind of consensus of blood with blood is admirably explained in the cure of a wound by the Magnetic Ointment, which we shall treat sufficiently (God willing) in the following chapter. Furthermore, the probability of this kind of sympathetic operation is confirmed by that well-tested conclusion regarding the Lodestone <note>Magnet</note>, so loudly proclaimed by some, by virtue of which communication has been made between friends living in far distant places. Two equally square boards are to be prepared in readiness, from the center of each of which a circle of equal diameter should be drawn. The areas of these circles must be hollowed out in the manner of that nautical instrument so necessary for sailors which the English call *the sea Compas* and the French *Le Compas marine*. ## CHAPTER IX.

->*On the various compositions of the Weapon or Magnetic Ointment, its properties, and its sympathetic operation through the blood.*<-

There is an extraordinary sympathy between things of the same nature, just as there is an admirable antipathy between contrary dispositions. To men overwhelmed by ignorance, this would seem impossible at first glance, had not the infallible properties of nature in different things been confirmed by ocular experience. Nor indeed is anything found outside of human nature that more clearly proves the sympathy of things than the very strong relationship of the magnet to iron, and its affection for the Pole Star. Nor certainly (to come to the kingdom of man) is there anything that more clearly demonstrates the sympathy and compassion between a man and the parts appropriated to his vital disposition, than that manifest logic observed between the ointment—composed of blood and other human parts—and the wound. It acts between the gore shed by the wounded man and the mass of blood still boiling within the injured body. Hence, by way of comparison made between the effects of the magnet and those of this ointment (since they are very similar), this is called the **Magnetic Ointment**.

First, therefore, we shall explain to you the ingredients of its composition and their measures, and we shall describe those effects which practice and experience (the teacher even of fools) have produced, so that you may more easily judge the human parts entering into it. Then, let me be permitted to draw forth the natural reasons for this occult and sympathetic work from the sanctuary or <term>myrothecium: a cabinet or vessel for storing perfumes and ointments</term> of my own mind, such as it is, through which I will briefly show you what my true feeling and opinion is on this matter.

->*The composition is as follows:*<-

Take: <term>Moscae seu Vineae ex Caluaria: "Moss of the Skull," a lichen (Usnea cranii humani) that grows on the skulls of those left unburied</term> of a man who has been hanging for a long time, or for lack of that, from the bones of a hanged man who was throttled by a noose, which have been long exposed to the air and hardened; take also human fat, 2 ounces each. Of <term>Mummy: ancient medicinal "mummy" was often made from the preserved or dried flesh of the deceased</term>, human blood, and <term>Armenian Bole: a red medicinal clay from Armenia used as an astringent</term>, 1 ounce each. Of linseed oil, 2 ounces. Let all be ground in a mortar until they are reduced to a fine ointment, which is to be stored in a small box and wisely reserved for use.

We see, therefore, in a composition of this kind, that this ointment is fashioned from things most suited to human nature, and consequently, that it has a great regard for his health and existence. Indeed, blood concurs in the first place in its composition, in which the power of life is situated. Here (I say) are present the bones of man and their essence in the form of the growing moss; here is his flesh, namely in the Mummy made from flesh and balsam; here the fat of the human body agrees with the rest for the perfection of such an ointment; and with all these, the blood (as was said) is mixed, which was the origin and nourishment of all the aforementioned. In this blood, the spirit of life, and with it the bright soul itself, is accustomed to hide and act in an occult manner. Thus, it seems that the entire perfection of the human body concurs in the making of this precious ointment. And this is why such a great relationship exists between this ointment and the blood of the wounded body: for it is necessary that some of the blood of the injured person be drawn out, even from the depth of the wound, as is clearly explained in what follows.

# On the Mystical Anatomy of the Blood.

When, therefore, a wound is inflicted on someone, either the weapon that caused the wound—smeared with blood—must be recovered, or, if that is missing, a sharp piece of wood must be thrust deep into the opening where the wound gapes so that it may be stained with blood. That instrument, whether it be a sword, a knife, an axe, or finally a piece of wood thus infected with blood, must be brought back to the location of the box <note>The "capsula" or box containing the medicinal salve</note> (however far removed from the patient). It should then be immersed in the ointment and left there until the cure is complete. In the meantime, the wound itself must be bound every morning with a fresh linen cloth soaked in the patient's own urine. And so (God willing) it will be healed without any plaster. This has been proven in the case of wounded men who were ten or twenty German miles away from the ointment itself. It is also useful for other pains, such as toothaches and the like, which are observed to arise from a corrupt disposition of the blood. Likewise, if a horse's foot is wounded by a nail, either through a blacksmith's negligence or by some other accident, it has been found that if a piece of wood is dipped into the bottom of the wound and placed in the box or small chest, the wound is healed within a few days.

In this treatment, however, one thing must be observed in passing: a strict and constant regimen must be maintained. For if this ointment is kept too warm, the wound will be affected by excessive heat; or if it stiffens with cold, the wound will also taste of that same indisposition. And now, from my own experience and knowledge, allow me to recount a story to you. A certain nobleman of the rank of Knight of the Garter <note>original: "eques auratus"</note>, named Sir Nicholas Gilbourne, my brother-in-law (as he married my eldest sister), a man who, in my opinion, is second to none of the English nobility in learning and philosophy—since by his office (which concerned the Royal Ships) the naval apparatus of England was under his care—this man, I say, keeping a box full of this ointment with him, heard that a certain carpenter hired to repair the ships had been severely wounded by an axe. Upon this news, he ordered the axe, whose edge was smeared with the blood of the wounded man, to be brought to him immediately. Rubbing the bloody edge of the axe with his ointment and finding it protected from the cold with linen cloths, he hung it on a nail in his chamber and departed, locking the door. Suddenly, the wounded man confessed that he felt relief, and day by day he continued to grow stronger. But truly, one day he complained greatly of his wound and of the pain and its intemperance; all those standing by wondered why, given no evident cause, he was afflicted with such sudden restlessness. They immediately fled to my brother; he himself hurried to his chamber at a fast pace and found that the axe had by chance fallen to the ground, stripped of its linen coverings, and the anointed part was exposed to the harshness of the air. Therefore, a second time he smeared the edge of the instrument with the ointment and clothed it in linen coverings; immediately the pain of the wound was mitigated, and it was restored to its former temperament, and so he soon recovered.

Now, indeed, we shall proceed to the natural demonstration of this sympathetic cure, so that we may speak not only with the mouth of experience (as is the manner and custom of mechanics), but that we may clearly depict the mystery of this action in the manner of philosophers, using reasons drawn from the hidden womb or storehouse of nature.

Since the air (as was said before) is the medium or vehicle of the spirit of any thing—which is also called the chariot of the soul itself, or of the celestial light, or of the primary agent—and furthermore, since the blood is the receptacle of all these, it follows that the movement of the blood in the vein or artery is from the impulse of the spirit itself, just as the spirit is driven by the light or soul within it, like a wind. In a similar fashion in man, this is incited by the intellectual spirit dwelling in the center of the soul, in the midst of which resides the Divine Mind as prince, emperor, and first internal agent, which is the principle of the Macrocosm <note>The "Greater World" or universe</note> made before all things (according to that passage in Ecclesiasticus: *Wisdom was created before all things*). <margin>Chapter 1</margin> This Mind, therefore, was the first breather into the mundane spirit in its organ, the first striker of the string of the Mundane Monochord <note>A philosophical concept of the universe as a single-stringed instrument tuned by God</note>, always moving in the lucid or Empyrean spirit, just as that spirit moves in the light or celestial soul, which also is carried with its spirit in the aerial spirit no differently than the spirit is carried in the blood. This, therefore, is the reason why blood is linked to the visible air by a bond of nature, no differently than the element of water is to the earth; and again, the air of the visible blood is linked to the invisible air implanted in it, as the element of water is to that of air. And also the lucid soul with its lucid vehicle is linked to the air (in which it is carried) as the element of air is to fire. Furthermore, the intellectual spirit is related to the soul as the celestial or ethereal substance is to the Empyrean, or the intellectual spirit as God is to the spirit of an angel, by which He is surrounded on all sides (according to the Royal Psalmist): <margin>Psalm 104, 2</margin> *God is clothed with light*, that is, with a fiery spirit. From these things it is manifest that the Blood and life are primarily moved by the Mind, but secondarily by the soul, by whose impulse the spirit is provoked, at whose nod the blood is moved in its vein. <margin>Pimander 10 <note>A reference to the Corpus Hermeticum</note></margin> This is also confirmed by Hermes Trismegistus in a discourse of this kind: *The human soul is carried in this manner: the Mind in reason, reason in the soul, the soul in the spirit, and the spirit in the body; and finally the spirit, diffused through the veins, arteries, and blood, moves the living creature on all sides, and sustains and carries about the suspended mass of the body.*

From these things, therefore, it is clear that insofar as the substance of the blood is joined to its spirit by an inseparable bond, and its spirit is nothing other than air in which the celestial soul dwells—and this by a continuous bond, no differently than ether to air—it follows that the relationship between the blood and its spirit is wonderful and firm. Similarly, since its spirit is nothing other than air enclosed in the blood, it adheres to the air in the macrocosm as a part to its whole, or as a drop of water is united with its whole in an inseparable way. # Section I. Portion III. Part III. Book II.

...just as water imbued with saffron, herbs, sandalwood, red dye, or ink—if it flows little by little from a dyer's workshop into a river—will nevertheless retain its distinct tinted appearance from the clear river water, appearing to mark and draw a certain line extended lengthwise in the middle of that river; and yet its substance will be so bound with the river water that it appears continuous with it. So also this **bloody spirit** <note>original: "spiritus sanguineus" — the vital essence or "breath" contained within the blood</note>, even though it has flowed out from the human laboratory <note>The body, viewed as a chemical workshop</note>, will nevertheless leave invisible traces of its nature in its likeness—namely in the air—wherever it is carried. Thus, from the wounded place from which it exited, all the way to the location of the box or casket filled with this kind of magnetic ointment, it seems to extend a certain invisible line of the nature of the visible blood (which is transferred via the wood or weapons to the little chest of health) and to imprint it upon its likeness, namely the air. 

For although all air is of the same nature and substance, it is nevertheless that **Worldly Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius mundanus" — the universal mediating spirit of the cosmos</note> whose parts seem to differ from others, not in respect to substance (since all agree in that), but in respect to the property of the place or body through which the air passed. Just as water is not changed from its watery disposition, yet it usually participates in a sulfurous, irony, or aluminous nature, as well as the colors and qualities of a place, by which it seems to differ from the nature or quality of fresh water. So also it is observed that the nature of the sweet river of the West Indians, called the **Amazon**, enters and penetrates for many miles into the salt sea before it seems in any way immensely altered or different from the nature of sea water, whether in shape, motion, or its sweet disposition. 

Therefore, this Worldly or sublunary Mercury, penetrating all things whether in heaven or finally on earth, after the manner of the celestial mercury, is capable of all qualities; and yet in its airy substance (which is nothing other than subtle water) it is always constant. Once it takes on an **animal force** <note>The "anima" or soul-force of a living creature</note>, it is not easy to lay it down suddenly; for a moist nature so greedily desires its own luminous form that, once acquired, it does not lay it down or lose it so quickly. 

From this it is clear that this spiritual line, invisibly drawn or extended in the air between the wounded person and the location of the box, carries its animal form with it. This soul-force is no less divided from its whole contained in the wounded body than a ray of the sun is from the sun. Therefore, just as a sunbeam swimming in the worldly spirit is like a messenger between heaven and earth, so also this animal ray is a faithful conductor of the health-giving nature from the **Balsam's apothecary-jar** <note>original: "Balsami myrothecio"</note> to the hurt and wounded body. Its medium—or directing line, or the spirit directing the health-giving power by means of the soul—is the spirit stretched invisibly in the air. Unless it were shaped in the air in an occult manner, the virtue of the ointment would flow here and there, and bring nothing of benefit to the wounded man. 

By a similar reasoning, we see that in **optical vision**, if there were no **pyramidal ray** <note>A 17th-century optical theory where vision occurs through a cone or pyramid of light/spirit</note>, the visual spirits could not go out to an object and then, by returning, make the senses more certain of the object's reality. For the sharp edge of the wounded man's soul's gaze is in the box, in which the expected health lies hidden; and that same magnetic power of the soul, looking into the object, attracts the spiritual strengths of that medicine by means of its ray moving in the spiritual organ. This ray is the pyramidal ray of the soul's own gaze, and such a gaze of the soul is full of compassion and love for its own subject or "tabernacle" <note>The body</note>, in which it attracts to itself what is healthful, just as by its antipathetic or hate-filled gaze it tries to repel and avoid objects. 

But to explain and demonstrate this mystical operation even more clearly: If a certain thread is stretched tightly from one place to another, we compare this thread to the occult line of the bloody spirit. If you strike one end of it with your finger, your soul pulsing here is related to the soul of the wounded man, emitting its ray through the spiritual line. The ray emitted by the pulsing soul is that virtue vibrating and shaking the entire thread from the starting point to the end point; it is like a messenger carrying through its spiritual organ the will of its "whole"—that is, the soul, which is the mistress of the whole and consequently of all parts. 

We see, therefore, that this stretched thread is so continuous in its parts that by a pulse at its beginning, its entire substance seems to resonate and vibrate. So, with the soul pulsing the airy part of that line continuous with the wound, that agitating force (which we called the "soul's ray" above) migrates by multiplication to the other end of the spiritual line, thrust into the depths of the box by means of the wood. By its attractive or magnetic power, it draws the nature of the ointment to itself more easily because it seems to symbolize and agree with it by a certain natural **sympathy**. For nature rejoices in its own nature; nature assists nature similar to itself; nature is accustomed to be refreshed by its own similar nature. 

Thus human blood is most easily delighted by, united with, and refreshed in its deficiency by its likeness in bones, lard, mummy <note>A common medicinal ingredient made from preserved human remains</note>, and blood (which concur in the composition of the ointment) through sympathetic consent and symphonic love. For a united force is stronger, and nature united to nature can conquer and overcome all things that are in any way contrary to nature. 

From this, therefore, arises that secret union and combination between wicked spirits and **evil-magicians** <note>original: "cacomagos"</note>, by which foolish men are shamefully deceived by the **Devil**. Hence the Devil, or the malignant spirit, at the invitation of this kind of "tribute," is eager to fulfill the will and commands of a sorceress. Whence a frequent commerce is made between them, so that the spirit, clothed in whatever shape, may daily drain a portion of blood by sucking it, whereby the spirit of the evil-magician lurking in the blood becomes one with that of the malignant spirit, and is thus converted into a diabolical nature, from which it is finally impossible to withdraw from diabolical worship. Indeed, for want of blood, sorcerers used to collect parts of a man originating from blood, namely bones from graves and hair from barbers, as one reads in **Apuleius**. It has been explained by the confession of those living in England: there is, I say, so great a harmony and sympathy between the spirit of one blood and its likeness, that if even a single drop of blood—or something originating from it—is treated by a magus <note>A practitioner of natural magic or spiritual science</note> in distant places, whether for ill or for good, the other person will either be tormented or affected by joy and health. By these means, it is best perceived how great a compassion <note>original: "compassio" — here meaning "feeling together" or resonance</note> exists between the blood of one and the blood of another, even in places far distant from each other. This indeed happens because of the hidden spirit enclosed within them, whose action is a ray of the soul. 

But perhaps someone might reply that an invisible line of this kind, stretched through the air from the wounded person to the site of the box <note>The container of the sympathetic ointment</note>, could be broken and divided into parts by the movement of men or animals, and that it would follow from this that the power of the ointment would work in vain, since its conduit is interrupted, and for this reason it cannot lead the healing power to the desired port. To this we answer: the principle is the same in the division of air as it is in water. For if a part of the water in some river is tinted lengthwise like a line, and a boat passing through its middle divides that tinted line, its parts are nevertheless perceived to rejoin each other in the blink of an eye; nor does it follow that air divided into two parts by a sword does not return to the unity of its substance.

We conclude, therefore, that the effects of the invisible spirit hidden in the substance of human blood are admirable and stupendous, both sympathetic and antipathetic. We have already spoken of the former above; we shall deal briefly with the latter below. And for this reason Arbatel <note>A reference to the *Arbatel de Magia Veterum*, a famous 16th-century manual of spiritual magic</note> (a man highly versed in supernatural mysteries) established an entire treatise on Microcosmic Magic, in which he denotes what the microcosm <note>The human being, viewed as a "little world" mirroring the universe</note> has effected through its spirit and the geniuses <note>original: "genios" — guardian spirits or guiding intelligences</note> added to it from birth, magically—that is, by spiritual wisdom—and how: and through that wisdom, the teacher of all things, the mind is carried into the human soul by means of its intellectual spirit, just as we understand the soul to be within the human spirit.

## CHAPTER X.

### *On the nature of both Macrocosmic and Microcosmic antipathy, and how the interior spirit of both is sometimes alienated from the soul inhabiting it, and is usurped by evil spirits.*

Concerning the sympathy of the blood—by means of its airy spirit—with its likeness even when placed in a distant location (and much more so when running in the same vein by which healthy life, or health and balance, is acquired by man), enough has been treated in the preceding sections. Now, however, our discourse will be established in this place briefly concerning the antipathy between the living soul and that evil, corrupting one—that is, one opposite to it in disposition—by means of the same spirit: and how this spirit, the vehicle of its own soul, may be alienated from its mistress and her care.

Just as it is impossible for any sympathetic harmony or symphonic society to exist where the airy spirit is diverse from its soul, or contrary in disposition (according to that saying of the Savior Jesus Christ: *a kingdom divided by opposition cannot long endure*), so also it is necessary that this alienation in the sublunary spirit <note>The spirit existing in the realm below the moon, i.e., the Earthly atmosphere</note> proceeds from a demon of nature contrary to the life-giving soul. For the air itself is of a moist and passive nature, and is led either by an internal agent naturally implanted in it from birth (by which it is made regular in its faculty of living), or by one coming upon it preternaturally, by which it is turned against its natural and ordinary course. It is then made rebellious to the living soul, and like the chariot of Phaethon <note>A mythological figure who lost control of the sun-chariot, nearly destroying the earth</note> carried outside the path of nature, it attempts to destroy the "lesser world" <note>The human body</note> either with fire or to submerge it with the flood of Deucalion <note>The Greek version of the Noah story</note> in deadly cold and moisture, headlong and in an insane manner, like those swine who, driven by evil spirits, cast themselves headlong into the sea. 

This inferior spirit, I say, is so fragile and so liable to defilements that, like a "celestial mercury," it is fit for the disposition of any demon or evil and foreign soul, however much it may be contrary to its own mistress, the vital soul. And this is the reason why the sublunary spirit, both in the Macrocosm <note>The universe</note> and Microcosm, is imbued with such great changes and inconstancy. From this it happens that it hungers with a constant appetite for new forms, and uses "privation" <note>A philosophical term for the absence of a quality</note> in the place of a temptress, by means of whom it constantly procures new loves for itself. Hence comes such great uncertainty in the sublunary world; hence the origin of the unhappiness of the human race and the beginning of sin. For (as I said before) although the air suffers in its moist nature, nevertheless the influences of the celestial bodies, flowing into it, serve in the place of agents or souls. 

But truly, insofar as we see that the influences are diverse, according to the varying nature of the planets predominating in the heavens, to that extent we observe diverse impressions and alterations produced in the air and inferior things, flowing from a variety of causes. For example, meteors are sometimes ignited, sometimes watery, and even windy, according to the diverse condition of the celestial influences in this or that region of the air. From this, however, it is right to elicit a variety—indeed even a contrariety—of celestial influences: namely, because the aspect of Jupiter is observed to be favorable and propitious to human nature, while that of Saturn is greatly opposed to it by a certain antipathy ordained by the Creator. For certain Saturnine aspects are most hostile to life and the human race, being cold and consequently contrary to human heat, and dry, which therefore in every way resist the radical moisture...

By these things it is clearly enough declared: that demons who are contrary to human nature and other things in their dispositions, as well as those who are favorable to the life of creatures, are contained in the air. In the air, according to the various predominances of the planets in heaven (from which they draw life and power), they exercise their turns in dominion and action. From this it happens that the blood, infected by malignant demons from the aerial element, is most easily corrupted and contaminated by contagious diseases, since the vital blood is nourished by the more subtle part of the air. Indeed, the air entering the human body through both breathing and nourishment sometimes draws and introduces with it a spirit that is malignant and hostile to human life. Whence no small alienation occurs between the aerial spirit and its own soul in this "lesser world" <note><term>microcosm</term>: the human being as a miniature reflection of the universe</note>, not otherwise than happens in the sublunary air of the "greater world" <note><term>macrocosm</term>: the universe or environment</note>, by whose presence the quiet air is disturbed by lightning and flashes, hail, rains, comets, and infinite other impressions, and seems to fall ill. And thus an incurable antipathy is sometimes created between a man's good genius <note>A protective guardian spirit</note> and the demon contrary to him, who attempts entirely to pollute the aerial spirit—the vehicle of the soul—and convert it into his own malignant nature.
