### On the Mystical Anatomy of Sperm.

The substance of the members composing the body is said to be formed by the most hidden action of nature; but the **seed** (which is something central and formal, and invisible within the sperm) relates to the sperm as the soul relates to the body. It is formed not from elementary matter, but from a celestial and ethereal substance, together with its light—indeed, with a super-celestial essence. Therefore, that definition which confuses elementary matter with its form—namely, <term>sperm<note>The visible, material fluid.</note></term> with <term>seed<note>The invisible, spiritual blueprint or 'soul' within the fluid.</note></term>—is inappropriately stated, since the two differ no differently than matter and form, of which one acts and the other is acted upon. 

We say, therefore, that sperm—that is, the visible mass—is like a cloud or air. By a breath, according to the nature of the breath of spirits or winds (both super-celestial and celestial as well as elementary) blowing from all corners or regions of the <term>microcosm<note>The "small world"—a traditional term for the human body as a reflection of the universe.</note></term>, it is condensed into the visible form of a white and fertile little cloud. For as we see in the <term>macrocosmic<note>The "great world" or the universe at large.</note></term> air, clouds change color because of the greater purity of their substance. According to the opinions of the ancient philosophers, if the substance of a cloud or cloudlet is procreated from a subtler vapor that is not so condensed, then it will be white in color, and its substance will be more rare, transparent, and bright, thereby denoting its airy purity. But if it is denser, and suggests a multitude of terrestrial humors or waters, then it will be dark or black, such that the solar rays cannot penetrate it. Therefore, this latter species seems to exist unnaturally in the world and brings about great rains or floods. 

The former species of clouds, however, seems to exist according to nature; these incline toward the nature of those fertile mists which are said 
<margin>Genesis 2:5.</margin>
to have ascended from the earth in the beginning, before any cloud appeared in the sky, to water its surface so that it might become fertile and more fit and convenient for the growth and vegetation of plants. In this same way, a white mist of this kind exhales from the quarters of the body (or the "earth"), and by the force of the internal spirit seizing and condensing it into a white cloudlet, it is introduced into the seminal vessels <note>original: *vasa seminaria*</note> as if into the "corner of the west." 

The manifest substance, therefore, is like the pure essence of the four elements that constitute the members of the microcosmic earth. This essence is first decocted and prepared within its members or vessels into a most subtle substance of air, which retains within itself the power of the four elements and consequently of the four humors, from which the body of the offspring is forged—no differently than from the seed, which first emanates from the heart, comes its divine soul. 

That this elementary and visible sperm is extracted from all the members of the body (as the essence of a composite mass by a "chemical" force for the composition of the born body, and not from any one particular part), we gather from three arguments: 

**First**, we see that after much intercourse all the members of the body are weary, numbed by a certain torpor, and exhausted. We observe the spirits of the brain to be dulled, the feet and even the muscles of the arms to be heavy, and finally the entire mass to be sluggish and almost lifeless. Indeed, even if one who engages in too much intercourse was affected in past times by <term>podagra<note>Gout of the foot.</note></term>, <term>chiragra<note>Gout of the hand.</note></term>, or hypochondriac wind—even if he is now almost completely cured—he will immediately feel pains and weariness in those specific members more than others after much intercourse. This is a most certain sign (as it seems to me) that a pure draft of the members, or the essence of the four elements, is drawn from them by a certain magnetic force and spirit (or wind) and introduced through the orifices of the small veins into the <term>vena cava<note>The primary vein returning blood to the heart.</note></term>; flowing through the blood mass, it is led downward and poured into the spermatic veins or vessels. There, by the power of the elementary spirit seeking a new form, it is held for complete preparation, so that it may better receive the impressions of its seminal form flowing from the heart through the great artery. 

**Second**, experience proves that a son participates in the incurable diseases of the parents. If some member is affected by such a deformity in the father or mother, we quite often observe that member similarly affected in the newborn: namely, gout in the feet, gout in the hands, or stones in the back or bladder, etc. The reason for this is that nature rejoices and desires to procreate like from like. 

**Third**, and most certain, is that a son or daughter for the most part displays the species and image of their parents: namely, a resemblance in the face, symmetry in the disposition of the members, and even the gesture and "icon" of the entire body. 

We conclude, therefore, that sperm (the more visible portion of the generative humor) is the essence of those four elements that constitute the members of the body. The members are the vessels in which it is decocted and prepared into the form of a misty smoke, a breath, or an elementary spirit seeking a new form. It drives this smoke before it with a successive motion, as wind drives smoky air, first from the fleshy parts into the blood mass of the vena cava through the orifices of the small veins arising from the trunk of the cava, and then later into the spermatic veins, in which that smoke gradually coagulates into a white cloudlet. 

From this it is manifest that sperm, being in this place of the body, is the origin and beginning of the fetus's body. And although it may appear to be a thick and bare mucus or matter, it nevertheless contains within itself the invisible parts of the whole thing to be begotten, which is the fruit of the members of the parent's body—no differently than the apple is the fruit of the apple tree, or the grape of the vine. Although this fruit is plucked from its tree, the tree does not die, but daily seizes a new power of generating for itself from the elements. And this is what the Philosophers mean when they say that the seeds of all things lie hidden in the elements. 

The immediate way in which this elementary spirit (which flies immediately from the extreme members after the emission of sperm into the womb, to successively fill the place of the emitted sperm) is nourished and refreshed is through the blood, which is procreated from the <term>chylous<note>Related to chyle, the milky fluid of digested food.</note></term> juice of nourishment. As for the mixture of this sperm with its seed, we shall deal with that point by point in the following chapter, where we will first treat the "form" of the seed or sperm.

## Chapter III.

### On the seeds or the mystical procreation of the hidden form of sperm: and how the true gold of life is made, sent from the heavens: Similarly, what the essence of offspring becomes.

How stupendous and admirable a creature the air is—how filled with influences of both life and death, and likewise how it is the source of vegetation and the formal "nurseries" of generation; indeed, it is the very receptacle of God as well as of angels and demons, as we have sufficiently and clearly demonstrated in the preceding sections. But truly, insofar as the sparks of life and generation swim in that aerial spirit alone, without which creatures (among whom we understand man to be the chief) cannot live for even a moment of time, it is therefore necessary that the inhalation of this air occurs every minute. Without it, the animal is immediately suffocated, for when the aerial spirit is taken away, its soul is also removed, which is the ethereal light coupled with such a spirit. By the former, the innate heat is nourished and refreshed; by the latter, the decreasing <term>radical moisture<note>In medieval medicine, the "radical moisture" was the essential fluid of life that acted as a fuel for the body's internal heat; its depletion led to aging and death.</note></term> is successively restored. 

Therefore, the animal—but more effectively, man—breathes this spirit into the left chamber of the heart. This occurs by the reason explained in our common anatomy: namely, by the contraction of the straight fibers of the heart and the consequent dilation of the oblique and transverse fibers. This movement is called <term>Diastole<note>The phase of the heartbeat when the heart muscle relaxes and allows the chambers to fill with blood (and, in this theory, air).</note></term>. During this interval, the heart draws air from the lungs through the <term>venous artery<note>Original: "arteriam venosam." In historical anatomy, this refers to what we now call the pulmonary vein, which was believed to carry air/spirit from the lungs to the heart.</note></term> into its left ventricle for the nourishment of the vital and generative spirits. This is not unlike how the liver is observed to attract the juice of nourishment into its cavity to regenerate the natural spirits destined for growth. In this laboratory of the <term>microcosm<note>The human body viewed as a "little world" reflecting the universe.</note></term>, perfect nature sets about completing the "anatomy" of the air, dividing it into its parts with equal partition. For here, it distinguishes the fiery substance of heaven and the ethereal spirit (which is its vehicle) from the smoky and morbid impurity of the air. These celestial elements it stores in its sanctuary called the <term>aorta</term>; the elementary parts, however, being subject to change and corruption and thus useless for the business of life, it turns into smoke and emits through the same path they were introduced, as superfluities unnecessary for the work of life. 

These are the shining atoms swimming invisibly in the ethereal spirit, reserved in the microcosmic storehouse. They are the <term>Phoebean seeds<note>Original: "Phębea seminaria." Phoebus is another name for Apollo, the sun god; thus, "solar seeds."</note></term> flowing from the fountain of the sun, which are said to differ from the nature and essence of the sun no differently than a ray differs from the sun itself. As the Royal Psalmist says, *God has placed a tabernacle in the sun*, meaning He is present centrally in the sun. But concerning this subject, God willing, we shall discuss more in the mystical dissection of the heart itself. Here, however, I shall turn myself chiefly to the way this solar spirit expands for the acts of life in the microcosm, and again to the reason for its contraction in the progress of generation.

As soon as this matter was separated from the impurity of the sublunary air in that most noble laboratory of the microcosm (the chemical workshop of the left chamber of the heart), it is introduced through three semilunar valves (which open inward and close outward) into the great artery or aorta, as if into the sanctuary of the microcosmic nature. By means of the trunk of this artery, it is dispersed everywhere through the entire body into infinite branches: namely, through the carotid arteries to the brain, through which the more super-celestial part of the chemical work (the solar substance, excelling in dignity the whole vital fountain) is raised to the cerebral heaven, or the <term>Empyrean<note>The highest, most refined part of heaven, associated here with the brain as the seat of the rational soul.</note></term> of the microcosm, as it is the seat of the intellect and the rational soul. 

Next, those cervical, humeral, and thoracic arteries, providing life to those parts, carry with them the spiritual impression of those parts. The coronary arteries bear the internal image of the heart and its spirit, and so it goes for the rest. Thus, the invisible spirit swimming here in the thinnest substance of the aerial spirit not only expands itself for the vivification of the body's members, but also by its own contraction (which usually occurs in the act of intercourse by a certain magnetic force, full of divine love), this spirit is drawn downward into the seminal arteries from all the members of the body, but especially from the principal ones. This invisible spirit—according to the model of that Archetype in which all things to be created were previously designed (just as the royal prophet David also boasted that he received the image of the temple entirely from the hand of God)—contains within itself the invisible figure for depicting the human body; that is, the [interior] of man...

## CHAPTER IV.

### On the exact method of mixing the seed with the sperm, by means of that wonderful plexus which the Greeks call Anastomosis.

**IN** my common anatomy, it was declared that two of the four preparing seminal vessels are veins, of which the right one sprouts from the *vena cava* below the emulgent <note>The renal vein.</note>, while the left one is drawn from the emulgent itself. The other two are arteries coming from the trunk of the great artery <note>The aorta.</note>, exiting below the emulgents; one of these turns toward the left side, joining its descending partner, while the right one meets its venous counterpart on the right side. For although these four vessels are divided into right and left sides (for in each side, one vessel relates to the artery as a female to a male), the veins and arteries are at first somewhat distant from one another. Afterward, however, they are so intertwined that the vein enters the artery and the artery the vein in a wonderful plexus. Thus occurs that remarkable and visually delightful mixture which the Greeks called <term>anastomosis <note>original: "ἀναστόμωσιν"; a Greek anatomical term for the opening of one vessel into another, or a connection.</note></term>. 

Indeed, this intertwining is prepared with the highest craftsmanship of nature, not only (as the Anatomists claim) to convert the "red seed" (as they call it) into a white color, but first so that it might separate the "spermatic substance" in the venous vessels and the "seminal substance" in the arterial vessels from the mass of blood—both the "natural blood" flowing from the liver and the "vital blood" which has its origin in the heart. 

The purpose is that, afterward, they might mix the "seminal form" with the "spermatic matter" according to the likeness of the species—not unlike how we observe the form of a thing spread through its entire elemental substance by natural mixing. This plexus or <term>Anastomosis</term> is a structure like the impression of a notable seal: in a man it is human, in a lion it is leonine, in an eagle it is aquiline, and so on. According to this scarcely perceptible impression, the sperm is shaped like clay, and is irrigated by its seminal spirit like water. By the divine power lurking in that spirit, it is brought back into a living soul. 

And so the sperm and its seed are tempered together according to the laws of nature. The seed is moved by the hidden divine power within it—much like a breath from a breather—to shape the sperm according to the image of its created species, as if some mole were setting out to build and fashion for itself a proper and comfortable home in the bosom of the earth. But the internal agent of this work is God, or the divine spirit, whence the royal prophet rightly said:

> By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the spirit from his mouth.

Thus, the spirit of man (which is his power of sensation) was formed originally from the divine spirit, and is moved and governed by the same according to His will, who "blows where He wills," as John testifies. And hence it was said by the wise man that no man has mastery over his own spirit.

<margin>Ecclesiastes 8:7</margin>
Therefore Job said: *In man there is a spirit, but the inspiration of the Almighty makes him understand*, as if he had said: within the created spirit of man there is also the uncreated spirit, which is its primary action. Whence Saint Paul concludes quite wisely that *man himself is the temple of the Holy Spirit*. We say, therefore, that the mixing of the celestial form (which is the vehicle of the mind) with the elemental essence (by which the generative spirit becomes a sharer of both sexes) occurs in this kind of wonderful plexus. In this place, the spirit—which was previously "golden" and hardly perceptible or distinguishable from the venous blood, as well as that ethereal spirit not yet selected from the arterial blood by the extraction or "chemistry of nature"—is reduced into the form of a mist, or a whitening cloud. This division of the generative spirit from the mass of blood, and the joining of the sperm with its soul or vivifying spirit...

### CHAPTER V.

#### *What the philosophers think regarding the method of introducing the sperm into the womb, and the operation or progress of that which is thus introduced: and thereafter the author's opinion on the matter is explained, supported by the testimonies of Philosophers and Theosophers as well as the Holy Bible.*

Regarding the sperm enclosing its own seed, and its introduction or ejaculation into the womb, it must be understood that two actions are required for this work: namely, a spiritual action, which concerns the intellect and its servants or handmaidens (memory and phantasy or imagination), and a corporal action, which operates through physical contact. The first action, the spiritual one, is concerned with the soul of the sperm or the seed. Hence, whether through the sense of sight or through the imagination, the rational spirit acts upon the consideration of a desired or loved object. For the impression or image of the loved thing is painted in the phantasy <note>Imagination or the "mind's eye."</note>. This phantastic faculty is directed by the rational faculty both before and during the act of generation, and in this operation of the soul, the ethereal seed is prepared. Its source is the heart itself, which previously introduced that seed from the "aerial sea" into its left ventricle through inhalation, in the manner described above. Therefore, through a strong imagination, the erection of the virile member occurs in this way: the animal spirits <note>In early modern medicine, "animal spirits" were subtle fluids that carried sensation and movement through the nerves.</note> mix themselves with the life-spirits by means of the carotid arteries; the heavenly fire of love excites a flame previously conceived in the imagination. This flame, raining its "magic smoke" <note>original: "fumum suum magicum"; likely referring to a subtle, invisible influence or vapor.</note> downward through the trunk of the great artery into the private member or penis, fills its capillary arteries with its breath. Thus, this member is vigorously erected by the power of the animal spirits diffused throughout it from the vital organs. By means of this erection, the sperm is drawn from the testes through the *vasa deferentia* into those vessels called the "prostates" or the "glandular overseers."

The second action, the corporal or elemental one, proceeds from material contact—namely, from the motion or friction that occurs in mutual copulation. In this act, delight and joy are excited in the whole body, and meanwhile the purest "marrow" of the elements is accustomed to leap from its foundations and is precipitated into the spermatic vessels; likewise, the seminal spirits, descending step by step from the parts of the body, are mixed with it. Thus it happens that the well-prepared and tempered sperm is urged to give place to these newly arriving spirits, and is enticed to exit into the depths of the matrix <note>The womb.</note> or into the light of the air by the strong friction exciting heat—not unlike fire struck from a flint by the collision of iron or steel. In this action, the celestial spirit also acts reciprocally and is delighted by an admirable sympathy. From this it is clear that in this dual action, the spiritual stands to the material as the soul to the body, or as heaven to the earth.

Once the sperm, with its celestial soul, has been injected into the womb, it is necessary (as some maintain) that the female sperm also meet this injected sperm at that very instant; they conclude that if this does not happen, no generation can occur. Just as the invisible seed in the masculine sperm was like a soul to the visible sperm, so also the whole mass of the man’s sperm is like a "form" to that of the woman. In this, human generation agrees with the creation of the greater world. For the Soul of the World <note>Anima Mundi.</note> is the luminous spirit of the super-celestial heaven, in which fire or light abounds in the simplest spirit; in the same way, the seed of the man, which is pure fire in a most limpid spirit, is compared with the nature of the sperm (the visible part of the generative humor in the man). Similarly, just as the informed substance of heaven or the ethereal spirit is the soul to the elemental world, so also the man’s sperm relates to that of the woman. Finally, just as God is present in the center of the world as Unity, from which both the watery matter and the luminous form—that is, duality and trinity—proceed.

So it is also in human sperm: namely, the acts of both its internal formal part and its external elemental part consist in its center or Unity, because it is the "breath of the Almighty," as the Holy Scriptures testify. Similarly, the menstrual blood observes the same proportion in respect to the sperm of the man and woman as the earth does to the more liquid elements and the celestial spirit. The menstrual mass <note>In early modern biology, it was believed the mother provided the "matter" (menstrual blood) while the father provided the "spirit" or "form" via the seed.</note> provides the earthly solidity to both and diligently offers the nourishment for growth; yet, because of its imperfection and impurity, the body which it builds is made liable to so many changes, subject to so many diseases, and so prone to an untimely death.

As for the preparation of the seed in the womb, accomplished through condensation and maturation, Galen <note>Claudius Galenus (129–216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity.</note> maintains that in the beginning, after the complete mixing of the seeds in their vessel or "philosophical egg" <note>An alchemical term for the womb or a specialized glass flask.</note>, a certain foam arises. From this, he seems to argue that *the secret spirit enclosed within the seed is a certain wind, working slowly toward perfection.* He then recounts that by the power of this kind of threefold wind enclosed within, *three prominent vesicles* <note>Small fluid-filled sacs or bubbles.</note> *are formed from the said foam, in each of which a different spirit is enclosed, by which the mass or matter is moved in every kind of motion. He says that each of these spirits intends the generation of its own material cause: namely, the middle one, which is vital, for the generation of the heart; the lowest, which is natural, for the completion of the liver; and the highest, which is animal <note>original: "animalis"; in this context, it refers to the "anima" or soul-directed functions of the brain, not "animal" in the modern sense.</note>, for the procreation of the brain.* He concludes, therefore, that as the windiness enters into the depth of the seed, *by the action of the three spirits, a certain vesicle is born in the middle, while another vesicle lies hidden above near it, and another below: from the first vesicle the heart is formed, from the second placed above, the brain, and from the third, the liver.* These are his words. From which it is evident that the internal spirit is nothing other than a three-fold wind, which is driven by a triple internal agent; all of these relate to the unity of life, which all three winds and their agents seem to obey.

<margin>Galen, *On Living Anatomy*</margin>
But this Galen of ours elsewhere describes the time when both the foam and the bubbles appear in words such as these: *For the first six days, foam appears in that matter at the end, and there are three bubbles set over the principal members. Afterward, through the three following days, the internal outlines and "punctuations" <note>The first visible dots or points of organs.</note> of the other members begin. During the first six days, nothing is drawn from the womb, because little or nothing of that matter is lost. During the six following days, as the windiness penetrates and the spirits tend toward the exterior, the branching of the veins and arteries is perfected. Through the following twelve days, blood enters through all the fleshy members, which is why in an abortion at that time, fleshy pieces appear; and in this space, the spinal medulla is also divided from the brain through the spine of the back. Likewise, through the nine following days, the members are distinguished from one another, namely the sides from the neck, the neck from the brain and head, the hips from the buttocks, and so in all others. Thus, in total, there will be 35 days, for the most part, although sometimes later, namely 40 days, and sometimes faster, namely 30 days, so that five days always intervene. The reason for the slowness is the lessening of heat, while the reason for the haste is its intensity.* Thus far Galen.

<margin>From Giuseppe Rosaccio, an Italian <note>A 16th-century Italian physician and cosmographer.</note>.</margin>
Others, however, hold that once the seed is received into the womb, the womb is immediately closed. From this point, in the space of 7 days, they say three bubbles are sufficiently clearly raised and formed, from which the three principal members of the body arise—namely the Heart, the Brain, and the Liver. Afterward, they recognize that these members, while still only in potential, are reduced into visible action and their natural shapes quite clearly over a space of fifteen days, so that the veins springing from the Liver, the arteries from the Heart, and the nerves from the Brain are in some way perceived. Then, with the internal heat working, the lungs, stomach, intestines, bladder, and finally all other members of the body are brought to light by the thirtieth day in a man, and the thirty-seventh day in a woman. Thus the fetus, possessing all its organs for the completion of its maturation, usually remains in the womb for nine months, receiving its nourishment through the umbilical vein descending from its mother's liver.

However, because the fetus, having completed that nine-month span of time, usually desires a wider range of air and more abundant food, it longs to go out from the darkness of the womb into the light of the world by a certain natural instinct. It strives with the greatest effort to obtain its freedom, which Astrologers assert happens because of the predominance of the Moon in that month of birth. They conclude that the child cannot live in the eighth month because of the governance of Saturn, nor in the sixth month, as that is when Mars has its dominion. But truly, the seventh month, which Jupiter presides over, grants it life. From these things, therefore, according to the opinions of almost all philosophers and anatomists, it is clear that the triple spirit—of one essence but different in property, after the manner of the Divine Trinity—is the operator and builder in the microcosmic machine of the world. Now, regarding the action and growth of the seed in the womb, and also the order and preparation of the parts to be produced, we shall say a few words according to our own opinion. First, we say that this seed is clothed with this triple spirit as a representation of the "Greater World" <note>The Macrocosm or Universe.</note>, in which three spirits are found, differing in position, nature, and dignity: namely the intellectual or super-celestial, which has an angelic and discursive nature; the ethereal or celestial, in which its vital soul resides (namely in the sun); and the aerial or elemental, where the faculty of changing, growing, and nourishing predominates. These are related in man to that rational or "animal" wind or spirit that raises and blows through the region of the brain; the vital spirit, by whose breath the heart is filled and built; and the natural spirit, by whose breathing the liver is established. We also say that an angel or "daemon" <note>In the Platonic sense, a guiding spirit or intermediary, not necessarily an evil demon.</note> presides over each of these spirits, each of whom excels the others in dignity and office—no differently than the spirits of angels in the worthier parts of the world are observed to have dominion over those daemons of the inferior spirits. For example, Michael the Archangel of the Ethereal Empyrean Heaven has dominion over the solar daemons, and these again over the elemental daemons, because they are accustomed to blow in the eastern region in the elemental world; for angels are the ministers of GOD, who perfect everything that has been ordained by GOD.

Therefore, although it may be said that God did this or that, it must be understood that He did it through the mediation of His ministers, among whom there are various orders differing from one another in dignity. And hence Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), a scholar and bishop whose encyclopedias were standard references in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> says that archangels are more worthy than the lower angels, as it is by their diligence that the lower angels are informed of the will of God. And again it is said that the Archangels receive their illuminations from the superior angels, and in turn pour these illuminations into the lower angels.

The Hebrew Doctors, setting down nine orders of angels, called the first of them *Haioth Kadosch* <note>original: "Haioth Kadosch", meaning "Holy Living Creatures" or "Animals of Holiness."</note>, that is, "the living beings of holiness" or "lives," through which angels the name *Ehyeh* <note>The Hebrew divine name "I Am."</note> bestows the gift of office. The third order they called *Arælim* <note>original: "Arælim", meaning "The Valiant Ones" or "Thrones."</note>, which is to say, angels who are great, strong, and robust; through these, the *Tetragrammaton Elohim*—or the name "Lord God" <note>original: "יהוה", the four-letter name of God.</note> pronounced with this conjunction—administers the form of flowing matter. Through the fourth order, called *Chaschmalim* <note>original: "Chaschmalim", meaning "The Brilliant Ones" or "Amber-colored ones."</note>, the God of bodies, *Eloah* <note>original: "Eloe".</note>, fashioned the outward shapes. From this we see that, according to the Hebrews, a God-like breath is provided by a single angel of the first order; from one of the third order, the seed or fluid matter is mixed with the "seed-form" or pattern for the perfection of life; and by one of the final order, the outline of the body's shape is drawn in the womb.

These angels, therefore, provide the mind, the vital spirit (consisting of subtle matter and life-giving form), and the natural spirit, which works toward the nourishment of the body and the completion of its shape. The Chaldeans and Egyptians seem to distinguish between "sacred spirits" <note>The text uses "dæmon," which in this context refers to a guardian spirit or tutelary genius, not an evil "demon."</note> and spirits of the stars—those of the "geniture" or birth, which come from the star predominating at the moment of birth—and elemental spirits, which are considered the worst of all. They claim the sacred spirits are those who, descending from the God of spirits himself, are assigned to rational souls. They say the duty of these is to direct the life of the soul, to always provide good thoughts to the mind, and to act within us by constant illumination, even if we do not always notice that action in the soul—except when we are purified and living tranquilly. Then this spirit is perceived by us, and seems to speak with us, as it were, clearly communicating its voice to us, though previously it was present in silence. It studiously endeavors to lead us toward holy perfection. They say the perfection of the "Socratic spirit" <note>The "Daemon" of Socrates, a divine inner voice he claimed warned him against mistakes.</note> was such that, by its virtue, we read that he avoided the malignancy of fate. And Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on theurgy and the soul's relationship to the divine.</note> speaks of this kind of spirit in these words: *It joins the soul to the body, cares for what has been shared, directs the soul’s own life, provides the principles for constant thought, and we perform such things as this spirit brings into the mind.* Jacob also felt the presence of this angel when speaking to his sons in his testament: *That angel who rescues me from all evil, may he bless these boys.* <note>Genesis 48:16.</note> And Christ himself acknowledged that this kind of angel is assigned to every person, as is clearly perceived from his speech when he says: *See that you do not despise one of these little ones, for I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven,* <note>Matthew 18:10.</note> as if he had said that every person has for their spiritual leader one of those seven angels who stand before the face of God. Of these it is said in the Book of Revelation: *Grace to you and peace from him who is, and who was, and who is to come, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne.* <note>Revelation 1:4.</note> And in the Book of Tobit: *I am Raphael, one of the seven angels who stand before the Lord.* <note>Tobit 12:15; original: "Iehouæ".</note> And in Luke: *I am Gabriel, who stands before God.* <note>Luke 1:19.</note> The effect of such an angel also appeared to the prophet Zechariah, as one who would speak to him familiarly, specifically because he was a purified man; *of whom it is said: The angel who spoke in me went out, and another angel went out to meet him, and said to him, "Run, run, speak to that boy, saying..." etc.* <note>Zechariah 2:3-4.</note> From this it is manifest, first, that one angel may command another even within the human body; and second, it is evident that two angels may manifest in one man, one of whom presides over the other in authority and dignity, for thus he commands here by saying, "Run, run, speak," etc.

Hence, we have first in that "wind" or spirit the "mover" or internal agent which inspires the "tabernacle in the microcosm"—I mean the brain with its organs—by its hidden spirit received immediately from God. It fills it with its spirit no differently than wind fills a bladder; and this wind is finally hardened by a "northern blast" <note>A metaphor for the cooling or condensing force in embryology.</note> and frozen into the solid substance of the brain, and grows through the steady arrival of nourishment to the perfect size of the fetus. In the same way, we see the spirit of the Divine Craftsman weave the labyrinthine web of a spider out of invisible matter, little by little and step by step, into a most exact shape.

Now, however, let us descend to the spirit of the middle heaven, or the "Olympic spirit," or the spirit of fate, which is subject to that highest Egyptian angel. This spirit has the immediate governance of life; insofar as it holds dominion in the middle, it participates in both good and evil. For "Olympic fate" rains down both favorable and adverse influences into the lower realms—favorable, I say, when the highest angel is working, but adverse when he ceases from his work. And this angel, or ethereal wind, is like a vehicle for that supreme one whom he serves; hence Hermes Trismegistus <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic corpus is attributed.</note> said: *In its descent, the mind took on the soul like a garment, because even the soul, being divine, uses the spirit as a vehicle, and the spirit runs through the whole living being.* The Cabalists made the World Soul the angel Metatron <note>A high archangel in Jewish mystical tradition.</note>, arguing from this that the shining form of the world is governed by such an Archangel. Just as particular souls [are governed] by lower angels...

And of this kind are those <term>daemons</term><note>The author uses "daemon" in the classical sense of a mediating spirit or "genius," rather than a "demon" in the modern sense of an evil entity.</note> whom the Egyptians called "stellar," and each of these daemons is also called a <term>genius</term>, because it is a daemon of generation. This genius descends from the arrangement of the world and the circuits of the stars that are involved in generation—determined by much more excellent witnesses—and it primarily takes care of the functions of life. This celestial wind prepares the tabernacle of the heart, and by its breath, it elevates its mass and condenses it into the northern spirit, continually drawing the proper nourishment of life from heaven through inspiration.

Finally, they hold that the third daemon of the newborn is the **elemental** one, which, by the permission of the supreme angel, has care over the elemental members and tends toward their growth and nutrition. Furthermore, unless the mind and its corresponding angel are at work, this spirit draws the soul away from the contemplation of heavenly things toward elemental delights and earthly enticements. It is by a spirit of this kind that the lowest, or natural, vehicles of the seed are inflated, which are condensed into the liver by the blast of a freezing wind. <term>Proclus</term><note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced much of medieval and Renaissance mysticism.</note> is also of this opinion, thinking that *one daemon rules the body, another the soul, and another the mind*. And all the Platonists similarly established three parts in man, which they call the **supreme, middle, and lowest**. By the "supreme," they mean the mind or the illuminated intellect, which Moses called the *breath of life* <note>original: "vitæ spiraculum"</note>, breathed into man by God or by His Spirit. By the "lowest soul," or the lowest elemental spirit, they understood that which is occupied with the flesh and worldly things; and this, Paul calls the *animal man* <note>original: "hominem animalem"; 1 Corinthians 2:14.</note>. The "middle spirit," however, is that ethereal and vital one participating in both extremes and connecting them both together—namely, the mind with the corporeal spirit. From this it follows that it tastes of the nature of both extremes. They conclude, therefore, that just as that highest portion never sins, never consents to evil, and always resists error and encourages the best things, so that lower portion—the animal or carnal soul—is always submerged in evil, sin, and concupiscence, and drags one toward the worst things. Of this, Paul speaks thus: *I see another law in my members, leading me captive into the law of sin.* <note>Romans 7:23.</note> But the middle spirit, since it is free by nature, can adhere to either as it pleases; if it constantly adheres to the superior portion, it is finally united with it and made blessed, until it is taken up to God. But if it adheres to the carnal spirit, it is depraved until it becomes an evil daemon.

The Platonists seem to confirm these preceding opinions. But since we made mention of angels above, I will briefly show what <term>Rabbi Moses</term><note>Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Jewish philosopher.</note> and <term>Rabbi Breseth</term><note>Likely referring to the author of Bereshit Rabbah, a midrashic text on Genesis.</note> think of them. Rabbi Moses calls the **active intellect** an angel, from which forms flow; he also calls it **Metattron** <note>Metatron, the highest angel in Jewish mysticism, often described as the celestial scribe or the "lesser YHWH."</note>, who is the prefect over the universe. By him, all individual human virtues are governed—the animal and vital as well as the natural—which are likewise called angels, and their multitude is infinite. For (says Rabbi Breseth), the Creator daily creates a host of angels, which others call "forms," inasmuch as they are formal substances with which the entire sphere of things that can be generated or corrupted is filled without number. Indeed, the divine poet <term>Hesiod</term> seems to recognize this, speaking in this sense: *Thrice ten thousand are there upon the earth, many enduring immortals, guardians of mortal men for Jove, who indeed watch over both justice and wretched deeds, clothed in air, going everywhere over the earth.* <note>Translated from Hesiod's "Works and Days."</note> Furthermore, the two powers of the will in man are called angels by the wise: that is, the author of good and the author of evil, as Rabbi **Asse** testifies in his *Collection*. And these are Hesiod's "guardians" mentioned before, who in Latin are called spirits, any one of whom is destined for the care of lower affairs.

Furthermore, according to <term>Reuchlin</term><note>Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), a German humanist and pioneer of Christian Kabbalah.</note>, angels or daemons are called "spirits" because they are, as it were, winds. Hence Rabbi **Tedacus Levi**, in his book on the *10 Numerations* <note>Referring to the Sephirot in Kabbalistic thought.</note>, after explaining the four winds (North, South, East, and West), finally writes: *And with those four winds He created four angels, who are set over them by day and by night*, and he concludes that many species are subject to them. Indeed, one reads in the *Gate of Light* <note>original: "Porta lucis", the Latin title for Joseph Gikatilla's "Sha'are Orah," a fundamental Kabbalistic text.</note> that from the earth to the firmament there is no empty space, but everything is full of forms, some of which are pure and capable of grace, and others foul, harmful, and tempting. Joseph Castaliensis also testifies to this. From these things we can gather that the reason for the variety of action in any of the vessels in the seed flows from the various natures of the formal spirits or winds, which nonetheless correspond to each other; and the lower ones obey the higher in the action of life, no differently than elemental daemons obey the celestial, and likewise the celestial obey the super-celestial, all of whom are of the same kingdom and dominion.

For example, the seven spirits who stand before the throne of God are those princes who have dominion over the spirits of the seven Planets, into whom they pour those illuminations which they received immediately from God. These planetary spirits, in turn, rain them down into the crowds of elemental daemons subject to that same Planet, who finally put them into execution by the power of the winds—indeed, in the form of winds. For example, the presiding or ruling Archangel of Saturn is **Sabathiel**, of Jupiter is **Zedekiel**, of Mars is **Samael**, of the Sun is **Michael**, of Venus is **Anael**, of Mercury is **Raphael**, and of the Moon is **Gabriel**. If Michael be the lord of the time, he rains the will of GOD into the Solar spirits at the hour of birth, and again the Solar spirits emit their influences to the Eastern winds or spirits, by whom finally care is taken of the exterior seed, just as the Solar spirit will have care of the life and the ethereal spirit, and Michael himself will be the guardian of the soul, and will have dominion over both the vital spirits (as they descend from the Sun) and the natural or elemental ones (since they breathe from the East, over which quarter of the world and its winds Michael presides). And so it is with the others. From this it is clear that, although human life is said to be a God-like breath, and man is said to be formed by God in the womb, nevertheless God does nothing in these lower things either naturally or miraculously, except—

...whether by the mediation of angels or His formal winds, which is also apparent from this: that although anger, mercy, and the protection of the Israelites in the desert are attributed to Jehovah, it was nevertheless His angel who worked all things—whether for punishment or for mercy and blessing—in the camps of the Israelites. For as Jehovah said: *Behold, I send an angel before you, to keep you in this way, and to bring you into the place which I have prepared; take heed of him and listen to his voice, do not provoke him, for he will not bear your rebellion, because my name is in him.* It is clear, therefore, that where the prince angel acts, there the divine essence is also present; and consequently, God is said to have performed this or that, since God is present by His name both in the execution performed by the angels and in the ordination of the same, decreed in His Archetypal counsel. For an angel is like a mediating power between God and nature, by which operations are performed in things that their own nature could not have done without it. The act of this power is the splendor of the divine will, which drives and agitates the angel (or wind) toward the goal proposed by God, just as a wind is observed to drive a cloud from one quarter of the world to the opposite side.

As for the order of the parts or members arranged and produced in the divine womb by this kind of instinct, and the manner of the inflation of each of them into the human form, there is no need to look to Pagan authors for this, since it is most exactly declared in the Holy Scriptures themselves. Indeed, it was described by the divine spirit in these words, which formed the members of man when none of them yet existed: *Have you not poured me out like milk, and curdled me like cheese? You have clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews; you have granted me life and favor, and your visitation preserves my spirit. But these things you have hidden in your heart; I know that this is with you.* Furthermore, it is said elsewhere: *I will put breath into you and you shall live, and I will lay sinews upon you, and will make flesh grow over you, and cover you with skin, and give you breath so that you may live.*

In these passages of the Holy Bible, we are taught first that God is the author of the human structure. His acting instruments are a double wind or spirit: the first acts toward the completion of the body and its organs, and is created from the angelic nature of the three regions of the world; the last is the God-like breath of life <note>original: "Deiforme vitæ spiraculum"</note>. Hence Job said in the place cited above, after the members of his body were already finished and formed: *You have granted me life and favor.* And Ezekiel, after the completion of the body: *I will give you breath so that you may live.* But in Ezekiel, this sequence is declared even more clearly; for after he had concluded these words: *And as I prophesied, there was a noise, and behold, a shaking, and the bones came together, bone to bone, and behold, the sinews and the flesh came up upon them, and the skin was stretched over them, but there was no breath in them; and the Lord said, "Prophesy to the breath, come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live," and the breath entered into them, and they lived, and stood upon their feet.*

From this it is clear that the spirit of life entered into man—made from muddy seed and adorned with all organs—from the four winds or the power of God filling the whole world, namely after his fabrication. Thus also in the perfection of Adam, it is said that his exterior was first formed by God from the mud of the earth. And Job said: *Remember, I beseech you, that you have made me as the clay.* But then afterward it is said that God breathed into the face of man, and man became a living soul. From this it is evident that the wind, by divine agitation, was involved in the shaping of the seed into the human fabric and image; but in the quickening of the same, the God-like breath was present. This is also clearly declared by the speech of that patient man <note>referring to Job</note>: *There is a spirit in man, but the inspiration of the Almighty gives him understanding.* And elsewhere even better: *The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty has given me life.*

Therefore, by the office of the first spirit, the body or external man with its organs is fabricated, by reason of which man is called "flesh," a "spirit" or "wind" that passes away and does not return. And elsewhere: *What is man that you should acknowledge him, or the son of mortal man that you should take account of him? Man is like a vanity,* etc. And elsewhere: *Naked man came from his mother's womb and naked he shall return thither.* And elsewhere: *Man is miserable and most abject.* And elsewhere: *Man decays like a rotten thing, like a garment eaten by moths.* And: *Man born of woman is of few days and full of trouble.* Similarly, man is elsewhere called weak and of short life. But in respect to the latter spirit, man is said to be created in the image of God; and elsewhere it is asserted that he is a little lower than the angels themselves, and that God has crowned him with glory and honor, and made him lord over the works of His hands, and put all things under his feet. By the power of the former, therefore, He fashioned the members of the body from the male seed by a hidden power or hidden breathing, according to this method:

---

First, therefore, He poured out the hidden and latent form of the external man like milk; that is, He reduced it into a spermatic nature similar to milk. Then He curdled that substance like cheese into a foamy substance, which—with the sinews, veins, and arteries first growing—He finally condensed into flesh and covered it with skin. Then He distinguished and stabilized the fleshy parts and members with bones and ligaments. Finally, when the members of the external man were thus produced, the Lord breathed into this mass the spirit of life, by which man was not only brought back into a living soul, but also, by reason of the inspiration of the Almighty, was endowed with intellect and reason, just as has been confirmed from the places previously brought forth from Holy Scripture.

## CHAPTER VI.

### In which it is declared that sperm is air in a "meteor" (either a small cloud or a dense mist) thickened by two opposite, health-giving winds, and that (contrary to the opinions of some) it is not nourished by menstrual blood in the mother's womb.

<margin>Book on Numbers</margin>
The temperance of the **West Wind** is likened by philosophers to the springtime; for it is temperate and fertile by nature. For this reason, it most easily produces herbs and flowers by its breath, and is thus called <term>Favonius</term> <note>The Roman name for the West wind, associated with "favoring" growth</note> because it favors the life-giving natures of natural things. For this same reason, by its constant breath, all species of animals apply and devote themselves to the generation and procreation of their own kind. Hence, this wind blowing from the western equinox is called <term>Zephyrus</term>, as if one were to say it "brings life and vigor with it." From this, the wind is attributed to the lord of spirits, <term>Raphael</term> (whose name means "Medicine of God"), and among the planets to **Venus**, who is fertile and gracious to vital nature. Furthermore, the **East Wind** (the <term>Subsolanus</term>) is called the wind to which all temperate things are attributed; for its spirit or breath is sweet, pure, subtle, and healthy—especially in the morning hours—since it does not tolerate poisonous spirits. Thus, it blows properly for both bodies and spirits, as we shall discuss more extensively in our treatise on the causes of health. For as <term>Tedacus Levi</term> <note>Likely a reference to a Jewish commentator or Kabbalistic source</note> says, **Michael** (the spirit governing the Eastern winds) belongs to the side of mercy, and the **Sun** (which is his planet) belongs to the side of life. These two opposite winds—merciful and promising for life and generation—are recognized as such not only by the teachers of the Hebrews but even by the most excellent of the Philosophers. These winds, breathing together, act upon the intermediate air—just as the male spirit acts with the female in the womb—to produce the <term>meteor</term> <note>In this context, "meteor" refers to any atmospheric phenomenon like a cloud or mist, not a space rock</note> dedicated to generation, namely the production of the spermatic humor. In this way are produced those yellowish cloudlets (evidence of clear air) which are often driven from the west toward the east and vice-versa by the force of the spirit predominating in the air. For contrary winds blowing together with equal vigor condense the intermediate air into a specific disposition through continuous pressure. However, the nature of the dominant wind will prevail more in that aerial "meteor" than the nature of its opposite. For example: if the West wind blows more strongly, the nature of the cloudlet will be moderately cold and moist in the manner of female sperm (which is the temperament of Venus), and the "meteor" will then migrate toward the East. But if the East wind blows more strongly, the nature of the cloudlet will participate more in the disposition of that wind; thus, the air condensed in that way will be hotter and drier—participating in the life-giving disposition of the Sun—and will be like the male sperm. Yet, the nature of the opposite wind will still hold some dominion within it. Therefore, the "meteor" procreated from the breaths of such healthy winds leads to generation in both the <term>macrocosm</term> (the great world/universe) and the <term>microcosm</term> (the small world/the human body). In this process, the eastern spirit acts as the hidden "active" principle in the seed, and the western spirit as the hidden "passive" principle, while their common womb is the milky or misty air in which the mysteries of these winds are enclosed. From this, in the macrocosm, such cloudlets or mists falling upon the earth provide "sperm" to plants and vegetables, by which they grow and produce their likeness, and their seeds are impregnated for a new generation.

In the microcosm, however, and also in other animals, these kinds of prolific "meteors" are produced most secretly within the bloody or aerial spirit by the breath of these spirits. These "meteors" fall into the microcosmic earth (that is, into the seminal vessels hidden in the viscera) and then leap from them into the female wombs, yearning to procreate their likeness in their own species. For there are two direct winds in heaven that blow for generation, namely these two, insofar as they belong to the side of life and mercy. But the other two direct winds, namely the North and South winds, tend mostly toward corruption (unless they are tempered by other winds), because they belong to the side of severity and disease. Hence, according to Rabbi Tedacus in the place cited above, **Gabriel** presides over the North in the power of judgment and severity, just as **Noriel** or **Uriel** presides over the South. In that southern region, a great demon named <term>Meririm</term> <note>The "Midday Demon" often associated with pestilence</note> is said to rage and seethe, producing almost all corrupt and putrid infirmities. From the heart in man, therefore—as if from the rising Sun—a generative and healthy breath is breathed toward the West (that is, into the seminal vessels). This breath, by its own blowing, condenses the air (the subtle part of the elements) drawn from the whole body into the venous spermatic vessels after it has been inspired by the East wind or the breathing Heart. Thus is produced the "meteor" of generation, for whose coagulation into bone and flesh the North wind's breath is required, by whose blowing...

Once the sperm is enclosed in the womb, it is necessary to understand by what nourishment it is fed so that it may reach the completion of the fetus. However, in the resolution of this doubt, philosophers and some physicians seem to disagree. Some believe that the substance of the retained <term>menstruum</term> <note>menstrual blood</note> concurs to compose the external or bodily part of the offspring; they believe this all the more because menstruation usually ceases in pregnant women. But others reject this reasoning for two reasons: first, because it is not likely that a thing so poisonous as a woman’s menstrual blood could build up flesh so tender and fresh, rather than destroying and corrupting it. For (as Pliny testifies) menstrual fluids are endowed with such malignancy that by their touch alone, nettles dry up, seeds become sterile, mirrors lose their brightness, the edges of knives are dulled, and dogs tasting them become rabid. Therefore, it is not right to believe that the healthy structure of a fetus and its growth could arise from a thing so impure. Second, because (they say) in pregnant women, the heat increases in respect to the living creature existing in generation, and consequently, the menstrual fluids are destroyed and consumed by it. 

However, I believe that the menstrual fluids do not appear at that time because their "subtle" part passes into the increase of the blood, so that the good blood which concurs for the nutrition of the fetus may be continually supplied. Furthermore, a portion of it, separated from its poisonous and earthy dregs through many "siftings," can contribute something to the generation of milk; for in the menstrual blood, there is a portion of good blood mixed with bad and poisonous blood. The fecal or waste parts are indeed expelled and flow out from the woman's body after the cleansing of birth. Nevertheless, physicians admit that the principal nourishment of the fetus is drawn from the liver by means of the umbilical vein. But the Holy Scriptures also teach us this clearly, in which we read: <margin>Wisdom 7:2</margin> *“A man is formed as flesh in his mother’s womb, curdled in blood in the time of ten months from the seed of a man,”* <note>original: "Homo ex vtero matris figuratus est caro tempore decem mensium coagulata cum sanguine ex semine viri"</note> where it does not say that the sperm is curdled into flesh, but the sperm *with* the blood—and not menstrual blood. Indeed, regarding that blood it is written: <margin>Levit. 12:2</margin> *“A woman, when she has brought forth a male child, shall be unclean for seven days.”* And elsewhere: *“she shall remain for thirty days in the purgation of her blood after birth,”* during which time she must not <margin>Lev. 15:20</margin> touch any holy thing, nor come into the sanctuary. Also in the time of her unclean flow or menstruation: namely, when the flow is in her flesh for seven days, let her be in her separation, and whoever touches her shall be unclean until evening. But regarding the "good blood" (which the wise man mentions here), it is understood where it is said that <margin>Genesis 9:4</margin> blood is the seat of souls. Therefore, from this kind of blood mixed with sperm, the substance of the infant is fashioned, according to the sentence of Solomon alleged above.

# CHAPTER VII.
## On the manner of infecting and corrupting sperm, by which purulent Gonorrhea is produced; likewise, that sperm held too long in its vessels sometimes contracts a demonic disposition.

Just as sperm is a most precious thing in its pure and unpolluted nature, insofar as it reaches toward the perfection of a rational creature and proceeds by the natural path of generation; so also, by the contrary path, if it be polluted by a preternatural reason and initiated by a foreign "form" and a pollution contrary to its nature, it does not tend toward generation, but vice versa toward corruption. That is to say, from the "meteorological" middle state, it is driven not toward the goal (generation), but back to the starting point—namely, into that which it was before—by a destructive nature. Thus, the southern spirits prepared for the generation of clouds and rain are hindered in their progress by the strongly resisting northern spirits and are driven back to their windy caves in the southern region. 

And the same reasoning applies to opposites: for if the northern spirits, previously predominating and producing snow and hail, are overcome by an opposite wind now predominating, those <term>meteors</term> <note>In the classical sense, any atmospheric phenomenon like rain or snow.</note> that were on the way to generation—namely, in the progression from the starting point (simple air) to the middle state, and then from the meteorological middle to a perfectly mixed substance—are suddenly dissolved by a southern breath. From the earthy hardness of hail or the dryness of snow, they are first turned into thick air, and then by an East wind they are converted into that thing which they were before; that is, they are led backward from the motion of generation to that of corruption.

From these things which have been said, we have revealed not only the internal active agents of the sperm but also its external passive recipients, which are derived from the purity or subtlety of the elements. We, however, contemplating the supercelestial agents a little more deeply, both in the elements and in the ether, have attempted to explain them—namely, the powers and efficacies of both good and evil angels, who are the intermediate instruments between God and man, or most swift ministers always ready to execute God’s commands upon the creatures of both visible worlds (the celestial and the terrestrial). ## CHAPTER I.

**JUST AS** Phoebus <note>A poetic name for the Sun or Apollo.</note> is observed sitting in the very center of the heavens, shining with golden hair and holding the scepter of the world like a king and Emperor, ruling and governing all things by the breath of his life—for in him, as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD).</note> and many others testify, all the virtues of the celestial bodies reside; indeed, Proclus <note>Another influential Neoplatonist (412–485 AD).</note> did not hesitate to assert that at the sight of the sun, all the powers of all the celestial bodies are gathered into one, which are finally scattered into this lower world through his fiery breaths: so also we see the heart conducting itself in the <term>microcosm</term> <note>The "small world"—a common Renaissance concept that the human body is a miniature reflection of the entire universe (the macrocosm).</note>. Heraclitus seems to explain this comparison to us very clearly, happening upon this discourse when he says: "If you take the sun out of the world, what is our poor body if the soul is missing?" In such a case, no pulsing vein is felt, no judgment remains to be sensed, no vital state exists within it, nor any respiration. For this reason, it has seemed to some—and not without consideration—to call the Sun the "heart of heaven," because just as the living spring and fountainhead of blood is found in the heart, gently moistening and watering the other members of the human body and pouring the act of life everywhere, both upward and downward, so also in the sun is seen the faculty of nourishing and preserving all things, both superior and inferior, as if enclosed in a sanctuary of life. For from the sun, life or <term>innate heat</term> <note>The natural, life-sustaining warmth believed by ancient and medieval doctors to be born with a person and seated in the heart.</note> is breathed into the lower things—and indeed even the higher ones—by means of its light.

This is according to that saying of <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic writings are attributed.</note>: *The spirit, diffused through the veins, arteries, and blood, moves the living creature everywhere; and it sustains the suspended mass of the body.* We see also that as the sun, by its motion and vital breath, inspires and gives life to all things in the visible world, similarly and in equal respect, the heart of man, by its own action through the vital spirit, floods and inspires all parts of the body by means of the arteries. If the sun is the fountainhead of health-giving heat and vital spirits, by a similar relation the Heart is a most overflowing source of innate and beneficial heat. Furthermore, the sun is observed never to cease its natural motion, and the human heart also shows itself constant in its motion—that is, immune from interruption. It is also situated in the middle of the chest no differently than the sun is in the center of the heavens. ## CHAPTER II.

### That the heart is the Eastern region of the microcosm, and how it relates to the East of the macrocosm.

**IN** the first book of this treatise, where we distinguished the microcosm into its quarters in imitation of the macrocosm, and also attributed to each of them its own proper wind or breath, we not unwisely assigned the eastern part to the heart. In the same way, we referred the spermatic vessels and the places adjacent to them to the point opposite the heart, for the reasons we have produced in this third book. Now, we shall begin to declare with clear reasoning in this place how the quarter or region of the microcosm assigned to the heart agrees in all things with the disposition of the worldly East.

First, therefore, from those things related in the preceding chapter, we can gather how great a relation exists between the solar body and that of the animal heart, and how close a friendship and kinship exists between these most principal bodies in both worlds; for the heart is, as it were, the son of the Sun, just as the Sun must be held as the father of the heart in a reciprocal manner. For as the Sun is the source and origin of life in the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>The "great world" or the universe at large.</note>, so also in the microcosm, the gifts of life are observed to gush forth from the sanctuary of the heart. Indeed, we observe the Sun to have its daily rising in the East, which is why that region is attributed by <term>Astrologers</term> <note>In the 17th century, astrology was considered a serious science of celestial influences on biology.</note> to the life of the newborn. For they call the first house of the Hemisphere the "angle of the east"—namely, that place where both the Sun and the remaining planets, rising upon our horizon at the moment of birth, claim for themselves the titles of "lords of the lineage and life."

For the first house, called the <term>Horoscope</term> <note>From the Greek "horoskopos," meaning "watcher of the hour." In this context, it refers specifically to the Ascendant, or the point rising in the East, which was believed to govern physical vitality.</note> (as the whole crowd of Astrologers testifies), signifies the life and body of the newborn, as well as the beginning of life and birth; hence they call it "life itself." To this house they assign <term>triplicities</term> <note>Groups of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element.</note>, and to each of them as many lords. The first lord affirms the life and nature of the newborn—namely, what he will love or what will happen to him at the start of his life; the second lord affirms the strength of the body and the state of life in middle age; and the third lord signifies the end of life.

From this it is evident how great the force of life is in this angle. Therefore, this <term>Cardo</term> <note>A "hinge" or turning point in an astrological chart.</note> or quarter is the fortress of life, the fan of life, from which its soul—namely the solar virtue—is breathed into the hemisphere of the world. Because of this, those well-versed in the mysteries of nature attribute the eastern angle to Michael (who is the Solar Archangel), whose duty is to resist the malice of evil demons and, consequently, to preside diligently and happily over the life and health of creatures, as we shall declare more broadly in the following chapter. 

Thus we see that after the intense darkness of night and the "death" of the hemisphere (or the deprivation of the previous day’s light and life), the Sun, rising as the sanctuary of life with new light, regenerates and revives the worldly spirit which was, as it were, deformed and overwhelmed by shadows. Hence we observe the origin of rising life and light to exist in the angle of the east.

In a clearly similar way, we see in the procreation of man that once the seed is corrupted (or after the loss of the previous seminal form), a new light of life and form usually rises in the dark mass of the fetus, removing its deformity and restoring a new human form. Thus, after the privative "night" in the sperm, the Sun of life rising in the angle of the heart (which is the East) or the "horoscope of the microcosm," strives to produce a new life, a new day, a new form and being, and a new man. From this it is clear that the heart is the beginning of man, the source of life, and the "Sunrise" of the microcosmic day, no differently than the Sun is seen to bring life, light, and a kind of new regeneration to the world from the macrocosmic east.

Conversely, in the region of the world opposite the east, where the sun sets, the hemisphere of the world seems to be "killed" by that setting—that is, it is weighed down by darkness and the deprivation of the daylight form. In the same way, we observe that the life-giving outflow of the heart (full of the rays and spirits of life, and most fit for generation), leaping out from the left chamber of the heart, "sets" into the place opposite it—where the stercoreous <note>Pertaining to excrement or waste; the author is referring to the lower digestive and reproductive organs.</note> and dark viscera (compared to the Western earth) are placed by nature—namely, into the spermatic vessels, and then it is cast down into the womb. Then it is likened to the setting of the Sun. This is why in several places in Holy Scripture, the grave is compared to the abyss and the lodging-place of hell. For we notice that a grain of wheat must be cast into the earth and die in its shallow depths before its spirit can rise again to life. In like manner, we say that the rising of the celestial sun in the world creates, as it were, a regeneration of a new day; the rising of the animal sun from the sperm in the womb, and the vegetable sun in the earth, also make a new day or life. Thus, this axiom of the Philosophers is best verified here: *the corruption of one is the generation of another, and consequently, generation follows corruption.* The reason for these opposite mutations in the world is that action and resistance which occurs between form and matter, so that matter, having entire dominion over the form...

# CHAPTER III.

->That the breath of life proceeds from the east in both the macrocosm and microcosm, and concerning the metaphysical reason for the life and souls of both worlds.<-

Since the heart is therefore the eastern region of the microcosm, no differently than the place of the sun's rising—the eastern angle called the <term>horoscopus</term> <note>The "ascendant" or rising point in an astrological chart, symbolizing birth and beginnings.</note>—it follows that a similar wind blows from such a pivot in man. And this wind breathes the soul of life into the entire human spirit, no differently than that macrocosmic wind of life is said to give motion to the spirit, or the air, or the human wind. Whence the Wise Man says that after the sun has set, it pants again for its place where it may rise, hastens to the south, and circles the North; from which words it is clear that the Sun—in which (according to the Platonists) the soul of the world is situated (and even the Psalmist says that God has placed His Tabernacle in the Sun)—is the principal mover and stirrer of the winds; and hence the Wise Man continues by joining this discourse 
<margin>Ecclesiastes 1:4</margin>
to the preceding: *The air (or as Jerome interprets it, the spirit) hastens, going round in its conversion, and according to its circuits the air returns,* which Pagninus interprets thus: *continually going round, the wind proceeds, and to its circuits the wind returns.* Jerome says: *The spirit proceeds, surveying its circuit, and returns into its circles:* by which speech the Wise Man argues clearly enough that the disposition of the air depends on the solar motion, as its rays are like a soul to it. Whence the air is naturally moved in no other way than by the motion of the sun, by whose action it is agitated in a circular motion. Hence it is that the winds are called the children of the Titans, Astraea, and Aurora, insofar as they are generated by the heat of the Sun, as Aristotle says, which renders the air subtle and thin, especially at the Dawn <note>original: "Aurora"</note>. But they are said to obey the commands of Juno insofar as they do not blow except in the air, which is called Juno <note>In classical mythology and alchemy, Juno often represents the element of Air.</note>. By equal reasoning, we see the spirit of life blow from the east of the microcosm—that is, from the chamber of the heart as if from the chest of the microcosmic <term>Aeolus</term> <note>The Greek god of the winds.</note>—and by its breath, it carries all the airy spirit of the blood with it as if in a whirl; by the mediation of its rays, that spirit lives, and by the life-giving motion, both northern and southern winds (that is, those of the spleen and liver), as well as western winds, are stirred in the microcosm. For as was said in the speech of the Wise Man above: 
<margin>Ecclesiastes 1:4</margin>
*The sun rises, and after it has set it pants again for its place where it may rise, hastens to the south and circles the north, the air hastens in its conversion,* etc. So also in the microcosm, in imitation of the <term>macrocosm</term>, we can say: the rising of the life-giving sun or vital heat, after it has set into the spermatic vessels, and then afterwards descended below into the womb or the south of the earth, it pants again for a new rising, as it were, and hastens through the branches of the aorta to the hepatic <gloss>liver-related</gloss> south and the splenic <gloss>spleen-related</gloss> north, and excites various breaths in them. For since the flame of the heart is the offspring of the sun and its true son (whence the heart is called the seat of the human soul, as the Sun is the seat of the world's soul; and that soul in the heart is called "natural fire" by Zeno and "celestial fire" by Prometheus, enriching man with life), it follows that it is moved by the motion of the sun, seeing as it is a ray of the same, which cannot be separated from it; thus it happens that the part is moved by the motion of the whole. And hence it was that <term>Mercurius Trismegistus</term> repeatedly called man the son of the world, and consequently his heart the son of the Sun, as by the heart's heat of internal light he is the son of the Sun, or the soul of the world. Whence, as from the center of the worldly Sun the seeds of life and life-giving light are ejaculated into the worldly spirit (which are also drawn in by the heart through the mediation of breathing), so also from the center of the microcosmic sun or the soul of the heart, vital heat is sown and scattered everywhere in the microcosmic spirit (which is also derived from the worldly air), which the royal prophet also 
<margin>Psalms 4:23 <note>Likely intended as Proverbs 4:23.</note></margin>
confesses in express words in this manner: *Guard your heart above all observation, because from it proceed the actions of life.*

But to approach the internal or metaphysical soul of the Eastern wind of both the macrocosm and microcosm, and its nature in both the sun and the heart: we have said that God originally breathed life into His creatures through His spirit, and this by the mediation of His angels, who are His fiery ministers, whose exterior or manifest part is air or wind, but whose interior is divine fire; whence it is written, *the name of Jehovah was in the angel 
<margin>Exodus 23</margin>
<margin>Psalms 103:4</margin>
whom God sent before the Israelites.* Hence therefore (says David), *Who makes your angels winds, and your ministers a burning fire, doing your pleasure;* we have also declared elsewhere that some angels have the care of life, others of the body, etc. But because it is known to all that the sun of the world is the fountain and origin of life, let us see, I pray, which angel presides over it, what his nature might be, and whether he be a Prince spirit having dominion over the breaths, or over life...
