### On the Mystical Anatomy of the Heart.

...whether he presides over worldly life or not, so that by this path we may come to the most intimate and more formal mystery of life, by which at last we may approach the first spirit of all things and the knowledge of the Lord of lords. <margin>Pico della Mirandola, *On Astrology*, Book 4, Chapter 4.</margin> As Pico della Mirandola says:
> *Human affairs are not ordered by the mystery of bodies, but of angels, who, being intermediate in nature and dignity between us and God, are governed [by Him]; therefore, when you descend from God to the earth, descend through the heavens; when you descend from God to men, descend through the angels.*

<margin>Reuchlin, *On the Kabbalah*.</margin> And all the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note>, and indeed the Rabbis more skilled in the Kabbalah <note>A tradition of Jewish mysticism.</note>, acknowledge that an angel is like a mediating power between God and nature, through which operations are performed in lower things. And elsewhere they affirm that all lower things are representative of higher things, and as it is done below, so it is also done above; and in this all Kabbalists agree. Therefore, in our inquiry we proceed thus: Rabbi Moses <note>Referring to Moses Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> says that the "active intellect" into which forms flow is an angel set over the universe, who is called **Metatron** <note>Metatron is a high-ranking angel in mystical Judaism, often called the "Prince of the Countenance."</note>, by whom all individual human virtues—both vital and natural—are governed. These are likewise called "angels," the multitude of which is infinite to us. And Rabbi Bereshit says that the Creator daily creates a "heaven of angels," whom others call "forms," as they are formal substances with which the entire sphere of things that can be generated or corrupted is filled beyond number. The doctors of the Hebrews made this prince-angel, Metatron, the **Soul of the World** <note>original: *anima mundi*</note>, about which we have treated abundantly in our Kabbalistic treatise. And more secret theologians have affirmed this to be the Archangel Michael, inasmuch as the guardianship of the Sun is assigned to him, which is the fountain of life and of living souls. And it is from this that all the Platonists said that the Soul of the World was in the Sun, and the Holy Scriptures say that **GOD** (who is the fountain of life and light) *placed His Tabernacle in the Sun*, and that in the Messiah or the Word (which is the light of the world) there was life. Michael, therefore, or Metatron (that is, the Soul of the World), is the internal intelligence or soul (in which, as it is written, is the name of God) moving, governing, and presiding over the Sun; hence it is that the lives of the world and its creatures are assigned to him. From this, therefore, the wise, agreeing with the Holy Scriptures, said that Michael with his angels and ministers fought for the souls of all against the ancient serpent: <margin>Archangelus [of Borgonovo] on the Kabbalah.</margin> And elsewhere it is said that he is the High Priest in heaven, offering rational souls to God; and again, he is handed down as the prince of the host of Christ, appointed over all souls to be received; he weighs them not with physical scales or balances, but with a balance possessing a symbolic measure. This, then, is that Michael who (witnessed by Archangelus in the Kabbalah) holds the primacy among the angels standing in the tribunal of divine justice. For as there are four evil angels who, in the army of Satan, carry the widest sails of the avenger—namely, Samael, Azazel, Azael, and Mahazael <margin>Reuchlin, *On the Kabbalah*.</margin>—so also there are four standard-bearers in the army of God: Michael, Gabriel, Uriel, and Raphael. Of these, Michael is the Prince; hence the Kabbalah says Gabriel spoke to Daniel: <margin>Daniel [10:13].</margin> *Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me.* Those more secret in theology also made him the Angel of Christ. <margin>Apocalypse 1.</margin> Whence it is written that this is the angel who appeared to John, *whose eyes were like a flame of fire, and his voice like the voice of many waters, who held seven stars in his right hand, and whose face shone like the Sun in its strength.* And from this it is declared that this is the internal spirit of the sun, in which consists the life and light of the seven planets, which are signified by the seven stars in his hand; hence it is said that he stood in the midst of seven golden candlesticks, denoting that he is that spirit in whom the name of God is written, who placed his tabernacle in the center of the sun—that is, in the midst of the planets. Therefore, with the wise, we call the Angel the internal fiery Word or name of **JEHOVAH**, which was that holy emanation or fiery power of the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, considered too sacred to pronounce.</note> which first shone out of the darkness—that is, that Wisdom created before all things, which has power over all other angels, and from which light and life were first imparted to the worldly spirit. This is that highest Archangel whom the spirits or angels who preside over the winds obey, no differently than the remaining stars are subjected to the command of the Sun’s exuberant glory and excellence. <margin>Apocalypse 7:1.</margin> Whence it is written of him in the Apocalypse:
> *I saw four angels standing on the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds of the earth, that they should not blow on the earth, nor on the sea, nor on any tree. And I saw another angel ascending from the east, having the seal of the living God; and he cried with a loud voice to the four angels of the earth, to whom it was given to hurt the earth and the sea, saying: Do not hurt the earth, or the sea, or the trees, until we have marked the servants of our God on their foreheads.*

From which it is clear that this was the Prince of the angels, insofar as he commanded them, and they in turn obeyed him. Furthermore, he seems to be that Archangel Michael who has dominion over the solar body; indeed, he is, as it were, its soul. <margin>Apocalypse 1:16.</margin> Whence John said: *His face shone like the Sun in its strength*; and this all the more because he is said to have ascended from the rising of the sun <note>original: *ab ortu solis*</note>, in which corner or pivot of the world Michael has his command. Finally, we can conclude from this place that it is in his power to permit the malignant angels, by means of the winds, to bring harm to the earth and to men, and again, at his pleasure, to send forth or recall and restrain the powers of those angels for the preservation and natural health of the air, the earth, and its creatures. Hence, those more skilled in secret theology hold that Michael is that great High Priest of heaven, sacrificing in the upper world, who presents the stainless souls <note>original: *animal* — here meaning the "living breath" or vital soul of a person.</note> of men to the blessed God, and subjects those who are unclean and burdened with vices to the devil. Following this pattern, the high priest in the lower world (as we have in Leviticus) is commanded to offer clean and innocent animals to God, but to deliver those burdened with crimes and a weight of harms to Satan. For in this way the Prince, although most inclined toward doing good and toward mercy, is nevertheless declared by God Himself to punish sins in a speech of this kind: <margin>Exodus 23:20.</margin>
> *Behold, I send an angel before you to keep you in the way, and to bring you into the place which I have prepared. Beware of his face, and listen to his voice; do not provoke him, for he will not bear your rebellion, because my name is in him.*

The Kabbalists affirm that this Angel was the tutor of Moses, and they assertively conclude that he is Metatron or Michael. And hence it is that winds of this kind are observed to be so healthy; regarding these, and especially the Eastern wind, it is said that under the sun, by reason of its innate moist and warm temperament (which is most similar to life), it renders waters clear and pure and of good taste, purifies the air, and makes it healthy and serene, preserves the body in health, and renders the spirit of the body like the air of the greater world <note>The "greater world" is the Macrocosm, or the universe itself.</note>—namely, serene, healthy, and subtle; for by its blowing, it makes the air pleasing with forms that are good and necessary for life.

The breath of Michael is therefore (which is nothing other than the solar spirit) benevolent toward life, as it disperses "solar seeds" everywhere through the aerial spirit. By these seeds, the lives of creatures are nourished through the path of inspiration <note>Literally "breathing in."</note>, and by the virtue of this cycle, the wicked angels cease from their evil breaths or winds, with which they infect the air to the ruin and destruction of life, as is declared from the passage cited above from the Book of Revelation. But if it should please the pleasure of the Supreme Spirit to chastise a creature in His anger for sins, then this good angel ceases his benevolent breathings and gives place to the avengers, who, dispersing themselves in the air, infect it. Whether by harming the trees or the fruits and cattle, they bring about famine; or by corrupting the air, the cattle, or the nutrients, they disseminate plague everywhere; or by horrendous storms on both land and sea, they destroy those who are forsaken.

But indeed, Michael, in whom is the Name of God and to whom the seal of the living God is committed, cries out to these infesting demons (as is declared in the passage cited above from Revelation): *Do not harm the earth, nor the sea, nor the trees, until we have marked the servants of our God on their foreheads.* <note>original: "Nolite nocere nec terræ, nec mari, nec arboribus, quouſq; ſignemus ſeruo. Dei noſtri in frontibus eorum." - Revelation 7:3.</note> From this it happens that in a plague, not all are destined for death and destruction, just as Lot with his faithful ones was preserved from the sulfurous storm among the others of Sodom and Gomorrah.

We conclude, therefore, that the Sun is the region of the "Eastern Microcosm" <note>The "Microcosm" refers to the human being as a reflection of the universe; the "Eastern" part refers to the heart/vital center.</note> because it is under the care and protection of the Archangel Michael. It is in his protection because it is the sanctuary of the microcosmic life which rains down from the Sun. The soul of the world, dwelling in the Sun, is the agent that pours down the seeds of life, to which (as is declared) the Eastern region and its wind are subject. Whence, just as a great consensus is observed between the heart and the Sun—since both are the fountains of life and the receptacles of the soul of each world (though the heart's life arises from the Sun's, since the Microcosm is the son of the Macrocosm)—it is necessary that the fiery spirit which inhabits the heart should flow from the breathing of Michael. For he is the fountain of worldly life, in whom the Word of God is inscribed, which is the true light of the world, first shining forth from the Father who lurks in darkness, and informing all things with the benefit of life; regarding which we have dealt abundantly in our metaphysical and Kabbalistic discourse.

## CHAPTER IV.
### *Of the matter or substance of human life: what it is, where it arises, and how it is constantly introduced into the left chamber of the heart for the sustenance of life, and there works by natural chemistry.*

Now, indeed, after we have spoken of the metaphysical act or first origin of the life-giving substance, it remains for us to delineate the essence of life itself and its hidden substance, insofar as it exists in the universality of things. That is, we must demonstrate the subject of that occult and invisible nature which is the beginning <margin>Aristotle, Physics Book 2.</margin> and the food of the life of creatures, by whose succession and fulfillment the life of every living thing is continued. **Aristotle** calls this kind of nature "the principle and cause of motion and rest in a natural thing, in which it exists primarily and by itself, and not by accident." But <margin>Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods, Book 2.</margin> **Cicero** defines it as "a certain force of motion necessarily moving in bodies." Others have called it a certain hidden force, not sensible to the touch but to the intellect, so instilled by God that it supplies the essence and any natural powers to every natural thing—namely element, animal, vegetable, and mineral.

But indeed, the true Philosophers, more certain in the mystical anatomy of natural <margin>The Art of Chemistry, Chapter 4.</margin> things, are accustomed to express the nature of this life-giving substance with a higher and clearer style, writing that it is a certain infinite force, procreating like from like, generating, increasing, and nourishing all things; the bond of the elements, the virtue of mixing, which effects the mixtures of elements in any thing of this sublunary world and imprints the form appropriate to its species, through which one thing in the kingdoms of nature is distinguished and separated from another. Therefore, it is said to have the names of all things within itself. It is of no color, and yet is a participant and shaper of all colors; of no weight or quality, yet the fertile mother of all qualities and things. Indeed, this kind of nature is so wonderful that the ancients hesitated over this: Whether God is Nature, or Nature is God.

Whence they concluded: that God is **Naturing Nature** <note>original: "Natura naturans" - the creative power of God acting within the world.</note>, that is, uncreated light, in which is life; and nature is not God, which they therefore called **Natured Nature** <note>original: "Natura naturata" - the created world or the physical laws of nature.</note> or created, by which they understood the moist spirit which exists by means of its uncreated light. Just as we said in our preceding treatise on sperm—that it is created from the seed as a celestial form and from the sperm as an elementary substance—so also we say that the internal part of life-giving nature is pure celestial fire, which is the throne of uncreated light; but its external part is the ethereal spirit, which is the dwelling place of the uncreated spirit; and the sublunary air is the common vehicle for both.

Hence it was that the ancients said, "Nature is God, and God is Nature," namely because God <margin>Pimander, 3.</margin> is within the moist nature, which He serves in place of life. Whence **Mercurius Trismegistus** affirmed that Nature consists in the divinity itself. And <margin>Pimander, 1.</margin> elsewhere he says that the Word cherishes the moist nature. This does not seem to differ at all from the sense of Holy Scripture, in which we find:

### On the Mystical Anatomy of the Heart.

*By the word of the Lord were the heavens established* <note>Original: "Quod verbo Dei firmati essent cæli." A reference to Psalm 33:6.</note>, *(that is, the structure of the moist spirit) and all their powers by the spirit from his mouth.* From these words it is clear enough that every form and every soul is derived from the Holy Spirit. Was it not also said in the construction of the world, that *the spirit of God moved over the waters* <note>Original: "spiritus Dei ferebatur super aquas." Genesis 1:2.</note>, (that is, over the moist spirit, imparting to it a fiery vigor), from which we see that the form of the primordial world-spirit emanates from the radiation of the divine spirit, by whose presence it was created. And so, the moist nature is called a "creature," but the primary informing form is the luminous power of the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note>, which the Kabbalists and Hebrew Doctors call the angel <term>Metattron</term> (whom they called the Soul of the World). In him, the name of <term>Jehovah</term> exists; that is, his Word, which is uncreated light.
<margin>Exodus 23.</margin>
And hence it is that in many places in the Holy Bible, we see an angel sometimes called "Jehovah"—namely, in respect to his uncreated form—and sometimes called by the name "angel," in respect to his external part, which is a created spirit. For this reason, <term>Rabbi Breseth</term> <note>Likely referring to the author of a commentary on *Bereshit* (Genesis).</note> called all forms floating in the air "angels," insofar as they receive a luminous life immediately from God in the manner of angels, yet they contract their external nature from the moist celestial nature. Hence it was that the philosophers established two species of nature: namely, the material, which they call the passive principle of motion, because it allows itself to be informed; and this is what <term>Merc. Trismeg.</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the *Hermetica*.</note> understands by the "moist nature." The other is the formal nature, which they recognize as more noble, as it informs the passive nature. Whence they called it the active principle, and this is the same as what <term>Merc. Trismeg.</term> understood by "the Word standing by the moist nature," which cherished that passive nature. Is this not the same thing that Saint Peter seems to hint at in his second and third chapters, where he says that *the heaven and earth were made out of water and through water by means of the Word*? And Saint John says:
<margin>By John 1.</margin>
*Through it all things were made, and without it nothing was made that was made.* In this active principle, therefore, is the presence of the Word or the divine spirit, which we signified above through the internal aspect of the angel Michael or Metattron. Hence <term>Merc. Trismeg.</term>
<margin>Pimander 1.</margin>
says that the Father of all, being Mind, Life, and Splendor, brought forth Man like unto himself; and from Saint John
<margin>John 4.</margin>
we receive that *Life is from Christ.* And the same Mercurius says, *The Soul is in the body, the Mind in the soul, and in the mind the
<margin>Pimander 12.</margin>
Word. Indeed, he asserted God to be their father.* From which he concludes, *that the Word is the image of God, the Mind the image of the Word, the Soul the image of the Mind, the Spirit the image of the Soul, and the Body the image of the Spirit itself.* It follows, therefore, that the purest portion of matter is air; of air, the soul; of the soul, the mind; and finally of the mind, God. Whence *God is centered around all things, the mind around the soul, the soul around the air, and the air around matter.* Thus he spoke. From these things it seems clearly explained that the celestial nature is the vehicle of the Word, just as the air is the receptacle of the celestial nature, by means of which it is introduced into the body, where it serves both for vivification and for generation.

We conclude, therefore, that the portion of nature which is called passive or moist is the celestial spirit, which Physicians call by another name, the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>Original: "humidum radicale." The essential life-fluid of an organism.</note>; but the divine fire acting upon it they have called the <term>innate heat</term> <note>Original: "calidum innatum." The vital warmth inherent in living things.</note> and the invisible fire, from which <term>Zoroaster</term> and <term>Heraclitus of Ephesus</term> taught that all things were generated. And this fire is the efficacy of the breath of life, which God is said to have breathed into created things when it was said at the birth of the world, *increase and multiply.* By the power of this breath, all things multiply themselves. But truly, because God *placed his tabernacle in the Sun,* according to the sentiment of the royal Psalmist <note>Psalm 19:4.</note>; (for there is nothing in the circle of the firmament that presents a greater likeness of God than the glorious light of the sun, since any thing claims for itself as much of God as it has light); therefore the Philosophers concluded that the Soul of the World was located in the Sun—which Soul the Kabbalists understood (as explained above) through the angel Metattron or Michael, the presiding governor of the Sun. Therefore, from the solar treasury <note>Original: "myrothecio." Literally a scent-box or storehouse of ointments, here meaning a divine treasury.</note>, by the most occult operation of Michael, such sparks or "Phœbean seeds" are daily disseminated into this lower world through the fiery breaths of the Sun. These are emitted from the inner vessels of the sun—like the sperm of a male from the seminal vessels—into the worldly womb, namely the air. In the moment of emission, they mix with the moist nature of the ether, or the passive sperm, no differently than the sperm of the male uses that of the female as a vehicle. Whence it is brilliantly explained by the wise that the air is everywhere filled with these solar seeds, like a great sea filled with tiny little fish.

Now, indeed, we must declare how these solar seeds are attracted into the human body, by means of which man lives; and it is said by the Wise Man that *the Sun and man generate man.* This invisible fire, therefore—this active nature, imbueing all paths, making all things sprout and vegetate, swimming in its nearest and most worthy spirit—and again, both of these having fallen from heaven into the sublunary spirit or air (that is, into their general vehicle), they are carried here and there by the breath of the Eastern wind, present to all things, nourishing all things, and intoxicating them as if with the nectar of life. Thus we have God everywhere present and assisting in the heavens and on the earth; sitting, namely, on the highest and deepest throne and tribunal of his handmaid, Nature, and assisting all. Thus we draw in our daily bread, thus the blessing of the Word, thus the food of life daily. For since, according to that axiom of <term>Parmenides</term>, *nature rejoices in nature,* the virtue of life situated in the center of the heart yearns to attract its like to itself by a certain magnetic force. Hence it is that the author, a most profound inspector into the mysteries of nature, falls into this admirable sentiment: *O Nature, multiplying the natures of celestial truth by the nod of God.* And again: *O strong Nature, nature conquering and overcoming, and making her own natures to rejoice.* This is that special and spiritual nature to which God gave power over the violence of fire, etc. By which he seems to hint that, by means of this celestial nature, the vital spirit and the flame enclosed within it are increased and multiplied, since by its power not only life, but also the fruit of generation is produced unto infinity. Nay, truly greater mysteries are revealed in the union of the fire of human life (the <term>microcosmic</term> nature) with the celestial fire (the active nature of the <term>macrocosm</term>), since by a bond of this kind the entire nature of the world has communication with that of man, by means of which they are able to perform stupendous things in <term>natural magic</term>. Moreover, the reason by which the appetite of human life is fulfilled in the attraction of its like—namely, the worldly nature—is the heart, which through its parts, both simple and organic, [is able] to work...

...is accustomed to being thinned. For it utilizes fibers of all kinds: by the contraction of the straight fibers and the dilation of the oblique and transverse ones, the heart draws the celestial air—the food of life—to itself from the lungs through the <term>venous artery</term> <note>original: "arteriam venosam." In pre-Harvey anatomy, this refers to the pulmonary vein, which was thought to carry air/spirit from the lungs to the heart.</note> and its branches. It then drives this air into its left ventricle. This air, along with its celestial treasure and clothed in divinity, is introduced through the two <term>mitral valves</term> (which open inward and close outward). By the chemistry of nature, it is prepared so that its impure and smoky part is separated from the subtle part. The gross substance that was first introduced by inhaling is then expelled by exhaling along the same path. 

This type of separation happens in the same way that those skilled in chemistry extract oil or essence from plants: namely, by means of a cooling vessel, in which the pure oil is revealed within a purer portion of water, while the coarser portion of water is rejected as useless. Or rather, it is like the essence of spices extracted by means of water is separated from its surplus watery medium or vehicle in a <term>bain-marie</term> <note>original: "Balneo Mariae." A "Mary’s Bath" or water bath used in alchemy for gentle heating.</note>. This cooling vessel or lukewarm bath is the Pericardium itself, a portion of which is always filled with water. In this water floats the depths of the heart, which acts as a "natural <term>alembic</term>" <note>An alchemical still used for distilling liquids.</note> in which this extraction is perfected. 

The subtle portion of the air serves as a vehicle for the fiery spirit of heaven (which is the matter of life), just as that spirit is the receptacle of reason, and reason is the receptacle of the mind. This is confirmed by the discourse of <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the "Hermetica," foundational texts for alchemy and Western esotericism.</note>: 
<margin>Pimander, 10.</margin>
*Mind is in reason, reason is in the soul, the soul is in the spirit (or thin air), and the spirit is in the body. The spirit, diffused through the arteries and the blood, moves the living creature in every part;* that is, by means of the celestial fire by which it is driven and stirred. And elsewhere he says that God is occupied with all things, the mind with the soul, the soul with the air, and the air with matter. 

Therefore, once this preparation is made—namely, by separating the gross from the subtle so that the internal agent may act and move more freely in its own spirit—it is collected and purified in the sanctuary of the heart. Through the other three <term>semilunar valves</term> (which open outward but close inward), it is placed into the casing of the aorta or "great artery" (which is the sanctuary of life). From there, it is dispersed everywhere through the entire body to perfectly perform the functions of life and generation. And from this most essential substance the "internal man" is fabricated, just as the "external man" is made from the subtle part of the four elements, as was explained more than enough in our treatise on the seed.

## CHAPTER V.

->How there are three motions or actions of the heart, which correspond to the three regions of the macrocosm.<-

<margin>Galen, On the Affected Places, section 5. On the Difference of Symptoms. Avicenna, first book, first doctrine, 6.</margin>
Just as three properties are counted in the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>The "great world" or the universe.</note> according to its three regions—namely, the **angelic**, which is to understand and act according to the pleasure of the divine mind; the **celestial**, which, by God’s command, grants the power of living to creatures; and the **elemental**, in which simple bodies are disposed by divine order—so also we observe in the <term>microcosm</term> <note>The "little world," referring to the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note> a threefold action corresponding to those three regions of the world. These are: the **intellectual** (which Physicians also call "animal") corresponding to the angelic heaven; the **vital**, corresponding to the ethereal heaven; and the **natural**, corresponding to the sublunary or elemental region. 

Truly, however, both Physicians and Philosophers have restricted these three actions (in both the macrocosm and microcosm) into a twofold property. That which pertains to the highest region of either world they have called **voluntary**; but the lower part (which involves both the vital/celestial region and the natural/elemental region in both worlds) they have named **involuntary**. 

From this, it is right to conclude in the first place that just as God, through the mediation of angels, acts upon the heavens and the elements originally and according to His will—while those things, whether they will or not (that is, involuntarily), are forced to receive the acts ordained by God and move according to them—so also those things which are ordained and acted upon by the supreme mind of the microcosm in its highest region are called **voluntary**. This is because they proceed from the beginning and from the "first act," and consequently are not involuntary, since nothing existed before them. From this it follows that there is nothing that can compel divine actions. Hence they are concluded to be voluntary and not involuntary. 

Such, therefore, are the supracelestial and divine actions in the macrocosm, and such are those intellectual and animal actions derived from the mind in the microcosm: namely, voluntary and not coerced. For thus we see the <term>First Mover</term> <note>original: "primum mobile." The outermost sphere of the universe in Ptolemaic astronomy, which moves all other spheres.</note> situated at the summit of the natural macrocosm, to which "will" is attributed, as it is moved according to the divine will through the mediation of His ministers. Yet all creatures of the ethereal heaven are revolved by a violent and involuntary motion by this same will; and again, the elements and things made of elements are snatched up by the motion of the celestial bodies. 

Hence, both the motion and action of the celestial and elemental things are snatched and carried along by the voluntary motion of the First Mover; for this reason, their motion and action is called involuntary. By a similar reasoning, Physicians and Philosophers have observed that the vital and natural actions in man receive their strength from the motion and summons of the intellect, and by the power of the mind's motion, they are twisted and stirred whether they will or not. From this they concluded that such actions are voluntary <note>note: the author appears to be arguing that while these lower functions seem involuntary to our conscious self, they are driven by the "voluntary" higher mind/will of the soul.</note>, as they are summoned not by their own proper motion, but rather by a hidden and excited motion, no differently than in the macrocosm the stars and elements are said to be moved and acted upon by their own intelligences, whose internal act or First Mover is God.

From this, therefore, the answer is given (unless I am mistaken) to that doubt debated among the leaders of physicians and philosophers: namely, whether the brain or the heart is to be preferred in generation. In this, Aristotle and the rest of the Peripatetic school strongly defend the idea that the heart holds the first place in generation. To them is opposed Hippocrates, asserting that the brain is the first member in generation; he seems to support this opinion with a certain experiment, because he observed that the head of a chick first appeared in the egg. And Isaac <note>likely Isaac Judaeus, a 10th-century physician/philosopher.</note> seems to agree with this opinion of Hippocrates, insofar as he thought man was like an inverted tree, and consequently the brain was most like its root. But we shall approach this opinion of Hippocrates therefore...

# On the Mystical Anatomy of the Heart.

<margin>fides [faith]</margin>

...therefore it is established, because it is certainly beyond question that the principle must be placed before the thing originated in time. Now, the brain is the receptacle of voluntary action, which does not precede involuntary action (such as that of the heart) in any other way than God precedes the creature, or the first act and motion precede secondary acts and motions. From the preceding will, therefore, all voluntary actions proceed, inasmuch as they are compelled to move at the instance of that preceding will. But voluntary motion descends from the brain and, through involuntary motion, causes the heart and liver to move regarding their functions, not unlike how the lower spheres are accustomed to be moved or turned by a quasi-involuntary motion from the East to the West according to the motion of the <term>Primum Mobile</term> <note>The "First Moved" sphere in Aristotelian astronomy, which was believed to drive the rotation of all other celestial spheres.</note> (to which the brain is compared). But let us return to the matter at hand.

<margin>Avicenna, *On Medicines of the Heart*, ch. 7.</margin>
They have established that this involuntary action in the heart (which they call "vital") consists of a threefold motion, corresponding to the three kingdoms or heavens of the greater world <note>The "Greater World" refers to the Macrocosm or the Universe.</note>. The first of these consists only in the **dilation** of the heart; in this action, the spirit in the heart is affected by good passions, such as joy, hope, and others. These types of sympathetic passions, full of pleasure, tend toward the <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>The highest, brightest heaven, believed to be the dwelling place of God and pure light.</note> of the microcosm—that is, the intellect. The last motion consists in the opposite act, namely, in **contraction** alone; in this action, the spirits destined for life are disturbed by malignant passions, namely, fear, sadness, and so on. Such antipathetic passions, burdened with vexations, regard the elementary heaven of the microcosm with dark mutations. The middle motion, however, consists between these two extremes, in both contraction and dilation, and its action participates in both extremes. For by dilation, the heart draws the food of its life from the mind, just as the Sun draws from the Word; and by contraction, it disperses that food to the lower parts. Therefore, through <term>diastole</term> <note>The phase of the heartbeat when the heart muscle relaxes and allows the chambers to fill with blood.</note>, it draws the benevolence of life from God by dilating itself, and through <term>systole</term> <note>The phase of the heartbeat when the heart muscle contracts and pumps blood from the chambers into the arteries.</note>, it communicates that life to the lower and natural parts by contracting itself. But we shall treat these matters more extensively in the following chapter, God willing.

### CHAPTER VI.
### On the mysteries of the involuntary actions in the heart, and how we can elicit from them the triple angel of man and their nature.

The mysteries of the involuntary actions of the heart are wonderful if we explore the matter a little more accurately and to its very core. For if, in the first place, we contemplate only the disposition of the heart to dilate, we shall perceive from the effect that it is occupied solely with super-celestial happiness, since through its mediation, the spiritual eyes (as it were) of the heart are opened. The heart (I say)—or rather the spiritual center of the heart—looking away from the darkness by its dilation, rejoices in a super-celestial vision. It exults upward by speculating upon the divine Idea of the Divine Mind; and by such contemplation, it draws the whole of human life from the lower things to the higher. Thus, the whole man is snatched from the cares of the <term>cacodemon</term> <note>An evil spirit or "bad daimon."</note> toward the felicity of the good angel and is lifted on high. It was by means of this kind of cardiac action that Saints John and Paul were snatched even into the third heaven, where they confess they saw things by no means to be revealed to the world. 

For in the spacious and sole dilation of the heart, the celestial spirits of life enclosed in the heart seek their freedom; they strive to visit their celestial brothers wandering everywhere in the air. In their light, they behold not only the source of the soul, but also the Mind within it, and in the Mind the Word, and in the Word and through the Word, God the Father, surrounded on all sides by a choir of Graces and the service of archangels—and they are ravished by that sight. This also seems to be confirmed by these words of the divine Synesius, speaking of the Mind: <margin>Synesius, *Hymn 1*, Ibid.</margin> *Yet there is, there is some light within closed eyes; there is also in those who have fallen down here a certain power calling them back to heaven, when, having emerged from the waves by force, they enter the holy place; they go to the palace of the Parent. Blessed is he who, after labors, after bitter earthly cares, having entered the paths of the mind, has seen the depth shining with divine light.*

And elsewhere: *Having conceived suppliant prayers from the perennial fountain of good things, ascend to the Parent; do not delay, leaving the earthly earth behind, for soon, joined with the Father, a goddess in God, you shall exult.* Indeed, this power of dilating the heart seems to be proven by its effect, since through it, good and delightful passions are introduced to the soul by reason of that hidden vision tending toward joy and beatitude. Although this cannot be discerned by a man seeing spiritually because of the "shadow-covering" of his flesh, yet his internal spirit seems to exult at the sight. From this it happens that joy, hope, confidence, love, mercy, and humanity follow this action of the heart—actions which are pious, placid, and closest to divinity. Solomon felt this regarding such a dilation of the heart, as well as its contraction, in these words: <margin>Proverbs 21:1 <note>The author likely means Proverbs 21:4 in the Vulgate numbering.</note></margin> *The loftiness of the eyes is the dilation of the heart; the lamp of the wicked is sin.* It is as if he had said: the eyes of the celestial spirits contained in the heart are exalted toward God by the dilation of the heart; but by its contraction, their lamp is sin—that is, darkness and error. Whence God also said: <margin>Jeremiah 30:21</margin> *Who is this that applies his heart to approach me?* Which speech can be translated into this sense: *Who is he who, by the power and fear of me, and by hope, charity, and joy, will so adapt his heart that he may reach the vision of me?* For the heart is dilated by good passions and habits, but by evil and impious ones, it is constricted. Hence David says in exultation: <margin>Psalm 107:1 [Vulgate]</margin> *My heart is prepared, O God, my heart is prepared; I will sing and give praise in my glory.* That is: *My heart is dilated, and by dilation it is prepared so that by the vision of Thee, who art my glory, I may sing and exult.* Here, then, is the joy of the spirits because of the heart’s dilation, which has arisen from the intuition of the divine Mind, by which the entire spirit of the body is also refreshed. Whence the Wise Man says: <margin>Proverbs 15:13</margin> *A joyful heart makes a cheerful face, but by the sorrow of the mind the spirit is cast down.* This can be interpreted in this way: the dilated heart cheers the spirit through the vision of invisible joy; but by the contraction of the heart, sorrow and sadness are produced, which oppress the spirit of life. Piety also...

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s exploration of the heart's "mystical anatomy." Having previously established that the heart’s motion reflects the celestial movements of the Macrocosm, Fludd now focuses on how the physical expansion (dilation) and contraction of the heart correspond to specific spiritual virtues and psychological vices.</meta>

### Section I. Portion III. Part III. Book IV.

Faith and religion are produced in the **dilation** <note>The phase of the heartbeat where the chambers expand and fill with blood; Fludd associates this physical openness with spiritual receptivity.</note> of the heart; for the fire of life, arising from its spirit fixed in the heart, beholds the vision of the mind and its glory with the highest pleasure. Thus, the person is rendered humble, pious, and just; hence it is said:

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 1:18; 2:20 <note>These references are to the Book of Sirach, also known as Ecclesiasticus.</note></margin>

> *The religious man will guard and justify the heart; he will give joy and gladness.*

Therefore, the Wise Man says here, proving the power of love through the dilation of the heart:

> *Those who fear the Lord will prepare their hearts, and in His sight, they will sanctify their souls,*

whereby he understands "fear of the Lord" not as slavish terror, but as love coupled with reverence. Even the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnici"</note> recognized that these pious passions of the soul proceed from the heart's dilation. Furthermore, regarding the production of faith, the Evangelist says:

<margin>John 14:1</margin>

> *Let not your heart be troubled; you believe in God, etc.*

It is as if he were saying: "Let not your heart be contracted within you, because you believe in God." For faith and hope arise from the dilation of the heart, and charity is also a pious passion that proceeds from this same expansion. Hence the Apostle says:

<margin>2 Corinthians 9:7</margin>

> *Let each one give as he has decided in his heart, not out of sadness or necessity; for God loves a cheerful giver.*

This means giving by expanding the heart and looking cheerfully toward God Himself—the supreme Mind—rather than by contracting it through secret grief and sadness, which is to give with an ill will. Furthermore, Ruth spoke of this kind of good action of the heart:

<margin>Ruth 2:13</margin>

> *I have found grace in your eyes, my lord, for you have comforted me and spoken to the heart of your handmaid;*

As if she had said: "My lord, by your speaking to the spirits of my life or my soul, hope and joy are produced in me." This, therefore, is that pious disposition of the heart in which a most free communication is established between the human spirits of heaven and those of the world. Through these, there is a spiritual view toward the object of Divine Majesty. Here, the seeds of celestial life in the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>The "Great World" or the universe.</note> and those adhering to the heart in the <term>microcosm</term> <note>The "Little World" or the individual human being.</note> are united. The Psalmist refers to this disposition when he says: *Place your hearts in His virtue,* which is to say: expand and open your hearts so that you may exult in the Lord.

From these things, we see that the action of the heart in dilation is the origin of good and pious passions. This is because the celestial spirits, enclosed in the chamber of the heart for the benefit of life, are refreshed through that copious expansion. They are refreshed by the vision of the mind—both macrocosmic and microcosmic—whereby they are snatched upward by a quasi-divine rapture from the cares and vexations of earthly disturbances to the contemplation of celestial and supersubstantial things. In such an ecstasy, they feel no small delight. Indeed, Paul and John experienced this action of the heart in the moment they were snatched up even to the third heaven and saw there wonderful and ineffable things.

Good passions follow this action of the heart: namely, joy or gladness, love and charity, faith, hope, mercy, humanity, piety, humility, and so on. All of these tend toward God and divinity and are numbered among the virtues. The "vision" through which these good passions are rendered visible to the body (though not always) is that of the soul or the spirits of life, whose seat is in the heart. But the soul's "eye" with which it gazes upon God is the human mind, free from every stain and contagion of the body. The "Idea" of God adheres to this mind no differently than a ray of the Sun to the sun itself, or the image of a thing to a mirror. The "affect" of the mind is reason, and its vision is the intellect.

It happens sometimes that some of these passions—such as joy, gladness, hope, love, and humanity—arise in men stained by sin. But in these cases, the "vision" which is the cause of these passions is not discerned because of the darkness of the body weighing down the soul. However, in holy men and Prophets, that blessed vision was revealed quite often, as in Paul, John, Elijah, Ezekiel, and others like them. This did not happen without a preceding and fitting preparation. Hence, it is required that he who desires to see the vision of God distinctly must have healthy eyes with which to look rightly. Those are said to have healthy eyes whose souls have been purged and removed from mortal desires. Indeed, no one can look spiritually in the right way unless he fixes the eyes of his contemplation in the light of God. Through that contemplation, he sees how great are the joys, the gladness, the serenity, and the delight. Health makes that vision secure; the right direction makes it straight; the vision itself makes it blessed. Therefore, when the soul is free from all dregs and washed of stains, it then holds itself most willingly within itself, fearing nothing and untroubled by any fault. Then, with a certain immense and incredible joy and confidence, it proceeds into God—that is, into the contemplation of truth. Thus the soul is first healed; once healed, it finds the valves of the heart open, through which its sight or vision goes forth. Having gone out, it is introduced to the divine object, and being introduced, it is refreshed and recreated.

But just as the soul or spirit of life (by means of those intellectual faculties) has its affections which exercise themselves in virtues, so too there are sometimes present passions contrary to these, by which it is disturbed and vexed. These are called the vices of the spirit or the passions that depress the soul. Just as the good passions or virtues arise from the dilation of the heart, so also its bad passions or vices usually proceed only from the **contraction** of the heart: namely, sadness, despair, fear, hatred, envy, anger, fury, shame, and so on. For when the heart inclines more toward contraction than dilation, the spirit is imprisoned too deeply in the abyss of the heart. Consequently, it can very rarely reach the vision of the divine mind. Thus the melancholic, furious, and sorrowful soul looks toward lower things, since the path to higher things is closed to it—and much more so to those supreme things. Such a soul has visions of demons <note>original: "Daemonum"</note> and is deprived of the divine vision. Driven by such passions, it affects the nature of a <term>cacodaemon</term> <note>An evil spirit or "bad demon," the opposite of an angelic or "agathodaemon" nature.</note> just as it used to take on an angelic nature in its blessed vision. Deprived of divine grace, it seems to taste the bitterness of darkness and to be subjected to the madness of elementary demons. It is vibrated and agitated by hypochondriac winds and turbulent waves of the air, and it is usually afflicted by mania, insanity, fear, sadness, despair, fury, and the like, and deluded by false and deceptive visions. Hence it is said:

<margin>Deuteronomy 28:67</margin>

> *He will give you a trembling heart and failing eyes, and a soul consumed with sorrow; and your life shall hang in doubt before you; you shall fear night and day, and have no assurance of your life:*

That is, because of the lack of the vision of truth (which happens due to the heart's contraction), these kinds of erroneous vices will vex your soul. Whence Job says:

### On the Mystical Anatomy of the Heart.

*My spirit is narrowed within me.* And the royal Psalmist says: <margin>Job 21:4.</margin> *My spirit is consumed, and I am made like those descending into the tomb; that is, my spirit is shrouded in darkness.* For which reason the Wise Man <note>A common title for King Solomon.</note> also says: <margin>Proverbs 4:19; Judges 16:16.</margin> *that the way of the wicked is dark, and they know not where they may fall*; hence we find elsewhere: *Their soul fails them and is harassed even unto death.* And Mercurius Trismegistus <note>The legendary founder of Hermeticism; the "Pimander" refers to the *Poimandres*, a central Hermetic text.</note> <margin>Pimander 10.</margin> speaks thus: *The soul, by the nature of things and the consciousness of the good, when deprived of bodily eyes, entangles itself in passions. The soul, corrupted after the fashion of an evil spirit <note>original: "cacodemonis"</note> and ignorant of itself, having cast off the body, serves deformed monsters; it carries its own body about like a hostile burden, not presiding over the body, but subjugated to it because of ignorance.* But truly Saint John <margin>John 14.</margin> offers a remedy of this kind for this disease: *Let not your heart be troubled; you believe in God, etc.* Where he implies that faith, by dilating the heart, is the cause of the cure for this passion. The Evangelist also teaches that sadness is produced by this kind of action in these words: <margin>John 16:6.</margin> *But because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.* Perversity and obstinacy are also caused by this, <margin>Exodus 10:19.</margin> whence it was said: *The heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not listen to them, just as the Lord had commanded*, that is, he had neither faith nor obedience.

The reason for this error of the soul is the obstruction of its vision; for it is blind because of the darkness of the closed heart and cannot see. This is gathered from many places in the Holy <margin>Isaiah 6:8.</margin> Scriptures: *Blind* (says God) *the heart of this people, lest they understand with their heart.* And elsewhere: *All saw Him and were troubled, etc.* and when the wind ceased, they were even more amazed among themselves, for their heart was blinded; that is, they could not see the vision of truth because of the contraction of the heart. And elsewhere: *This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.* And elsewhere: <margin>Mark 6:52</margin> *They did not glorify Him as God, nor give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened.* And elsewhere: <margin>Mark 7:6.</margin> <margin>Romans 1:21.</margin> *According to your hardness and impenitent heart, you treasure up for yourself wrath on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God.* From these passages, it is explained quite clearly that these passions—namely fear, error due to a defect of vision, sadness or mourning of the soul, despair and distrust, the narrowing of the spirits, the darkness of the soul, and the deceptive delusions arising from its failure, perversities or obstinacy, blindness, and its separation from divine contemplations—proceed from this foul and ill-fated action of the heart: namely, its long-lasting **contraction**. This occurs when the heart is more inclined toward contraction <note>systole</note> than toward dilation <note>diastole</note>, whereby it happens that the spirit of life is shrouded in darkness and does not know how to judge rightly concerning divine matters, according to that saying of the Wise Man: *The body which is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that muses upon many things; and we hardly guess aright at things that are upon earth, and with labor do we find the things that are before us, but who shall search out the things that are in the heavens? And who shall know your counsel, unless you give wisdom and send your Holy Spirit from on high, etc.* <note>Quoting the Wisdom of Solomon 9:15-17.</note>

We conclude, therefore, that while the primary passions arising from the dilation of the heart cause the ethereal spirits in the heart to cling to super-celestial things, the latter passions derived from the heart's contraction cause them to become neighbors to the sublunary <note>The earthly realm below the moon, subject to decay and change.</note> realms. Thus we see the celestial nature sometimes participate in the nature of the Empyrean <note>The highest, fiery heaven, the dwelling of God.</note> and sometimes in the elemental nature, as it pleases. If its spirit descends downward, it mixes itself with wicked demons; but truly visiting the super-celestial kingdoms, it participates in the angelic nature. This same relationship exists between the spirit of life in man and his intellectual spirit in the brain, and that natural spirit in the liver; for just as the spirit of life vivifies invisibly, so that natural spirit in the liver causes visible growth. From this, it is denoted that the liver belongs to the part of the flesh and the elemental kingdom.

But that action of the heart, which is in the middle between these two extremes, is that which participates equally in both extremes, so that it may serve the necessity of life alone. In this work, there is a relationship of the middle to both extremes: namely, the nature of the middle heaven or ether to that nature of the Empyrean or angelic heaven, and again its respect to the elemental nature. From the super-celestial heaven, therefore, it draws the intellectual spirit; the ethereal part holds the vital soul within itself and is carried in the sublunary air with its super-celestial soul, and finally is enclosed in the opaque body for the complete composition of man. Hence, it is that by the motion of the heart (which is the seat of the middle spirit)—specifically **Diastole**—the soul dilates itself, so that it may indefinitely attract to itself its likeness: both the rational from the Empyrean heaven wandering everywhere in the air, and the vital from its ethereal kingdom (that is, from the higher regions, which action is completed by dilation), and by its **Systole**, through which by contracting it separates the impure from the pure.

From this, it is clear that the action of life imitates the action of the *World Soul* <note>original: "anima mundi"</note>, or the primary emanation from **Jehovah**, which the ancients (skilled in occult Theology) called the World Soul and the Messiah. This is the power of the **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter name of God, YHVH.</note>, which the Kabbalists identified as the angel **Metattron** or **Michael**, who has command over the malignant angels who are enemies of human life. By the dilation of its principal organ, therefore, the soul attracts friendship and the gifts of life and reason from heaven—namely, by means of the motion of Diastole—just as a bellows draws air to itself to provide fuel for the fading fire of life, so that the fire itself may always burn in its vigor. In this metaphor, the man standing is like the soul of life, the moving bellows are likened to the lungs, and the air drawn into the bellows is of the same kind as that drawn into the lungs. Just as the air drawn by a man through bellows nourishes the flame of an external and artificial fire, so too the similar air drawn by the heart through the lungs preserves life and, with successive replenishment, aids the internal fire of life and the natural flame. By the growth and preservation of this flame, man continues and progresses in his state of living.

The soul, therefore, in this kind of motion of life, is the internal agent or formal principle as far as we are concerned, just as its internal agent is the Mind or the Word. The instrumental causes are the heart and the lung; the material cause is the life-giving part of the air; and the effect is life. It follows that the involuntary motion called Diastole, through the dilation of its organ, attracts the benevolence of God (which, according to Holy Scripture, is life and being), and Systole, by contracting, expels the useless parts of the introduced air—not unlike how the flame of a fire selects the pure part from the air blown to it by bellows for its nourishment, but expels the impure and superfluous in the form of useless smoke. The heart, therefore, must be cared for above all things, just as the

### Section I, Portion III, Part III, Book IV.

<margin>Proverbs 4:23.</margin>
The Wise Man <note>Referring to King Solomon</note> speaks in this manner: *With all watchfulness guard your heart, because from it life proceeds.* <note>original: "Omni custodia conserua cor tuum, quia ex illa vita procedit."</note> From this, a great mystery in nature is explained: namely, that in this movement of life, measured by the nature of the pulse, there must be an equality. This is no different than how we see the ethereal heaven held in an equal position between the highest fiery heaven <note>The Empyrean</note> and the lower world of the elements, since the balanced temperament of life and the elements consists of this quality. For if the equality of this movement is corrupted, or if it fails in its beat, it is inevitable that an error will also occur in the bond of the four elements, which is the **fifth essence** <note>The *quinta essentia*, a celestial substance that Fludd believes binds the physical elements of the body together.</note>. This essence, by its nature, agrees with every quality of the elements; consequently, it lives peacefully with them and binds them together in harmonious peace. 

For the strength of life lies as much in the attraction of light (which is similar to itself) as in the expulsion of the superfluities of darkness (which are opposite to its nature). Thus, when the **systole** <note>The contraction of the heart.</note> is weakened while the **diastole** <note>The dilation or opening of the heart.</note> remains in its natural state, nature becomes burdened with waste. In this case, the introduction of waste is strong while its expulsion is weak. So, even if the natural heat remains at its proper level, the smoky and empty vapors tend to produce <term>Orthopnea</term> <note>Difficulty breathing unless upright.</note> and <term>Dyspnea</term> <note>Shortness of breath.</note>, acting unnaturally. Moreover, both with and without these symptoms, fevers are stirred up because of the rot contracted from the corrupt, useless, and empty air remaining in the body. This air ought to be expelled through exhalation, but by its thickness, it tends to suffocate and block the useful passages of life; by its useless nature, it easily turns to corruption. 

From this arises an equality of pulses combined with speed (due to the narrowing and compression of the blockage), and from here comes the origin and beginning of fevers and acute diseases, whether they be putrid or contagious. Indeed, physicians to this day have not fully perceived this. For where the expulsive power is not present in the celestial fire of life, there **Michael**—who is the Prince of Life and the expeller of evil spirits—rests from his office by the divine will because of the sins of men. Consequently, demons who are contrary to the nature of life, and who inhabit the superfluous and useless air (that is, the more "empty" air), take possession of the human spirit. Thus, they become the authors of breathing difficulties, feverish conditions, or other diseases, according to whichever winds and elements are most agreeable to these wicked demons. 

This, therefore, is the inequality of the action of life or the heavens. Since nature has disposed this balance in both the **macrocosm** <note>The universe.</note> and the **microcosm** <note>The human being.</note>, it follows that if a person departs from this natural state, the condition of life becomes unnatural. Furthermore, if the movement of the *systole* is longer and more lasting in its time than the *diastole*, it follows that wicked spirits and enemies of life hold great dominion over such a sick person. For in that case, very little "food of life" <note>Fresh air/vital spirit.</note> is attracted, but much superfluous air is retained along with its spirits, who are children of darkness and consequently enemies of life and light. Diseases of this nature are for the most part "cold" diseases, or indeed mixed and melancholic diseases. 

From this, it is evident that the movement of the heart, if it is to tend toward an exact disposition of healthy life, must be equal in Diastole and Systole. The middle point between these two movements is that rest <note>The pause in the heartbeat.</note> which refers to the nature of the "middle heaven." In this rest, there is an equal portion of **radical moisture** <note>The fundamental fluid of life.</note> and **innate heat**. In their equality consists the "Sabbath" or rest of life. Just as the *systole* relates to the airy or elementary heaven, the *diastole* dilates and extends itself toward the super-celestial or empyrean realm (from which the intellectual spirits descend). By means of this movement, the intellectual light of God and the life-giving spirit of nature are enticed and attracted into the chamber of the heart. 

In its strength, therefore, the Diastole performs the office of Michael in the expulsion of wicked and useless spirits from the "human heaven," who without his assistance would bring harm to life and its functions. The Diastole joins strength to strength through a natural path; hence, nature rejoices in its own nature and is exalted. Thus, the animal life is continued and preserved. The Diastole brings and introduces raw and unrefined matter into the left ventricle of the heart; the Systole purges and prepares it, and finally expels the thick dregs. The rest between these two retains the "proven" and purified matter as being most suitable for the functions of life. This exact operation of nature consists in the equality of these movements, which also denotes the harmony of the elements and the firmness of nature's bond, which is achieved through that virtue of life derived from heaven. But if there is an inequality in the progress of these movements, it proves an inequality of the elements and a violation of that natural bond; from this follow infirmities, which are nothing other than a lack of balance caused by the inequality of movement.

Here, however, a question may arise: in the beginning of life, does the Diastole or the Systole claim the first place? To this doubt we can answer, and not without consideration, that Diastole claims preeminence in life, because it is necessary that attraction occur before any expulsion can take place. This is proven from the words of Holy Scripture, where we find: 
<margin>Genesis 2:7.</margin> 
*God breathed the breath of life into the face of the earthly Adam, who then became a living soul.* <note>original: "Deum in faciem Adami terrestris, inspirasse spiraculum vitæ, qui inde factus est in animam viuentem."</note> 
From this, it is clear that the inhalation and the lifting of the lungs came before the exhalation or the depressing of the lungs; consequently, the movement of Diastole was prior in its act to that of systole. For it is necessary that bellows first receive air before they are able to breathe it out.

Furthermore, we have gathered a notable observation concerning life or death in the extreme danger of the sick, based on the action of these movements of the heart as they relate to one another. For both I and others have noticed, in the extreme danger of death and in what is almost the final gasp, that if the inhalation or the movement of Diastole is long, and that of the systole very short, the patient often lives, provided the disease arises from a lack of innate heat. The reason for this is clear: namely, because the natural heat still left in the body of the sick person acts strongly in attracting what is similar to itself. By this attraction, its failing vigor is so multiplied and refreshed that it is now able to resist the wicked spirits opposed to life, and thus the patient is usually restored to their former health. But truly, if the movement of the systole (by which exhalation occurs) is long, and the Diastole is short and sudden, this is the greatest sign of death; for the natural heat, already weak, [exhausts] its remaining strength in the strong expulsion of waste...

# On the Mystical Anatomy of the Heart.

...expends and consumes <note>Referring to the heat and energy of the heart mentioned on the previous page.</note> through its motion, and because of its weakness in attraction, it snatches almost nothing celestial for itself by which it might be refreshed and increased; thus it happens that it is gradually extinguished. From this also arises the reason for the double breathing in **Melancholics** <note>In Fludd's time, "Melancholy" was one of the four humors, associated with black bile, coldness, and sadness.</note>; namely, because the inhaled smoky air or wind is not totally exhaled, which prevents a full inhalation, wherefore nature is forced to redouble its force and action. So also we see that when the stomach is filled with winds, the swallowing of nourishment is hindered, so that one must swallow two or three times before the food can be drawn down through the esophagus to the bottom of the stomach by means of the straight fibers.

Finally, upon these foundations, we can firmly consider, first, what kind of angels they are who have power over the internal man, likewise how many there are, and what their duties are. We have spoken abundantly about these in the preceding book on the *Mysteries of the Seed*, and also in our *Genethlialogical* <note>original: "Genethlialogico" — referring to the study of horoscopes and the influence of the stars at birth.</note> treatise (of which we treated in the technical history of the microcosm). Thus, as we see three actions centered in the heart—of which the **highest** consists only in dilation, the **middle** in dilation and contraction together, and the **lowest** in contraction alone—so also it is very easy to determine that each of these actions has a respect or relation to the three regions of the world. These are: the **Empyrean** <note>The highest, fiery heaven, the dwelling of God.</note> or super-celestial; the **Ethereal** or celestial; and the **Elemental** or sublunary. 

For pious, good, and just passions (which are produced by the dilation of the heart) belong to the angelic nature, and consequently are placed under the super-fatal angel who is the guardian of the mind, whose proper dwelling is in the super-celestial kingdom. By means of this angel (as **Iamblichus** <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> testifies), <margin>Iamblichus.</margin> we perform such things as he brings to our mind, and he governs us to that extent, until we exchange the dominion of the sacred prefect for a **daemon** <note>original: "dæmone" — in this context, a guiding spirit or lesser deity, not necessarily an evil "demon."</note>. Then this angel, yielding to God, ceases from his work or leads us to the same. Furthermore, the actions of a convenient life (which are excited by the equal dilation and contraction of the heart together as if by instruments) proceed primarily from the **Olympic** or fatal angel (having dominion in the celestial world). This angel is subject to that angel who is the guardian of the mind, and he has care of the soul or life in no other way than his superior is the director of the mind. 

Whence the aforementioned Iamblichus says (wrongly attributing only a single daemon to the internal part of man): *this daemon was in the archetype before the soul fell into generation; as soon as the soul received him as a leader, the daemon stands by it, subsequently a filler of lives; he binds the descending soul to the body, he himself cares for its common animal nature, directs the soul's own life, and whatever we reason, he provides the principles of reasoning; we do such things as he brings to mind, and he governs us, until, purified by sacred works, we receive God as our leader instead of the daemon, etc.* 

And certainly, we most rightly acknowledge that the later actions are ascribed by Iamblichus to the primary angel or the angel of the mind. But that he is also the immediate guardian of life, we utterly deny, since we see that the actions of life and mind are sometimes different. Thus the "middle soul" is said by the **Platonists** to neglect the mind and adhere to the animal soul or sublunary nature. If there were only a single angel attributed to the mind, the soul, and the spirit, it would follow that the operations of one and the other would always be in agreement. Experience teaches us that this is false, demonstrating that Sadness, Joy, Hope, Despair, Envy, and Hatred are entirely opposite things. Their unique action—namely dilation—is derived from the super-celestial nature, while contraction is derived from the sublunary. 

We conclude, therefore, that there is one angel of the mind and another of the soul; but we say the angel of the soul is subject to the mind in no other way than the soul itself is subject to the mind, of which it is the vehicle. And although the celestial angel or **Olympic daemon** has that angel of the mind as his prince, yet sometimes he is found rebellious and perverse toward his prince, according to that scripture: <margin>Job 4:18 <note>Fludd cites Job 4:17, but the text corresponds to 4:18.</note></margin>
> *Behold, those who serve God are not stable and firm, and in his angels God finds wickedness.* <note>original: "Ecce qui seruiunt Deo non sunt stabiles & firmi, & in angelis suis reperit Deus prauitatem."</note>

Hence, the Platonists recognized three things in the internal man: namely, the **Mind**, which is his supreme part, corresponding to the Empyrean heaven; the **Spirit**, the middle part, binding the vital soul with the supreme, and thus participating in both. They want this portion to differ from that supreme part as life differs from intellect in spiritual things, and as the heart differs from the brain in material things (which are vessels fit to receive these two gifts of the heavens); it also differs from the lower part as celestial things differ from elemental things. Finally, they call the lowest part the **animal or sensible soul**, which is composed of the elemental spirit. 

They conclude, therefore, that the mind never consents to evil, always resists error, and exhorts toward the best things. But the lowest portion is always submerged in evil, sin, and concupiscence, and drags one toward the worst; for **Paul** felt this when he said: <margin>Paul.</margin>
> *I see another law in my members, and it leads me captive in the law of sin.* <note>original: "Video aliam legem in membris meis, & captiuantem me in lege peccati." — Romans 7:23.</note>

They say the mind is never condemned, but when its companions are punished, it departs unhurt to its own region. They believe the middle spirit, since it is free by nature, can adhere to either extreme at will. They say that if this middle nature constantly adheres to the higher part (the mind), it is finally united to it and beatified until it eventually passes to God. But if, neglecting the mind or superior part, it inclines toward the lower portion, they assert it is depraved and corrupted until it becomes an evil daemon. From this, it is gathered that the natures of these three parts of one man are diverse from each other, and consequently, they have leaders of various conditions presiding over them. Of these daemons, the one who possesses the care of the lower portion is the worst, and is, as it were, a born **evil genius**, just as the superior is called one's **good genius** or Archangel. We could expand this discourse infinitely, for its field of debate is so wide; but truly, since other things call us away, leaving behind the spiritual heart and its actions, we shall say a few words about the material heart.

### CHAPTER VII.

#### On the material heart, its instruments, and the manner of its nutrition.

Taught by the experience of anatomy, we observe that just as the left ventricle of the heart is occupied with invisible spirits and turns its entire focus toward the creation of those vital spirits, so also the duty of the right ventricle is not only to fabricate, establish, and repair the material elements of the heart, but also to build, nourish, and maintain the heart's fan <note>original: "flabellum" — Fludd refers to the lungs as a cooling fan or bellows for the heart's heat.</note> in a healthy state. For that same motion in the heart which proceeds toward the heart's expansion, called **Diastole**, besides the introduction of airy spirit, draws blood from the **vena cava** <note>The large vein carrying deoxygenated blood into the heart.</note> into its right ventricle. During the period of rest, that introduced blood is prepared and thinned; its denser and heavier part passes through a small branch of the vena cava ascending to the base of the heart, which is called the **coronary** vessel, for the nourishment of the heart's substance. By means of this branch, the venous blood ordained for nourishing is dispersed throughout the entire material heart, not unlike how, on the opposite side, a branch proceeding from the **aorta** (before it exits the heart) imbues it with invisible spirits of life. This serves for the vivification of its substance, just as that branch from the vena cava serves those natural parts destined for nutrition. However, a thinner portion of the blood prepared and thinned in the heart is transferred into the substance of the lung (or the heart's fan) for its growth, preservation, or nutrition. This occurs through the three semilunar valves by means of the **arterial vein** <note>original: "vena arteriosa" — the pulmonary artery. In Fludd's time, it was called the "arterial vein" because it had the structure of an artery but carried blood like a vein.</note>, in which it disperses itself everywhere through small branches or streams. And in this way, this principal organ is built and repaired, assisted in its work by the lung. The heart, therefore, prepares for itself both spiritual and material nourishment by which it is sustained and exists in its state, and it preserves its being by its instruments or bellows, without which it is plainly crippled and deficient in its work.

Therefore, while these organs of life persist in their complete state, the entire microcosmic machine <note>The human body, viewed as a miniature version of the universe (the macrocosm).</note> is both watered by the spirits of life and everywhere vivified and illuminated by the rays of native heat. This is no different than the presence of the Sun, which draws its being from God as if from a fountain, by which the entire world is sustained; it draws its life, its being, its light, its spirit, its whole self from God, and then afterwards liberally nourishes all things contained in the world. Just as that Sun of the visible world (whom **Plato** calls the visible son of God) is the pattern of His invisible Son, or the uncreated spirit, and the light or emanation, so also the visible heart has its spiritual counterpart, in whose likeness it is formed. We call the invisible spirit of the thing that in which the soul dwells, just as the mind dwells in the soul, and the Word in the mind, to speak with <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>original: "Merc. Trismeg." — A legendary Hellenistic figure to whom a body of mystical and philosophical texts, the Hermetica, is attributed.</note>. And it is from this that the mystical Doctors among the Hebrew and Kabbalistic teachers agree: namely, that all lower things are representative
