## CHAPTER I.

->*Where the Brain in the microcosm is compared, both in its position and function, to the Empyrean Heaven of the Macrocosm.*<-

<margin>*Ps. 68:34* <note>Psalm 68:34: "To him who rides on the heaven of heavens, which were of old."</note></margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' depicting a scholar seated at a desk in a study, surrounded by books, a globe, and other instruments of learning.</image-desc>
**M**ERCURY Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with hermetic philosophy.</note> recognized that the mind is the presiding ruler of the vital soul; he also stated that the celestial or vital soul has the same relationship to the elementary spirit (which is subject to it) as the soul has to the mind, to which it usually offers similar obedience. Therefore, Photinus <note>This likely refers to Plotinus, the Neoplatonist philosopher, though the OCR reads "Photinus."</note>, along with other Platonists, recognized and established three parts in the internal man: namely, the highest, the lowest, and the middle. By that highest divine part, they understand the "mind" or the "illuminated intellect," and they made this mind the superior portion of the internal man. This is what Moses intended to signify by the "breath of lives" <note>original: "vitarum spiraculum"; referring to Genesis 2:7</note> breathed into us by God or His spirit. Thus, just as in the external man the brain claims the third or highest place—being enclosed on all sides by a bony, stone-like fortification—so also the interior of the brain is the intellectual world, in which mind and reason reign. This is no different from how the Word of God and His rational creatures—namely, the angels—have their seat in the third or highest heaven, which for that reason is called "intellectual and rational" by Bede, Isidore, and others. The spiritual brain is, therefore, like a soul to that material brain; and just as we find in Sacred Scripture that Mount Zion is the holy rock in which God dwells, so also within the walls of this eminent rock [the skull], the Illuminated Intellect has its seat and dominion in its Empyrean spirit. For as the Empyrean Heaven <note>The highest, fiery heaven in medieval cosmology, the dwelling place of God.</note> relates to the celestial and elementary realms, so also the spiritual brain must be considered in relation to those spiritual regions subject to it, namely the chest and the abdomen. For just as God is said to have His habitation in the "heaven of heavens" <note>original: "coelo macrocosmi coelorum"</note> of the macrocosm, so the mind, or the breath of lives, possesses its throne in the region of the microcosm’s regions: specifically, at the summit of the entire body. Therefore, insofar as the spiritual brain is the seat of intellect and reason, it is certain that it claims for itself that very place in the microcosm which the spirit of the Empyrean heaven holds in the macrocosm. Furthermore, it is said that God breathed the breath of lives into Adam's face—not into his chest or belly, but into the highest portion of man, which He chose for the seat of His divine breath, much like the "heaven of heavens of old" where He Himself sits.

<margin>*Pimander 12.*</margin>
<margin>*Pimander 10.* <note>References to the "Pimander," a core text of the *Corpus Hermeticum* attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note></margin>
From these points, we believe it has been explained clearly enough that the brain holds primacy not only in its location, but also in dominion and dignity over both the heart (which resides in the middle region of the microcosm) and the liver (which is the prince of the lowest region). This is because the rational soul of the brain has power over both the vital soul (whose palace is the heart) and the natural soul (which reigns in the liver). Hence, Mercury Trismegistus says: *In whatever souls the mind presides, it illuminates them with its own brightness, resisting their evil habits.* From this, he concludes elsewhere *that a soul destitute of the presence of the mind is able neither to do nor to say anything.* Thus it is clear that, as the mind excels the soul in dignity, it also follows that its dwelling place—namely, the brain—is to be preferred to that soul by many degrees. From these things, it is right to gather that the brain in the microcosm has the same relationship in its arrangement as the Empyrean heaven has in the greater world [the macrocosm].

### CHAPTER II.

-> On the mystery of the choroid plexus, and on the wonderful endeavor of nature in <-
-> the reduction of material and coarse blood into a subtle and spiritual essence, <-
-> by which we are taught that its aim is to return <-
-> earthly things to a celestial nature. <-

Those more skilled in anatomy, equipped with quite pertinent observations, say that the choroid or "choriform" plexus in the brain—which Laurentius <note>André du Laurens (1558–1609), a prominent French anatomist and physician to Henry IV.</note>, on account of its stupendous structure, called the *rete admirabile* <note>Latin: "wonderful net."</note>, and Columbus <note>Realdo Colombo (c. 1516–1559), an Italian anatomist who described pulmonary circulation.</note> called the reticular plexus—takes its origin from the "wonderful net" woven from the *pia mater* <note>The delicate innermost membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord.</note>. Indeed, it is composed of a labyrinthine texture of small veins and arteries running through a small portion of thin membrane. As for its position, we are taught that this membrane or web is located in the anterior ventricles of the brain, in which it floats upon the clear fluid contained within them, not unlike how we see the heart bathing in the fluid of the pericardium. They believe this plexus is useful for expiration, inspiration, and the breathing of air into the anterior ventricles, for the brain moves through *systole* and *diastole* <note>The rhythmic contraction and expansion, usually associated with the heartbeat.</note> just like the heart. This is done to "cook," prepare, alter, and thin the <term>animal spirits</term> <note>In Galenic physiology, these were the "refined" spirits responsible for sensation and movement.</note>, which are still coarse and like smoke while contained in this plexus, before they reach the natural sense or the "third ventricle." In that third ventricle, the preparation of said spirits is finished and perfected so that they may be moved to the fourth or final ventricle. Therefore, Columbus among others concludes that the use of these structures is primarily destined for the generation of animal spirits.

In the second book of this work, where we treated the mysteries of the blood—specifically in the third chapter, where we explained the chemical laboratory of nature in the microcosm along with its vessels—we demonstrated that there are three evident vessels or organs by which nature separates the pure juice from the impure in a subtle way, and transmits each separated element of the mass into its own proper receptacle. Each of these vessels holds a preeminence over the others in the dignity of its work, namely: the liver (which is the second vessel of natural <term>Alchemy</term>) over the stomach (which is its first vessel); and the heart (which is its third vessel) over the liver; and these choriform plexuses (which are held in the highest place of nature's laboratory). 

For the stomach—which is nature's "circulatory vessel," placed in the lowest part (serving not the kitchen, but the human viscera) to purify its subject—is that hidden organ in which the first extraction of pure <term>chyle</term> <note>A milky fluid consisting of lymph and emulsified fats, produced during digestion.</note> from the fecal impurity occurs. Their final separation happens in the intestines through filtration performed by the mesenteric vessels, not unlike how we see a skilled chemist separate and extract the <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>Distilled alcohol or ethanol.</note> with its phlegm from its dregs through a preceding circulation in a water bath. And just as we see this "water of life" (*aqua vitae*), still impure and mixed with its own wateriness, placed in a second vessel and exposed to the "dew of the bath" <note>An alchemical term for gentle, indirect heating, often using steam or warm water.</note> so that the purer spirit of wine may be divided from its impure and watery parts, so also the matter of the chyle, divided from its terrestrial dregs by the filter, is cooked in its second vessel (the liver, which is more tender and delicate than the first). This happens by means of the vapor of the viscera surrounding the liver; in this cooking, the watery mass is separated from the "airy" or bloody mass and is expelled downward into the "mother of the bladder" through the kidneys. The coarse blood, likened to coarse air, is then poured out everywhere through the body to nourish its coarse limbs. 

Furthermore, for an even more exact purging of the spirit of the vein from its wateriness, it must be placed in the third vessel, more worthy than the others: the heart. From there, this blood of the first preparation rises through the ascending *vena cava*, and a portion of it is sent into the right chamber of the heart, where it is circulated by the "fire of the third regime" (likened to the heat of the sun) and thinned into a more fiery nature. Thus purified, that blood serves as the light food for the lungs and behaves like pure, visible spirit of wine. The "airy dregs" (which are also thinned and purified by this kind of boiling) contribute to the nourishment of the vessel itself, namely the heart. 

From these things, it must be noted that the dregs of the first operation, performed in the stomach, are **earthy**, and their receptacle is the colon intestine. The dregs of the second operation (which happens in the liver) are **watery**, and their receptacle is the bladder; this is called the serum of the blood. The dregs of the third operation are **air**, and they are useful for the nourishment of the heart's substance. Finally, the depurated portion of both arterial and venous blood ascends to the brain and establishes those reticular plexuses there by its texture.

Here, however, it must be observed with diligence that just as the elements of wine naturally seek the region destined for them by nature—as has been proven by our own experiments and explained in the history of the Macrocosm and Microcosm, where we depicted water floating above earth, air above water, fire above air, and the <term>quintessence</term> (or the element of heaven) above fire—so also the celestial part of the blood seeks the third and highest region of man by a natural inclination. This was the subject of an enclosed experiment involving wine which I once dedicated to our most Serene King <note>Likely King James I of England, to whom Fludd dedicated several works.</note>, to his great admiration. The fiery part holds the middle region, and the lowest region contains the air. Therefore, it is necessary to believe that the blood, both venous and arterial, which ascends to the plexuses of the brain, is exceedingly subtle and thin, and behaves like the most subtle...

### CHAPTER III.

#### *How, by means of the choroid membrane (that is, its wonderful plexus and texture), a spiritual and invisible generation is achieved in the brain for the forming of rational ideas—exactly as a physical and visible generation is achieved by means of that wonderful plexus formed by the seminal vessels, called <term>Anastomosis<note>original: "Anastomosis," a Greek term for the interconnection between blood vessels; here used to describe the "interweaving" of vessels.</note></term> by the Greeks.*

Hermes said in his Emerald Tablet, <quote>That which is above is like that which is below, and vice versa.</quote> And the Doctors, both of the Hebrews and others more skilled in the <term>Kabbalah<note>A school of Jewish mysticism; Fludd often uses "Christian Kabbalah" to link mystical traditions with anatomy.</note></term>, assertively say that all lower things are representative of higher things, and as it is below, so it is also above. We even find this expressed in specific words in the Holy Scriptures, such as these: <margin>Hebrews, chapter 11.</margin> Through faith we acknowledge that it has always been thus with the world through the word of God: that from those things which could not be seen, those things which can be seen were made. Who is so ignorant as not to know that the image or visible form of a man—even an infant—was first outlined in his internal or invisible self? Since this very thing is clearly declared by the Holy Scriptures, saying, <margin>Psalm 139:16.</margin> > Your eyes saw my unformed substance, and in your book all these things were written, from which they were fashioned day by day, when as yet there was none of them. By these words it is declared that the visible image of a bodily thing was first invisibly depicted in its spirit before the visible appearance emerged.

But truly, by Hercules, it seems that a spiritual effigy of this kind was outlined in the intellectual spirit (according to that preceding verse: "your eyes saw my unformed substance, and my members were written in your book, when none of them yet existed") before either the heart or the liver were formed, according to the opinion of Hippocrates. For just as the divine mind existed before the soul of life—since it is by the presence of the mind that life exists—so also the Spirit of God depicted the human form in the invisible mundane spirit before it appeared visibly to the eyes. Thus, we think it not inept to conclude that this kind of hidden and spiritual action always remains in the brain, where it is prepared to fashion invisible forms—not only fantastic and imaginary ones, but also essential and true ones. These descend invisibly through the great artery into the seminal arterial vessels and produce the seed of the sperm, which is the soul, or the internal man being generated.

This is clearly demonstrated by that famous "Genoese coitus," where it was observed that from the strong imagination of a black Moor painted on the canopy of a bed and seen during the act of conception, an infant both Moorish and black was procreated by those white parents. From this it is clear that the effigy of the one being generated was first invisibly depicted or fabricated in the spiritual workshop of the brains of both parents before it was produced into a visible act. Do we not also forge visions and strong imaginations, both in sleep and in waking, which arise from the false air breathed in through the nostrils, or from that air enclosed in poorly tempered blood? But he who is sound in mind and reason produces sound, true, and lasting ideas in the brain, which are offered daily to God like sacrifices; these establish the governance of life and the whole man, and produce visible effects in carnal procreation. Therefore, the Wise Man wishes this to be understood regarding such spiritual generation where he says, <margin>Wisdom 4:1.</margin> > The memory of a chaste generation is immortal, for it is known before God and men.

Regarding the mysteries of such spiritual generation, we shall deal briefly here. Since we have declared above that it takes place principally in the brain, we must first see what the relationship is between the organs of physical generation and those of spiritual generation. We say, therefore, that for physical generation, two spermatic vessels are arranged on both the right and left sides of the abdomen, one of which is a vein and the other an artery. To these correspond two <term>choroid<note>original: "choriform." The term refers to the chorion (a fetal membrane), noting the similarity between the brain's membranes and those of the womb.</note></term> membranes, and in the composition of each, a small vein and artery meet: one of which is located in the right part of the brain, and the other in the left. Furthermore, for physical generation, a wonderful plexus is made called <term>Anastomosis</term>, in which the vein is entwined with the artery, and the artery with the vein, in a wonderful texture like a web or ivy. Do we not see, in exactly the same way, a similar plexus called <term>Anastomosis</term> made from the intertwining of an artery and a vein in these two membranes of the brain? Then, after that, at the base of the lower intertwining destined for physical generation, we see there are two vessels called the processors or <term>epididymides<note>original: "epididimes." Coiled tubes behind the testes where sperm matures.</note></term>, since they "cook" and unite the sperm mixed with the seed. In a clearly similar way, we see that the two anterior ventricles of the brain serve as a cooling chamber for the purpose of coagulation...

And such an "infant" is so pure that it joins itself with God. As we shall declare below.

# CHAPTER IV.
### *On the most spiritual regeneration, which produces the infants of reason and intellect.*

**J**ust as the intellect and reason are far more eminent in dignity than sensation and movement, so it is necessary that two types of spirit—one more noble than the other—be required to perform these two functions of the soul. For one will behave like the soul to the body, and the other like the body to the soul. For as sensation and movement are closest to bodily things, being immediately concerned with bodies, so also reason and intellect are neighbors to the highest spiritual things and are concerned with the contemplation of Ideas. Therefore, animal spirits of a coarser disposition are required for sensation and movement, whereas thinner and purer spirits are needed for reason and intellect. Just as the ethereal spirits relate to the empyrean and super-celestial ones, or as the airy spirits relate to the ethereal ones, so too do those animal spirits which work to fulfill the duties of sensation and movement relate to those that deal with rational and intellectual matters. For the empyrean spirits of the heaven in the <term>macrocosm<note>The "great world" or the universe as a whole.</note></term> (which are also called "intellectual spirits") correspond to the animal spirits in the <term>microcosm<note>The "little world" or the human being, seen as a reflection of the universe.</note></term> in terms of their respective purity. 

Hence it is clear that the entire animal spirit, or "sperm" (which is invisible), is prepared in the choroid plexus and perfected in the third ventricle. In every way, it is assimilated to the visible sperm destined for material generation. Just as material sperm is composed of a coarse part (called "sperm") and a most subtle part (called "seed")—the former contributing to the constitution of the body or the "outer man," and the latter to the soul or the "inner man"—so indeed the invisible or animal sperm is forged from a coarse spirit (which deals more with the senses) and a most subtle spirit (which tends toward the operations of the intellect). Therefore, reason or intellect is awakened by the <term>quintessence<note>The fifth and highest essence; the purest part of a substance.</note></term> of this animal spirit or sperm alone, and movement and sensation are stirred by both together. 

Thus, the sperm of movement and sensation is prepared by the choroid plexus and finished in the third ventricle. Passing through the opening from the third to the fourth ventricle between the "buttocks"—namely, through the "anus" <note>original: "anum." An anatomical term for the opening of the cerebral aqueduct into the fourth ventricle.</note>—all this animal sperm is sent in. The more spiritual part of this spirit is separated by hidden organs and kept in the chamber of memory; the remainder is spread throughout the entire body via the nerves to produce the faculties of sensing and moving. For the spirit primarily enters the nerves to provide the faculty of the senses: specifically, it enters the optic nerves for the sake of seeing; the fifth pair of nerves for the sake of hearing; and the third pair of nerves so that taste may operate, and so on for the others. 

From here also, movement and touch are granted to every member of the body, both through the said nerves and especially through the sixth pair (which carries the power of sensation and movement to all the organs of the chest and abdomen), and by means of the spinal cord <note>original: "nuca," a term derived from Arabic anatomy referring to the spinal cord.</note>, whose root begins in the <term>calamus scriptorius<note>original: "calami argutia," literally the "sharpness of the pen," an anatomical feature in the floor of the fourth ventricle of the brain.</note></term>—that is, in the rear corner of the fourth ventricle. That this kind of spirit, destined for sensation and movement, is of a more servile and inferior condition than that of reason or intellect is clearly shown. For reason, shining in the light of the "active intellect" through the "theater" of the brain, as it were, sits upon a high judgment seat like a judge. It commands like a king in his kingdom and judges the desired object: is it useful or not? Should it be pursued with hate or treated with love? The "common spirit," however, fills the role of a messenger, who carries the commands of reason down to the muscles by means of the nerves. Finally, the muscles, stirred by the animal spirits and illuminated by intellectual rays, as it were, long to perform and complete the commands of their prince or queen. 

From this it is evident that the spirits of reason are more worthy than the others, and they hold eminence over other types of animal spirits just as the spirit of the Sun holds eminence over the other stars, or the element of fire possesses dominion over the other elements. The more subtle (I say) and more imperial part of the primary animal sperm is kept in the sanctuary of memory for the use of the royal reason; and this part, thus enclosed in the hidden chest of memory, is again prepared into a "sperm" of the highest degree of spirituality by most secret ways and means,

# CHAPTER V.

->*On several organs found in the Brain, which are referred to those of carnal generation: And how it is probable that they contribute to the generation of the third or supreme order.*<-

Those well-versed in anatomy recognize, and we also understand through taught experience, that after the "furnace" <note>likely referring to the heat of the central brain ventricles</note> at the edge of the brain toward the cerebellum, and at the ends of the posterior part of the third ventricle, several protruding parts are seen, bearing the likeness of "testicles." <note>original: "testium seu testiculorum." In modern anatomy, these are the *inferior colliculi* of the midbrain.</note> From this, they have not undeservedly claimed the name of "testicles" for themselves among anatomists. Near these "testicles," two other small parts offer themselves, slightly larger and more elevated than the others, which because of their shape are called "buttocks." <note>original: "clunes" or "nates," referring to the *superior colliculi*.</note> Between these is situated that hole or entrance which leads from the third to the fourth ventricle (where the seat of memory is), and this passage is marked with the name "anus" because of its similarity. Furthermore, in the front part of the "testicles" extending toward the third ventricle, another small portion of the brain presents itself, which expresses the image of the female "pubis" or "vulva" not unsuitably, but indeed quite elegantly. Moreover, near this small body, a somewhat hard gland is seen, of a different color from the brain substance—that is, somewhat yellow—covered with a thin membrane; and this gland is attached to the "wine-press" <note>original: "torcular." Likely referring to the *torcular Herophili*, the confluence of the sinuses, or the pineal region's connection to the vascular system.</note> and has the shape of a "penis" or "virile rod." <note>original: "penis seu virgae virilis." This refers to the pineal gland, which Fludd and his contemporaries noted for its phallic shape and central position.</note> From all these things it may be seen, and it is even said by similarity, that all the members of generation are present around this same place in the brain—or at least the likenesses of the genital members—namely, the testicles, buttocks, anus, vulva, and the penis itself. These are arranged among themselves in this place in no other way than the members destined for carnal generation are in the lowest region of the body. 

However, as for the utility of these parts thus arranged in the brain, authors seem to disagree and are hardly consistent with themselves. For Columbus <note>Realdo Colombo (c. 1515–1559), a famous Italian anatomist and surgeon.</note> thought the "penis" was ordained by nature for the division of vessels. Others feel it was created by nature so that through it, like a plug, the animal spirits or the sperm of the first degree might be enclosed in the fourth ventricle. Others say it is for preserving the "species" or images of memory, etc. Concerning the use of the other parts, they have been able to judge nothing at all, and (as if nature had made something in vain) they have rendered them as if useless and superfluous. Regarding the use of the "penis" according to Columbus’s opinion: surely its shape, its varied color, its covering of thin membrane, and finally its attachment to the "wine-press" must denote some other hidden use than merely being ordained for the division and partitioning of vessels, or serving as a plug according to the opinions of others—especially since we see that office performed in many parts of the body by a craftsmanship far different from this. 

Furthermore, why do these parts agree so much in location, shape, and arrangement with the testicles, anus, buttocks, and vulva placed near them, unless they have a hidden relation to those instruments of corporal generation—not only in shape, but also in action and property? Or, since the other members are arranged in relation to the disposition of this "penis" or "little rod," why is some particular use attributed to this one and not to those, when nature does nothing in vain? Indeed, I, instructed by probable demonstration, have been forced to fall into this opinion: namely, that the buttocks and anus, as well as the testicles and the rod, have a secret power in spiritual and rational generation. Specifically, the anus and buttocks serve for the secretion of the coarse animal sperm from the subtle part, after that spiritual sperm of the first degree has been completed in the third ventricle. Its thicker part is extended to sense and motion through the nerves and spinal marrow, while the subtle part is hidden and reserved in the secret "box of memory," which is adjacent to the "wine-press" to which the "penis" is attached. # Section I. Portion III. Part III. Book V.

...is cast out, and thus perhaps rational offspring or concepts are drawn as much immediately as mediately—that is, from the storehouse of memory. Or, if all the "sperm"—both the subtle and the thick portions—is destined for the action of sense and motion, then it will be possible to derive the origin of that intellectual sperm from the **wonderful net** <note>original: "rete admirabile"; a network of blood vessels at the base of the brain. While prominent in many mammals, it is less so in humans, but early modern physicians believed it was the site where "vital spirit" was refined into "animal spirit."</note>, since it is necessary that the spirit refined in its intertwinings be of a more eminent and worthy nature and property than that which is thinned and prepared in the **choroid plexuses** <note>original: "plexibus choroidalibus"; networks of vessels in the brain's ventricles that produce cerebrospinal fluid.</note>. For just as the folding made in the choroid membranes is woven from a small vein and a small artery, so indeed in the **wonderful net**, it is not a vein joined with an artery, but an artery joined with an artery in a marvelous intertwining. For the small arteries from which it is woven are branches or "forks" rising from the ascending Carotids, which grant their strength and texture to the choroid only secondarily. From these things it is manifest that the spirit springing from such a plexus is worthier and of a nobler kind than that prepared from the choroid plexus; for in the composition of the former, a single celestial—that is, vital—spirit (to which the intellectual spirit strongly adheres) concurs, whereas for the consistency of the latter, a sublunary or "bloody" spirit—whether venous or celestial (that is, vital or arterial)—comes together.

From this it is right to gather that this most noble and fiery sperm—the only kind worthy to receive the rays of reason or intellect—is prepared in the plexus of the **wonderful net** and raised through hidden passages to the "testes" <note>In brain anatomy, certain rounded structures like the *colliculi* were historically referred to as the "testes" and "nates" (buttocks) due to their shape.</note>, in which it is purged of superfluous vapor. For the more this spirit is purified, the clearer and more transparent is that man’s intellect, and the more effective and certain the result of his reason. The arguments for the probability of this matter are various: namely, the location of the **wonderful net**, the exalted property of its spirit, the necessity of the intertwining (called *anastomosis*) for mixing the "female" sperm with the "male," the observation of the triple generation in man, and finally, the diversity of the generated effects.

Regarding the location of the **wonderful net**, we see indeed that its seat is immediately beneath the brain, so that unless the brain is removed, it does not appear; therefore it is clear that its location is near these instruments of generation, whose "pubes" is attached to the **wine-press** <note>original: "torcular"; referring to the *torcular Herophili* or confluence of sinuses, a drainage point for the brain's blood, which the author likens to a reproductive structure.</note>, and consequently it is contiguous to the cerebellum. Furthermore, the "testes" are deeply immersed and are not far distant from the **wonderful net**. From there, through hidden passages by means of a magnetic force, the spirits prepared in the plexus of this net can be attracted, and from them be brought through the "penis" into the "womb." Then, through the exalted purity of the spirits refined in such a plexus, we can denote that they serve a most simple and excellent virtue, such as that rational or intellectual power which holds itself in the **microcosm** <note>The "small world"—the human being.</note> just as angelic intelligence does in the **macrocosm** <note>The "great world"—the universe.</note>, to which the fiery or Empyrean spirit, which is the purest, thinnest, and simplest of all, corresponds or serves.

After this, the *anastomosis* or wonderful intertwining of the **wonderful net** proves that it was destined by God and nature for a most high business—that is, the preparation of a most excellent sperm. For just as in the mixing and preparation of sperm with its seed for carnal and visible generation there is a folding of a vein with an artery, so also for the production and mixing of "animal sperm" a similar plexus is ordained, which is called the choroid. By its operation (as anatomists testify) "animal spirits" of a coarser order or first degree are procreated, which differ from those of the second degree no differently than venous blood differs from arterial, or as aerial spirit (which is thick) differs from ethereal spirit (which is subtle). In such spirits of the first degree, the soul of the senses and motion lies hidden; these, migrating into the fourth ventricle and penetrating as much through the pairs of nerves as through the spinal cord, procreate sense and motion through the whole body.

Furthermore, we see that the **wonderful net** also claims such intertwinings for itself; therefore the nature of its fabric denotes a property similar to the other preceding plexuses. For if it were true what the anatomists affirm—namely, that the sole use of this net is to contain the vital spirits ascending from the heart to the brain—we could object that such a disposition of a net or plexus is not required for that work. We see far larger branches of arteries, supplying vital spirits to the brain, dispersed everywhere within the brain; therefore, for such a common task, a net-like plexus so noble, remarkable, and wonderful is not required. **Columbus** <note>Realdo Columbus (c. 1516–1559), a famous Italian anatomist and surgeon.</note> acknowledges that at the ends of the arteries forming the net-like plexus, the **pineal gland** <term>pinealis: a small pea-shaped gland in the brain, famously called the "seat of the soul" by Descartes.</term> or "pine" is present; and elsewhere he relates that this plexus is attached to the **wine-press**. He says from his observation that this "wonderful plexus" is constructed of four arteries, and elsewhere he says that this work is wonderful and constructed with unspeakable art by the Highest Architect—concerning whose wisdom and providence he thought it better to remain silent than to say too little, as if he wished to argue from this that its office and property are hidden and not revealed to him.

From these things it is right to gather that the closeness of the "testicles" to the "penis," the attachment of the "penis" to the "wine-press" (to which the **wonderful net** also adheres), and the adaptation of the "womb" to the "penis," produce a wonderful probability for intellectual generation. For what shall I say? Is the **wonderful net** destined for the sole preservation of vital spirits or not? Since arterial vessels dispersed everywhere through the body are accustomed to perform this same office. But nature has done nothing in vain; why then did she strive to perfect through many efforts that work which she could have brought to the desired end through fewer? What? Is the "penis" only for the division of the ventricles? Were the "testicles" and "womb" created in vain? What of the shapes of the "buttocks" or "cheeks" <note>original: "natium seu clunium"; referring to the *corpora quadrigemina* of the brain, known as the *nates* (buttocks).</note>? What? Is the office of the "anus" plainly vain and empty? Will it not seem impious to godly men, and a sin wandering from virtue, to suggest such things exist in nature? Would nature not have to be accused, she who is usually and ought to be prudent and most sharp-eyed in the fabric of man, if she had formed so many images and figures in vain in a substance so noble as the brain? She made such images in the lowest region of man for the sake of generation; wherefore it seems likely that she...

### On the Mystical Anatomy of the Brain.

...produced such images in the brain for the same reason, since the form of an external object paints the image of the internal. For in this way GOD is revealed through his creatures—that is, through a demonstration from what comes after—and thus the soul is depicted through its body; for as has often been cited above: *All lower things are representative of higher things, and as it is below, so it is acted above.* <note>original: "Omnes res inferiores sunt repraesentatiua superiorum, &, vti sit inferius, sic agitur superius." This is a variation of the famous Hermetic maxim, "As above, so below."</note> Hence, by the "higher," the heaven and spirit of a thing are denoted, and by the "lower," its internal or visible aspect. For there is nothing external and visible that <margin>To the Hebrews 11.</margin> does not have its internal and invisible likeness from which it proceeds; for the Apostle says: *It has always been done in the world through the Word of God, so that from those things which could not be seen, those things which can be seen were made.* <note>A paraphrase of Hebrews 11:3.</note> Finally, three such generations in the body are revealed by their effects: for the effect of corporal sperm is the visible or elemental man; the effect of the invisible generation of the first degree is the **phantastic** <term>phantasticum: relating to the "phantasy" or imagination, the faculty that processes sensory images</term> and what is depicted in the imagination, whose likeness is diffused everywhere into the body through both internal and external sense, as well as through motion. This "infant" is a medium between the sensible and the intelligible, just as the heaven of the **macrocosm** <term>macrocosm: the "great world" or the universe as a whole, which early modern thinkers believed was mirrored in the "microcosm" of the human body</term> is situated as a medium between the elemental and the ethereal. For the generated body is an element; the procreated "phantastic" part is likened to the matter of heaven; and finally, the offspring of reason or intellect has an angelic composition within itself. Thus, an element is reduced back into heaven by dissolution, and the nature of heaven takes on an angelic form by **subtilization** <note>original: "subtiliatione"; the process of refining a substance into its most pure, spirit-like state</note> and purification. This is no different than how the thick and elemental blood of the liver, combined with that first and ethereal blood of the heart, creates by subtilization the animal sperm of the first degree—that complex **choroid** <note>original: "choroidem"; the vascular membrane in the brain</note> which is made from a vein and an artery. And this same substance is reduced to its ethereal likeness through the **wonderful net** <note>original: "rete admirabile"; a network of blood vessels at the brain's base</note> by subtilization into the spiritual sperm of the final degree. We have here, therefore, a sensible generation attributed to the body; we have that "phantastic" generation assigned to the imagination; and finally, the generation destined for reason claims the highest place for itself. But **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of wisdom (Hermetica) that blends philosophy, magic, and anatomy.</note> also seems to declare this clearly in these words: *The Idea of the body is air; of air, the soul; of the soul, the intellect; and of the intellect, GOD. Therefore, GOD is around all things, the intellect or mind is around the soul, the soul is around the air, and the air is around matter; through matter he denotes the effect of generation, through air the phantastic faculty, in which spirit the soul acts, penetrating by subtilization to the intellect, which reaches to divinity itself.*

### CHAPTER VI.

->On the excellence of the eye, and the notable mystery of the pupil.<-

**H**ow great is the nobility of the eyes, how great their power, and how many mysteries are to be contemplated in them—and that they are as much spiritual as corporal—we are taught even by the Holy Scriptures. Indeed, the difference in the nature of the eye is no less than that between this temporary bread and that spiritual bread which is the Word, or between heaven and earth. We also derive this from Genesis, chapter 3, verse 5, where it is said *that the eyes of the man and the woman shall be opened. You shall be as Gods, knowing good and evil.* And elsewhere: *The eyes of Balaam were uncovered by Jehovah so that he might see the angel.* The Evangelist speaks of this kind of dull and <margin>Matthew</margin> perceptive vision from the admonition of CHRIST: *I speak to them in parables because seeing they do not see, etc. But blessed are your eyes because they see.* From this it is clear that eyes are both spiritual and corporal. <margin>Proverbs</margin> Hence, eyes are also attributed to God himself, no differently than bread is attributed to angels. Thus it is said: *Let your eyes <margin>Proverbs</margin> and Jehovah look toward what is right.* And elsewhere: *The eyes of Jehovah are in every place, watching the good and the bad.* And Job most excellently <margin>Job 10</margin> declares what the eyes of God are like: *The eyes of God,* he says, *are not of flesh, nor do they see as mortals do.* And the Psalmist says: *The eyes of God see all things, and nothing can be hidden from them.*

By these things it is clearly explained that all the mysteries in the world are encompassed in the essence of the internal eye, since it has familiarity with God, with angels, and even with all hidden things in the mundane spirit. Do we not also see, in the contemplation of the greater world, two eyes in it conducting and governing the whole mass of the visible world and all its members? Namely, the Sun—which the Platonists quite aptly called the right eye of the world—and the Moon, which they called its left eye. And yet, we recognize that within the visible sun there is an invisible eye of the world, which is called the "invisible light of the world" by the Holy Scriptures, inasmuch as He "placed his Tabernacle in the Sun." For it is not the solar mass that illuminates the world and looks upon all things in it, but it is that divine mind which, descending from its Empyrean and supernatural throne, establishes its natural Tabernacle in the center of the sun (as a worthier substance), providing it with the power of seeing, illuminating, and quickening. In plainly the same way, it is not the human eye that sees, but that spirit—illuminated from the Empyrean seat of the intellect or mind, carried downward on the wings of reason—which penetrates through the visual organs or optic nerves. It descends into the circles of vision and, in their centers—namely, the **crystalline humors** <note>The lens of the eye, which early anatomists believed was the primary organ of sight.</note>—it builds its palaces as seats more suitable for its clarity. From their centers, through the pupils of the eyes, they emit their power...

Section I. Portion III. Part III. Book V.

...emit a bright light to see some object, no differently than the worldly Sun sends its rays to a portion of the earth or a cloud. These rays, flashing with the invisible brightness of the mind and leaping out from the center of the **crystalline humor** <term>crystalline humor: the lens of the eye, which early scientists believed was the primary organ of sight</term>, gradually and step-by-step expand themselves. This occurs just as two lines of an angle, proceeding from a single point, are observed to move further apart from each other the further they extend in length from that center. From this it happens that the base of these projected rays is formed and terminated at the object seen, while the tip or "cone" remains in the center of the eye. From this we can contemplatively perceive a divine truth: that just as the point or "unity" of this pyramidal motion is in the middle point of the crystalline humor, while the final "multiplicity" of that same motion is in the object seen; so also it is concluded that the first actor in that center or point has a very close relationship with God. For He is the **One and the Monad** <note>original: "vnus & monas"</note> who immerses Himself through His emanation into multiplicity, just as the ray of the mind travels here from the center—the cone of the pyramid—to its base. In this emanation, it always immerses itself more and more into the depth of matter until it reaches the pyramid's base. For in this way the world was made, and the divine spirit immersed itself deeper and deeper into the fabric of the world, from the center of unity into the worldly multiplicity. 

Therefore, as we see in the emission of solar rays, at the object where the base of the pyramid is located, the superficial rays meet and are reflected back into the center of the base. There, both extremes meeting together in the middle, they radiate with equal resistance in a direct motion back to the center of the sun. (This motion is called the **axis of the pyramid**, which is the formal line tending through the middle of the pyramid from the center of the base to its cone.) This is further confirmed by what we see in a round concave mirror: all the exterior rays are contracted in the center, and through their resistance in that spot, the entire image being viewed appears to leap out from it in a straight line. The matter is exactly the same with the rays reflecting from the center of the eye to the base, and from the base through its center back to the cone; for by this straight reflection, the truth regarding the external nature of the object is declared to the sense of sight. In this way, by a spiritual messenger, that image of truth is carried back from the center of the eye to the **throne of reason** by a certain backward or "retrograde" motion. Reason then judges this image and, accordingly, instructs the natural soul with either hatred or love, appetite or loathing, or neutrality; and through its messengers, it instructs all the members of the body either to avoid the thing seen or to embrace it with love.

First, therefore, the **animal sperm** <term>animal sperm: here referring to the "animal spirit," a highly refined fluid or "breath" that early physiologists believed traveled through the nerves to facilitate sensation and movement</term>, or the animal spirit of the first degree, is prepared in the **choroid plexus** <note>a network of blood vessels in the brain's ventricles</note>. Its purpose is to serve the senses and motion. It is a messenger sent by the intellect to conduct such an inquiry, carrying the command of the mind to the "crystalline palace" of the eye. That command in this **microcosm** <note>the "little world" of the human body</note> is like the Word of God in the **macrocosm** <note>the great world or universe</note>, surrounded on all sides by intellectual light and divine brightness. This is the first act of both life and vision, which has placed its tabernacle in the microcosmic eye, no differently than the Word of **Jehovah** <note>original: "Iehouæ"</note> in the sun. 

The spiritual sperm of the second degree or purification is the immediate vehicle for this intellectual light or brightness. It is carried upon the wings of the first spirit just as the celestial spirit or soul is carried upon the wings of the air or wind. For this spirit is extracted from the "cream" of the vital spirit, which flows and floats abundantly in the **rete admirabile** <term>rete admirabile: Latin for "wonderful net," a complex of blood vessels at the base of the brain where spirits were thought to be refined</term>. This floating, invisible cream, created by purification, relates to the coarse animal spirit as the **ether** (in which super-celestial qualities abound) relates to the air. For in it, the brightness of not only life but also the intellect holds dominion. This is the reason that the images in the pupil of the eye are seen as living and sparkling; it is because of the abundant presence of these flashing rays. Nevertheless, in people near the extreme danger of death, these rays are observed to be absent and failing for three days before passing, which is a most certain sign among physicians of the death to follow. The reason for this is ready at hand: namely, that due to the weakness of nature, the animal faculty is unable to prepare and purify its "sperms," through which the intellectual brightness must be carried and conducted to the crystalline seat of vision. This is also the reason why the sight of those suffering from an external and long-lasting disease is so weak and dull that it cannot look at light or tolerate the sun's rays. Clearly, because nature is weakened by sickness, it operates only slowly and feebly in the company of the animal spirits; consequently, the divine brightness of the mind is emitted only sparingly to the "crystalline mountains" or watchtowers of the eyes. From this it follows that due to the lack of this shining soul-light, the eyes are rendered tender and weak.

# On the Mystical Anatomy of the Brain.

It is observed that quartan fevers <note>original: "febres quartanas"; fevers that recur every third day, historically difficult to treat and here linked to spiritual causes</note>, which are usually produced by the worst attacks of besieging malignant spirits, are driven back and cured by this part; this could certainly not be accomplished unless a great celestial power and efficacy were present in this <term>petrous</term> <note>original: "petrosæ"; the "stony" part of the temporal bone at the base of the skull, the hardest bone in the body</note> part, as we shall explain more extensively elsewhere. But truly, regarding the cure for <term>Epilepsy</term>, it has been observed by some diligent investigators that in the skulls of certain hanged men (which they say happens and is found only in those who die a violent death) a certain whitening cross is found in some small portion of this whole bone, about this size: **+**. This portion especially contains the faculty for curing <term>Epilepsy</term>. Indeed, they are accustomed to hold that little piece at a great price, and they believe that no small power and most hidden properties are contained within a transverse bone of this kind.

Furthermore, even the Philosophers most highly versed in the hidden mysteries of nature have made mention of a certain bone hidden in the human body, which they themselves called the <term>Luz</term> <note>A bone from Jewish tradition, sometimes identified as the coccyx or a bone in the skull, believed to be indestructible</note>. Concerning its internal property, the ancients certainly declared great and stupendous things. For these things are written about it: *There is in the human body a certain very small bone, which the Hebrews call <term>Luz</term>, the size of a cleaned chickpea; it is subject to no corruption, nor is it even conquered by fire, but is always preserved unharmed. From it, just as a plant grows from a seed, our animal body will sprout again in the resurrection of the dead.* And they conclude that these powers are declared not by mere reasoning but by experience. And certainly, this is that wonderful little portion in man which never departs from the human body, and through it, it shall remain as a guardian until the final day.

It came into my mind to write these things to you (benevolent readers) so that you might understand that not all things are known to men of common understanding; indeed, as you yourselves may freely admit, more things are hidden from men than have been revealed to them up to this time. Therefore, I would wish for you to receive this <term>anatomy</term> of mine in good part and with calm brows <note>meaning with an open and favorable mind</note>. I implore you to read, re-read, and consider everything point by point before you rashly and thoughtlessly condemn these labors of mine, which (in my opinion) should by no means be lightly rejected. For you have everything we have spoken and committed to writing confirmed both by reasons drawn from the foundations of philosophy, and by the testimonies of philosophers and <term>God-bearers</term> <note>original: "Theophorum"; divinely inspired men or those who carry the spirit of God</note>, and indeed even of the sacred scriptures. Nor is it enough to say that this teaching of ours ought to be rejected or cast aside because it seems new and has been very little opened or publicized until this day; rather, we think it should be weighed all the more in the scales of justice, as we find the treatment of philosophy and medicine among us to be more uncertain and deceptive. However, in our next treatise, which discusses the causes of diseases, we hope to make all these things clearer—indeed, to make them so evident that we believe no one endowed with a sound mind will doubt these matters any longer. In the meantime, we pray from the heart for sound minds in sound bodies for you. <note>original: "mentes sanas in corporibus sanis"; a reference to Juvenal's famous ideal of health</note>

->THE END.<-

# JOHANNES KEPLER,
## MOST CELEBRATED PROFESSOR
### OF MATHEMATICS <term>Mathematics (Mathesis): In this era, this term referred to the "quadrivium"—arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy—viewed as a single interconnected body of knowledge.</term>.

<image-desc>A large square woodcut decorative initial 'Q' containing a figure amidst foliage.</image-desc>*Because your letters (given on a brief occasion) reached my hands so suddenly (Most Excellent Man), I have been bathed in no small joy and drenched in unexpected delight. Nor indeed would I wish you to think that I have emerged happy and eager solely from their long-desired presence, since from them—as well as the Defense* <note>original: "Apologia"; this refers to an appendix Kepler added to his 1619 work *Harmonice Mundi*, where he attacked Fludd's "theosophical" methods.</note> *annexed to them—I noticed that your indignation toward me has flared up publicly. On the contrary, my sadness in this matter would be increased and doubled, had I not perceived that you (by no means called or incited to this) have plunged a finger, armed for the violation of my honest reputation, into my works with a rash appetite. But because your Defense, emerging recently into the light like a public envoy, seems in a certain way to excuse its master to me and to the world—in that very matter where provident caution warned me and compelling necessity urged me to sharply accuse him in my Analytical Discourse. Truly, by Hercules! You say you wonder what necessity reduced me to responding with a Discourse to your Analysis, since you promised nothing, asked nothing, and objected to nothing. Is it thus, my Johannes, that you play with us? Do you not know that I can still judge colors? Or do you think I am fashioned from a spirit plainly insensible or not at all subject to the touch of the tongue, as if I were one who knows not how to feel the hard blows of words and the burning wounds of writing? But who, by curious observation or diligent deliberation within himself on this matter, would conceive in his mind that a man—so exalted by the light of the intellect, second to none in mathematical science, most celebrated throughout nearly all of Europe for his various gifts of mind, and singing the Harmony of the Heavens* <note>original: "Harmoniam"; Kepler's masterwork *Harmonice Mundi* (The Harmony of the World) argued that the same mathematical ratios governed planetary orbits and musical scales.</note> *in his own divine mathematical manner—could have fallen into such a moral antipathy? To the point that, by way of comparison and with no evident cause preceding it, he would bruise a man quite unknown to him—one who was not striking back nor providing him with any just occasion—as if with a leafy club of words, and pursue him with the thick and hostile heels of ill-will? And did you think you would carry away my insults with impunity? Or did you believe that the vexation of such a great injury should be passed over in silence, and not washed away by a pen soaked in the sharpness of truth? For what mortal would not strive to repair his own reputation and dignity, wasting away under the splashes of insolence, and restore them with a mutual effort, as it were, and with the balm of truth* <note>original: "Opobalsamo"; a rare, precious resin used in ancient medicine, here used metaphorically for a healing or purifying truth.</note>*? Since even the fly is endowed with its own spleen, and the little worm with gall* <note>Fludd invokes the Latin proverb "habet et musca splenem" (even a fly has a temper), meaning that even the humblest person will defend themselves when provoked.</note>.

# PREFACE.

...fortified against the invasions of enemies and the insults of opponents in every way, they seem to declare this by a certain natural instinct. But indeed, you dream of yourself established in the pulpit as usual, and you do not blush to assert that you spoke from it as if to instruct your readers; as if this were a just and fit excuse for the insult offered to Ptolemy and Robert—namely, that by means of it, with no question to be raised in this matter hereafter, you might produce the established foundations of their science upon the public stage like a kind of victim to be offered up to your will. What? Is it because that once great and royal Ptolemy (now buried in the earth by the cruel smallness of fate) cannot plead his cause with a living voice or repel the injuries and crimes of error brought against his honor and dignity; did you therefore think in your mind that Robert—who survives Ptolemy in life though not in glory—would not descend into the arena for his own harmonic cause? Did you think he would not manfully stand his ground, even with Johannes <note>Johannes Kepler</note> fiercely attacking him, even if Johannes had emerged far more learned in the matter of symphony, and even if he were hemmed in by a whole chorus of listeners and disciples and accompanied by the entire crowd or troop of his sect? 

Behold then, and see: beyond your expectation (for you say I have arisen unexpectedly from the crowd, since it was not my own will but a just reason that impelled me to a contest of this kind), I appeared at the next-to-last Spring Fairs <term>Spring Fairs: Refers to the Frankfurt Book Fair (Messkatalog), the primary venue for scholarly debate and book distribution in 17th-century Europe.</term>; I came, I say, into the public view under the title of *Analytic Discourse*. For hey you! You who had begun the comparison—the offspring of this present contention—and who first cast your speech against the laws of my Harmony; you who inquire more curiously than is fair into the deeds of another's business with the subtle gaze of Lynceus <note>A figure from Greek mythology noted for his incredibly sharp sight.</note> himself and the manifold eyes of Argus <note>The hundred-eyed giant of Greek myth.</note>; let it not grieve or shame you if I, returning like for like, have destined a profusion of wordy coins of the same condition for the reward of a slanderer or detractor. For this is a Christian admonition: that we should not do to another what we would not want done to ourselves. We find it commanded in the scriptures that an eye must be restored for an eye, blood washed away with blood, and wordy reproaches must sometimes be repressed with the like; for it is said that poison is expelled by poison, and a scorpion crushed into a pulp is said to heal the wounds of its own sting. 

Truly, I was not thinking of building or contriving anything contrary to you or your Harmony out of malice, nor was I stirred to such an end driven by the stings of envy. Rather, a double occasion invited me, and a twin caution persuaded me, to act boldly in my own cause against those casting errors upon me: namely, that I might first show the learned of the world how much easier it is for one skilled in Philosophy than for one endowed with even mediocre gifts of genius to defend the foundations of his Philosophy—however much they are obsessed and attacked by words steeped in insult. This is especially true since they are fortified by a triple demonstration, like an invincible faction of armed men—armed, I say, with the most powerful reasons of Physics, crowded with the frequent authority of both Philosophers and Theosophers <term>Theosophers: Here referring to those who study divine wisdom through nature and revelation, a title Fludd claimed for himself in contrast to Kepler's more mathematical "Astronomy."</term>, and finally (which is more effective than any argument) derived and confirmed by a most certain chorus of ocular conclusions from the hidden mystery of the five elements and their spiritual operations. 

Afterward, I acted so that I might indicate to the reader—borne aloft on the wings of justice—that it is just as possible for me, Robert, to reject and make cheap the laws of Johannes's Harmony with eyes closed and a hardened heart, as it is for you, Johannes, to refute or inflict injuries upon his own. For it is not difficult for one who is willing to fashion those lies and things least consistent with the truth—supported by some probability from the most depraved opinions and arguments—which seem either new to the ear or arduous beyond the reach of common thought; which, nevertheless, if they are inspected a little more accurately, are judged not only evident to be discovered, but truly possible, indeed easy to do. Therefore, the [laws] of the Harmony of Physics...

# PREFACE.

...of Robert’s [har]mony, you have tried to overturn with astuteness and mathematical subtlety. If indeed, with equal skill and with reasons gushing from nature’s own storehouse, I should attempt to tear down those foundations of Johannes in a reciprocal effort, would anyone think that Johannes—stirred to an unjust indignation even beyond the measure of the deed (an experience familiar to scholars wrestling with wordy swords in the castle of Minerva <note>original: "castro Minervae"; a metaphor for the university or the goddess of wisdom's domain</note>)—would rage against me? Since when like is returned for like, is it not deemed fair and honorable? 

But at the end of your *Defense* <note>original: "Apologiae"; referring to Kepler’s *Apologia adversus Fluddum* (1622)</note>, you say you were provoked by frequent injuries and had cause for lighting up in anger everywhere. By Hercules, you are singing my song! I, who—striking only once at you who strike twice—having already been hit by a double blow, would have had a double cause for anger compared to your single one, had I not heard you yourself on page 50 kindly asserting that the wit and jokes of debaters were merely the sauces <term>embammata <gloss>savory sauces or condiments used to season meat</gloss></term>. 

Just as I have now been present as a guest at two of your "philosophical banquets" by invitation, and there I discovered that the arrangement of the feast was not so much composed of physical harmony as it was seasoned with the bitterness of words; so also I feel you at my own table and meager meal—which is hardly dissimilar, though I feel you are weighed down only once by my invitation, more out of indignation and weariness than by the food, despite it pleasing the palate—and so I see each of us inclined toward peace and quiet. Therefore, with the vessels of ill-will’s food quickly removed, and the harmful cups of this enmity banished into exile beyond the northern <note>original: "hyperboreos"</note> mountains, let us finally be so reconciled; let us (if it please you) conclude these complaints—or rather, these philosophical brawls. 

Let us approach friendship according to your wish; let us cement it, though begun from a dispute (albeit a philosophical one); let us indulge it; let us, I say, hold its reins most loosely, and so that I may correspond almost word-for-word to your speech delivered on page 50: Behold, you find me mitigated and appeased by that equanimity of yours, and I do not see (provided you act with fairness and goodness) what will prevent us in the future from cultivating a literary friendship <note>original: "amicitiam literariam"</note>, and that whatever talent <note>original: "Talentum"; referencing the biblical Parable of the Talents</note> each of us has received from God, he should bestow it to the praise of the Creator and the instruction of his neighbor without the disparagement of the other; and whatever well-written things one finds from the other, he should accept and enjoy with a grateful heart, venerating the spirit of the Giver. 

Indeed, I truly judge that man worthy of suffering the extremes—if there is anything more extreme than the last extreme—who, without being compelled or incited, delights in preferring brawls and contentions to the peaceful contemplation of God and Nature. Whosoever of us, therefore, shall attempt in the future to resist the rules of this friendship first offered by you, let him be deservedly struck. But in the meantime, I would have you know this: just as I have proposed to myself to think nothing to your ruin hereafter, nor to act against the laws of your *Harmony* <note>original: "Harmoniae"; likely Kepler's *Harmonices Mundi*</note>, so also may God grant me better than that, through even the slightest negligence of mine, any part of either the *Harmony* or my own *Physical Works* should suffer even the smallest bit of indignity or insult. Rather, if anything in your *Defense* should look unfavorably upon any member of them, I shall not cease to wash it away with arguments drawn from the fountain of truth (with your permission and with the bonds of our friendship remaining safe); in which business I hope Johannes will admit the effectiveness which Robert, in this his **Reply**, desires neither to twist toward a serene brow (as he says on page 4), nor to hurl back at anyone except the one who strikes.

# REPLY TO THE APOLO-
## GY REGARDING ANALYSIS I.

Whether Johannes <note>Johannes Kepler</note>, in his comparison, seems to accuse me of ignorance—albeit secretly—I gladly leave to you, Reader, who weighs all things in the scales of justice. And who is to be found in this deceptive world so just, and so sincere in the truth of the matter, who, when comparing his own work with another's, does not usually prefer his own, or place his own after another's, however much more excellent it might be? Johannes made a voluntary comparison between his own Harmony and that of Robert <note>Robert Fludd</note>. What then is more to be expected than that Johannes, being closest to himself, should bestow extraordinary honors upon his own Harmony, but contaminate that of Robert with the foulest opinions? He tries, with his mathematical astuteness, to make those things seem like lies which are most truly put forward by us, and are felt to be easy in the doing. But even now, the outcome will prove the deeds. For:
> *On page 41, he breaks out into these words: I have uncovered more of the divine works in my harmonies than you have in yours, you who indulge in private conceptions of the world, confirmed by no sense-perception.*

But because I would by no means wish the Reader to be burdened by a multitude of pages on my account, I set out here to recite and re-measure those few parts of Johannes's Comparison—those which cast I know not what errors upon me. By these, it may be shown more clearly to the benevolent and just Reader that a just occasion was offered to me for repelling the insults of my attacker, and for washing and wiping away my dignity—stained by the outbursts of envy—as if with the waves of truth. These are his words:
> *Text 10. Therefore, in his own work there are many pictures; in mine, there are mathematical diagrams provided with letters. What? Or why this comparison between pictures and mathematical diagrams, unless he would thereby intimate to the world the vanity of pictures, but the utility of mathematical diagrams?*
> *Text 11. Let him see that he himself is greatly delighted by the dark riddles of things, while I strive to bring the things themselves, though wrapped in obscurity, into the light of the intellect. That former way is familiar to the Chemists, the Hermeticists, and the Paracelsians <note>followers of Paracelsus, a Swiss physician known for occult and chemical medicine</note>; this latter way is proper to Mathematicians.*

Here, indeed, it seems to be made known to the world that my Harmony is useless because it is wrapped in dark riddles; and thus he unjustly attempts to draw learned men away from my Harmony with his foulest opinions. But indeed, so that his own work might be held in respect and honor, he claims that it is open, clear, and entirely devoid of parabolic shadows.
> *Text 12. Where he treats the same material as I do, this is the difference between us: what he himself takes from the ancients, I dig out from the nature of things and establish from the very foundations. Those things he has received, he uses in a confused way because of the varying opinions of those handing them down, and he uses them uncorrected. I proceed in a natural order, so that all things are amended according to the laws of nature, and confusion is avoided.*

He seems to proclaim many things about himself in this place, O most welcome Reader; but if you look into the matter a little more accurately, you will feel that while mountains are promised, barely little hills are produced. But in the meantime, it must be gathered from the above how austere a judge and how unjust an arbiter he is toward me (my cause having been barely heard, or being entirely unknown to him).
> *Text 13. Where I expressly refute the ancients who differ concerning the causes of consonances, there he follows them without any risk of doubt; he does not even think of truer causes.*

Proceed, then, to fix the wordy trophy of your victory; but in the meantime, I warn you to beware lest you be deceived by your incomplete knowledge of the causes of harmony. Indeed, I perceive clearly enough from your writings that you have not yet tasted the sweetness of the <term>Heliconian spring <gloss>a spring on Mount Helicon sacred to the Muses</term>, or that you have never visited <term>Parnassus <gloss>the mountain home of the Muses and Apollo</gloss></term>, the seat of the Muses. But proceed, I say, with your Comparison, which (on page 5 of this work) you manage to call a "comparison" and not an "accusation."
> *Text 14. Where he introduces Music into the world. Here, indeed, there is a massive difference between us. First, those Harmonies which he intends to teach are mere <term>symbolisms <gloss>symbolic representations or allegories</gloss></term>, about which I say the same thing I say about the symbolisms of Ptolemy: that they are poetic or oratorical rather than Philosophical or Mathematical.*

By Hercules, I see that Johannes holds my Harmony to be poetic symbolisms rather than philosophical ones because he observed that its basis is that **Chaos** mentioned by Ovid, and the **Waters**, **Light**, and **Darkness** so often sung of by Homer and Hesiod, and indeed by Virgil. But indeed, no wise man will judge that there is no Chaos, no waters, or light, or darkness simply because they were celebrated by the Poets. Finally, all Philosophers—both pagan and Christian—confess that these are the original subjects of Physics. What, therefore, shall prevent the foundations of my Harmony, if they be held as symbolisms, from being *philosophical* symbolisms?

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s point-by-point rebuttal to Johannes Kepler. On the previous page, Fludd introduced the idea that Kepler’s "comparison" of their two systems is actually a veiled attack. Here, he delves into the philosophical nature of geometry and numbers, arguing that both he and Kepler use them as symbolic tools to understand the divine.</meta>

# Reply of Robert Fludd

...more than those of Johannes <note>Johannes Kepler</note>, which are founded upon a circle in the soul and its divisions. On pages 16 and 17, he proves that this necessarily follows because the soul is the image of God; and from this, he seems to say that all geometric figures are derived in a plane. But is this anything more than symbolic and parabolic? For the Soul is called a "Circle," and even God himself is so called, but in an analogical and plainly metaphorical way. Nor do I wish or desire to detract anything from Johannes's laws of Harmony, since number is also said to have been the primary pattern <note>original: *exemplar*</note> in the mind of the Creator for the things to be created. But in what way? Namely, insofar as the infinite is declared through it; for nothing is more infinite than number. Furthermore, God's immutability is declared through it, insofar as nothing is more unchangeable than number and its properties.

Therefore, number suggests a simple God insofar as he is immutable; it suggests a wise God insofar as he is foreknowing; it suggests an incomprehensible God insofar as he is infinite; and it suggests a wonderful and singular God in these three aspects. And this is the reason why Theology chose the number three <note>the Trinity</note> as primary and most perfect, wishing to express the first form of all things, arguing from there that He is the origin of all forms and of Light. Furthermore, his greatness is explained through number, which is why mathematicians ascribe the triangle to him, as that figure cannot be broken down into others, nor is it subject to any prior principles. Instead, it is the beginning in every composition of geometric figures and the end in their resolution; for the square, the pentagon, and the remaining figures proceed from it and return to it. It is, therefore, like the first form from which matter received its being, and without which it cannot exist. Furthermore, form is incapable of receiving accidental changes.

From these things, it is clear how God, or the Mind itself (which participates in God), was called a number, or a circle, or a triangle by the Sages <note>the *Sophi*, referring to ancient philosophers and mystics</note>—not because He is truly so, but through likeness and by way of parabolic speech. Therefore, if there is a symbol in my *Harmony*, it is indeed a philosophical one, just as I confess that of Johannes to be a mathematical one; and this I hope is without injury to either his Harmony or mine.

> *Text 15. In his first volume, he divides the world into three regions, where, according to that most famous axiom of Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus; the axiom "As above, so below"</note>, he makes the upper things similar or analogous to the lower. But for this analogy to succeed in all things, the things being compared on both sides must often be dragged by the hair <note>a Latin idiom meaning "forced" or "strained"</note>.*

But now, let the Reader very easily observe where this "Comparison" of Johannes's is heading: let him see whether this is properly a comparison or, as he himself said, an accusation. He continues, however, and treats me generously thus:

> *Text 17. He <note>Fludd</note>, trusting in the ancients, believed that the force of Harmonies came from abstract numbers; let him be satisfied if he demonstrates a concordance between parts, and let him encompass them with numbers in whatever way, with no care for what kind of units are accumulated in that number. I nowhere teach anyone to seek harmonies where the things between which the Harmonies exist cannot be measured by the same measure of quantity.*

But here, good Johannes, you have erred by a whole heaven in this assertion of yours, as is clearly explained in my *Analytical Demonstration*. There, I especially proved that you have not at all understood the physical sense of my Harmony. I also proved that the units of my harmony—taken in an external and mathematical way on the world monochord <note>an imaginary single-stringed instrument representing the universe's proportions</note> (which I fashion as the axis of each Pyramid, where the degrees of form and matter are best explained)—are ordered well, harmoniously, and in just proportion to worldly things according to the pleasure of your Plato and Proclus. I shall not despair of demonstrating this quite openly in this little Treatise. Observe again, good Reader, with what timeliness he presses me here:

> *Text 18. Furthermore, he divides the whole world into three equal parts by means of a radius, knowing well enough that those parts are not at all equal. But he does so only because the first unit is the elemental world, the second the ethereal world, and the third the empyrean <note>the highest, fiery heaven</note>: and truly, units cannot be depicted otherwise than by equality of lines.*

Here Johannes finds much error in the "bad application of units," since he seems to recognize none except those depicted in the equality of lines. He is indeed a man vigorous in Mathematics and so addicted to geometric demonstrations that he has forgotten truly physical and formal Units, which are determined by no dimensions. If it please you, Reader, I implore you to read my *Analytical Demonstration* in this context. Who, then, from this speech of his, would not choose to call it a refutation rather than a Comparison?

You will observe that Texts 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, and 25 are of the same sort and grain <note>original: *farinae*, literally "of the same flour"</note>, if you inspect them with a fair mind. Finally,

> *Text 26. He concludes thus: From these few things, I think it is established that even if the deepest Philosophy which Robert transmits is joined together to understand mysteries, the knowledge of Harmonic proportions is altogether necessary. Yet he who has thoroughly learned even my whole work will still be a good deal further from those most perplexed mysteries than those mysteries themselves have receded from the most accurate certainty of mathematical demonstrations.*

From these things, therefore (as I believe is not hidden from the Reader), Johannes has attempted not a comparison, but rather an express refutation of my Harmony and Physics through the entire discourse of his *Appendix*, and has tried it with every effort. This is so even though he seems to deny it in many places of his *Apology*, among which I have proposed to recite a few here:

> *I have long since asked of you, Robert, that you hold me excused from the crime of detraction or malevolence. I thrust no disgrace upon either you or Ptolemy because you use symbolisms that demonstrate nothing directly. Page 31.*

> *I have established a comparison, not an accusation, for the instruction of the Student of Philosophy. Page 5.*

> *In the title of the Preface: I wonder what necessity drove you to respond, to whom I previously promised nothing, asked nothing, and objected to nothing. Page 3.*

He argues that Kepler’s "comparison" is actually a hostile refutation that ignores the "physical and formal" reality of the universe in favor of abstract lines.</summary>
