### In the Apology for Analysis II & III

> *I have done you no wrong, Robert; I have fixed no mark of envy upon your work out of malice, but I have written about the work for the Reader, as it was born from its own nature. Page 11.*

> *You complain that I attempt to reveal your ignorance and lack of skill to the world. You are clearly deceived, or you deceive. I, as I said, compare my things with yours so that I might instruct the Reader. Page 14.*

> *I say that no injury has been brought upon your doctrine by my comparisons, while I call my harmonic boundaries "Mathematical," but yours "enigmatic, pictorial, and Hermetic <note>Hermetic: Referring to the mystical, alchemical, and occult traditions of Hermes Trismegistus, which Fludd followed.</note>." Page 33.*

> *I do not refute your things, Robert, but I compare my own, so that the Reader may know what to seek from you and what from me. Page 37.*

> *In vain do you arm yourself, Robert; I do not come as an attacker, but as a guest saluting you from a distance. Page 40.*

> *This desire of yours for vengeance could have found more excuse than it does now, where I have used mere comparisons and often built a fence for the benefit of the Reader between your Harmony and mine. Page 47.*

But now I shall turn the thread of my speech to you, Johannes, and I will say boldly that my Physics <note>term: *Physica* — In this context, natural philosophy or the study of the physical world through a spiritual lens.</note> pertains neither to you nor to your mathematical harmony. Therefore, the mark of envy is to be assigned to you rather than to me, for it was you who began this kind of contention or dispute between us, and you were the first to cast your speech against my Physics. Therefore, let the eye of the reader and of justice bear witness—to whom I commend my present case—whether that speech of yours delivered on page 41 is appropriate or not. "Nor now," you say, "ought I to wink in silence, but rather demonstrate my indignation, because I see you irritated by the envy of injury (which you imagine for yourself from the fact that I gave God His due, having performed my duty by distinguishing between your things and mine); you are," you say, "driven to distraction, haunted by the revenges for this slight offense," and so on.

You are deceived and you deceive, Johannes: for I do not burn with envy, nor do I begrudge your virtue; indeed, I would rather praise it, had I not perceived you—without being called upon or previously provoked by me—rushing headlong against me and my Harmony. For I was attempting nothing against you or your dignity or your Harmony of my own accord, but was compelled and provoked, as befits a wise man, to repel foreign violence with my own strength, and I have undertaken to defend with the utmost effort my fortification against the attempts of an invading enemy. Therefore, let the vice of envy and rivalry be cast upon you, who started these philosophical complaints. For in truth, as far as I am concerned, I praise your inventions in mathematical matters, and I do not envy your success in astronomical matters; but I only ask of you that, since you are eminent in both morality and doctrine, you should not consider it fair or honest to belittle someone equal to you in every science without reason, or to afflict his doctrine with reproach and calumnies, unless you have first been summoned by him into the philosophical or at least the mathematical arena. But I proceed thus to your Apology.

### On the Apology for Analysis II

Whether I might desire to claim some glory for myself in this Analysis, I commit to the Reader, who is carried on the wings of justice. He will undoubtedly find this assertion of yours to be as true as those terms of yours: *Putrefactions, Calcinations, Sublimations, and Reverberations* <note>These are alchemical terms for the breaking down and refining of substances; Fludd is mocking Kepler for using them out of context.</note>, as they pertain to the matter or subject of your Apology or my Analysis.

### On the Apology for Analysis III

I do not wish to dispute further concerning the sense of words or their grammatical application. For let that which was said by you suffice: namely, that you place no part of the distinction in the number of words. Therefore, I shall rather prepare myself for the material parts of this Apology of yours, whose primary intention concerns the contraction or dilation <note>meaning: the shortening or expanding of an argument</note> of speech in teaching about both Harmonies, and likewise in the method of explaining the means and the more convenient and suitable invention or demonstration of the *Diapason* <note>term: *Diapason* — The musical interval of an octave, which Fludd viewed as a fundamental cosmic proportion.</note> consonance.

As for the copious series of words, I acknowledge that it is very necessary and useful for public professors, who are accustomed to preach the art they deal with from a pulpit to their auditors. This is so they can first explain and demonstrate the secrets of the art they profess with a multitude of words and circumlocutions to make them easier for the listeners to grasp, and secondly, so that the space of the appointed hour does not pass by in vain. Therefore, I do not envy Johannes his flow of words; indeed, I rather praise it. Yet it does not follow that Robert’s succinct method of demonstrating in musical matters and his indications through figures should be entirely rejected or neglected, since he has never exercised the public profession of Mathematics <note>term: *Mathesis* — The study of mathematics and its related disciplines like astronomy and music theory.</note>, nor did he propose to exercise it for himself. For although (I confess) the condition and duty of a Public Professor is highly laudable and most worthy of reverence, I nevertheless feel myself neither ready nor fit for such business, being impatient of such great labor and by no means excelling in volubility of tongue.

Certainly (thanks be to God), no such necessity compels me to spend my diligence on any work or condition contrary to my nature or inclination for the sake of obtaining food and clothing; for my once most dear Father, distinguished with the honor and title of a Knight <note>original: *Equitis aurati*, literally "gilded knight," a Knight Bachelor.</note>, and occupied in the Commonwealth in offices of no low condition, and sufficiently fortunate in riches and possessions, left to me a portion or patrimony (which, though not so large, is nonetheless sufficient for the youngest son), by means of which I am able to lead and conduct a life quite elegantly and sumptuously by myself without the help of any Profession or Art. And although the profession of Medicine...

# Robert Fludd’s Reply

I now embrace this profession <note>The profession of medicine and natural philosophy.</note> willingly and gladly, as a science most full of the mysteries of nature and divinity. However, I acknowledge that I am more often absent from its daily practice than engaged in it, because the peaceful contemplation of God and Nature calls me away from worldly business for the most part. This, therefore, is the reason why I have dealt only briefly with various sciences—the fruits of my youth—contracting them into short summaries. My goal was not to instruct completely unrefined or raw students in the manner of a Professor, but rather to advance those already moderately versed in Physics <note>term: *Physics* — In the 17th century, this referred to "Natural Philosophy," the study of the physical world and its underlying spiritual causes.</note> and the liberal arts toward perfection. I wrote succinctly, I say, and I have clearly delineated the matter to the eyes with vivid pictures, so that one might supply the deficiency of the other, and the mystery of Science might be more quickly drawn out by the diligent Searcher.

But Johannes here seems to mock those who strive to teach the eye in place of a multitude of words. He considers very little that sight is more excellent than all the other senses and more existing in itself: for a thing seen is accustomed to make more powerful impressions on the mind than that which is explained by words alone. We say, therefore, that the "marrow" or core of an art is more quickly grasped by a teacher when it is explained with both pictures and words than if it were struck into the ears by speech alone. I praise Johannes’s wordiness <note>original: *prolixitatem*</note> only insofar as I am not ashamed or weary of Robert’s succinct way of writing, mixed with the demonstrations of pictures.

As for what pertains to harmonic means and the discovery of the Diapason <note>term: *Diapason* — The interval of an octave, considered the most perfect consonance in music theory.</note> consonance, and even the revelation of the keys of B-flat and B-natural <note>original: *b. b.* — Referring to the "soft B" (flat) and "hard B" (natural/sharp) which were fundamental to the medieval and Renaissance system of hexachords.</note> from the foundations of Nature: since you, Johannes, so belittle my knowledge in Music and Mathematics, I shall speak of them below in their proper place. There, I hope to make the learned world perceive with open eyes that I am not entirely ignorant of the nature and condition of Johannes’s foundations, and that he has been "as far as the whole sky" <note>original: *toto cœlo erraſſe* — A Latin idiom meaning to be completely and utterly mistaken.</note> wrong in his rash judgment of my works. Yet, you will perceive that I do not, according to my promise, bring anything against you or the laws of your Harmony. For you should know that I have not done this foolishly (however much I have been harassed by insults throughout this *Apology* of yours), but rather I study to soften you through the sweetness of morality throughout this little treatise of mine, rather than to inflame you with indignation or wrath.

### On the Apology for Analysis IV.

And certainly, I distinguish natural Music from artificial music not without justice, even though both are produced from the same foundations. For we do not call a house, or a clay vessel, or glass "natural things" simply because they are all derived from the same natural base—namely stones, wood, clay, herbs, and sand. Rather, they are "artificial," insofar as the foundations of nature (that is, the elements) are mixed, composed, and shaped by the industry of Art according to the Craftsman’s pleasure. From these things, therefore, the Reader may gather whether I am a difficult man in such an assertion, or not?

### On the Apology for Analysis V.

Concerning the manifold division of your time; concerning your wonderful experiment between the low and high strings constituting the sound of the Diapason, by which you say you measure the space between the *systole* and *diastole* <note>The contraction and expansion of the heart during a pulse beat.</note> of the human pulse; whether the measurement of the "beat" <note>term: *tactus* — The basic unit of time or "pulse" in Renaissance music.</note> has no place, as you say, in the Harmonies of the Planets; whether the Harmonic proportions of the planets consist in the length of their periodic times, or not; and if they appear in the real motions of the planets, as if from the center of the Sun, are these the Harmonies to be sought? Whether the motion of the *Auges* <note>term: *Auges* — The apogee or the point in an orbit farthest from the center; Fludd is questioning the physical nature of astronomical points.</note> is not physical?

I say that sharp and tedious disputes and controversies can be made about all these things. But I do not intend to judge or debate them in this place, lest I should bring boredom to the Reader or be troublesome to you and your studies by inciting you to further anger. Whether the "time of duration" can be considered in the Harmonies of the Planets, as it is in human song: you deny it, and yet they are distinguished from one another by time (namely, the duration of motion). It seems to me they do not behave according to only one respect of time. But I acknowledge all these things (to speak with your own mouth) have been "entirely poured into the divine power of Robert’s genius" <note>Fludd is here quoting Kepler’s sarcastic or backhanded compliment back at him.</note>. But whether Robert is deceived in these matters or not, I do not wish to inquire too curiously, nor to contend further with you, since these things pertain to *your* Harmony, against which, according to my promise, I wish to produce nothing adverse hereafter, lest I make you more resentful or excite you to new anger.

### On the Apology for Analysis VI.

Tones can be called dissonant intervals in one respect, but consonant in another; therefore, I have not denied the assertion of the ancients in this either. For according to Guido the Monk <note>Guido of Arezzo (c. 991–1033), the medieval music theorist who developed the musical staff and solmization.</note>, "Consonance is as if sounding together"; unless two voices sound together, it cannot be a Consonance. Yet the tone is counted among the Consonances, of which he himself makes eight in number. Furthermore, practice has taught me that a low string produces a sound with a B-flat <note>original: *B. molli* — Literally "soft B."</note> together with another in B-natural <note>original: *B. duro* — Literally "hard B."</note>; and although that meeting is somewhat rough and harsh, nevertheless, by a sudden inclination, the agreement is made pleasant in its identity. Moreover, we see two tones of the same interval produce sounds differing in number. Nor do I play here with equivocation (as you say), since both the tone and the interval are sounds and harmonize with each other; for otherwise a Tone would not be called a consonance, just as a tone sounds identically with a tone. Nor do I argue that there is a difference in the *kind* of interval between one tone and another, when I have said that the tone of a single string...

### Against the Remarks on Analysis VII

Pythagoras would never have arrived at the mystery of this science without the practice of the striking of hammers. Furthermore, it is also read that Tubal Cain <note>A biblical figure mentioned in Genesis as the first smith; traditionally credited with discovering the principles of harmony from the sound of his hammers.</note>, the primary inventor of Music, was most highly skilled in the practice of musical instruments: Ptolemy also is said to have been by no means ignorant of the practice of Music. Therefore, I do not push these men away from the theory of Music; on the contrary, I confirm them in it even more.

Finally, stirred by I know not what anger, you fall into this exclamation: "O wretched little Philosophers <note>original: *O misellos Philosophos*</note>, who thrust forward their speculations on the work of Creation, when they themselves have created nothing." And indeed, Johannes, you who are so vigorous—I will not say "wretched little"—a philosopher, and such a great Mathematician, what in the name of God have you created? Do you truly know what creation is, what the forging of the world is, or what God left in the power of men, with whom He permitted His Wisdom to remain forever, so that she might instruct him in all things and teach him what is acceptable to God, and how the world was made? Or do you know what Robert [Fludd], since he is a man created in the image of God, is capable of: how much he is engaged in the true practice of Creation? Do you think his science is imaginary, or uncertain in the manner of common Mathematics (I except yours here)? Or do you believe that infallible demonstrations of his Mosaic science <note>Philosophy based on the teachings of Moses and the Book of Genesis.</note>—indeed, even ocular ones—are lacking? You are mistaken, you are mistaken, Johannes, and you wander throughout your whole external heaven, even though you believe you perceive the positions and harmonic motions of the Planets from afar through your optical telescopes. You do not know how to judge the internal mind of man or its more hidden actions. 

Therefore, I will say boldly: if Johannes abounded in as much skill in his Art as Robert does in his, he would stand in a better and more correct state of Worldly Harmony than he does now. And I confess that I exult in this, that I am worthy to be numbered among the disciples of Moses, from whose Theosophical and Philosophical art all other sciences are derived—indeed, even that most sacred and only true Astronomy and Astrology, in which few are engaged, which neither your Proclus <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> nor Copernicus ever tasted, or seem to have tasted. Therefore, do not cry out, I pray, against men not so well known or familiar to you, calling them wretched little Philosophers according to your whim, as if you judged no one comparable to yourself. I know indeed and confess that you are well-versed in common Mathematics; I praise your industry, I magnify your invention, and I do not deny that a pleasure, perhaps not a common one, can be found in it. But yet, this must be felt as unseemly in your acquired glory: that you do not hesitate to so easily condemn men unknown to you for the crime of ignorance. But I attribute this to your bitterness, since I see that you wrote this in an angry mood.

### Against the Remarks on Analysis VIII

Here I will leave you hidden in your corner, since your musical instruments and that new subject of your comparison pertain to nothing. For either you have added superfluous things, or you have cited them for the sake of mocking; I disregard both, and value them at a straw <note>original: *flocci pendo* — a Latin idiom meaning "I value it at a tuft of wool," or "I don't care at all."</note>.

### Against the Remarks on Analysis IX

You say that Pythagoras considered the strikes of hammers before the causes of Music were discovered, and yet you conclude that Robert has today handed down "new" instruments. But Robert seems to reply that although they are new in character or shape, the causes of their Harmony are most ancient, and extracted from the very bowels of nature. Next, you assert that because your book lacks my instruments, you have provided the causes of consonances to your Reader. I respond that I have completed this same work for the Reader (but under another form), though in words not so copious. 

But I would wish you to confess frankly here: do no accidents <note>term: *accidents* — In Aristotelian philosophy, these are non-essential qualities of a thing (like color or size) as opposed to its essential substance.</note> (as you say) except those quantitative and mathematical ones concur in the true explanation of a physical thing? Then you proceed by affirming that among accidents the first kind is quantitative, and you learned this from Aristotle; you say all the rest are secondary. I ask, therefore, what quantity does a substantial form <note>term: *substantial form* — The essential nature or "soul" that makes a thing what it is.</note> admit, which is the first act and the principle of motion, stripped of every external accident? Or what do you make of formal quality? After this, you say that harmony requires both mathematics and physics for the discovery of causes. This is denied, because it is in the nature of harmony to seek out its own causes: indeed, by the very manifestation of its own hiddenness through its admirable motion in the fabric of both the old and the new world—that is, both the macrocosm and the microcosm—harmony is accustomed to manifest its causes even to scientific eyes, with no recourse had to mathematical things. Yet I do not deny that Nature can in some way also indicate through mathematics, though not so openly and naturally. Furthermore, let this also be said by me without sin: that my sacred Physics is the same as Metaphysics.

That Robert uses the word "Harmony" in the widest sense (as he says), I am not ashamed, since I acknowledge a single soul of the world <note>term: *Anima Mundi* — The "Soul of the World," a spiritual force believed by Fludd to animate all nature and connect the stars to the earth.</note> expanded everywhere, which is seen to strike the string of the world's harmony, which is the universal spirit, whose instrument is the entire gathering of the world itself. It is not an error for me that I have placed Music among the Liberal Arts, although it is but the husk and shadow of true formal Music. For who will rightly affirm...

# Reply of Robert Fludd

...will he claim that external things are to be preferred to internal ones, or the circumference to the center, or bodily things to spiritual ones, or the coarse to the subtle? I do not acquiesce (as you seem to imply) in sensible Music <note>Music that can be heard with the physical ears.</note>, but in elemental music entirely, for in it dwells the pulsating form; nonetheless, I say that formal music has formal and internal sounds, just as material music has external ones. For the voice of the spirit is one thing, that of the body another; one is of God, another of an Angel, and another of a man. In this, I seem to stray neither from my Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the divinity of numbers and harmony.</note> nor indeed from the Holy Scriptures. The reason for concords and discords the world will see (I hope) hereafter, and will see that I am no more ignorant than Johannes himself, nor less versed in the Harmony of Plato, Porphyry, Iamblichus, or Proclus. And as you say you have corrected their dogmas according to the rule of Catholic doctrine, so indeed I, insofar as I am a Christian, shall not follow them in all things.

I say the same Music is truly in all things, just as the same **World Soul** <note>original: *Anima mundi* — the vital force that Fludd believed animated the entire universe like a single living creature.</note> is generally speaking; but truly you know that voices or sounds are produced differently according to the proportion of the agent’s action upon the patient <note>The "agent" is the force acting, and the "patient" is the object being acted upon.</note>: just as the same blow makes a different sound in copper, tin, iron, lead, and in the earth, but in the air it is scarcely heard. Furthermore, a strong blow gives a stronger sound in the same subject, and a weaker one a more feeble sound; for a more obedient spirit renders a lighter and more insensible sound, so that bodily things rightly agree with bodily things, and spiritual with spiritual. Do you see here how my Harmony is "equivocal," as you call it? But I say that all Music consists of sounds, although some are sensible <note>perceptible to the senses</note>, while others are by no means subject to the senses. And although I grant that these voices—whether sensible or not—can be demonstrated well enough by mathematical proportions, nevertheless such a demonstration is more analogical, symbolic, and accidental than that **Physical** one, in which the thing itself is explained in its own nature as it is; for nature is closer to its own nature than to something foreign, and it rejoices more in real substance than in imaginary accidents <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that does not affect the essential nature of a thing (e.g., its color or size).</note>. I do not condemn the mathematical arts, my Johannes; indeed, truth compels me to praise and extol them. Yet, in the demonstration of nature, I am compelled to prefer nature itself and its real physical motions—which distinguish the degrees to the eyes—above all mathematical things. For who, except by way of imagination, or by chance, or by analogy, can rightly and infallibly declare the form or the motion and act of form in passive nature through the industry of Mathematics alone?

->In the Defense against Analysis X.<-

Here, you, Johannes, say that my Book abounds in pictures engraved in copper <note>original: *picturis ære excusis* — copperplate engravings, which Fludd famously used to illustrate his complex ideas.</note> by my own admission. I confess it, and I did not feel myself angered by it. But I wonder what delight moved you, or what necessity in your comparison, that you cast words about my pictures and your diagrams, since this would be familiar to any reader—unless it is because you yearn to prefer your diagrams to my pictures. If this is not the case, then what you said was superfluous and useless to your comparison.

You conclude, Johannes, too pompously, as it seems to me, and boastfully, with these words: *“Let me even now bring forth a clearer voice. He who loves the certainty of Mathematical Disciplines receives more utility in learning the harmonic part of Mathematics from my harmonic work than from that of Robert Fludd. But he who desires to feed his eyes on pictures of the character of mystic philosophy (which is usually handed down through enigmas) will not find what he seeks in my book.”* To which I reply: from the mere contemplation of my **monochord** <note>A single-stringed instrument used by ancient and Renaissance theorists to demonstrate the mathematical ratios of musical intervals.</note>, by rightly applying it to the world and the soul of the world, I am able (if I wished) to explain and teach more of the internal truth of harmony to readers in the space of a single day—provided they were even moderately versed in Philosophy—than Johannes can in his many inventions. But I see very well that Johannes has either read nothing but the titles of the books and chapters, or in reading them, he took for enigmas those things which, to one truly looking, are very clear, transparent, and confirmed and demonstrated by visual conclusions. And in truth, I see no reason why Johannes proclaims my "enigmas" to the world, and yearns to publish everything written by me as obscure and parabolic <note>allegorical or told in riddles</note>, while his own work is "lucid and manifest." Yet it is certain and well-known by experience that men well-versed here in England in both Theology and Philosophy—and indeed, even several Nobles of both high and low rank—have become so learned in my physical works by the mere reading of my books (the concatenation and connection of the passages being well observed), that they have blown the trumpets of praise for my philosophy [perhaps beyond my merits], neglecting and almost condemning the **Peripatetic** <note>Aristotelian philosophy, which Fludd viewed as "heathen" and inferior to his Christian-Hermetic system.</note> philosophy of the heathens, and appearing to delight wonderfully in the contemplation of mine. I refer, therefore, myself and my physical Book to the judgment of benevolent readers, praying them again and again that (unlike Johannes) they do not look at the titles alone, but immerse themselves in its true marrow before they judge it. And they will see, I hope, that the matter is far otherwise, and further removed from enigmas than Johannes injuriously and unjustly seems to trumpet—whose sole argument, often chanted, is this: *"What Robert wrote are dark enigmas and hieroglyphs, while I strive to bring the things themselves, involved in obscurity, into the light of the intellect."* It is as if he were saying: "Come, embrace my doctrine, for it is clear, easy, transparent, and pleasant; flee that of Robert, for it is enigmatic, Hermetic, and dark." But Robert denies this argument of yours, and says that there is greater difficulty in perceiving the foundations of your Harmony (as we shall declare below) than those of mine, if the matter is properly considered.

# Regarding the Apology to Analysis XI

You think you burden and vex me much here with these words, "Hieroglyphic" and "enigma," and you have me as a supporter of the fact that I have used hieroglyphics in my writings. It is conceded that I said my Musical Temple <note>Fludd refers to his complex diagram of a "Temple of Music" from his *Utriusque Cosmi Historia*.</note> stands in place of a hieroglyphic sign; but I would particularly want the Reader to understand that a hieroglyphic either remains veiled in its own obscurity and mystery, or it is revealed and manifested once its curtain or veil is drawn back, its interior disclosed, and it is explained by letters and interpretations. I say the Musical Temple, without the keys and notes expressed within it, would be a Hieroglyphic image, a thing as obscure as the pyramids of Memphis; but with the keys and notes expressed in it, it differs not at all from the Musical System of Guido <note>Guido of Arezzo (c. 991–1033), the monk who developed the staff notation and the "do-re-mi" system still used today.</note> and others most skilled in Music. Furthermore, we have demonstrated every part of it with letters and writings, and so it is with my other pictures. Here then, Johannes, you have a Hieroglyphic that is open and not hidden. And how, I pray, do the mathematical images explained in your books differ from such hieroglyphics, if they were not demonstrated and explained by letters and writings? Moreover, if the Reader looks at your *Forerunner* <note>original: *Prodromum* — referring to Kepler’s *Mysterium Cosmographicum* (1596).</note>, he will find there new pictures closer to hieroglyphic characters than mine. Therefore, these voices and words of yours are empty; and consequently, what you have written in so many lines must be neglected and rejected in a single word. Furthermore, if I produced the opinions of wise men, both the "God-bearers" <note>original: *Theophororum* — those divinely inspired, like Hermes Trismegistus or Moses.</note> and Philosophers, regarding the approval of silence and secrecy, I did not do this to excuse myself for my enigmatic writings, but against your assertion, as you seemed to condemn parabolic writings and enigmas.

Hence, here you seem to afflict me with threats and strike fear into me with "foot-and-a-half-long" words <note>original: *sesquipedalibus* — a literary joke from the Roman poet Horace, referring to long, pretentious words.</note>. Your words are these: > *I would wish you to look to yourself more carefully in the future, lest you harm your own reputation. For as far as I am concerned, I need neither your recantation nor your contrary praise. Nor will you achieve by this persistence that I decline to skirmish with you as often as I can do so without my own expense and with some profit to the Reader.* These are your words, to which I say: I know well enough that my reputation (I warn you here) is in no way placed in your power, such that you could harm it either with your elegance or your mathematical demonstrations. Behold, then, Robert in the philosophical arena (if you should attempt anything against him), prepared to repel any injury offered by you; there you will find me not disturbed by fear of your words, nor struck dumb in a stupor, but armed partly with the shield of truth and partly with the sharp darts of wit. Where shall I seek such philosophical virtue in you? When shall I see it? By what means could I be forced to recant the things I have alleged, or hold you and your power in philosophical matters in such great admiration with unworthy praises? Good God, what boasting words these are, how unbecoming to a man of such fame and learning! Nor would I wish you to think that I brought anything against you for the purpose of preventing you from skirmishing with me; on the contrary, I expected rather an impulsive force from the region of your divine genius. And if in the future you attempt to examine my Works with an even more scrupulous investigation, I would have you expect that I shall pay you back with the same coins of lashes, or at least similar ones; this is the earnest-money <note>original: *arrhabo* — a down-payment or pledge.</note> of my promise: and believe for certain, I lack neither the power to perform it, nor indeed (once the bonds of friendship offered by you and reciprocally accepted by me have been violated) the will.

Finally, you conclude this part of the Apology with these words: > *I fear, as the nation is perverse today, that this injustice might extend beyond words into actual deeds, if some of the readers believe you rashly without inspecting my text.* Would that you, Johannes, had drawn back this tragic curtain, or folded up this theatrical veil, so that I might discern whether this was said by you for good or ill. What, my Johannes, have you suddenly changed from a Mathematician into a Chemist? Do you now delight in speaking enigmas, you who just now rejected parables? Is it because I said, following Holy Scripture, that I acquire the secrets of the sciences through the acquisition of the Holy Spirit, that you speak perversely about me in an enigma, as if any science could be acquired through new inventions without the assistance of the Holy Spirit? I see that you have been spurred into anger by the goads of my Analysis; therefore, I willingly forgive what has been said by you while incensed.

### Robert Fludd’s Reply

I have done this only to show you that it is just as easy for me to notice your errors or mistakes through careful investigation as it is for you to find them in mine. Do not believe this was done out of envy or arrogance, but in the manner of disputants, whose role it is to argue for and against any proposed subject; a task I have begun and brought to a conclusion. Regarding those matters pertaining to your Harmony set forth in this analysis, I will say nothing of them yet, but we believe three things in particular must be addressed by us. 

The first is to explain my own view regarding the natural foundations of your Harmony, a task I would not have approached had I not been invited and incited by these words of yours on page 17, line 11: *“Now go, Robert, and first overturn these parts of nature: undermine these foundations: then finally deny that I have fulfilled my promise or proceeded naturally.”* 

The second is to briefly uphold several philosophical assertions put forward by me (which you have attempted to subvert in this part of your *Apology*). 

The third is to show myself, contrary to your allegations, to be sufficiently well-versed in the Harmony of the ancient Philosophers, and consequently to demonstrate clearly that my Harmony is not so imperfect, so devoid of true demonstrations, or so hidden and veiled in hieroglyphics and enigmas as you, Johannes, have sought to imply in many places. 

As for the natural foundations of your Harmony, you seem to explain them with these words on page 16, near the end: *“It is clear (I say) that I have unearthed the causes of this matter from the nature of things. Do you wish to know, then, what that nature of things is? The human soul is a part of nature: in the Soul shines the Circle with its divisions through regular planes, because the soul is the image of God. From the division of the circle, which exists in the very essence of the soul, the terms of intellectual harmonies are established according to Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who argued that mathematical concepts exist innately in the soul.</note>—in the world, like yours, or in the intelligible world, like Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD), another Neoplatonist who emphasized the mystical and mathematical structure of the universe.</note>, or as I do in the divine mind, of which the human mind is the pattern, retaining the character of geometric things from the birth of man from its Archetype. Furthermore: Hearing is a part of nature, and it testifies to sounds and their quantities, which the common sense represents to the intellect. If a proportion is found in these that was already shining in the intellect from its origin, these sounds are judged to be harmonic: from this arises delight from them. This is so in general. Now specifically, the Triangle is a part of the nature of intelligible things, the Square is another part, and so on for the others; and each one divides the circle into parts, which by their quantity or length become the terms of some harmonic proportion. To the number of consonances thus established follow the remaining natural things that exist in artificial song.”* 

Now go, Robert, etc., as was said before. 

Behold, my Johannes, I, your Robert, am ready to show you courteously what I think of these foundations of your Harmony, in words that are succinct, yet neither hieroglyphic nor parabolic.

As it seems to me, from these foundations of your Harmony, various questions and doubts arise that are not easily resolved: namely:

> I. Whether the human soul is a part of nature.
> II. Whether the Circle with its divisions through regular planes shines in the Soul because the soul itself is the image of God.
> III. Whether the terms of intellectual harmonies are established from the division that exists in the essence of the soul itself in the divine mind, as Johannes Kepler wishes: of which the human mind is here the pattern, retaining the character of Geometric things from the birth of man from its Archetype?
> IV. Whether Hearing is a part of nature and testifies to sounds and their qualities, which the common sense represents?
> V. If a proportion (from the aforesaid) were found shining in the intellect from its origin, are the sounds to be judged harmonic, and does delight arise from them or not?
> VI. Whether the triangle is a part of the nature of intelligible things, and the square another part, and whether each divides the circle into parts which, by their quantity or length, are terms of some harmonic proportion; and whether to the number of consonances thus established follow the remaining natural things that exist in artificial song?

Regarding the most important of these questions, my Johannes, I begin in order—not to contradict you in any matter or to bring any harm to your Harmony, but solely for the sake of disputation, and as one Philosopher provoked by another toward the resolution of certain questions beyond his own opinion:

### Is the Human Soul a Part of Nature?

->*Contrary to your expectation, I hold the negative view on this question:*<-

1. Because Nature, insofar as it has the character of the universal soul <note>original: *anima vniuersalis* — the "World Soul" or *Anima Mundi*, a concept suggesting the entire universe is a living being.</note>, functions as a whole, and is not divided into essential parts, as Plato testifies.
2. Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the *Hermetica*, texts on philosophy, magic, and alchemy that Fludd frequently cited.</note> says that the Soul—namely, the human mind (which he did not hesitate to call the nature of God)—is no more separated or divided from God than a ray of the Sun is from the Sun.

# In Defense against the 12th Book of the Annals

3. Plato, along with Aristotle, seems to affirm that the Creator of all things possessed the Soul as a complete whole before any division. And Plato called this soul "Universal Nature" <note>original: "Vniuersalem naturam"</note>.
4. Plato says that the Soul, when separated from bodily laws, does not become a "number" possessing quantity, nor is it divided or multiplied into parts, but is uniform.
5. And Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who focused on theurgy and the soul's relationship to the Divine.</note> seems to agree that the Soul, although it appears to contain all principles and forms within itself, is nevertheless always determined according to some single unity.
6. Finally, Pythagoras and all other philosophers endowed with some divine insight recognized that God is one and invisible. Thus, we argue by way of syllogism:

> That which was a complete whole before any division is not a part of any thing,
> But the Soul was a complete whole before division,
> Therefore, it cannot be a part of nature.

The "minor" premise is proven by the third axiom cited above. 
But if you say to the "major" premise that the Philosopher <note>Commonly referring to Aristotle, though here used generally for the authorities cited.</note> understood this to mean the World Soul <note>original: "Anima mundi"</note> or the Total Soul, while you are speaking of the human soul, we reply with the fourth axiom: that the Soul separated from bodily laws is not a number, nor is it divided. But that World Soul—which according to Plato and the third axiom is Nature itself—is separated from bodily laws; therefore, the human soul cannot be counted as a "part" of it, since it is indivisible, according to axioms 2, 3, and 4.
Or I shall deal with you another way, taking an argument from your own mouth:

> The Image of God is not a part of any thing,
> But truly, by your own concession, the human soul is the image of God,
> Therefore, it is not a part of Nature.

The major premise is clear, because God is one and indivisible, according to axiom 6. 
The minor premise is your own assertion, as declared in the second question, and the discourse of Hermes Trismegistus <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the "Hermetica," a body of texts on philosophy, magic, and alchemy.</note> regarding the vastness of the Mind declares this. (Axiom 2).
Now indeed, we shall hurry to the second question:

## Does the Circle, with its divisions through regular planes, shine forth in the Soul because the Soul is the Image of God?

I shall not hesitate to deny this question as well, supported by the strongest votes of the Philosophers and incited to this by the following: 
1. First of all, Plato says that the Soul, separated from bodily laws, is not a number having quantity, and thus it is neither divided nor multiplied. Rather, it is uniform, returning into itself, and rational, surpassing all bodily and material things.
2. Aristotle and Plato say that the Creator retained the soul as a complete whole before division; and Pythagoras makes it "one" within itself, and says that it has its unity in the intellect.
3. Pythagoras, writing to Eusebius, recognizes that God is unity and indivisible, and says that duality is the Devil and evil, since in duality there is multitude and materiality. And Plato holds that all good exists through the "one," but that Evil exists because of confused multitude.
4. Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), the Roman statesman whose philosophical works often blended Stoic and Platonic thought.</note> says that there could be no perfection of order in all the parts of the world, unless they were made continuous by a single, divine, and continuous spirit.

5. God can neither be defined, nor divided, nor composed.
6. God, infused in all things, is called by the Platonists the "World Soul," which they say has the character of the whole, insofar as He, being universally diffused, fills and invigorates all things.
<margin>Duns Scotus.</margin> <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major High Medieval scholastic philosopher and theologian.</note>

8. The Pythagoreans and Platonists, enclosing the Soul within seven limits, say that it rests in the first limit within the highest intellect, and they then say it is made one and the same with it.
<margin>The Art of Chemistry.</margin> <note>Likely referring to the "Ars Chimica" or alchemical tradition, which Fludd integrated into his philosophy.</note>

10. Hermes Trismegistus says that God is a center of any thing, whose circumference is nowhere.

Thus, therefore, we argue against your assertion based on these Axioms of the Philosophers.
**Argument I.**

> That which, taken by itself, is not a number and has no quantity, certainly does not receive within itself a quantitative figure (such as a circle).
> But the Soul, separated from bodily laws, is not a number, nor does it have quantity,
> Therefore, the Soul does not receive a quantitative figure (such as a circle) within itself from its origin, and consequently, the circle does not shine forth in it at all.

### Robert Fludd’s Rebuttal

The major premise is evident in this: that which is not a quantity cannot receive quantities, just as "one" does not admit a multitude and, consequently, is not a number.

The minor premise is confirmed by the first axiom, and similarly by the second and third, by which the Soul is proved to be "One." If you respond that the Soul, as you define it, is not separate from physical laws because it is human, I say that you have misunderstood the essence of the soul. As appears in the following sections, the essence of the soul existing within a human does not differ from that of the "World Soul" <note>original: "magni mundi" (the Great World or Macrocosm)</note>, which is the subject of the first Axiom in the second question, and the second Axiom of the first, where it is proved that the essence of the soul cannot be divided from God. Or otherwise, argue it thus:

> *If the Soul is the image of God, it is neither a quantity nor a number,*
> *But, as you yourself confess, it is the Image of God,*
> *Therefore it is neither a number, nor does it admit quantity.*

The major premise stands because God is neither a "what" <note>a specific substance</note>, nor a "quality," nor a "quantity" according to the seventh axiom, insofar as He is outside and above every logical category.

Furthermore, as for the confirmation of your own opinion (proving the soul to be the image of God), that is supported by the seventh axiom, which testifies that the Soul at some point rests in God, and is made one with Him at the highest limit of its essence. And by the second Axiom in the first Question, the mind is not divided from God.

> *If a circle with its divisions through regular planes shines within the Soul from its origin, as you say, then the Soul is either divided or multiplied.*
> *But the Soul is neither divided nor multiplied, Therefore [your premise is false].*

The major premise stands because if a circle fills the soul—whence it is called a "circle" by the Platonists (though in metaphorical speech)—and that circle is divided into parts by regular planes, it follows that the Soul is also divided by the divisions of that circle.

The minor premise is confirmed by the first Axiom; moreover, through the second Axiom, it is clear that the Creator possessed the Soul as a total whole <note>original: "totale quiddam"</note> before any division. Thus, from the beginning, neither did a circle shine within it, nor did it admit the divisions of a circle through regular planes. But this is declared even more clearly by the following argument:

> *The human soul (even by your own agreement) is the image of God,*
> *But God can neither be divided nor composed of parts,*
> *Therefore, neither can the human soul.*

The major premise stands from what has been conceded.

The minor premise is explained first by the third Axiom, where Pythagoras makes God indivisible. Then by the fifth Axiom. Furthermore, the Platonists call God the "Soul of the World," from which Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a syncretic blend of Greek and Egyptian philosophy; Fludd frequently cites him as a primary authority.</note> says the human soul can no more be divided than a sunbeam from the Sun. And this also agrees with the Holy Bible, where we find that God is the Sun providing man’s life and glory. From these points, therefore, I infer that if the Soul is the image of God, it follows that its divine essence is the same as God's, through which it is also made one with God.

Finally, that axiom of Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), Roman statesman and philosopher.</note> also denotes that God is a single, alone, and continuous—that is, not divided—spirit, by means of which there is a perfection of order in all parts of the world. And this Spirit, as has been said, the Platonists accept as the World Soul; they say it has the character of a "whole," insofar as it is universally diffused, fills all things, and continually governs and preserves them through the power which it liberally pours from the perennial fountain of its spirit into created things daily. It is not, however, as if a circle shone within Him, or in His breath <note>original: "inspiraculo suo"</note>—which imparts life and fiery love to the "waters" <note>likely referring to the primeval waters of Genesis</note>—even though the human soul is also continuous. Rather, He is said to be in all things, or all things in Him, just as numbers are within unity, or as all the straight lines of a circle are within the center, or as the powers of the limbs are within the soul.

For just as unity is the common measure, source, and origin of all numbers, containing every number joined uniquely within itself, and is the principle of all multitude—yet is itself indivisible and innocent of multitude, always the same and immutable—so in like manner created things relate to the Creator. And just as the individual human soul exists as the ruler of its body, present as a whole to the whole body and to every part of it, so similarly God is everywhere in this world and presides over all creatures in it. And this is what Hermes seems to declare clearly when he defines God as "the center of every thing," and elsewhere: "whose center is everywhere, whose circumference is nowhere."

Therefore, as a center is a point scarcely imaginable, and a point is the smallest part of quantity, so it does not seem likely that the largest and most capacious figure of Geometry <note>the circle</note> could be received within its being, much less be divided into smaller parts. And yet from that point, majesty and power shine forth into infinity—namely, from a center where no periphery is found, because within Himself is everything that is, and He emits rays of life outside Himself as He pleases into infinity. And this is the reason why He is affirmed truly to be neither defined, nor divided, nor composed, and yet He has all these properties in metaphorical speech—in which sense He is also said to hear, speak, be angry, see with eyes, and touch with finger and hand. Yet that this is metaphorical speech and taken from likeness, I think is hidden from no one endowed with reason. And this same thing can be said of the Soul; wherefore Iamblichus speaks not unwisely in these words: *The soul, although it seems to have all principles and species, yet is always determined according to some single unity.*

These things being so, there is no need to proceed to the explanation or refutation of the four following questions; for when the cornerstone of any structure is weak or fashioned from shifting sand,

# In the Apology for Analysis XII.
## Cc

...breath, it must necessarily melt and be reduced to nothing by itself, and the whole edifice must collapse of its own accord and be reduced to nothingness without any force pushing it.

But nevertheless, God grant me better than that I should do any violence to the principles or foundations of Johannes [Kepler] in this place; rather, I hope—indeed, I know—that he used metaphorical speech there, where he says that the human Soul is a part of nature, and that in it a circle shines forth with its dimensions through regular planes, etc. Yet I shall not imagine his Harmony to be "Symbolic" or "Poetic," as he does mine; for who can explain the wonders of God or of Nature—or of the first-born wisdom—except through likenesses to created things? For God is known through His creatures to be immense, ineffable, unthinkable, above all imagination, above all thought, above all intellect and essence, unnameable, to be preached only by silence in the heart, an incomprehensible depth, an indivisible Trinity, and an immutable essence. Of this, therefore, our very own universal Soul is the image. Whence it is impossible to truly know or imagine that a circle can be found in God, or in that breath of life which He communicated to man, except in a certain allegorical respect; much less that Geometric figures could be found or represented in it by a real or spiritual impression, except by speaking through **analogy** <note>original: "ἀναλογίαν"</note> and likeness. Therefore, the Philosophers spoke of God according to their own capacity and not as He truly is, nor could they judge concerning divine mysteries, which are indeed above all imagination, above all intellect, above all essence, and are incomprehensible. For God the Creator is "enclosed within himself," <note>original: "in feipso claufus est"</note> and no one can know the Father except the Son, nor are His mysteries to be revealed except through His own Spirit.

Yet it is granted to Physicists <note>Natural philosophers</note> and Mathematicians to elicit prior causes through respect to posterior effects. For Physicists—through the due adaptation of the grades of matter to form in the worldly spirit and the elements, as if of the passive or female to the action and the male—derive the harmony of the world from the throne of God. Mathematicians, through Arithmetic and Geometric proportions with proper numbers and measures, attempt to provide this same thing quite skillfully. Physicists describe the spirit of God as being nearest to the throne, most thin and most simple. Mathematicians rise from the multitude toward God by the way of Geometry—namely, from the solid body to the surface, and from that through lines to the point of the angle—or they seek the Harmony of the world from the division of the circle into triangles, quadrangles, etc., and by the apt application of these to the parts of the world; or they seek it via the Arithmetic path by regression from number (that is, multitude) to unity. Physicists seek to strip away form and cast off the confusion of matter, for they believe that by this path there will be an entrance to the sanctuary of the knowledge of God, whose seat is indeed inaccessible light; and they conclude that the more light something has in itself, the more it can claim God for itself; and by these steps they truly perceive and gather the Harmony of the world. Mathematicians seek to demonstrate this same thing through the simplicity of solid figures, through the mean square and resolution into the root. Therefore, a Physicist is not to be despised by a Mathematician because he does not use his own [the mathematician's] invention to demonstrate Harmony; nor the Mathematician by the Physicist, though he may not be so well-versed in physical demonstration; **for one travels from Prague toward Rome by various routes with an effect that is hardly different.** <note>Fludd uses this proverb to suggest that his mystical approach and Kepler’s mathematical approach (Kepler being based in Prague) seek the same truth.</note> Let us therefore join Mathematics to Physics, so that the power thus united may be stronger and more valid for perfecting this work; for a great power and discipline—indeed, an Ocean—is required for the description of worldly Harmony. And yet, in the end of our searching, we shall perceive ourselves as remote from the investigation of the mysteries of God as we were at the beginning; for as the Prophet says, the mystery of God is a great sea, into which many rivers have entered.

Simonides the Philosopher, when asked by the tyrant Hiero what God was, requested the space of one day for the resolution of this question. Returning again the next day into the tyrant’s sight, he was urged a second time to answer his question, but he requested two more days to clarify the matter. Finally, when the term was finished and the tyrant pressed him more often to give an answer to his doubt, the Philosopher used to double his days at every turn. But at last, when the tyrant diligently sought the reason from him, he is said to have received an answer of this kind: "Because," he said, "the more I revolve this matter in my mind by thinking again and again, the more obscure and mystical it indeed becomes to me." The same is also testified by the Holy Scriptures: for just as God is said to be "clothed in light," so indeed is that Light inaccessible. And hence in Wisdom, chapter 9, we find that no one knows the counsel of God, nor can anyone think what God wills; because the reasons of mortals are fearful, and their thoughts unstable. This the leader Moses seems to confirm best in very few words in Deuteronomy 29:29: "The secret things of God no one knows, but they belong to God; however, the manifest and revealed things are known to us and our children." Wherefore it is manifest that even through posterior effects, it is impossible to arrive at the knowledge of the hidden mysteries of God, unless it be through the revelation of the Holy Spirit. But let us hear what the Philosophers say in your favor, among whom I shall here recite the opinions of your Proclus.

First, Proclus seems to assert that the division of the soul is not according to matter or inferior things, but proceeds from an efficient cause: he therefore divides it through its perfect measures of all things, looking toward which the Creator had need to divide this universality in a similar way into intelligible patterns; and he affirms that this division into a multitude is gathered through a harmonic order making the various parts similar.

Plato asserts the Soul to be both divisible and indivisible: namely, he makes it divisible when not separated from bodily laws, but truly describes it as not being a number having quantity, and consequently, neither divided nor multiplied into parts.

Aristotle says (with whom Plato also agrees) that the Creator established the Soul as a certain "total something" <note>original: "totale quiddam"</note> before division.

<meta>This page continues Fludd’s argument that mathematical and geometric terms used by ancient philosophers to describe the soul—such as "circles" or "numbers"—are metaphors for divine unity rather than literal measurements. He draws on a wide range of authorities, including Francesco Giorgio, Plato, Pythagoras, and the Hermetic tradition, to support his mystical interpretation of harmony.</meta>

### Robert Fludd’s Reply

**Francesco Giorgio of Venice** <note>original: "Franciscus Georges Venetus"; Giorgio (1465–1540) was a Franciscan friar whose work "On the Harmony of the World" attempted to reconcile Christian theology with Neoplatonism and Kabbalah</note>, who wrote wonderfully and divinely on the **Harmony of the World**, says that the substance of the soul is a certain unique thing that simultaneously possesses parts—namely, unity and a multiplicity gathered from a wondrous Harmony. He says that whoever wishes to correctly perceive the soul must not apply the limit of their industry or labor to mathematical contemplations, but must elevate themselves as much as possible toward the place most suited to the animal substance. One must weigh in right balances that it is a threefold whole: one part of which is *before* its parts, another *from* the parts themselves, and the last *within* each of the parts. The whole which arises from the production of parts is not consumed, but remains; for that which gives the parts is good and does not even dissolve the composition of the parts. Indeed, this dissolution is a property of a malignant spirit and not a good one. Whence it happens that the whole which precedes the parts survives and remains, while that which is made of parts is dissolved and perishes through the dissolution of those parts. For that which is from the parts is lower, and this is what **Plato** designates through those circles into which the soul is divided. He concludes, therefore, that the Soul is unique and multiple, having its unity in the intellect, and its quality and multitude insofar as it has respect for lower things. Therefore, the soul existing through itself is unique and simple, but descending toward lower things, it is said to be divided. And this is the reason for generation and corruption in lower things. Hence, **Pythagoras** says when writing to Eusebius: **God is in unity, but in duality is the Devil and evil**, for in duality there is material multitude.

Hence it is clear how varied the opinions of writers are regarding the division of the Soul; some wish it to be so according to matter, while others only insofar as it participates in material things. For in truth, the interior soul (which is God himself) neither suffers nor admits divisions; its division, therefore, is in respect to the matter in which it resides, and not from its own essence, which is the same as God, from whom it first emanated. This is according to **Hermes Trismegistus** in the *Poimandres*, book 12: **The Mind indeed is born from the very essence of God, if indeed He has an essence; therefore it is by no means divided from the essence of God, but is connected to it in the same way that light is to the body of the Sun.** This Mind is God in men, and therefore some among the number of men are Gods. Thus says Hermes. From these things, therefore, it is clear that division exists in the multitude which is in matter, and not in the essence of the form. Thus we see the infinite rays of the Sun mingling themselves with the spirit of the world, distinguishing it into infinite parts, though nevertheless those rays are not divided or distinguished from the solar body.

**Plato**, as was said above, seems to divide the Soul into circles, and elsewhere he called the soul a circle. But **Aristotle** is said to have rejected Plato's propositions, not to refute what Plato wrote, but to condemn those terms which sound common and yet have another meaning. Aristotle did this so that people would not fall into error because of the metaphorical writings or terms frequently used by Plato (in which he used to enclose and hide a profound meaning). Francesco Giorgio of Venice provides an example of this: "When," he says, "they read in Plato that the soul is a circle or a number, it must not be believed that this was said according to material mathematics or common arithmetic. Similarly, when he says that all things are but one, it should not be understood as one composite thing or any particular thing; rather, all things are called 'one' insofar as they have the power of existing through the One, just as all numbers have their being from the Unity expanded into them." So says Giorgio.

By clearly similar reasoning, God is called a **Circle** by the Platonists—a circle that does not take its origin from elsewhere than itself, and, tending toward itself, leads all things with it. And yet, by these same thinkers and by Hermes Trismegistus, He is called the **center** of every thing. Furthermore, the same Hermes (as Francesco Giorgio testifies) explains the **Trinity** under the riddle of the **Sphere**, when he says that **God is a Sphere whose center (that is, the Father) is everywhere, but whose circumference (that is, Wisdom and the Son) is nowhere**, because He is incomprehensible, yet He comprehends all things. But indeed, the mutual respect—that is, the harmony and the bond of love—between the center and the circumference, which occurs through the regularity of the proportions of similar radii, is denoted by the **Holy Spirit**. The Spirit is called that **Golden Chain** in the world <note>The "Golden Chain" (*catena aurea*) is a classical and alchemical concept of a vertical link connecting all levels of existence from God down to the lowest matter</note>, preserving all the joints of the world (namely the elements) in peace and concord by its amorous embrace. This means imparting the fiery vigor—the amorous power of life and multiplication—to the waters (the mundane spirit), and filling all things with its harmony in the vast hollow of the world, so that no vacuum should again be given in the nature of things. That verse from *Ecclesiasticus* seems to confirm this interpretation of the circle: **"I alone," says Wisdom, "have compassed the circuit of heaven, and I have penetrated into the depth of the abyss."** Furthermore, it is said that by the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the Spirit of His mouth. That the periphery of this circle is beyond human grasp is clear from these words of the holy man, **Job** (chapter 11:9): **The Wisdom of God is not to be found, for it is higher than the highest heavens, and deeper than the lowest grave; its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea.** You see here, therefore, how enigmatic is the meaning of the Philosophers, and how remote from common understanding, when they call God or the Soul a "Circle," or say that a "Circle" is within them.

Indeed, through the **Harmony** of the same Word leaping forth from the chains of darkness and overcoming the marks of death, all things shall return to the unity from which they previously departed. This is according to that passage of **Saint Paul** previously cited, by which we are clearly taught that not only men, but all other things are led back to their true harmonies through the blood of Christ. His words are of this kind: **"Peace-making through the blood of His Cross all things which are on earth and which are in the heavens."** This extension of the Son (namely Wisdom) from the center (namely the Father), whom the **Cabalists** called the **Dark Aleph** <note>original: "Aleph tenebrosum"; in Kabbalah, the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet represents the infinite, hidden Godhead (Ein Sof) before creation</note> (that is, the hidden God), means that the Son (the Light, the Word) leaping out from this center in every direction like a circle, is called by them the **Bright Aleph** <note>original: "Aleph lucidum"; representing God as He reveals Himself through light and creation</note> (that is, the revealed God). We shall speak of these things sufficiently and copiously below. And the Platonists received this Wisdom of the Hebrews and the Messiah of the Christians, and the Cabalis-

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s defense of his mystical philosophy, specifically focusing on the relationship between the Archangel Metatron, the World Soul, and the mathematical proportions that govern the universe. He bridges Pythagorean number theory with Kabbalistic interpretations of the Hebrew Tabernacle.</meta>

### In the Defense regarding Book XII of the Annals

...Metatron <note>A powerful celestial being in Jewish mystical tradition, often identified as the "Prince of the Countenance" or the mediator between the divine and the human.</note>, and the Word of the Prophets and Apostles as the true **Soul of the World**, which they said harmonically filled all the intervals of the world in the triple, its square, and its cube: namely 3, 9, and 27. This formal and most perfect proportion acted upon the material proportion—2, 4, and 8—as the active upon the passive, the male upon the female, form upon matter, and perfection upon imperfection. Therefore, the active Spirit of Wisdom (namely the angel Metatron) pulses through the aforementioned proportions of perfection into the passive spirit of the world. This passive spirit receives the measures—the impressions of harmonies—from the pulsing spirit, just as a string receives them from a Musician, or a pipe from a blower. Yet the pipe itself, the instrument, is the vast cavity of the World itself, which when the soul strikes it, the divine breath fills it, just as the force of the blower fills the cavity of a flute with his breath.

And here it is demonstrated clearly enough in passing that just as the proportion of harmony (namely of sounds and consonances) was in the flute or the string, and not in the blower or the player, so too the circle—from whose parts you say harmony arises in the soul—was in the thing measured, and not in the measurer. That is, it is in the numbered thing and not the numbering mind, as I will immediately show in a physical manner.

But let us return to the matter: just as the Platonists reduced every act of mundane Music to the cube of the number three <note>3 cubed is 27.</note>, so to explain the harmony of the world, they expressed the three **enneads** <note>A group of nine. Here, Fludd refers to three sets of nine numbers (1-9, 10-90, 100-900) to reach the mystical number 999.</note> concurring in the composition of that cube in a twofold way. That is, insofar as the cube of three is 27, they produced or arranged them from right to left in this way: **999**, by adding three nines gathered into one. Therefore, they attempted to mathematically demonstrate mundane Harmony through the cube, proving the harmonic proportions of form through its parts in the world, as we shall declare below.

**Pythagoras**, most skilled in numbers, intended this same thing when he asserted that perfect harmony is completed through cubes. Whence the Pythagoreans called cubes "harmony," because among other figures, they have angles proportionally equal in sides and surfaces. **Plato** and the **Cabalists** seem to include wonderful mysteries of mundane harmony, both metaphysical and physical, in this series of enneads (999). For according to the Algorithm of the Arabs and Hebrews:
*   The first number toward the right is a simple number contained under the number ten. Because of its simplicity, they attributed to it the formal essence and the **nine Orders of Angels** who are in the intelligible world.
*   The second ennead, which is of tens and in which there is composition, they applied to the **nine heavens**.
*   The last ennead, which is of hundreds, in which the composition is even more material and compact, they applied to the **nine degrees of generable and corruptible things** in the elementary world.

All of these terminate in **Man**, who is like a passage and a medium through which those things pass to celestial things, and from those are again exalted to the intelligible things. And through these intervals perfectly filling the world—so that no vacuum or emptiness is left in the nature of things—the most exact Harmony of the Sages, both of the world and of the soul, is elicited. Yet to specify these things exactly with the Philosophers and Mathematicians is a most difficult task.

Truly, the **Zohar** <note>The foundational work of Jewish mystical thought (Kabbalah).</note> demonstrated this threefold division not by numbers, but by analogy or likeness. For it says there are three things that correspond and are shaped after the pattern of the **Archetype** (the primary Idea): namely, the **Tabernacle of God** prepared by Moses, the **Temple of Solomon**, and the **Human Body**. These correspond to the three aforementioned numbers in the **Macrocosm** <note>The "Great World" or the universe as a whole.</note>:
1.  The **vocal** or operative part, which is drawn from measure to the elementary world.
2.  The **formal** part, which is elicited from the vocal to the celestial world.
3.  The **rational** part, springing from the formal toward the intelligible world.

For the Tabernacle represented by Moses seems to symbolize the three worlds in both the macrocosm and microcosm in this way:
*   **The First Portion:** Which is not covered but open to the air, exposed to winds, rain, hail, snow, and other atmospheric impressions in the sublunary world. It is in perpetual change and alteration. Access is granted here to the common crowd and animals, and there was a constant vicissitude of life and death because of the continuous sacrifices offered there. This portion of the Tabernacle denotes the **Elementary World**, which is composed of grosser waters as a fluid substance, unstable and never remaining in the same state. Whence this is properly called the "World of Shadows and Obscurity," where the Tempter and the Prince of Darkness has his habitation and dominion. Thus it is subject to death, corruption, and mutations. In man himself, this is denoted by his **body**.
*   **The Second Part:** Gleaming with gold and adorned by the candelabrum with seven points (which are undoubtedly symbols of the **seven heavens of the Planets**), denotes the **Celestial World**. It participates in both light and darkness, which correspond to water and fire. Whence the Heaven is called by the Hebrews *Eschamaim* <note>original: אשמים *Eschamaim*</note> from *esch* <note>original: אש *esch*</note> "Fire," and *mayim* <note>original: מים *maym*</note> "Water." From this, "ether" is also called as if it were *aeth-aer*, that is, "fiery air." And hence, although this part is imbued with a body, yet because of the prevailing disposition of the lucid form in it and a certain intellect governing it (as the rational soul governs the body), it does not submit itself to corruption. In man, such is his **soul** or spirit of life.
*   **The Third Part:** The Temple is the **Holy of Holies**, showing the super-celestial or intellectual world in the macrocosm, totally fused from perfect and intelligible light and fire. It is the seat of the Angels ministering before the great God **Tetragrammaton** <note>The sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH.</note>. This is denoted by those two golden **Cherubim**, who are depicted as elegant and extending their wings toward the altar and the Mercy Seat.

This world, therefore, moves the celestial world, and that in turn moves the Elementary. The Super-celestial World is thus "male" to the Celestial, acting upon it as a male upon a female; the universal matrix of the Celestial is the **Sun**, which fills the other stars with its light. Likewise, the Celestial is "male" to the Elementary, whose matrix is the **Earth** itself. In a similar way, such is the relationship or comparison between the outer part of the Tabernacle and the **human Body**; in turn between its middle gilded part and the **human Soul**; and finally between the Holy of Holies and the **Reason, Intellect, and Mind** in man. And hence it is that man is also called by the Apostle the **Temple of the Holy Spirit**.
