# Robert Fludd’s Reply

And from here it arises that, through that respect which is held for the number 999, the division of the fruits and goods of the earth was made in the Mosaic Law: for one hundred portions were destined for the people, and a tenth part for the men of the Church, from which part again a tenth portion was extracted for God himself. Thus, the hundredfold numbers, being more material, coarse, and immersed in the multitude, were reserved for the people, the commoners, and the profane; the tenth for the priests; and the unity for God, who, existing as all in all, is nonetheless nothing but unity. From these things it is clear that all things are nothing but one, when viewed in respect to God, though by the grasp of human reason, things seem to be many and manifold.

And so, as far as the Philosophers are concerned, the Soul and God himself seem to be a Circle, and to receive divisions within themselves, from which they desire to draw out sciences and find various formulas of worldly Harmony. But I would wish that they rightly understand what Jeremiah says on this matter in chapter 9: <note>Jeremiah 9:23–24</note> *Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong in his strength, nor the wealthy in his riches, but in this: that he knows and understands God.* Yet truly, the Wise say one thing and understand another, as has been proven before. But to proceed in this Discourse, and to open the mystery of the ternary number <note>The number three</note> with an even wider gap: the Kabbalists and the Wise of the Hebrews say that this number 999 is found in the Hebrew letters of the most powerful intelligence, **Metatron** <note>original: מטטרון; in Jewish mysticism, the highest archangel and celestial mediator</note>, whom they called the "Prince of Faces," because he has the office of introducing before the face of the Lord those whom he wishes to be called; others take him for that **Soul of the World** described by the Platonists. This Metatron, namely the Soul of the World, was (according to the tradition of the Wise) the first created thing, retaining in himself the perfection of all other Creatures: whence it seems to me that he was that very **Wisdom**, of which it is said in Ecclesiasticus, chapter 1: <note>Sirach 1:4</note> *Wisdom was created before all things, and the understanding of prudence from everlasting:* as will also appear from what follows.

The more secret Theologians and those most expert in the true Kabbalah have said that just as the Mind has dominion over the human Soul, so also Metatron presides over the celestial world (in which he governs the Sun), and the soul of the Messiah over the angelic world, and **Adonai** <note>The Lord</note> over the Archetype <note>The divine blueprint or original world</note> itself. And just as the light of the soul is the active intellect (that is, the Mind itself), so also the light of the Angel Metatron himself (or the Soul of the World) is **Shaddai** <note>Almighty</note>, and the light of the soul of the Messiah is **Elchai**, which signifies the "Living God," and the light of Adonai himself is **En-Soph** <note>original: EnSoph; the Infinite or Boundless nature of God before emanation</note>, signifying the infinity of the Divinity. Therefore, the Soul of the World is Metatron, whose light is that Soul of the Messiah (or the power of the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH</note>), in which is the light of the living God, in which is the light of the En-Soph, beyond which there is no progression. From these things it is clear that in Metatron himself (that is, the soul of the world, or the wisdom created before all things and existing from eternity with God) is the power of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Whence God intended him (as the Wise have explained) when He spoke to the Israelites in these words in Exodus 23: <note>Exodus 23:20–21</note> *Behold, I send my Angel before your face, who shall keep you in the way; listen to his voice, and do not provoke him, etc., for my name is in him.* This "Name" is the Tetragrammaton, which is the Symbol of the Trinity.

Behold, therefore, how powerful and how close to God the Creator himself is that soul of the world, and how profoundly (namely from the En-Soph or the infinity of the divinity) she draws the origin of that spiritual and fiery Harmony, which is the active and formal harmony in the world. This was signified by the Platonists through the ternary numbers 1, 3, 9, 27 (or 999). Its harmonic acts are impressed upon imperfect matter through the binary numbers 1, 2, 4, and 8, according to the Philosophers, following the dignity and proportion of the matter in its purity, subtlety, thickness, or opacity. By its lucid power, it fills the worldly spirit—whether it be thinned by subtilization or thickened by congelation—to a greater or lesser degree. And just as by the act of this universal soul, the unity of the deformed and dark *hyle* <note>term: hyle; ancient Greek term for "prime matter" or raw substance</note> is divided into a multitude (just as we perceive the Sun dividing the worldly spirit into infinite parts with its rays), so also the Platonists understand all those parts created in the beginning to be joined back together by that fiery love. This love is called the "glue" or the "fiery bond of nature," joining its creating form with the things created in material multitude by a harmonic knot: as we see in numbers, where 3 joins 2 to 4, and 6 joins 4 to 8, and so in the rest.

And from here arose the discovery of the triple means—namely, the Harmonic, Geometric, and Arithmetic. Among these, the harmonic mean is truly natural and pertains to physics; the others look to mathematics rather than to nature. From this, therefore, is derived the discovery of the Platonists and Pythagoreans regarding the **Heptachord** <note>A seven-stringed musical scale</note>, where they make their mixtures of the odd number with the even number. They denote by this the "unions"—namely, the progressions or harmonic connections—made between male and female, between light and darkness, between matter and form, between heaven and earth, between the creator and the creature.

This can be approached either by ascending from the lowest base of the multitude toward unity (that is, simplicity), as did Aristotle and the Peripatetics, who used to outline Nature and its consensus through "posterior" demonstrations <note>term: a posteriori; reasoning from effects back to causes</note>. That is, they ascended in their demonstration from the nature of sensible things, through the explanation of the mysteries of the elements and the principles of lower things, up to the heavenly machine and no further—and this through the quaternary number, which is corporeal, material, and sensible. (This number, according to the doctrine of Pythagoras, participates in matter and body just as the ternary number participates in form.)

Or, one can approach by descending through "prior" demonstration <note>term: a priori; reasoning from causes to effects</note> from the supreme Creator of all things down to the lowest level of creatures. This is done through the ternary number, in the manner of the order of the **Sephirot** <note>The ten emanations of God in Kabbalah</note>: first from the intellectual heaven into the ethereal one, and from that into the four elements (the elementary heaven). And from there I have derived my "natural Demonstrations," from the composition of two pyramids—one formal and one material—disposed in a transverse way <note>Fludd is famous for his diagram of two interlocking pyramids: one of light descending from God, and one of darkness/matter ascending from the earth</note>. From these, the degrees and connections of watery matter and lucid form in worldly nature are drawn—that is, the intersections of the **World Monochord** <note>term: Monochord; a single-stringed instrument used by Fludd to symbolize the harmony of the entire universe</note> with their intervals linked to one another in a harmonic bond, about which I have written copiously...

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s philosophical defense against Johannes Kepler. On the previous page, Fludd discussed the mystical number 999, the Hebrew intelligence Metatron, and how the divine Unity relates to the material world. Here, he contrasts various philosophical schools—Peripatetics, Platonists, and Hermeticists—and argues that the World Soul and the human soul are indivisible emanations of God, like light from the Sun.</meta>

### In the Defense of the 12th Analysis

We have treated these matters in the physical *History of the Macrocosm* <note>The "Macrocosm" refers to the universe as a whole, which Fludd detailed in his massive work *Utriusque Cosmi Historia*</note>. From this, it should be noted in passing how varied the methods of philosophizing are among men, and how divided the discovery of the true worldly Harmony has been. Some begin through numbers, and among them, some start with the **binary** <note>the number two</note>, such as the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>; others with the **ternary** <note>the number three</note>, such as the Platonists. Of these, the latter strives to demonstrate matter through form, while the former endeavors to explain the mysteries of form through matter. The Pythagoreans used both formulas. The Kabbalists, the Sages, and the Hermeticists <note>Followers of the mystical teachings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note> attempt to achieve this through the observation and contemplation of the real and living action and passions of nature.

Regardless, all have recognized and confessed that **Golden Chain** <note>original: "Catenam illam auream"; a reference to the Homeric Chain connecting Heaven and Earth</note>, the first link of which they believe is fastened and fixed to the Throne of Jupiter. Slanting downward from that point and stretching through the very marrow of all nature even to the center of the world, it delineates the consonances and intervals of worldly harmony by its links; Jupiter himself strikes and compels the harmonic string of the worldly instrument to vibrate in symphony. This, I say, is that **Jacob’s Ladder** <note>The ladder seen in the dream of the biblical patriarch Jacob (Genesis 28)</note>, by means of which the Angels—that is, the divine minds of men—lean down from heaven and ascend to heaven in an admirable harmony. 

The instrument of this harmony, I say, was that **Stone of Jacob** <note>The stone Jacob used as a pillow</note>, possessing and representing in itself the likeness and harmony of the entire world; for it was called the House of God. Its image was that three-part Tabernacle of Moses, described by us before and related to the three regions of the World. Indeed, in that **Microcosm** <note>Man as a "little world" mirroring the universe</note>, the true temple of God, the true harmony of the world is seen with living eyes: the ratio of formal numbers, the primordial consideration of the binary and ternary, the clear arrangement of darkness and light, the union of passive nature with active nature, the progression of element into element according to the laws of nature, the ratio of perfection of the number three, and the production of that number seven springing from the admirable connection of matter and form (that is, 4 and 3). 

It also explains the **Sabbath day**—namely, the rest in the Lord—and provides a clear demonstration of the seven steps of Jacob’s Ladder: namely, the path through the earth, through the thick water, through the impure air, through the thick fire, through the ether of life (which they establish as the fifth element or the fiery and pure air), through the purely fiery heaven (namely, the sixth element), and finally to the ineffable revelation of the divine essence and majesty, where inexplicable rest and peace—the Sabbath and glory—are most clearly explained forever. For Jacob said: *God is here, and I did not know it.* <note>Genesis 28:16</note>

Here, therefore, the true harmony of the world is explained; here is the first illumination of the divine philosophers and the discovery of the science of Music, which they adapted to external mathematical numbers and figures. Just as we declared that the secrets of both the archetypal and typical worlds were drawn out according to the model of Solomon’s Temple or the Mosaic Tabernacle, this is usually done in a symbolic or analogical manner. This occurs when it is done through the numbers of common Arithmetic, the figures of external Geometry, or through visible things—since there is no true or certain vision in corporeal things (for they are seen and yet are not). Rather, the certainty of all visions is in the center of the form, namely the intellectual form, because within the "womb of form," Wisdom (that is, the Word, the Light of the Messiah) is said to shine back, just as it is said to be in **Metatron** <note>The highest archangel in Kabbalistic tradition</note>, who is the World Soul.

From these things, therefore, it stands clearly enough (unless I am mistaken) that when Philosophers have said God is a **Circle**, or that a Circle is in the soul—dividing it into geometric parts, namely the triangle, quadrangle, pentagon, etc.—that, my dear Johannes <note>Addressing Johannes Kepler</note>, is said only in an analogical and metaphorical manner. And yet I still hope that I shall achieve so much before the world that, since we are now joined in literary friendship (as I hope), I may bring it about that we both agree on the same foundations of Harmony. Thus it will appear to the world that there is no need for further contention between us, but that we may rest together in peace hereafter, as becomes good Christians.

You say, therefore, that the human Soul is a part of nature, and that a circle with its divisions through regular planes shines within the soul because the mind is the image of God. But I say that the Soul, insofar as respect is held for its essence, cannot be divided from nature as a part from a whole, according to that saying of **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: "Mercur. Trismeg. Pim. 12"</note> in the *Pimander*, book 12: *The Mind is by no means divided from the essence of God, but rather connected to it in the same way that light is to the body of the Sun.* For we see the solar rays are joined with the solar body, and in truth are not at all to be divided, because the essence of Light is one, and not to be divided into parts. 

But truly, in respect to us who are occupied in the multitude <note>The world of many separate things</note>, we say the Soul of this person differs in number and species from that of another, even though all souls nonetheless have a continuous relation to the one World Soul or Metatron, like the light of the Sun to the Sun. There is, therefore, in truth a plurality in matter and not in form, which is nothing other than a continuous emanation from God (namely, the Word), imparting life and essence to all Creatures. By the withdrawal of this, life is taken away, according to **Psalm 104**: *When God gives to them, the creatures gather; when He opens His hand, they are filled and satisfied with good; when He hides His face, they are troubled; when He takes back His spirit, they breathe their last and return to dust; when He sends forth His spirit, they are recreated.* And **Job** chapter 12, verse 10 says: *that in God’s hand is the soul of every living thing, and the spirit of all flesh.* And **Psalm 146**: *The kindness of God preserves all things forever.* And elsewhere it is said: *that God is the Sun, giving life and glory.*

For God, as has been said, is present everywhere by His essence through the world, and dwelling in His Metatron, clothed in Light (as the Holy Scriptures say), He fills all things and preserves them continually by His presence. Hence all the works in creation were called "good," which had been esteemed "evil and void" before Creation. This goodness arose from God (who is the sole and highest good) and from participation in His essence. By this "glue" and harmony, all things in the world are connected in concordant peace and eternal bonds. I conclude, therefore, that just as God’s essence is indivisible, so also Nature herself—which is His emanation into the world—is in every way a single form and indivisible in itself. Insofar as God is "divisible" into three Persons (arguing from the offices and properties produced for the perfection of this world), so also the soul is said to be divided into various parts, whence sometimes it is sense, now...

Those who are eager to consider the Soul as it is placed within perishable things will observe that it is distinguished from the body and its properties by corporeal eyes. But whoever penetrates his own inner passages by returning to himself and to his own center—neglecting the external world as if it were a deceptive shadow—will perceive with spiritual eyes that there is neither division nor quantity within the soul. Nor can numbers or geometric figures be investigated within God (who is above "how much" and "of what kind," and with whom the essence of the soul is continuous). Therefore, the circle and its divisions are imaginary, existing in the created passive spirit and not in the creating soul. But indeed, insofar as the soul, through its essence, fills the three-fold and formal steps of the harmonic scale and is said to be present everywhere and to comprehend all things, the thing comprehended is nonetheless no different in nature (that is, in the essence of the comprehender) than a Creature is in the essence of the Creator. But the worldly Circles are said to be in the luminous soul just as darkness, once illuminated, is in the light, or as worldly water is in fire; so too a multitude can be said to be found in light—namely, in the matter encompassed by Light—even though that Light is individual, unique, and indivisible in itself. Therefore, a circle does not exist in the essence of the soul, but in that material thing, namely the worldly spirit, to which the soul gives being and which it embraces on every side like a circle. Nevertheless, in that circle, neither a center nor a circumference is found, according to that passage of Job cited above in chapter 11:9: "The wisdom of God is not to be found, for it is higher than the highest heavens, and deeper than the lowest grave; its measure is longer than the earth, and wider than the sea."

This spirit is sustained by the act—that is, the power and virtue of the world soul—and is enclosed as something limited and finite within a thing that is indeterminate and infinite. Thus, this circular spirit is enclosed by the fiery soul of the world surrounding it, with whose smallest parts the fiery force and symphonic love of that soul are mixed, just as the human soul is in the whole and in every part of the whole. I also acknowledge that by the spherical art of Mathematics, this substance can be partitioned and distinguished into parts by both arithmetic numbers and geometric figures—through an imaginary path and a concept of the mind—whereby we can arrive at a more perfect knowledge of God and nature through demonstration, whether from the effect or from the cause. However, Mathematicians and Philosophers ought to know that they occupy themselves in mathematics for that purpose because, in truth, there are neither numbers nor external figures in the world soul considered by itself, since it is continuous and devoid of division. Rather, demonstrations are made through analogy or likeness, since the true subject of Physics and its harmony is Spirit (or Water) and Light (or Soul)—that is, matter and form. Therefore, in a mathematical manner, Johannes [Kepler] has well described the harmony of the visible world, but by a more abstract reasoning; likewise, Robert [Fludd] has explained his Harmony in a physical manner, but by a more concrete reasoning. Since, therefore, both of us are established upon the same firm foundations of nature, I do not see why Robert could justly reject Johannes's mathematical way in describing the Symphony of nature, or likewise why Johannes should repudiate Robert’s physical path in the explanation and demonstration of his Harmony, since (I say) the foundations are the same, the object and goal are the same, and only the progress in demonstrating is different.

But where you are seen to assert that those divisions and intervals of Harmony were in the archetypal world from the beginning, and were infused from there into the human soul, I say that no division occurs in the divine essence, seeing as it is indivisible, nor can it receive the impressions of circles or figures (unless speaking metaphorically). For it is like a *Diapason* <term>the Greek term for an Octave; here representing the most perfect and complete musical consonance</term>, which, arising from its own virtue, returns into it again, and this remains one. The soul is the same way, according to that saying of Plato mentioned above, insofar as it is free from corporeal laws, since it is a ray of that divinity from which it arose. Whence it should be known that, just as in the nature of things the Sun is a complete whole and one without division, yet it nonetheless emits infinite rays (which are of the same essence as their whole) into the spirit of the world, distinguishing it into infinite species; or as Unity in Arithmetic is indivisible, yet from it a multitude flows; so also God, who is always one and the same and in every way indivisible, is dispersed into a multitude—that is, into matter and its parts—while He Himself remains this one and indivisible thing. For this reason, He is called by Philosophers versed in Theology the "Being of beings" and the "Father of creatures." He is therefore one, infinite and indivisible, insofar as He is considered in and by Himself; and yet, in relation to us and common understanding, He is divided into harmonic parts and proportions, insofar as He attributes life to every worldly proportion and creature by sending out His rays of life and being from a single center (as it were) to infinite points of the circumference, and distinguishing one from another. Whence all things are said to live in God and to exist in Him; that is, they are thought to derive life and existence from His very essence. And if not, it must be asked why a new system of worldly harmony should not be granted to both John <note>Johannes Kepler</note> and Robert <note>Robert Fludd himself</note> just as much as to any of those who have applied themselves to the search for the World's Harmony.

<margin>7.</margin>We read, first of all, that Terpander <note>A Greek poet and musician from the 7th century BCE, credited with increasing the strings on the lyre</note>, upon inventing the seventh string (that is, the heptachord), finally made it equal to the number of the planets. Others among the ancients found a fourfold kind of Harmony in both the Great and Small Cosmos <term>Macrocosm and Microcosm; the universe and the human being</term> corresponding to the elements. Specifically, they judged that the **Dorian** mode agreed with Water and Phlegm, the **Phrygian** with Fire and Choler, the **Lydian** with Air and Blood, and the **Mixolydian** with Earth and Black Bile <note>These are the four "humors" or bodily fluids thought to govern health and temperament</note>. Similarly, Nicomachus assigned the Tetrachord <note>a scale of four notes</note> invented by Mercury to the four elements; he claimed that its single string *Hypate* resonated with and indicated Earth, *Parahypate* or *Mese* Water, *Nete* or *Diazeugmenon* or *Hyperbolaeos* Fire, and *Paranete* Air. Others, looking at the number and power of the heavens, assigned the **Dorian** to the Sun, the **Phrygian** to Mars, the **Lydian** to Jupiter, the **Mixolydian** to Saturn, the **Hypophrygian** to Mercury, the **Hypolydian** to Venus, the **Hypodorian** to the Moon, and the **Hypomixolydian** to the starry sky. 

Some, again, make the space lying between the Earth and the Moon an interval of a Whole Tone. (At this, I know John <note>Kepler</note> would surely mock me, by Hercules, if he had found a tone of such great length in my Harmony!) Then, from the Moon to Mercury, he makes half that space a semitone, and just as much from there to Venus. From there to the Sun, however, he establishes a triple tone and a half, making a *Diapente* <note>A musical interval of a Perfect Fifth</note>. From the Moon to the Sun, making two and a half tones, he establishes a *Diatessaron* <note>A musical interval of a Perfect Fourth</note>. From the Sun to Mars, they want to have again as much interval as from the Earth to the Moon, making a tone. From there to Jupiter, half of that, making another semitone, and just as much from there to Saturn, constituting a semitone, from which to the orb of the stars there lies another space of a semitone. Thus, from the Sun to the starry heaven is a *Diatessaron* (namely, of two tones and a half), but from the Earth, a perfect *Diapason* <note>A musical interval of an Octave</note>, namely, of six whole tones. 

According to others, a Harmony—the sweetest of all, they say—results from the proportion of the movements of the Planets to one another and with the eighth heaven. This proportion of Saturn to Jupiter is two-and-a-half times (double sesquialter); of Jupiter to Mars, sixfold (sescuple); of Mars to the Sun, Venus, and Mercury (which complete their journey equally), a double proportion; of those to the Moon, twelvefold; and of Saturn to the starry orb, one thousand two hundredfold. Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, a famous 16th-century occultist</note> maintains that Saturn, Mars, and the Moon have more "voice" than "concord." He says Saturn has sad, hoarse, deep, slow sounds, as if compressed toward the center. Mars has harsh, sharp, threatening, swift, and angry voices. Between these, the Moon observes a middle ground. Jupiter, the Sun, Venus, and Mercury possess concords. Jupiter, therefore, claims for himself deep, constant, intense, sweet, cheerful, and pleasant concords. The Sun possesses venerable, pure, and sweet ones. Venus, playful, luxurious, and voluptuous ones. Mercury, more relaxed, multifaceted, and happy and pleasant with a certain vigor. From these particular and proportioned concords, the tone obeys the nine Muses: Jupiter has the grace of the eighth and fifth notes (the Octave and the Fifth); the Sun obtains the melody of the eighth note (the Octave), and likewise fifteen tones (the Double Octave). Venus holds the grace of the fifth note (the Fifth). Mercury has the *Diatessaron*, the grace of the fourth note. And so on for the others.

Plato and Pythagoras draw the demonstrations of their Harmony from the logic and mutual concatenation of numbers and proportions. Aristotle attempts to explain the matter through physical principles and things derived from principles. Likewise, there are others who imagine the Harmony of the human Soul to consist of the due temperament and proportion of its virtues and operations, which are the **Desiring**, the **Spirited**, and the **Rational** <note>original: "Concupiscibilis, Irascibilis, & Rationabilis"; the three parts of the soul in Platonic philosophy</note>. They say their proportions are as follows: the Rational and Desiring have the proportion of an Octave (*Diapason*); the Rational to the Spirited has a Fourth (*Diatessaron*); and the Spirited to the Desiring has the proportion of a Fifth (*Diapente*). And there are various other such inventions according to the minds and intentions of Philosophers and Mathematicians philosophizing in diverse ways.

From these examples, therefore, it clearly appears that it is just as permissible for John <note>Kepler</note>, following the concept of his own soul in his mathematical fashion, to proceed in the demonstration of worldly Harmony, as it is for Robert <note>Fludd</note> to explain the laws of his own natural Symphony according to his own invention and imagination. For it is established by the testimony of the writers cited above that it is a common and familiar thing among Philosophers to commit the mysteries of nature to writing in their own peculiar manner and method.

# Robert Fludd’s Reply

...I shall declare to you and to the world in a brief discourse that Robert [Fludd], in the invention of his Harmony and the arrangement of proportions, did not err as gravely as you perhaps thought at first glance. But before I descend into the discourse of my own Harmony, I will now speak of the Harmony of the ancients, for two reasons that compel me to do so. First, to indicate to the learned that I am not entirely so ignorant of the Harmony of the ancients as I have been proclaimed by Johannes [Kepler] in many places. Second, so that I might more correctly and easily adapt the proportions of their Harmony to my own world monochord <note>The "world monochord" is Fludd's famous diagram of a single-stringed instrument stretching from the earth to the highest heavens, illustrating how God "tuned" the universe.</note>, so that you (most esteemed readers) might more rightly judge that comparison of mine.

We find it recorded in writing, according to both the Pythagoreans and the Academics <note>The followers of Plato</note>, that both the world and its souls were to be described as conveniently as possible through harmonic proportions. And since three types of melodies—that is, the genera of harmony—were chiefly in use and practice among the ancients: namely, the **Diatonic**, which proceeded through a Whole Tone, a Whole Tone, and a Semitone, together constituting the consonance of the <term>Diatessaron (the interval of a perfect fourth)</term>, in all the tetrachords (originally found for the arrangement of the four elements); this genus is somewhat harsh, but nevertheless natural. Next is the **Chromatic**, receding from the natural Diatonic and sounding softer; it decreases through a semitone, a semitone, and three semitones, which joined together also make a Diatessaron. And finally, the **Enharmonic**, which is sung in all tetrachords through a <term>Diesis (here understood as half of a semitone)</term>, another Diesis, and a ditone, all of which added together also measure out the consonance of the Diatessaron. 

From these, the divine Plato chose the **Diatonic** for describing his harmony of the world and the soul, because he perceived that genus to be more natural, simple, and noble. Consequently, it was better suited by its nature to originally depict and describe the bonds—the symphonic duties and harmonic proportions—of the world and the soul (that is, of aquatic matter and lucid form, or of the passive and active), both within each part and between them. He was all the more led to this choice because it was noticed through diligent observation by him and Timaeus of Locri <note>A Pythagorean philosopher featured in Plato's dialogues</note> that this genus possessed in its nature a certain governance over rational life—just as the Enharmonic presides over all life suited to a body, and the Chromatic has regard for the bodily idea. But since among these properties of the soul, reason is more eminent and noble, and the Diatonic genus is more natural in its arrangement, he therefore chose it above the others for his investigation of worldly harmony. 

Indeed, just as the ancients proceeded through this in tetrachords <note>four-note scales</note>, so Plato—imitating Nicomachus for a better and more proportional demonstration of his Harmony—expanded it to the nature of the <term>Heptachord (a seven-stringed scale)</term> conformed to seven limits. He began from unity and doubled it until reaching the cube of two (namely, 8), and then triple it until reaching the cube and solid of three (namely, 27) <note>This refers to the "Lambda" diagram in Plato's *Timaeus*, using the series 1, 2, 4, 8 and 1, 3, 9, 27 to describe the soul's proportions</note>. According to this proportion of numbers, the Academics believed the fabric of both the soul and the world was arranged and brought to completion, following those ancient teachings of Pythagoras. Pythagoras equated the proportions of the number three to the soul, as if to a masculine, acting perfection and to light; and he equated the proportions of the number two to matter, as if to an imperfect, feminine, passive principle and to water. From the conjunction of these—namely, from matter and form—all things in this world are procreated and propagated. 

Therefore, those most skilled in the science of numbers assigned the **Monad** (Unity) to the Creator God, the **Dyad** (Duality) to matter, the **Triad** (the Virgin Three) to the forms themselves, and the **Heptad** (Seven) to life and man. And from this, Plato ordered his Diatonic Harmony toward the Heptachord, because he adapted it to both the internal world (the soul) and the corporeal substance, whose proportions he deduced from the aforementioned 1, 2, and 3. The cubes of these numbers complete the structure of both the soul and the world: the cube of three (namely, 27) for the soul, and the cube of two (namely, 8) for the body or matter. 

But one may best gather these proportions in the fabric of the world, as it seems to me, from the account of the Priest Moses: *The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters.* <note>Genesis 1:2</note>. Here, the Spirit of the Lord is the formal unity, just as the water is the material unity. Then the doubling was made when the Creator commanded that universal matter be informed, saying: *Let there be Light.* Next, the square of that two (4) was produced when that general mixture was reduced into the four elements, which are dispersed through the vast cavity of the world. Finally, through the cube of that two (8), the bodies of the elemental creatures were propagated: namely, the stars from the mixture of celestial elements, and minerals, vegetables, and animals from those sublunary elements. In this way, the material and feminine creature was proportionally completed in this world according to the arrangement of triple dimension—namely length, breadth, and depth (line, surface, and body). These correspond in the Macrocosm to the most thin substance of the Empyrean heaven, to that of the middle heaven, and to the Elemental realm. As we said in our *Harmony*, these regard the root, the square, and the cube in the number two. 

Finally, all the intervals of those numbers are filled with the triple numbers of the same proportion, without which they cannot exist; for without these, a vacuum and emptiness would follow in the feminine mass. Hence in Genesis, all created things are called "good" and filled with divine rays, insofar as they participate in the goodness of <note>original: "Elohim"</note> **Elohim**—that is, the Holy Spirit, which proves the number three in its divine property. Without this, all things would be, as they were before its appearance, darkness and void. Therefore, one must proceed through the masculine power (the number three) in the same proportion with the feminine power toward the cube; for it was this masculine virtue that attributed grades and proportions to the feminine substance, filling its intervals with life, essence, and action. It established the most perfect harmony in the world: namely, the proportion of the most perfect consonance, the <term>Diapason (the Octave, a 2:1 ratio)</term> in the Angels and the intellectual Spirit; and that less perfect one, the <term>Diapente (the Fifth, a 3:2 ratio)</term> in the Olympic Daemons and the ethereal heaven; and the imperfect <term>Diatessaron (the Fourth, a 4:3 ratio)</term> in inferior things, such as in animals, vegetables, and minerals. # In Defense of the 12th Annals

Plato therefore filled the intervals of his harmony according to the example of the Soul of the World; but we Christians attribute the logic of this Harmony to the spirit of life, the tree of life, and the fountain of life, which is the life of the world and is called its true **Metatron** <note>In Jewish mysticism, Metatron is a supreme angel and mediator between the divine and the human; Fludd identifies this figure with Christ.</note>, the highest Wisdom of the world and the basis of true Harmony—namely, the cornerstone of which Jacob preached so much. He argued that through His Harmony alone, as if by his ladder, it was given to men to ascend into the kingdom of heaven, concerning which Paul, in the place previously cited, speaks thus: <note>original Latin: "Pacificans per sanguinem suæ Crucis res omnes quæ in terra & in cœlis sunt."</note> *Making peace through the blood of His Cross for all things which are on earth and in the heavens.* From this, it seems to follow that not only men, but indeed all other things have been led to their true harmonies through the blood of Christ.

The ancient Sages, both the Academics <note>Followers of Plato.</note> and the Pythagoreans, attempted to explain the pattern of this mystery through the shadowy formulas of numbers and figures; for we are taught how great was their knowledge in the divine mystery, and how admirable their science, seeing that to them—although they were Pagans in religion—the mystery of the Holy Trinity was revealed. It is for this reason that the title of "divine" is not foolishly attributed by us Christians to **Hermes Trismegistus** and **Plato**.

Our Christ, therefore—the God made manifest arising from the rock of Jacob, sprouting from the earth as if from the center of the hidden Father or God, expanding Himself everywhere and extending Himself into infinity beyond and outside all things (since divine Wisdom has no end)—attempts to lead all created things back to the Creator through a **Harmony of more-than-perfection**. In this harmony, that excellent consonance sounds most clearly, and the glorious Sun—that is, the Divine Light giving life and glory—sounds for eternity. This leads from the imperfect consonance of the <term>Diatessaron (an interval of a perfect fourth)</term>—that is, the life of the Creature buried in darkness—through the consonance of the <term>Diapente (an interval of a perfect fifth)</term>, which is of lesser perfection—that is, through the ethereal spirit where one first tastes the delights of perfection and bliss—to the <term>Diapason (an octave)</term> itself, which ends in God Himself, when we shall have been made one with God through Christ by means of that true consonance of perfection.

And just as according to Plato’s description of the heptachord <note>The "Pythagorean Lambda" or "Platonic Lambda," a triangular arrangement of numbers representing the harmony of the universe.</note> there are four steps in both the "female" and "male" progression—namely 1, 2, 4, 8 or 1, 3, 9, 27—which four series are arranged thus: 1, 2, 3, 4; so in this general system of Harmony:
*   **1 to 2**, which is a double proportion, denotes that consonance of more-than-perfection ending in unity, namely God: the **Diapason**. Here, all things proceeding from unity into multiplicity are observed to return again into their own unity and simplicity.
*   The **sesquialter** proportion, **2 to 3**, indicates the consonance of lesser perfection: the **Diapente**.
*   The **sesquitertian** proportion, **3 to 4**, proves the imperfect consonance: the **Diatessaron**.

For we see that things behave exactly this way in this world. Namely, on account of this kind of imperfection, such as is in the Diatessaron, we observe all sublunary things <note>Things below the moon, i.e., on Earth.</note> to languish and be subjected to constant alterations. We are taught that in the ethereal heaven, things are immune to corruption because of the perfection of the Diapente. And in the angelic heaven, we know that the highest bliss is acquired through "more-than-perfection" via the Diapason.

Wherefore the **Diatessaron**, consisting of four and held in sesquitertian proportion as 3 to 4, proves the four sublunary elements. The **Diapente**, denoting the five and the middle perfection of the celestial region, held as 2 to 3 in the sesquialter, is called the **Quinta Essentia** <note>The "Fifth Essence" or quintessence, believed to be the pure substance of the stars.</note>. And the **Diapason** pertains to the more-than-perfection of the angelic heaven, which is measured by six tones and is called the **Sixth Essence**, held as 1 to 2 in the double proportion. And this consonance, defining the fountain and ultimate goal of more-than-perfection in God, leads all things that flowed out from unity into multiplicity back again into divine unity. It is called the **Rest of the Sabbath** in the **En Soph** <note>Hebr. *Ein Sof*, the Infinite or "Without End," referring to God before manifestation.</note>, which ends in the number 7, since the Diapason consists of that many intervals.

The progression from unity into multiplicity goes as far as the number one thousand, beyond which, according to Aristotle, there is no further progression in numbers. This number is described by the Hebrews through a "Large Aleph," just as unity is described by a "Small Aleph." This letter, among the Kabbalists, is the sign and character of divinity in unity; and it is from this that God is called by Saint John the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. Therefore, the progression from the Small Aleph (unity) is made toward the multiplicity of 999, according to the teachings of the Platonists; if the Large Aleph is added to this number, it produces 1000, through which the return of things from multiplicity occurs.

I have rightly said, therefore, that the sublunary world is imperfect and liable to changes, because in it is the smallest portion of Light, that is, of the mundane soul—just as we believe the soul is more in the head and heart of a man than in his shins or legs; for there, matter has dominion over the proportion of light. Again, by the same proportion, I explained that corruption is rejected from the ethereal region, and that a middle perfection dwells there because of the equality of dominion and the proportion of light to that of the mundane matter; hence I placed the Sun in its center, not without reason. This is proved to be so because, by the Philosophers and those more skilled in the practice of secret mysteries, "ether" is called as it were "fiery air" or "ignited air," from the equality of the proportion of air (or water) and fire (or light) in it, and especially in the place where the Sun passes.

Finally, I showed in that same place that the angelic region, immense because of the dominion of fire (or light) in it over the thinnest mundane spirit, was most perfect in its essence, and rightly compared to the highest Diapason. Hence the empyrean heaven is named from the Greek word *pyr* <note>πῦρ</note>, meaning fire or fiery. Indeed, I have depicted all these things—because of the contrariety of the fiery form and the watery matter—as being in every way opposite. While unity, the perfection of Light, essential action, subtlety, motion, and entity are in opposition to multiplicity, opacity, passivity, thickness, and rest, I depicted them under the form of **two pyramids**, similar in figure and quantity, but opposite in site and position. For as the progression of the motion and resolution of multiplicity (matter) occurs from the number one thousand into unity, so the proportion of created Light is equivalent to that of the number one thousand, but in unity. Thus, the more it proceeds from multiplicity to unity, the more the unity (the lucid form) conquers, and claims more dominion for itself over matter.

Hence, therefore, according to Plato’s proportion, as between the binary (female) matter and the ternary (male) form—which agree with each other in proportion—there is a discre-

Anyone who desires to forge this Heptachord <note>A seven-stringed musical scale or system.</note> of his out of several perfect consonances according to the intervals of proportions between 1 and 8, or 1 and 27, I shall prepare myself to describe it with the following apparatus.

The Platonic Heptachord (which Plato himself applied and arranged to demonstrate the Harmony of the world and the soul) consists of seven strings, as it were, or proportions, partly even and partly odd—namely 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 27. Although Porphyry and Proclus <note>Neoplatonist philosophers who commented on Plato’s works.</note> drew these out into a single line, Adrastus and Calcidius adapted them to the sides of a Triangle or Pyramid in this manner. At the summit, Unity is expressed as both material and formal, thereby confirming the opinion of Synesius and other divine philosophers that God is everything that exists; for from Him, in Him, and through Him are all things. He is male and He is female, or as Hermes Trismegistus <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the "Hermetic" tradition of wisdom and magic.</note> says, "most fertile in both sexes." He is power and He is act; He is form and He is matter; indeed, in truth, there is nothing that He himself does not exist as. Six other figures correspond to the opposite side: namely, the proportions of the even numbers once, and the odd numbers three times, so that any formal proportion of the number three corresponds directly to those of the opposite even numbers in this way:

In these numbers, therefore, the primary kinds of all things in Creation are clearly demonstrated along with their Harmony, as well as the subordinate and intermediate species contained between these proportions, specifically for the completion of the spirit and soul of the world. But in this Heptachord of Plato, your Proclus seems to have found no small imperfection because, as he says, some intervals in it are not complete—chiefly that space between 1 and 2. He claims there is no middle term between these two unless unity is broken into parts. Here indeed Proclus speaks not as a Christian but as a Pagan, and is seen by Christian Philosophers to be deceived with his eyes wide open; for God—in whom alone resides a consonance more than perfect (namely the <term>Diapason [Octave]</term>)—holding Himself in a double proportion as 1 to 2, produced this consonance of greatest perfection into His archetypal Light when He begot Wisdom, that is, His Word, before the ages. This Word was nonetheless not divided from the divine Being, but was the same and one with it eternally. Hermes Trismegistus seems to confirm this from philosophy in these words:

> The Monad <note>original: "Monas"</note> generates the Monad and reflected its heat into itself;

arguing from this that before the Creation of the world the Son—that is, God manifesting out of the darkness, and the bright <term>Aleph</term> <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, used here to represent the beginning or the divine "One."</note>—shone forth or went out from the Father—that is, God hidden in the darkness, and the dark Aleph. This dark Aleph was not divided from the essence of the Father during or after Creation, although by property and office in the Creation of the world He is called the Second Person, distinct from the First, as 2 is from 1. Furthermore, we gather from the Holy Scriptures that the Son is one with the Father, remains in the bosom of the Father, is in the mouth of the Father, sits at the right hand of the Father, and is the mediator for us men to the Father, having no medium between Himself and the Father, but joined to Him in such a way as the light of the Sun is to the solar body, or the diameter of a circle to its center. And hence it is imagined by the Poets that Apollo and Cupid are the sons of Jove, thereby declaring Christ shining in the world and casting His loving rays everywhere through the mundane spirit. Or, regarding the first Creation, He is called Jupiter—that is, the powerful and manifest God—who was the son of Saturn—that is, the dark and hidden God. From this it is clear that, contrary to Proclus’s opinion, this interval is filled without a middle term, insofar as it is of one continuous essence, descending through the more than perfect consonance of the <term>Diapason [Octave]</term> from the archetypal world into the one to be created. That is, from 1 (denoting pure, simple, and ineffable uncreated light) into 2 (the unity of matter), where the uncreated, bright, and formal 1 creates and activates the one that is dark, shapeless, potential, and material, mixing Himself with it; and thus the first light was created as the first creature in the world, the subject of all forms, through a spiritual Octave. Then 3, which is the hidden middle between 2 and 4, describes the nature of the ethereal heaven or firmament; this is the middle between 2 (the Empyrean heaven, which is the receptacle of the first bright Creature) and 4 (denoting the four sublunary elements). Therefore, in the production of this region of the world, there concurred the nature of the first Creature, which was Light or the Soul of the World (acting as its soul or form), and the substance of the water created by its presence and now called by the name "firmament." Between the first heaven, filled with the first bright Creature, and this ethereal heaven, there is a distance and a ratio of composition from matter and form in a <term>Sesquialtera [3:2 ratio]</term> proportion (namely 3 and 2), from which is forged and in which consists the less perfect consonance of the <term>Diapente [Perfect Fifth]</term>. Hence, this part of the world is called the <term>Quinta essentia [Fifth Essence]</term>, just as the others are the sixth and seventh. For as the Fifth is a consonance of lesser perfection, so the Octave is a consonance of the highest perfection; thus the ethereal heaven (the kingdom of the visible Sun) relates to the Empyrean (presided over by the spiritual and invisible Sun). Finally, 4, which is the square of the Root 2, denotes the elementary heaven, divided into 4 stations called elements.

# In the Defense of the Annals, Book XII

It is directed toward the matter of the sublunary world, since that celestial spirit is like an active principle or a sea relative to the elemental world. For this reason, it is said by the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> that superior things act upon inferior things through motion, light, and influence. This is proven by the harmonic path—namely, by the logic of the difference between consonances. Just as the **Diapente** <note>A perfect fifth (ratio 3:2).</note> is a consonance of lesser perfection, so too is the **Diatessaron** <note>A perfect fourth (ratio 4:3).</note> an imperfect consonance; and whatever perfection it possesses, it receives from the heavens. Between 3 and 4 there is a **sesquitertia** proportion <note>A 4:3 ratio.</note>, which denotes the proportion of the Diatessaron consonance. Finally, from 2 to 3 and 3 to 4—that is, from the Diapente and Diatessaron—is fashioned the material **Diapason** <note>An octave (ratio 2:1), formed by adding a fifth and a fourth.</note>; that is, that most perfect proportion found in the mundane nature, whose soul is the spiritual Diapason.

As the 1 in that Heptachord <note>A seven-numbered scale: 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 27.</note> is the primary soul and the **Ensoph** <note>The Infinite or Divine Source in Cabalistic thought.</note>—that is, the infinity, the original and archetypal Diapason consonance in the divine essence—it gives life equally to the watery matter and to the formal Light created at the beginning. This is clearly indicated by its placement according to Porphyry, Severus, and Proclus <note>Neoplatonist philosophers.</note> in a straight line thus: **1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 27**. Here all these things appear more clearly; for the material 2, by a formal bond with 1 itself, becomes a being in act through the supreme Diapason. The nature of the material number 2 is united by a formal bond to the matter that is double itself. Therefore, 1 is the form to 2—namely, God to the unformed matter, which is signified by the Platonists by the number 2, and which the Pythagoreans call the "confusion of units," and is like a Chaos. But by the emanation of the luminous spirit 1 into the deformed spirit 2—or **Iod** into **He** <note>The first two letters of the Hebrew Divine Name, YHWH.</note>—that created Light is made. This uncreated unity, plunging itself more deeply into the confused matter, creates 3, or Heaven, which is like the form and soul to 4—that is, to the sublunary Elements. 

Thus, 1, as the primary root and supreme element of fire, produced the Empyrean light, which is Element 2; and then, plunging itself more deeply into multiplicity, it created the ethereal spirit, which is Element 3. Then later, penetrating into the lowest region of the world, it created and arranged the other 4 Elements, which are gross; each of these it suspended in its proper place according to the dignity of the matter and bound them with its fiery glue. These are indeed the 7 steps from God. But if the root is left in its archetypal kingdom and the elemental composite is added (which is signified by the cube), there will be in the nature of things 7 steps leading to the supreme Monad <note>The "Monad" represents the indivisible Unity of God.</note>.

Furthermore, if we consider the formal side of the Triangle, we find there that 3 is the form corresponding to 2 and 4. Whence it is said that the Spirit of the Lord—that is, **Elohim**, or "the Gods" in three Persons as some wish—moving in one spirit by arguing <note>original: "arguendo," perhaps meaning "proving its presence."</note> was carried over the 2 waters, imparting to them a fiery and loving vigor and the virtue of life. Hence "Waters" are denoted by the Cabalists by the Hebrew **Mem** (מ), which the Pythagoreans marked by 2; and they made the character **Schin** (ש), the sign of fire, the hieroglyphic of the Holy Spirit, arguing from its three horns that it is a single spirit operating in a threefold way. This spirit, plunging itself more deeply into the waters, divides itself proportionally into 9 parts, and finally tripled those 9 parts by penetrating to the center according to its threefold nature; that is, it divided each into 3 other parts, namely 27. Therefore, 3 (or the fiery spirit) created 2 (the empyrean heaven) and divided it into three Hierarchies of Angels according to its own exemplar. Thus the spiritual heaven was formed. Descending deeper according to its triple nature, it dispersed itself into the multitude of material heavens, and thus each of them is informed. Finally, tripling itself again, it informed the composite creatures. And this was done according to that word of the Psalmist:
> By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the Spirit from his mouth. <note>Psalm 33:6</note>

Finally, from the proportions **sesquialtera** <note>3:2 ratio.</note> (4 to 6) and **sesquitertia** <note>4:3 ratio.</note> (6 to 8), just as from the Diapente and Diatessaron, the Diapason of composite creatures is produced. This is a heavy and bass Harmony made in the likeness of the spiritual Diapason of the world, which was formed after the exemplar of the more-than-perfect consonance in the intellectual spirit. In these proportions, the Pythagoreans attributed the **Hexad** <note>The number 6.</note> to the human composition, and the **Heptad** <note>The number 7.</note> (situated between 8 and 6) to his life or soul. To the life of all other creatures, they equated the **Ennead** <note>The number 9.</note>, which is the square of three. 

In this way, we see how God is bound to His creatures: first, 1 (the Monad in act) to 1 (the Monad in potential), which becomes a **Dyad** <note>The number 2.</note>. Then the Monad united to the Dyad produced the **Triad** <note>The number 3.</note>. And the Monad glued again to the Triad produces the **Quaternary** <note>The number 4.</note> number. Thus, through this Harmony, the world was fashioned in the first three days of Creation. God is said to fill all things; the formal or divine unity was the agent, while the material unity (existing in potential before time) was the patient, or the female. This, I say, is the true Harmony of the world. Those who desire to explore more curiously beyond this by themselves, without divine influence, deceive and are deceived. For to dispute directly and specifically about God and His works would be an immense, impossible, and unsearchable task. The works of God are wonderful and least understood by human capacity, except where God has given His Wisdom and sent His Holy Spirit from the holy heavens, according to that saying of Solomon in chapter 9:
> The body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly thought presses down the sense that thinks many things; and with difficulty do we judge the things that are on earth, and we find with labor the things that are in our sight, but who has searched out the things that are in the heavens? And who shall know your sense, unless you have given wisdom, and sent your spirit from the highest? <note>Wisdom of Solomon 9:15-17</note>

But let us now proceed in the description of the **Platonic Harmony**, and let us admit that "scruple" of Proclus: that no mean is to be found between 1 and 2. And then later, that although only the number three is found between 2 and 4—which (as he seems to suggest) since this proportion is only "with a half" compared to the smaller 1, and that compared to the smaller is found in the sesquitertia proportion—whence he concludes that the intervals...

### Robert Fludd’s Reply

...intervals cannot be harmonically filled. And by these same diminished proportions, the number 6 comes between 4 to complete the corporeal Harmony <note>Physical or bodily harmony, as opposed to purely spiritual harmony.</note>. And likewise in similar cases: he rightly says that in Plato’s fundamental and primary harmonic numeration, an odd number is observed in the **sesquialtera** <note>A 3:2 ratio, which creates the musical interval of a Perfect Fifth.</note> and **sesquitertia** <note>A 4:3 ratio, which creates the musical interval of a Perfect Fourth.</note> proportions—namely, 6 between 3 and 9, just as in the aforementioned 3 between 2 and 4; and 18 between 9 and 27, just as in the aforementioned 6 between 4 and 8. He seems to conclude, therefore, that the harmonic intervals cannot be filled by such an arrangement of numbers.

And yet, as it seems to me (with all due respect to Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD) whose commentaries on Plato’s *Timaeus* were essential to Renaissance music theory.</note> and others of his opinion), where there is a **sesquialtera** proportion (which is as 2 to 3), there consequently follows the **Diapente** consonance <note>A Perfect Fifth.</note>, in the measure of which are understood intervals of three and a half tones. Similarly, where the **sesquitertia** proportion occurs (which is as 3 to 4), it is necessary that three intervals be understood there—namely, two tones with a semitone—and both of these proportions joined together constitute the **Diapason** <note>A Perfect Octave.</note>. It follows, therefore, that if the **Diatessaron** consonance <note>A Perfect Fourth.</note> sounds, or that of the **Diapente** or the **Diapason**, all the parts of these consonances are necessarily understood to be present.

Between 1 and 2 is the **dupla** <note>A 2:1 ratio.</note> proportion, which is the sign of the **Diapason** consonance with the filling of all those intervals contained beneath it. Similarly, between 2 and 3 is the **Diapente**. And finally, between 3 and 4 is the **Diatessaron**. Furthermore, 4 relates to 8 as 1 relates to 2. Moreover, even in the **ternary** <note>The "triple" series of numbers: 1, 3, 9, 27.</note> or masculine order, 2 comes between 1 and 3, being in a **dupla** proportion to 1 and **sesquialtera** to 3; and between 3 and 9 occurs the number six (**senarius**), where the proportion is **dupla** to 3 and **sesquialtera** to 9. Finally, between 9 and 27, by the same logic, 18 intervenes.

But let him proceed in his own way: I say that he, rejecting the number 27 (under which all primary types of things are comprised) due to a perceived lack of "filled" intervals, chose another larger number. Nonetheless, this larger number observes the same limits and proportions as the primary ones, though (as I say) it is of a greater quantity so as to fill the aforementioned intervals more exactly. Therefore, so that he may reduce any proportions into their whole small parts, he takes the number six (**senarius**) in place of unity <note>Instead of starting the scale at 1, he starts at 6 to avoid fractions in his calculations.</note>. This 6 relates to 12 as 1 to 2; doubled in progression, it produces 12, 24, 48; and tripled, it makes 18, 54, 162.

He concludes, therefore, that all intervals are filled by this figure of numbers, since the means between the two extremes of 6 and 12 are 8 and 9. Here, the mean of 9 exceeds 6 by an equal proportion of numbers and is exceeded by 12. Furthermore, from the lesser extreme of 6 to the lesser mean of 8 is a **sesquitertia** proportion—that is, 6 and its third part, which is 8—from which leaps forth the **Diatessaron** consonance. This also occurs from the greater mean to the greater extreme. But from the lesser extreme to the greater mean is a **sesquialtera** proportion—namely, 6 and its half part, which is 3, making 9—from which proportion the **Diapente** consonance is drawn. From the lesser extreme of 6 to the greater extreme of 12, a **dupla** proportion is found, from which arises the **Diapason** consonance. The interval of a **Tone**, therefore, is that which lies between the two means—the lesser 8 and the greater 9.

From these, the Platonists say all Harmony is born, which is composed of tones. This same process must be done with the triple number, where the extremes are 6 and 18, and the means are 9 and 12. Its other extremes are 18 and 54, whose means are 27 and 36, and so on, proceeding proportionally from 54 to its extreme. The means of all these respond to the extremes among themselves in the same way as those double or doubled proportions.

Therefore, the **Arithmetic mean** <note>A mean where the difference between numbers is the same (e.g., 6, 9, 12; the difference is always 3).</note> between the two extremes 6 and 12 is 9, for it is a certain proportion of numbers exceeding the other in a proportional progression, as 6, 9, 12—where as much excess is found in the greater extreme of 12 over 9 as there is a deficiency in the lesser 6 below 9, namely 3. But the **Harmonic mean** <note>A more complex musical mean; between 6 and 12, the harmonic mean is 8.</note> proceeds from the multiplication of the lesser term (6) by itself, and dividing the product 36 by the mean... <note>Fludd’s mathematical shorthand here describes the calculation of the harmonic mean.</note> which produces 8, which is the harmonic mean. For it excels the lesser extreme by the same proportion that the greater extreme surpasses it. For just as 8 exceeds 6 (or half of the whole) by 2, so 12 (which is the whole) exceeds 8 by 4, which is double 2. Similarly, the matter stands in 3, 4, 6, where 4 is the harmonic mean. Therefore, the harmonic mean does not seem to differ much from the **Geometric mean**, since this is a certain proportion of proportions, from two of which the Harmonic mean results. By these rules, I say, Proclus teaches how to fill all the intervals of the world, except for semitones and **dieses** <note>Very small musical intervals or quarter-tones.</note>.

# Robert Fludd’s Reply

Truly, from this kind of correct order of Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who wrote on music and philosophy.</note> and Proclus <note>A later Neoplatonist (412–485 AD) who commented on Plato’s "Timaeus," the source of these musical-cosmic theories.</note> (where feminine degrees are linked with masculine according to nature's arrangement), it is very easy to discern the connection in composite things and their Harmony. This harmony is established between the ethereal spirit—which we understand through the number 6, representing the second Platonic term—and the elemental spirit, indicated by 8, which is the sign of the fourth term. Both of these, through the luminous form of 9, relate to the Platonic trinity along with the earthy body of 12, which is the proof of the 8th term, or Plato’s feminine cube. By arguing from one to the other, we see that 6, through the vivifying and luminous unity which makes 7, joins the most worthy and first-created spirit with the worldly elements 8. Then, that same unity, plunging itself deeper into the multitude, turns 8 into 9. This unity is the medium for joining the golden spirit to the body, just as in the septenary <note>A group of seven.</note> it joins the ethereal spirit to the elements, especially to the sublunary air. For the luminous form, possessing here the <term>arithmetic mean</term> <note>The simple average between two numbers.</note> as if it were a seat of justice, causes the geometric spaces (the intervals between 8 and 6, and 8 and 12) to return a harmonic consonance. Indeed, the number 8 denotes the <term>harmonic mean</term> <note>A more complex average used in music theory to find the "Perfect Fourth."</note> or the worldly spirit, which is vibrated and animated by the luminous soul of 9; and so it is with the rest.

But now let us proceed to that description by Proclus concerning the invention of the Semitone and the <term>Diesis</term> <note>A very small musical interval, often called a "microtone" today.</note>. By thinking more precisely about the filling of intervals, Proclus progressed by adding minor semitones to this Platonic Harmony in his own fashion. Even though the Pythagoreans, who were most skilled in numerical science, completely rejected semitones because a <term>superparticular proportion</term> <note>A ratio where the numerator is one greater than the denominator, such as 9:8 or 4:3.</note> cannot be divided into two equal parts, it is clear that a Semitone cannot properly be given. Nevertheless, Ptolemy and those who wrote after him did not hesitate to divide the tone into unequal parts. The larger of these they called the <term>Apotome</term> <note>original: "Apotomen"; the "major" semitone in the Pythagorean system.</note> or major semitone (with which Timaeus of Locri wished the smaller intervals to be filled), while the smaller they called the <term>Limma</term> <note>original: "Lemma"; the "minor" semitone or "remainder."</note> or minor semitone. Our Proclus, by imitating Plato in this (who chose the Diatonic genus of Harmony to explain the harmony of the world), chose to reject the Apotome species entirely in favor of the minor semitone for filling the smaller intervals. But before I say a word about the placement and arrangement of the minor Semitone in my Platonic or Proclerean Harmony, I will offer here a familiar demonstration of the invention of both the major and minor semitone based on what was said before, so that Proclus's indication of the deeper multitude may be more easily understood.

First, it is clear from the above that a Tone consists of a <term>sesquioctave ratio</term> <note>A 9:8 ratio.</note>, such as 9 to 8. But here no middle number is found between these two. Therefore, we double these means, and 16 and 18 arise, between which the number 17 stands in the middle. Thus, 17 placed against 18 claims the sesquioctave proportion for itself, which interval, as stated, measures a tone. But the middle number 17 does not divide this proportion equally. If 17 is compared to 16, it contains the whole of 16 plus its sixteenth part (one unit). But if 18 is compared to 17, it contains the whole of 17 plus its seventeenth part (one unit). Thus it is quite clear that this middle number exceeds the smaller part and is exceeded by the larger part in unequal portions, since the 17th part is smaller than the 16th. These are the parts of the tone called Semitones—either minor or major, according to their deficiency or excess. The same is true for the mean of 3 between 24 and 27.

But let us proceed with Proclus's invention of the Semitone. He denies it is possible for <term>sesquitertia</term> <note>A 4:3 ratio, the interval of a Perfect Fourth.</note> proportions to be divided into sesquioctaves and minor semitones using the terms previously described. For, as said before, the proportion between 8 and 9 is a sesquioctave, and this interval is the measure of a tone; because it is a measure of unity, it cannot be divided into parts. Therefore, to perform this task more effectively, he first tried multiplying 8 by itself, starting from the number 64, since from that number it was possible to form three sesquioctaves. By tripling 64 again, it produces 192. If its sesquitertia (one-third more), which is 64, is added, it makes 256. If its sesquioctave part (one-eighth), which is 32, is added to this, it produces 288. These hold the arithmetic mean between 192 and 384 (which is the double proportion of 192, and a sesquitertia to 288). But since he found it impossible to form two sesquioctaves from the number 288—because its sesquioctave, 324, does not have an eighth part—he concluded that a sesquioctave proportion could not be fabricated from this number, as its eighth part is 40 and a half (a fraction). 

Therefore, for the exact discovery of the Semitone, he was forced to plunge himself into the abyss of the multitude. He proceeded by doubling all the aforementioned numbers: 192 becomes 384, and so on for the rest. Or, let the number 384 stand in place of the number 6, or the unity of the lesser extreme. Because the sesquioctave proportion assigns the interval of a tone, its sesquioctave part (which is 48) is added to this number, and the sum—432—will measure a tone from 384. Then, its own sesquioctave part (which is 54) is also added to this product, and it will make 486, designating the second tone. However, a sesquioctave proportion is not found in 486, because after division 6 remains. Thus, a semitone occupies this interval between 486 and 512. Next follows the sesquitertia part to be added to 384, which will produce 512; this is the lesser mean, or harmonic mean, between the two extremes 384 and 768. But if the sesquioctave proportion is added to this lesser mean, the greater or arithmetic mean will be produced, namely 576, which is another tone. Afterwards, if its sesquioctave part is added to this, it will give 648, and there will be the space of another tone between 576 and 648. Again, if the sesquioctave part of 648 is added to it, it produces 729. Because a sesquioctave part is not found in 729 without fractions, the <term>Limma</term> <note>Minor semitone.</note> fills the space between 729 and the greater extreme, which is 768. In this way, we have seven intervals filled with five tones and two <term>Limmas</term> or minor semitones, of which the first three intervals...

### In the Reply to Book 12 of the Annals

...are filled with two tones and a semitone, and produce the harmony of a **Perfect Fourth** <note>original: *Diatessaron*</note>, and the four following parts are measured with three tones and a semitone (that is, a <term>limma</term> <note>A small interval in Pythagorean tuning, slightly less than a modern equal-tempered semitone.</note>), which constitute the harmony of a **Perfect Fifth** <note>original: *Diapante*</note>. From these two harmonies joined together, the most perfect harmony, the **Octave** <note>original: *Diapason*</note>, is derived. Clearly, one must proceed in a similar way by making the greater extreme in the first octave and the lesser in the second, producing the greater by doubling the lesser. For example: the lesser extreme will be 768, and the greater 1536, which is double the lesser. And so one must proceed with the means and all other numbers which grew out of the addition of the <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>A ratio of 9:8, which defines a whole musical tone.</note> proportion of itself. Thus, twice 432 is 864; twice 486 is 972; twice 512 is 1024; twice 576 is 1152; twice 648 is 1296; twice 729 is 1458; and so one arrives at the greater extreme, which is 1536. And in this way, we have a second complete harmony of an **Octave**. After this, we proceed according to the general order of natural things 1, 2, 4, 8 to find the third and fourth Octave harmonies, always proceeding by doubling, so that the lesser extreme rises to the greater, as will be explained more clearly in the following demonstration.
